questions.q: Which component is present in a nucleotide but absent from the corresponding nucleoside?
o: A nitrogenous base
Both nucleosides and nucleotides contain a base.
A pentose sugar
Both contain ribose or deoxyribose.
A phosphate group
Correct: a nucleoside is base + sugar; adding one or more phosphates makes it a nucleotide.
A 3′ hydroxyl group
The 3′ OH is on the sugar, which both molecules share.
questions.x: A nucleoside is just a nitrogenous base attached to a pentose sugar by an N-glycosidic bond. Adding one or more phosphates to the sugar, usually at the 5′ carbon, turns it into a nucleotide (for example adenosine vs. AMP/ATP). The base, sugar and its hydroxyl groups are shared by both, so only the phosphate distinguishes them.

questions.q: Which pair of DNA bases are both purines?
o: Cytosine and thymine
These are single-ring pyrimidines.
Adenine and guanine
Correct: A and G have the fused double-ring purine structure.
Adenine and thymine
This is a base pair: one purine (A) and one pyrimidine (T).
Guanine and cytosine
This is a base pair: one purine (G) and one pyrimidine (C).
questions.x: Purines (adenine and guanine) have a fused two-ring structure, while pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have a single ring. Every Watson–Crick pair joins one purine with one pyrimidine, keeping the helix width constant. So any true base pair, like A–T or G–C, can never be two purines.

questions.q: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 22% thymine. What percentage of its bases are guanine?
o: Confuses G with A; A equals T at 22%.
Correct: A + T = 44%, so G + C = 56%, and G = C = 28%.
This is A + T, not G alone.
This is G + C combined; split it evenly between G and C.
questions.note: Chargaff: in dsDNA, A = T and G = C.
questions.x: Chargaff's rules for double-stranded DNA: A = T and G = C because each base pairs with its partner. If T = 22%, then A = 22% and A + T = 44%, leaving 56% for G + C. Split equally, G = 28%. The common trap is stopping at 56% or assuming G equals T.

questions.q: Why does a DNA duplex with higher GC content have a higher melting temperature?
o: G–C pairs are joined by covalent bonds across the two strands
Base pairs are held by noncovalent hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds.
G–C pairs form three hydrogen bonds and stack more strongly than A–T pairs
Correct: extra H-bonding and stronger stacking make GC-rich DNA harder to separate.
GC-rich DNA contains more phosphodiester bonds per base pair
Every nucleotide has one backbone linkage regardless of base identity.
Only G–C pairs contain a purine
A–T pairs also contain a purine (adenine).
questions.x: Melting separates strands by disrupting noncovalent interactions, not covalent bonds. G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds versus two for A–T, and GC-rich stretches also have stronger base stacking, so more energy (higher Tm) is needed to separate them. Every nucleotide contributes exactly one backbone phosphodiester bond regardless of base, so backbone bonds cannot explain the difference.

questions.q: What does it mean that the two strands of a DNA double helix are antiparallel?
o: One strand runs 5′→3′ while its partner runs 3′→5′ alongside it
Correct: the strands have opposite chemical polarity.
The two strands coil with opposite helical handedness
Both strands wind in the same right-handed helix in B-DNA.
The sugar–phosphate backbones face inward and the bases face outward
Backbones are outside; bases are stacked inside.
Purines on one strand pair with purines on the other
Each pair is one purine with one pyrimidine.
questions.x: Each DNA strand has polarity: a free 5′ phosphate at one end and a 3′ OH at the other. In the double helix the partner strands run in opposite directions, one 5′→3′ and the other 3′→5′, which is what antiparallel means. It describes chemical direction, not helical handedness; both strands of B-DNA wind in the same right-handed helix.

questions.q: Which bond links adjacent nucleotides within a single strand of DNA?
o: A hydrogen bond between neighboring bases
Hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together, not neighbors in one strand.
An N-glycosidic bond between neighboring sugars
N-glycosidic bonds attach each base to its own sugar.
A peptide bond between neighboring phosphates
Peptide bonds join amino acids in proteins.
A phosphodiester bond from one sugar's 3′ carbon to the next sugar's 5′ carbon
Correct: phosphodiester bonds form the covalent sugar–phosphate backbone.
questions.x: Within one strand, the 3′ OH of one sugar is linked through a phosphate to the 5′ carbon of the next sugar, forming a covalent phosphodiester backbone. Hydrogen bonds act between strands, pairing complementary bases. N-glycosidic bonds attach each base to its own sugar and do not link neighboring nucleotides.

questions.q: RNA is hydrolyzed in alkaline solution much faster than DNA. Which structural feature explains this?
o: Uracil lacks the methyl group found on thymine
The U/T difference affects base identity, not backbone stability.
RNA phosphodiester bonds join 2′ and 5′ carbons
RNA backbones are 3′–5′ linked, just like DNA.
The 2′ hydroxyl of ribose can attack the adjacent phosphodiester bond
Correct: the 2′ OH acts as an internal nucleophile; deoxyribose lacks it.
RNA lacks N-glycosidic bonds between bases and sugars
RNA bases are attached by N-glycosidic bonds too.
questions.x: Ribose carries a 2′ OH that deoxyribose lacks. In base, this 2′ oxygen is deprotonated and attacks the neighboring phosphorus, cleaving the RNA backbone through a cyclic phosphate intermediate. DNA cannot do this, which is one reason it is the more stable storage molecule. The U versus T difference affects base identity, not backbone chemistry.

questions.q: Cytosine in DNA can spontaneously deaminate to uracil. How does using thymine rather than uracil in DNA help cells repair this damage?
o: Any uracil found in DNA can be recognized as damage and removed
Correct: since U never belongs in DNA, uracil-DNA glycosylase can excise it without ambiguity.
Uracil cannot base-pair, so it stalls the replication fork
Uracil pairs readily with adenine, which is why it is mutagenic.
Deamination of cytosine produces thymine, which pairs with guanine
Cytosine deaminates to uracil; it is 5-methylcytosine that yields thymine.
Uracil forms three hydrogen bonds with guanine and distorts the helix
Uracil pairs with adenine using two hydrogen bonds.
questions.note: Thymine is essentially methylated uracil; the methyl tag marks it as belonging in DNA.
questions.x: Cytosine deamination produces uracil, which pairs with adenine and would cause a C→T mutation after replication. Because DNA normally contains thymine (methylated uracil), any uracil in DNA is unambiguously damage, and uracil-DNA glycosylase removes it to start base excision repair. If U were a normal DNA base, the cell could not tell a damaged C from a legitimate U.

questions.q: A researcher slowly heats a DNA solution while measuring absorbance at 260 nm. As the strands separate, what happens to absorbance?
o: It decreases, because single strands absorb less UV light
The opposite is true; stacking suppresses absorbance.
It stays constant, because the number of bases does not change
Absorbance depends on stacking, not just base count.
It increases, because unstacked bases absorb more UV light
Correct: this is the hyperchromic effect of denaturation.
It increases, because heat breaks phosphodiester bonds
Melting breaks hydrogen bonds; covalent backbone bonds stay intact.
questions.x: Bases absorb UV near 260 nm, but stacking in the double helix suppresses that absorbance. When heat breaks hydrogen bonds and the strands separate, the bases unstack and absorbance rises: the hyperchromic effect. The covalent backbone stays intact during melting, so the increase reflects unstacking, not bond cleavage.

questions.q: Sequence-specific DNA-binding proteins most often recognize base sequences by contacting which part of B-form DNA?
o: The major groove, where base edges expose distinctive hydrogen-bonding patterns
Correct: the major groove displays more distinguishable chemical groups for each base pair.
The minor groove, which displays more base-specific information
The minor groove is narrower and less informative about sequence.
The sugar–phosphate backbone, which differs for each base
The backbone is identical for every nucleotide, so it gives no sequence information.
The stacked bases in the helix core, by inserting into the duplex
Base faces in the core are not accessible without disrupting the helix.
questions.x: In B-DNA the major groove exposes the edges of base pairs with a distinctive pattern of hydrogen-bond donors, acceptors and methyl groups for each pair, so proteins can read sequence there without unwinding DNA. The minor groove is narrower and offers less distinguishing information. The backbone is chemically identical for every nucleotide and so carries no sequence information.

questions.q: Histones bind tightly to DNA largely because they are rich in which amino acids?
o: Aspartate and glutamate
These are negatively charged and would repel DNA.
Cysteine and methionine
Histone–DNA binding is not based on sulfur chemistry or disulfides.
Lysine and arginine
Correct: their positive side chains attract the negatively charged phosphate backbone.
Leucine and phenylalanine
Hydrophobic residues would not interact well with the charged backbone.
questions.x: DNA's phosphate backbone is strongly negative. Histones are rich in lysine and arginine, whose side chains are positively charged at physiological pH, so they bind DNA tightly by electrostatic attraction regardless of sequence. Acidic residues such as aspartate and glutamate would repel DNA instead.

questions.q: The core of a nucleosome consists of about 147 bp of DNA wrapped around which protein structure?
o: An octamer containing two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4
Correct: the histone octamer forms the nucleosome core.
A single molecule of histone H1
H1 is the linker histone that sits outside the core particle.
A tetramer of four H1 molecules
H1 is not part of the core and does not form the octamer.
A hexamer containing two copies each of H2A, H2B and H3
This omits H4 and has the wrong number of subunits.
questions.x: The nucleosome core particle is about 147 bp of DNA wrapped roughly 1.7 times around a histone octamer: two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3 and H4. Histone H1 is the linker histone, binding DNA where it enters and leaves the core and helping compact chromatin further. H1 is therefore not part of the octamer itself.

questions.q: Recruiting a histone acetyltransferase to a gene's promoter generally has what effect?
o: It adds positive charge to histones, tightening chromatin
Acetylation removes positive charge from lysine.
It methylates cytosines in the promoter, silencing the gene
That is DNA methyltransferase activity, not acetylation.
It removes acetyl groups, promoting heterochromatin formation
That describes histone deacetylases, the opposite enzyme.
It neutralizes lysine charges, loosening chromatin and increasing transcription
Correct: acetylation weakens histone–DNA attraction, opening chromatin.
questions.x: Histone acetyltransferases add acetyl groups to lysine side chains, removing their positive charge. This weakens histone–DNA attraction, loosens chromatin and recruits activating proteins, so transcription generally increases. Deacetylases do the opposite, and DNA methylation is a separate mark made by DNA methyltransferases on cytosines, not histones.

questions.q: Compared with euchromatin, heterochromatin is:
o: Loosely packed and highly transcribed
This describes euchromatin.
Densely packed and mostly transcriptionally inactive
Correct: tight packing limits access for transcription machinery.
Present only during mitosis
Heterochromatin persists in interphase nuclei.
Free of histone proteins
Heterochromatin is still built on nucleosomes.
questions.x: Heterochromatin is tightly packed chromatin that limits access for RNA polymerase and transcription factors, so it is mostly silent. Euchromatin is loosely packed and active. Both are built on nucleosomes and both exist in interphase nuclei; heterochromatin is not just condensed mitotic chromosomes.

questions.q: Heavy methylation of cytosines in CpG islands near a eukaryotic promoter usually has what effect on that gene?
o: Transcription increases because RNA polymerase II binds methylated DNA
Methylation generally blocks, not attracts, the transcription machinery.
The amino acid sequence of the encoded protein changes
Methylation is epigenetic; it does not change the coding sequence.
Transcription of the gene is repressed
Correct: promoter CpG methylation recruits repressive proteins and compacts chromatin.
The mRNA is spliced in a new pattern
Promoter methylation affects whether the gene is transcribed, not splice choice.
questions.x: Methylation of cytosines in CpG islands near a promoter is an epigenetic mark that represses transcription. Methyl-CpG-binding proteins recruit histone deacetylases and other repressors, compacting chromatin and blocking the transcription machinery. It changes whether the gene is expressed, not the DNA sequence or the protein it encodes.

questions.q: What is the main function of telomeres at the ends of linear eukaryotic chromosomes?
o: Protecting genes from erosion and keeping chromosome ends from being treated as breaks
Correct: repetitive noncoding caps buffer end loss and are shielded by proteins.
Attaching sister chromatids to spindle microtubules
That is the role of the centromere and kinetochore.
Serving as the only origins of replication
Origins are scattered along the chromosome, not only at the ends.
Encoding the histone proteins
Telomeres are short noncoding repeats.
questions.x: Telomeres are repetitive noncoding sequences (TTAGGG in humans) at chromosome ends. They buffer the gradual loss of end sequence caused by the end-replication problem and, bound by protective proteins, keep natural ends from being recognized as double-strand breaks and fused. Spindle attachment happens at centromeres, not telomeres.

questions.q: The centromere is the chromosomal region where:
o: Telomerase adds repetitive sequences
Telomerase acts at telomeres, the chromosome ends.
Sister chromatids are joined and the kinetochore assembles
Correct: centromeres link sisters and anchor spindle attachment.
Replication of every chromosome begins
Replication starts at many origins along each chromosome.
Ribosomal RNA genes cluster to form the nucleolus
That describes nucleolar organizer regions.
questions.x: The centromere is a constricted region where sister chromatids are held together and where the kinetochore protein complex assembles to attach spindle microtubules. This lets chromatids be pulled to opposite poles in mitosis and meiosis. Chromosome ends are telomeres, and replication starts at many origins, not at the centromere.

questions.q: E. coli grown for many generations in ¹⁵N medium are moved to ¹⁴N medium. After two rounds of replication, what DNA densities are seen?
o: All hybrid density
This is the result after only one generation.
Half hybrid (¹⁵N/¹⁴N) and half light (¹⁴N/¹⁴N)
Correct: semiconservative copying keeps each old strand paired with a new one.
One-quarter heavy and three-quarters light
This would occur with conservative replication.
A single band lighter than hybrid
This would occur with dispersive replication.
questions.note: Each round halves the hybrid fraction; heavy/heavy never reappears.
questions.x: In semiconservative replication, each daughter duplex keeps one parental strand. After one generation in ¹⁴N, all DNA is hybrid ¹⁵N/¹⁴N. In the second round, each hybrid gives one hybrid and one fully light duplex, so DNA is half hybrid and half light. Conservative replication would have kept a heavy band, and dispersive replication would give one band of intermediate density.

questions.q: Why is primase required during DNA replication?
o: Primase unwinds the double helix at the fork
Unwinding is done by helicase.
Primase seals nicks between Okazaki fragments
Sealing nicks is the job of DNA ligase.
Primase removes RNA primers after synthesis
In E. coli, primers are removed by DNA polymerase I.
DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing 3′ OH
Correct: primase lays down a short RNA primer that provides the starting 3′ OH.
questions.x: DNA polymerases cannot start a chain from scratch; they can only add nucleotides to an existing 3′ OH. Primase, an RNA polymerase, synthesizes a short RNA primer that provides this 3′ OH, and polymerase extends from there. Unwinding (helicase), primer removal (pol I in E. coli) and nick sealing (ligase) are done by other enzymes.

questions.q: Why is the lagging strand synthesized as Okazaki fragments?
o: Its template is exposed in an orientation that forces 5′→3′ synthesis away from the fork
Correct: polymerase must restart repeatedly as new template opens behind it.
Its template strand is made of RNA
Both template strands are DNA.
Helicase unwinds that side of the fork only in short bursts
Helicase unwinds continuously; the problem is polymerase direction.
The lagging-strand polymerase lacks proofreading
Proofreading is unrelated to whether synthesis is continuous.
questions.x: DNA polymerase synthesizes only 5′→3′ and the two template strands are antiparallel. On one side of the fork, synthesis can follow the fork continuously (leading strand). On the other side, synthesis must run away from the fork, so polymerase repeatedly restarts on newly exposed template, making short Okazaki fragments. Helicase unwinds continuously; the limitation is polymerase direction.

questions.q: In E. coli, which enzyme removes RNA primers and fills the resulting gaps with DNA?
o: DNA polymerase I
Correct: its 5′→3′ exonuclease removes primers while it fills the gap.
DNA polymerase III
Pol III is the main replicative enzyme but lacks 5′→3′ exonuclease activity.
DNA ligase
Ligase seals the final nick only after the gap is filled.
Primase
Primase makes primers; it does not remove them.
questions.x: In E. coli, DNA polymerase I has a 5′→3′ exonuclease activity that removes RNA primers as it moves forward and fills the gap with DNA (nick translation). Pol III, the main replicative polymerase, lacks this activity. DNA ligase then seals the remaining nick in the backbone.

questions.q: A temperature-sensitive E. coli mutant accumulates many short DNA pieces at the restrictive temperature, while leading-strand synthesis looks normal. Which enzyme is most likely defective?
o: Helicase
Without helicase neither strand could be synthesized.
Primase
Without primase, lagging-strand fragments could not even begin.
Topoisomerase
Loss of topoisomerase would stall fork movement on both strands.
DNA ligase
Correct: without ligase, Okazaki fragments are made but never joined.
questions.x: Okazaki fragments are primed and extended normally, but joining them requires DNA ligase to seal the final nick. If ligase fails, lagging-strand fragments accumulate unjoined while leading-strand synthesis proceeds. Defects in helicase, primase or topoisomerase would block fork progress or prevent fragments from being made at all.

questions.q: DNA polymerase proofreading depends on which enzymatic activity?
o: 5′→3′ exonuclease activity that removes RNA primers
That activity clears primers and does not check new nucleotides.
3′→5′ exonuclease activity that removes a mismatched nucleotide at the growing end
Correct: the polymerase backs up and excises the wrong nucleotide.
Endonuclease activity that cuts both strands near the error
Proofreading does not make double-strand cuts.
Ligase activity that rejoins the corrected strand
No ligation is needed when proofreading at the 3′ end.
questions.x: Replicative DNA polymerases proofread with a 3′→5′ exonuclease: if a mismatched nucleotide is added at the growing 3′ end, the enzyme backs up, removes it and tries again. This raises fidelity roughly 100-fold. The 5′→3′ exonuclease of pol I works ahead of the enzyme to remove primers and does not check new nucleotides.

questions.q: What do single-strand binding proteins do at a replication fork?
o: Keep separated strands from re-annealing and protect them from nucleases
Correct: SSBs coat exposed single-stranded DNA.
Break hydrogen bonds to unwind the helix
Unwinding is the job of helicase.
Synthesize short RNA primers
That is primase.
Relieve supercoiling ahead of the fork
That is topoisomerase.
questions.x: Once helicase separates the parental strands, single-strand binding proteins coat the exposed DNA, preventing re-annealing and hairpin formation and protecting it from nucleases. They keep strands apart but do not unwind DNA themselves. Unwinding requires helicase, and supercoiling ahead of the fork is relieved by topoisomerase.

questions.q: What supplies the energy to form each new phosphodiester bond during DNA synthesis?
o: Cleavage of the incoming dNTP, releasing pyrophosphate
Correct: the dNTP's own high-energy bonds drive the reaction, aided by PPi hydrolysis.
A separate ATP hydrolyzed by DNA polymerase
Polymerase does not need extra ATP for each nucleotide.
GTP delivered by elongation factors
GTP-bound elongation factors work in translation, not replication.
A proton gradient across the nuclear membrane
Nuclear processes are not driven by proton gradients.
questions.x: Each incoming nucleotide arrives as a dNTP. The 3′ OH of the growing chain attacks its α-phosphate, forming the phosphodiester bond and releasing pyrophosphate; hydrolysis of PPi by pyrophosphatase makes the reaction effectively irreversible. Polymerase therefore needs no separate ATP or GTP per nucleotide.

questions.q: Eukaryotic chromosomes have many origins of replication, while the E. coli chromosome has one. What is the best explanation?
o: Eukaryotic genomes are much larger and forks move more slowly, so many origins are needed to finish in S phase
Correct: multiple origins let a huge genome be copied in a limited time.
Eukaryotic polymerases can replicate in only one direction from an origin
Eukaryotic origins fire bidirectionally, just like bacterial ones.
Circular chromosomes are unable to use more than one origin
This is not a physical rule; size is the reason.
Eukaryotes lack primase and need extra origins to compensate
Eukaryotes have primase (part of pol α/primase).
questions.x: Eukaryotic genomes are many times larger than bacterial genomes, and eukaryotic forks move more slowly, partly because of chromatin. With a single origin, replication would take far too long, so thousands of origins fire in S phase, each producing two forks. Origins in both bacteria and eukaryotes are bidirectional, so direction is not the difference.

questions.q: What causes the end-replication problem in linear chromosomes?
o: Helicase falls off before reaching the end of the leading strand
The leading strand can be copied to the end; the lagging end is the issue.
Once the last primer on the lagging strand is removed, no upstream 3′ OH exists to fill the gap
Correct: polymerase cannot fill that terminal gap, so ends shorten.
Telomerase removes nucleotides from chromosome ends
Telomerase adds sequence; it counteracts shortening.
DNA ligase cannot join fragments on linear DNA
Ligase works on linear DNA; the gap itself cannot be filled.
questions.x: On a linear chromosome, the last lagging-strand fragment starts from an RNA primer near the very end. When that primer is removed, there is no upstream 3′ OH for polymerase to extend into the gap, so it cannot be filled and the chromosome shortens each round. The leading strand can be copied to the end; the problem is specific to the lagging strand.

questions.q: How does telomerase extend chromosome ends?
o: It copies the complementary DNA strand as a template
No DNA template exists beyond the end; telomerase brings its own RNA.
It uses its own RNA as a template to add repeats to the 3′ overhang
Correct: telomerase is a reverse transcriptase carrying an RNA template.
It ligates premade repeat fragments onto the end
Telomerase synthesizes repeats nucleotide by nucleotide.
It adds repeats to the 5′ end of the strand
Like all polymerases, it extends a 3′ end.
questions.x: Telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein reverse transcriptase: it carries its own RNA template and uses it to add DNA repeats onto the 3′ overhang of the chromosome. The complementary strand is then filled in by primase and DNA polymerase. Like every polymerase it extends 3′ ends, and it synthesizes repeats nucleotide by nucleotide rather than ligating premade pieces.

questions.q: Which cell type would be expected to have the lowest telomerase activity?
o: An embryonic stem cell
Stem cells maintain telomerase to keep dividing.
A cancer cell
Most cancers reactivate telomerase to avoid senescence.
A mature skin fibroblast
Correct: most differentiated somatic cells express little telomerase.
A spermatogonium
Germ-line cells express telomerase to protect chromosomes for offspring.
questions.x: Telomerase is active in cells that must divide indefinitely, such as germ-line cells, embryonic stem cells and most cancer cells. Most differentiated somatic cells, like mature fibroblasts, express little telomerase, so their telomeres shorten with each division until they reach senescence. Cancer cells commonly reactivate telomerase to escape this limit.

questions.q: How does the sliding clamp (β clamp in bacteria, PCNA in eukaryotes) speed up replication?
o: It unwinds the DNA ahead of the polymerase
Unwinding is done by helicase.
It removes mismatched nucleotides
Proofreading is done by polymerase's 3′→5′ exonuclease.
It tethers polymerase to the template, greatly increasing processivity
Correct: the ring keeps polymerase from falling off after each nucleotide.
It synthesizes RNA primers
That is primase.
questions.x: A sliding clamp (β clamp in bacteria, PCNA in eukaryotes) is a ring loaded around DNA that binds the polymerase and keeps it on the template. This raises processivity from a few nucleotides per binding event to thousands. It does not unwind DNA, proofread or make primers.

questions.q: Replication of a circular bacterial chromosome begins at a single origin and proceeds bidirectionally. How many replication forks form?
o: Bidirectional replication moves two forks in opposite directions.
Correct: one fork travels each way around the circle until they meet.
Each origin produces one bubble with two forks, not four.
It depends on chromosome length
The number of forks per origin is fixed at two.
questions.x: Replication from an origin is bidirectional: the origin opens into a bubble with a fork at each end, and the forks move in opposite directions. On a circular bacterial chromosome with one origin, the two forks travel around the circle and meet at the terminus region. Chromosome size affects how long replication takes, not how many forks one origin makes.

questions.q: A mutant DNA polymerase lacks 3′→5′ exonuclease activity but has normal polymerase activity. What is the most likely result?
o: Replication continues at a near-normal rate, but the mutation rate rises
Correct: synthesis is intact, but misincorporated bases are no longer removed.
Replication stops completely
Polymerization does not require the exonuclease domain.
Okazaki fragments are no longer joined
Joining fragments is the job of ligase.
The mutation rate falls because fewer bases are removed
Losing proofreading lets more errors stay, not fewer.
questions.x: Polymerization and proofreading are separate activities. Without the 3′→5′ exonuclease, the polymerase still synthesizes DNA at a near-normal rate, but misincorporated nucleotides are no longer removed. The result is a mutator phenotype with a much higher mutation rate, not a stop in replication.

questions.q: Which replication enzyme uses ATP hydrolysis to break hydrogen bonds and separate the two parent strands?
o: Helicase
Correct: helicase is an ATP-driven motor that unwinds DNA.
Single-strand binding protein
SSBs hold strands apart but do not unwind them.
Primase
Primase synthesizes RNA primers.
DNA ligase
Ligase joins fragments; it does not separate strands.
questions.x: Helicase is a ring-shaped motor that uses ATP hydrolysis to move along DNA and break the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, opening the fork. Single-strand binding proteins then keep the separated strands from re-annealing, but they do not provide energy or unwind DNA themselves.

questions.q: How does the E. coli mismatch repair system know which strand of a mismatched pair is the newly made one?
o: The parent strand is methylated at GATC sites while the new strand is briefly unmethylated
Correct: hemimethylation marks the new strand as the one to fix.
The new strand contains uracil instead of thymine
Normal replication puts thymine in the new strand.
The template strand still carries RNA primers
Primers are on the new strand and are removed quickly.
The new strand is always shorter than the parent strand
Length cannot identify strands at a local mismatch.
questions.x: In E. coli, Dam methylase methylates adenines in GATC sequences, but only after a short delay following replication. In that window the parental strand is methylated while the new strand is not, so the mismatch repair proteins (MutS, MutL, MutH) can nick and correct the unmethylated new strand. This ensures the error, not the original template, is fixed.

questions.q: Which lesion does UV light most commonly cause, and which pathway repairs it?
o: Thymine dimers, repaired by mismatch repair
Mismatch repair fixes replication errors, not bulky UV lesions.
Double-strand breaks, repaired by base excision repair
UV mainly causes pyrimidine dimers, and BER fixes single bases.
Thymine dimers, repaired by nucleotide excision repair
Correct: NER cuts out the bulky dimer within a short oligonucleotide.
Deaminated cytosines, repaired by nucleotide excision repair
UV's signature lesion is the pyrimidine dimer; deamination is fixed by BER.
questions.x: UV light causes covalent bonds between adjacent pyrimidines on the same strand, most commonly thymine dimers, which distort the helix. Nucleotide excision repair recognizes this bulky distortion, cuts out a short oligonucleotide containing the lesion, and fills the gap. Mismatch repair handles replication errors, and base excision repair handles small single-base damage.

questions.q: Tumors from patients with inherited loss of MSH2 show many expansions and contractions of short repeated sequences. Which repair pathway is defective?
o: Mismatch repair
Correct: polymerase slippage in repeats creates loops that only mismatch repair corrects.
Nucleotide excision repair
NER removes bulky lesions such as thymine dimers.
Base excision repair
BER removes single damaged bases, not slippage loops.
Homologous recombination
HR fixes double-strand breaks, not small insertion/deletion loops.
questions.note: Microsatellite instability is the hallmark of mismatch repair defects.
questions.x: MSH2 is a core mismatch repair protein. When polymerase slips in short repeats, it creates small insertion/deletion loops that mismatch repair normally corrects. Without it, repeat lengths change frequently, a pattern called microsatellite instability, as seen in Lynch syndrome. NER and BER handle bulky lesions and damaged bases, not slippage loops.

questions.q: How does base excision repair begin?
o: A DNA glycosylase removes a damaged base, leaving an abasic site
Correct: the glycosylase cuts the N-glycosidic bond of the bad base.
An endonuclease removes a 12–30 nucleotide stretch around a bulky lesion
That is nucleotide excision repair.
The entire newly synthesized strand is degraded
No repair pathway removes a whole strand.
Ligase directly joins the ends of a broken chromosome
That resembles nonhomologous end joining.
questions.x: Base excision repair starts when a DNA glycosylase recognizes a single damaged or inappropriate base (such as uracil or an oxidized guanine) and cleaves its N-glycosidic bond, leaving an abasic site. An AP endonuclease then cuts the backbone, polymerase inserts the correct nucleotide, and ligase seals the strand. Removing a longer stretch around a bulky lesion is nucleotide excision repair.

questions.q: Why is homologous recombination a more accurate repair of double-strand breaks than nonhomologous end joining, and when is it mainly used?
o: It copies an intact sister chromatid, so it operates mainly in S and G2
Correct: a matching template restores lost sequence, and sisters exist only after replication.
It copies RNA transcripts of the gene, so it operates mainly in G1
HR uses a DNA template, not RNA.
It ligates ends without processing, so it works in any phase
Direct ligation describes NHEJ, which is error-prone.
It uses telomerase to rebuild lost sequence, so it works in M phase
Telomerase acts only at chromosome ends, not at internal breaks.
questions.x: Homologous recombination uses an intact homologous sequence, normally the sister chromatid, as a template to restore any sequence lost at a double-strand break, so it is accurate. Sister chromatids exist only after replication, so HR is used mainly in S and G2. Nonhomologous end joining simply ligates processed ends, works in any phase including G1, and often leaves small insertions or deletions.

questions.q: A point mutation changes a codon into a different codon for the same amino acid. What type of mutation is this?
o: Silent
Correct: the protein sequence is unchanged because of code degeneracy.
Missense
Missense mutations change the amino acid.
Nonsense
Nonsense mutations create a stop codon.
Frameshift
Frameshifts come from insertions or deletions, not one-base swaps.
questions.x: Because the code is degenerate, many amino acids have several codons, often differing only at the third position. A point mutation that changes one codon to another for the same amino acid leaves the protein sequence unchanged: a silent mutation. Missense changes the amino acid, nonsense creates a stop codon, and frameshifts require insertions or deletions.

questions.q: Which mutation is most likely to destroy the function of the encoded protein?
o: Substitution at the third position of one codon
Third-position changes are often silent.
Insertion of three nucleotides near the end of the coding sequence
This adds one amino acid and keeps the frame.
Insertion of one nucleotide near the start of the coding sequence
Correct: it shifts the reading frame for nearly the whole protein.
Substitution deep within an intron, far from splice sites
Most intronic sequence is removed and does not affect the protein.
questions.x: Inserting or deleting a number of nucleotides that is not a multiple of three shifts the reading frame, so every codon downstream is misread and a premature stop codon usually appears. Near the start of the gene, this scrambles almost the entire protein. A three-nucleotide insertion keeps the frame and adds just one amino acid, so it is usually far less damaging.

questions.q: Which change is an example of a transition mutation?
o: A purine replaced by a pyrimidine, such as A → T
Purine ↔ pyrimidine swaps are transversions.
Insertion of a single nucleotide
Insertions are not substitutions at all.
Deletion of one complete codon
This is an in-frame deletion, not a base substitution.
A purine replaced by the other purine, such as A → G
Correct: transitions swap purine for purine or pyrimidine for pyrimidine.
questions.x: Base substitutions are classified by base type. A transition swaps a purine for the other purine (A↔G) or a pyrimidine for the other pyrimidine (C↔T). A transversion swaps a purine for a pyrimidine or vice versa, such as A→T. Insertions and deletions are not substitutions at all.

questions.q: Intercalating agents such as ethidium bromide slip between stacked DNA bases. Which kind of mutation do they most often cause?
o: Thymine dimers
Thymine dimers are caused by UV light.
Transitions from mispairing of a base analog
Base analogs, not intercalators, act by mispairing.
Methylation of guanine
That is the action of alkylating agents.
Frameshift mutations from small insertions or deletions
Correct: the inserted molecule distorts spacing so polymerase adds or skips bases.
questions.x: Intercalators are flat aromatic molecules that slide between stacked base pairs, distorting the helix and its spacing. During replication this makes polymerase add or skip a nucleotide, producing small insertions or deletions and therefore frameshift mutations. Base analogs cause transitions by mispairing, and UV causes pyrimidine dimers.

questions.q: In the Ames test, a chemical is mixed with rat liver extract before exposure to histidine-requiring Salmonella. Why is liver extract added?
o: To supply histidine so the bacteria can grow
Supplying histidine would defeat the selection for revertants.
To kill bacteria that do not mutate
Liver extract does not select against nonmutants.
To mimic metabolism that can turn harmless compounds into mutagens
Correct: liver enzymes activate many procarcinogens, as would happen in the body.
To provide DNA repair enzymes to the bacteria
Repair enzymes would reduce, not reveal, mutations.
questions.x: Many chemicals are not mutagenic themselves but are converted to reactive mutagens by liver enzymes such as cytochrome P450s. Adding rat liver extract to the Ames test simulates this metabolic activation, so procarcinogens that would be dangerous in the body are detected. Without it, such compounds would falsely appear safe.

questions.q: In the Ames test, why do colonies appear on histidine-free plates?
o: The test compound provides histidine to the bacteria
Mutagens are not a histidine source; colonies reflect genetic change.
The liver extract supplies histidine
The extract contains enzymes, and the plate is designed to lack histidine.
Reverse mutations restored function of a histidine-synthesis gene
Correct: only his⁺ revertants can grow without histidine.
Bacteria import histidine made by neighboring cells
All the starting cells are his⁻ and cannot make histidine.
questions.x: The Ames test uses Salmonella strains that are his⁻ and cannot grow without histidine. A mutagen raises the rate of reverse mutations that restore the histidine-synthesis gene, and only these his⁺ revertants form colonies on histidine-free plates. More colonies than the control plate indicate a mutagen; the compound and extract do not supply histidine.

questions.q: Why does expansion of an in-frame CAG repeat inside a coding sequence not shift the downstream reading frame?
o: CAG is a stop codon, so translation ends before the repeats
CAG codes for glutamine; stop codons are UAA, UAG and UGA.
Each repeat adds exactly one codon, preserving the frame
Correct: inserting multiples of three nucleotides keeps the frame.
Repeats are spliced out of the mRNA
In-frame coding repeats remain in the mature mRNA.
Ribosomes skip repeated codons
Ribosomes read every codon in turn.
questions.x: The reading frame shifts only when the number of inserted or deleted nucleotides is not a multiple of three. Each CAG repeat adds exactly three nucleotides, one codon for glutamine, so downstream codons keep their frame. That is why CAG expansions in diseases like Huntington produce proteins with extra glutamines rather than truncated proteins.

questions.q: How many different codons make up the standard genetic code?
o: That is 4², which would code for too few amino acids.
That is the number of standard amino acids, not codons.
61 is the number of sense codons; three more are stop codons.
Correct: 4 bases at 3 positions give 4³ = 64 codons.
questions.x: Each codon has three positions, and each position can hold any of four bases, giving 4³ = 64 possible codons. Of these, 61 are sense codons that specify the 20 standard amino acids and 3 (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop codons. A doublet code (4² = 16) would be too small for 20 amino acids.

questions.q: The genetic code is described as degenerate. What does this mean?
o: A single codon can specify several different amino acids
That would be ambiguity; each codon has one meaning.
Most amino acids are specified by more than one codon
Correct: 61 sense codons encode only 20 amino acids.
The code differs among most organisms
The code is nearly universal.
Adjacent codons overlap and share nucleotides
The code is read in nonoverlapping triplets.
questions.x: Degeneracy (redundancy) means most amino acids are encoded by more than one codon, since 61 sense codons cover only 20 amino acids. The code is still unambiguous: each codon specifies exactly one amino acid. Do not confuse degenerate with ambiguous, or with non-universal.

questions.q: According to the wobble hypothesis, how can one tRNA recognize more than one codon?
o: Nonstandard pairing is allowed at the codon's first base
The first two codon positions pair strictly.
Nonstandard pairing is allowed between the codon's third base and the anticodon's first base
Correct: relaxed pairing at that position lets one anticodon read several codons.
Each tRNA can carry several different amino acids
A charged tRNA carries one specific amino acid.
The ribosome can skip a base when reading the codon
Skipping bases would cause frameshifts, not wobble.
questions.x: Codon and anticodon pair antiparallel, so the codon's third (3′) base pairs with the anticodon's first (5′) base. Pairing at this wobble position is relaxed, allowing for example G–U pairs or inosine pairing with U, C or A. Thus one tRNA can read several codons that differ only at the third position, while the first two codon positions pair strictly.

questions.q: An mRNA codon reads 5′-GCA-3′. Which tRNA anticodon pairs with it, written 5′→3′?
o: This is the complement written in the wrong direction.
This is identical to the codon, not complementary.
This is simply the codon reversed.
Correct: the antiparallel complement of 5′-GCA-3′ is 3′-CGU-5′, which reads 5′-UGC-3′.
questions.note: Write the complement 3′→5′ under the codon, then flip it to read 5′→3′.
questions.x: Codon and anticodon pair antiparallel. Write the complement under 5′-GCA-3′ in the opposite orientation: 3′-CGU-5′. Reading that anticodon in the standard 5′→3′ direction gives 5′-UGC-3′. The common error is writing the complement CGU as if it were already 5′→3′.

questions.q: A DNA template strand reads 3′-TACGGT-5′. What mRNA sequence is transcribed from it?
o: 5′-AUGCCA-3′
Correct: the mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template, with U for T.
5′-UACGGU-3′
This copies the template sequence instead of complementing it.
5′-ACCGUA-3′
This is the right complement written backward.
5′-ATGCCA-3′
This is the coding-strand DNA sequence; RNA uses U, not T.
questions.x: RNA polymerase builds mRNA complementary and antiparallel to the template strand, using U instead of T. The template 3′-TACGGT-5′ pairs with 5′-AUGCCA-3′. That mRNA matches the coding strand (5′-ATGCCA-3′) except for U in place of T, which is a quick way to check answers.

questions.q: The coding (nontemplate) strand of a gene reads 5′-ATGTTC-3′. What is the mRNA sequence?
o: 5′-UACAAG-3′
This is the complement of the coding strand, matching the template instead.
5′-GAACAU-3′
This is the reverse complement, the template read 5′→3′ with U.
5′-CUUGUA-3′
This reverses the coding sequence without complementing it.
5′-AUGUUC-3′
Correct: mRNA matches the coding strand with U in place of T.
questions.x: The coding (nontemplate) strand has the same sequence and orientation as the mRNA, except DNA has T where RNA has U. So 5′-ATGTTC-3′ becomes mRNA 5′-AUGUUC-3′. Complementing the coding strand gives the template instead, which is the most common mistake.

questions.q: Which codon begins translation of most mRNAs?
o: UAG
UAG is a stop codon.
UGA
UGA is a stop codon.
AGU
AGU is a sense codon (serine), not a start signal.
AUG
Correct: AUG is the start codon and encodes methionine.
questions.x: Translation nearly always starts at AUG, which codes for methionine (N-formylmethionine in bacteria) and sets the reading frame. UAA, UAG and UGA are the stop codons. Memorizing the start and stop codons is essential for reading-frame problems.

questions.q: A ribosome translates the mRNA 5′-AUGUUUUAAGGC-3′ starting at AUG (UAA is a stop codon). How many amino acids are in the resulting peptide?
o: Misses that UUU after AUG is also translated.
Correct: AUG (Met) and UUU (Phe), then UAA stops translation.
Stop codons do not add an amino acid.
Translation ends at UAA, so GGC is never read.
questions.x: Reading 5′→3′ from AUG in triplets gives AUG (Met), UUU (Phe), then UAA, a stop codon. Stop codons are recognized by release factors, not tRNAs, so they add no amino acid. The peptide is therefore two residues long; nothing after the stop codon (GGC) is translated.

questions.q: Which biotechnology result depends most directly on the near-universality of the genetic code?
o: PCR amplifies a stretch of human DNA in a tube
PCR copies DNA by base pairing; no codons are read.
Bacteria carrying a human insulin cDNA make the correct insulin sequence
Correct: bacteria read human codons the same way human cells do.
Restriction enzymes cut human DNA at specific sites
Cutting depends on recognition sequences, not the code.
Gel electrophoresis separates human DNA fragments by size
This depends on size and charge, not on codon meaning.
questions.x: The genetic code is nearly universal: almost all organisms read each codon as the same amino acid. That is why a bacterium given human insulin cDNA (with a bacterial promoter) produces a protein with the correct human sequence. PCR, restriction digestion and electrophoresis act on DNA directly and never involve reading codons.

questions.q: A gene has a one-nucleotide deletion in codon 5 and a one-nucleotide insertion in codon 8. What is the most likely effect on the protein?
o: Every amino acid after codon 5 is changed
The second mutation restores the original frame after codon 8.
The protein is unchanged because the mutations cancel
Codons between the two mutations are read in the wrong frame.
Only the amino acid at codon 5 is changed
The frameshift persists until the compensating insertion.
Amino acids encoded by codons 5–8 change, but the downstream sequence is normal
Correct: the insertion restores the frame shifted by the deletion.
questions.note: A nearby compensating indel limits damage to the region between the mutations (assuming no stop codon arises there).
questions.x: A one-base deletion in codon 5 shifts the frame, so codons are misread from that point. The one-base insertion in codon 8 restores the original frame, so codons after it are read normally. Only the stretch between the two mutations is altered, assuming no premature stop codon appears there. This compensating-frameshift logic is how Crick showed the code is read in triplets.

questions.q: Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase transcribes protein-coding genes into pre-mRNA?
o: RNA polymerase I
Pol I makes the large rRNA precursor.
RNA polymerase III
Pol III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA.
RNA polymerase II
Correct: pol II makes pre-mRNA and most snRNAs and miRNAs.
Primase
Primase makes short primers for DNA replication.
questions.x: Eukaryotes have three nuclear RNA polymerases: Pol I makes the large rRNA precursor (28S, 18S, 5.8S), Pol II makes pre-mRNA plus most snRNAs and miRNAs, and Pol III makes tRNA and 5S rRNA. A quick mnemonic is that the polymerase numbers follow the order rRNA, mRNA, tRNA. Primase makes RNA primers for DNA replication only.

questions.q: How does RNA polymerase differ from DNA polymerase?
o: RNA polymerase synthesizes in the 3′→5′ direction
Both enzymes synthesize 5′→3′.
RNA polymerase uses deoxyribonucleotides
It uses ribonucleoside triphosphates.
RNA polymerase can start a new chain without a primer
Correct: RNA polymerase initiates de novo at promoters.
RNA polymerase has stronger proofreading and fewer errors
RNA polymerase makes more errors than replicative DNA polymerase.
questions.x: Both RNA and DNA polymerases synthesize 5′→3′ and read the template 3′→5′. The key difference is that RNA polymerase can start a new chain de novo at a promoter, whereas DNA polymerase needs a primer with a free 3′ OH. RNA polymerase uses ribonucleotides and has much weaker proofreading, so it makes more errors.

questions.q: What is the role of the sigma factor in bacterial transcription?
o: It ends transcription by pulling RNA polymerase off the DNA
That describes Rho termination factor.
It recognizes promoter sequences and positions RNA polymerase to begin transcription
Correct: sigma binds the −10 and −35 elements.
It adds a protective cap to the 5′ end of the transcript
Bacterial mRNAs are not capped.
It splices introns out of the transcript
Bacterial genes generally lack introns.
questions.x: Bacterial RNA polymerase core enzyme can transcribe but cannot find promoters on its own. The sigma factor binds the core to form the holoenzyme and recognizes the −35 and −10 promoter elements, positioning polymerase to start. Different sigma factors let bacteria switch on different gene sets. Termination by Rho and RNA processing are separate.

questions.q: What is the role of the TATA box in many eukaryotic promoters?
o: It is the start codon for translation
Translation starts at AUG in the mRNA.
It is bound by TATA-binding protein to help position RNA polymerase II
Correct: TFIID binds about 25–30 bp upstream of the start site.
It signals cleavage and polyadenylation
That is the AAUAAA signal near the 3′ end.
It is the branch point used during splicing
The branch point is an adenine within the intron.
questions.x: The TATA box is a core promoter element about 25–30 bp upstream of the transcription start site in many eukaryotic genes. TATA-binding protein, part of TFIID, binds it and bends the DNA, nucleating assembly of other general transcription factors and RNA polymerase II. It acts in DNA at the start of transcription, not as a codon or an RNA processing signal.

questions.q: Cells are treated with a low dose of α-amanitin, which selectively blocks RNA polymerase II. Synthesis of which RNA falls most?
o: 28S and 18S rRNA
These come from RNA polymerase I.
tRNA
tRNAs are made by RNA polymerase III.
Pre-mRNA
Correct: pol II transcribes protein-coding genes.
5S rRNA
5S rRNA is made by RNA polymerase III.
questions.x: α-Amanitin, the toxin in death cap mushrooms, inhibits RNA polymerase II strongly at low concentrations, while Pol III is inhibited only at much higher doses and Pol I is resistant. Pol II makes pre-mRNA, so mRNA synthesis drops most. rRNA from Pol I and tRNA and 5S rRNA from Pol III are largely spared.

questions.q: How does Rho-dependent termination end transcription in bacteria?
o: A GC-rich hairpin followed by U's forms in the RNA
That describes Rho-independent (intrinsic) termination.
Release factors recognize a stop codon
Release factors end translation, not transcription.
Rho binds the transcript and moves along it to release RNA polymerase
Correct: Rho is an RNA helicase that catches up with the polymerase.
The RNA is cleaved and a poly(A) tail is added
That is eukaryotic 3′-end processing.
questions.x: Bacteria end transcription in two ways. In Rho-dependent termination, the Rho protein, an ATP-driven RNA helicase, binds the transcript and travels along it until it reaches the paused polymerase, then unwinds the RNA–DNA hybrid and releases the RNA. Rho-independent termination instead relies on a GC-rich hairpin followed by a U-rich stretch.

questions.q: A bacterial intrinsic terminator consists of a GC-rich inverted repeat followed by a run of U's. Mutations that prevent base pairing within the inverted repeat would most likely cause:
o: Transcription to stop earlier than normal
Disrupting the terminator weakens termination.
Failure of RNA polymerase to start transcription
Terminators act at the end of the gene, not the promoter.
Premature stop codons in the protein
The terminator is downstream of the coding sequence.
Transcription to continue past the normal termination site
Correct: without the hairpin, polymerase does not pause and release.
questions.x: In intrinsic termination, the GC-rich inverted repeat folds into a stable hairpin in the RNA, causing polymerase to pause, and the weak rU–dA pairs that follow let the transcript dissociate. Mutations that prevent hairpin formation abolish the pause, so polymerase reads through and transcription continues past the normal end. Terminators do not affect initiation or the protein's coding sequence.

questions.q: How do eukaryotic enhancers differ from promoters?
o: Enhancers must sit immediately next to the transcription start site
That describes the core promoter.
Enhancers are transcribed and translated into regulatory proteins
Enhancers are DNA binding sites, not genes for proteins.
Enhancers can act from far away and in either orientation, upstream or downstream
Correct: DNA looping brings distant enhancer-bound activators to the promoter.
Enhancers are found only in prokaryotes
Enhancers are a hallmark of eukaryotic regulation.
questions.x: Promoters sit at the transcription start site and work in a fixed orientation. Enhancers are DNA elements that bind activators and can act thousands of base pairs away, upstream, downstream or within introns, and in either orientation. DNA looping brings enhancer-bound activators into contact with the promoter machinery through coactivators such as Mediator.

questions.q: During transcription, RNA polymerase reads the template strand in which direction?
o: 5′→3′, producing RNA 5′→3′
Antiparallel pairing means the template is read 3′→5′.
5′→3′, producing RNA 3′→5′
RNA is never synthesized 3′→5′.
3′→5′, producing RNA 5′→3′
Correct: the new RNA is antiparallel to the template.
Either direction, depending on the gene
Direction is fixed; which strand serves as template varies by gene.
questions.x: Nucleic acids are always synthesized 5′→3′ by adding nucleotides to a free 3′ OH. Because the new RNA is antiparallel to its template, RNA polymerase must read the template strand 3′→5′. Which strand serves as template varies from gene to gene, but the direction of synthesis never does.

questions.q: Many bacterial mRNAs are polycistronic. What does this mean?
o: One gene yields several mRNAs by alternative splicing
Alternative splicing is a eukaryotic process.
One mRNA carries several 5′ caps
Bacterial mRNAs are not capped.
One mRNA is read by many ribosomes at once
That describes a polysome, which can occur with any mRNA.
One mRNA encodes several proteins, each with its own start and stop codon
Correct: operon genes are transcribed together into one mRNA.
questions.x: Bacterial operons transcribe several functionally related genes from one promoter into a single polycistronic mRNA. Each coding region has its own ribosome-binding site, start codon and stop codon, so several separate proteins are made from one transcript. A polysome, in contrast, is many ribosomes translating the same mRNA.

questions.q: Why can bacteria begin translating an mRNA before its transcription is finished?
o: Bacterial ribosomes read mRNA 3′→5′
All ribosomes read mRNA 5′→3′.
Bacterial RNA polymerase also forms peptide bonds
Peptide bonds are formed only by ribosomes.
Bacterial mRNA is spliced as it is made
Bacterial mRNAs typically are not spliced.
There is no nuclear envelope separating transcription from translation
Correct: ribosomes can bind the 5′ end of the RNA while it is still being made.
questions.x: Bacteria have no nucleus, so transcription and translation occur in the same compartment. Ribosomes can bind the 5′ end of an mRNA and begin translating while RNA polymerase is still synthesizing the 3′ end, called coupled transcription and translation. In eukaryotes, the nuclear envelope separates the two processes and mRNA must be processed and exported first.

questions.q: A 3 kb region upstream of a gene is linked to a reporter. Deleting it lowers expression 10-fold, and inverting it restores full expression. This region is most likely:
o: A silencer
Deleting a silencer would increase expression.
The core promoter
The core promoter is right at the start site and is orientation dependent.
A TATA box
A TATA box is a short element about 25–30 bp upstream, not 3 kb away.
An enhancer
Correct: needed for high expression and works in either orientation at a distance.
questions.x: An element required for strong expression that works when inverted and sits 3 kb from the gene fits the definition of an enhancer, which acts from a distance and in either orientation. A silencer would have the opposite deletion effect, raising expression. Core promoter elements such as the TATA box lie close to the start site and are orientation dependent.

questions.q: Gene-specific transcriptional activators in eukaryotes typically contain which two functional regions?
o: An RNA polymerase active site and a proofreading site
Activators do not synthesize RNA.
A DNA-binding domain and an activation domain that recruits transcription machinery
Correct: one region finds the site; the other contacts coactivators.
A ribosome-binding domain and a peptidyl transferase site
These are translation features.
A nuclease domain and a ligase domain
Activators do not cut or join DNA.
questions.x: Eukaryotic activators are modular. A DNA-binding domain (such as a zinc finger, helix-turn-helix or leucine zipper) recognizes a specific sequence, often in an enhancer. A separate activation domain recruits coactivators, chromatin-modifying enzymes and the general transcription machinery to raise transcription. Activators do not synthesize, cut or join nucleic acids.

questions.q: By mass, which type of RNA is most abundant in a typical cell?
o: rRNA
Correct: ribosomal RNA makes up roughly 80% of cellular RNA.
mRNA
mRNA is a small fraction and turns over quickly.
tRNA
tRNA is abundant in number but second to rRNA by mass.
snRNA
snRNAs are a tiny fraction used in splicing.
questions.x: Ribosomal RNA makes up roughly 80% of cellular RNA by mass because ribosomes are extremely abundant and their rRNAs are large. tRNA is numerous but small, and mRNA is only a few percent and turns over quickly. So even though mRNA carries the coding information, it is a minor fraction of total RNA.

questions.q: What is the 5′ cap of a eukaryotic mRNA?
o: A string of about 200 adenines
That is the poly(A) tail at the 3′ end.
A CCA sequence added to the 3′ end
CCA is added to the 3′ end of tRNAs.
A methyl group added to the 3′ hydroxyl
The cap is at the 5′ end and is a whole nucleotide.
A 7-methylguanosine linked by a 5′–5′ triphosphate bridge
Correct: the cap is a modified guanosine joined in reverse orientation.
questions.x: The 5′ cap is a 7-methylguanosine attached to the first nucleotide of the mRNA through an unusual 5′–5′ triphosphate linkage, added co-transcriptionally. The poly(A) tail is at the opposite, 3′ end, and the CCA sequence belongs to tRNAs. The reversed 5′–5′ linkage leaves no free 5′ end for exonucleases.

questions.q: Which function does the 5′ cap serve for a eukaryotic mRNA?
o: It signals RNA polymerase II to terminate transcription
Termination is linked to 3′-end signals.
It directs the mRNA to the endoplasmic reticulum
ER targeting uses the signal sequence of the growing protein.
It provides the splice sites for intron removal
Splice sites are sequences at intron boundaries.
It protects the mRNA from 5′ exonucleases and helps recruit ribosomes
Correct: it stabilizes mRNA and is bound during translation initiation.
questions.x: The 5′ cap protects mRNA from 5′→3′ exonucleases, aids nuclear export, and is recognized by eIF4E so the small ribosomal subunit can load and scan for the start codon. ER targeting depends on a signal sequence in the protein, and splicing depends on sequences at intron boundaries, not on the cap.

questions.q: How is the poly(A) tail added to eukaryotic pre-mRNA?
o: It is transcribed from a run of T's at the end of the gene
Genes do not encode the poly(A) tail.
RNA polymerase II adds it during elongation using the template
The tail is added after cleavage, without a template.
Poly(A) polymerase adds it to the 5′ end of the transcript
The poly(A) tail is at the 3′ end.
The transcript is cleaved downstream of AAUAAA, then poly(A) polymerase adds A's without a template
Correct: the tail is not encoded in the DNA.
questions.x: The poly(A) tail is not encoded in the gene. The pre-mRNA is cleaved about 10–30 nucleotides downstream of an AAUAAA signal, and poly(A) polymerase then adds roughly 200 adenines to the new 3′ end without a template. The tail stabilizes the mRNA and promotes export and translation.

questions.q: The spliceosome that removes introns from pre-mRNA is made of:
o: Ribosomal RNA and ribosomal proteins
That describes the ribosome.
Small nuclear RNAs bound to proteins (snRNPs)
Correct: snRNAs pair with splice sites and help catalyze the reactions.
Transfer RNAs bound to amino acids
tRNAs carry amino acids for translation.
Protein enzymes only, with no RNA
RNA components are central to spliceosome function.
questions.x: The spliceosome is a large ribonucleoprotein complex made of small nuclear RNAs bound to proteins (snRNPs such as U1, U2, U4, U5 and U6) plus many other proteins. The snRNAs base-pair with the 5′ splice site, branch point and each other, and the RNA is thought to carry out catalysis. It is distinct from the ribosome, which uses rRNA.

questions.q: In what form is an intron released during pre-mRNA splicing?
o: A linear fragment with normal 3′–5′ ends
The intron is looped into a lariat first.
A closed circle joined by a 3′–5′ bond
The loop is joined through a 2′–5′ link and has a tail.
A lariat with a 2′–5′ bond at a branch-point adenine
Correct: the branch A's 2′ OH attacks the 5′ splice site, forming the loop.
A short mRNA that is then translated
Excised introns are degraded, not translated.
questions.x: Splicing proceeds by two transesterifications. First, the 2′ OH of the branch-point adenine attacks the 5′ splice site, creating a 2′–5′ link that loops the intron. Then the freed 3′ OH of exon 1 attacks the 3′ splice site, joining the exons and releasing the intron as a lariat with a tail. The lariat is debranched and degraded, never translated.

questions.q: A mutation changes the invariant GU at the 5′ end of intron 3 of a gene to AU. What is the most likely consequence?
o: Transcription of the gene cannot begin
Splice sites do not control transcription initiation.
The protein is unchanged because introns are not translated
The mutation changes how the intron is removed, so exons can be affected.
The poly(A) tail is not added
Polyadenylation depends on a 3′-end signal, not intron sequences.
Intron 3 is not removed correctly, altering the mature mRNA
Correct: the 5′ splice site is lost, causing intron retention or use of other sites.
questions.x: Introns almost always begin with GU at the 5′ splice site and end with AG at the 3′ splice site. Changing GU to AU destroys the 5′ splice site, so the spliceosome cannot remove intron 3 normally; the intron may be retained, a cryptic site used, or an exon skipped. Although introns are not translated, their boundaries determine which sequence ends up in the mature mRNA.

questions.q: What does alternative splicing allow a eukaryotic cell to do?
o: Translate one mRNA in several reading frames
Alternative splicing changes exon content, not the frame used.
Fuse mRNAs from different chromosomes into one protein
Standard splicing joins exons within one transcript.
Translate intron sequences directly into protein
Introns are removed before translation.
Make several protein isoforms from one gene by joining different exons
Correct: different exon combinations give related proteins.
questions.x: Alternative splicing joins different combinations of exons from the same pre-mRNA, for example by skipping an exon or choosing between alternative exons. One gene can therefore produce several related protein isoforms, often in different tissues. This helps explain how about 20,000 human genes produce a much larger variety of proteins.

questions.q: A eukaryotic gene spans 12 kb, but its mature mRNA is only 2 kb. What best explains the difference?
o: The mRNA was partly degraded during export
Degradation would not produce a consistent, functional mRNA.
The poly(A) tail was trimmed
The tail is only about 200 nucleotides.
Introns were removed by splicing
Correct: most of the gene's length is intron sequence.
The promoter was not transcribed
The promoter is short and never part of the mRNA anyway.
questions.x: Most eukaryotic genes contain introns, which are transcribed into pre-mRNA but removed by splicing in the nucleus. Here about 10 kb of the 12 kb gene is intron sequence, leaving a 2 kb mature mRNA of exons plus the cap and tail. The promoter is never transcribed, and the poly(A) tail is only about 200 nucleotides, far too small to account for a 10 kb difference.

questions.q: A mature mRNA is hybridized to the single-stranded template DNA of its gene and viewed by electron microscopy. Several loops of unpaired DNA appear. What do the loops represent?
o: Introns that are present in the gene but missing from the mRNA
Correct: DNA with no matching mRNA sequence loops out.
Exons that failed to base-pair
Exons are in the mRNA and pair with their DNA.
The poly(A) tail of the mRNA
The tail is RNA with no DNA partner; it would not form DNA loops.
The 5′ cap of the mRNA
The cap is a single modified nucleotide.
questions.x: When mature mRNA hybridizes to the template DNA of its gene, exon sequences pair with their complementary DNA. Intron sequences in the DNA have no matching mRNA because they were spliced out, so they bulge out as single-stranded loops. The number of loops shows the number of introns. This R-loop experiment was early evidence for split genes.

questions.q: Which processing step occurs for a typical eukaryotic mRNA but not for a bacterial mRNA?
o: Synthesis by an RNA polymerase
All mRNAs are made by RNA polymerase.
Translation starting at an AUG codon
Both use AUG as the usual start codon.
Addition of a 7-methylguanosine cap
Correct: capping is a eukaryotic modification.
Degradation by ribonucleases
mRNAs in all organisms are eventually degraded.
questions.x: Eukaryotic pre-mRNAs undergo processing that bacterial mRNAs do not: a 5′ 7-methylguanosine cap, a 3′ poly(A) tail and splicing. Synthesis by RNA polymerase, AUG start codons and eventual degradation are features of mRNA in all organisms. Bacterial mRNAs are translated directly, often while still being transcribed.

questions.q: Where does pre-mRNA splicing take place in eukaryotic cells?
o: In the nucleus
Correct: splicing occurs before mature mRNA is exported.
In the cytoplasm on free ribosomes
Ribosomes translate mature mRNA after export.
In the rough endoplasmic reticulum
The RER handles protein synthesis and folding, not splicing.
In the Golgi apparatus
The Golgi modifies and sorts proteins.
questions.x: In eukaryotes, capping, splicing and polyadenylation happen in the nucleus, many of them co-transcriptionally, before the mature mRNA is exported through nuclear pores. Only fully processed mRNA is normally exported and translated in the cytoplasm. This compartmentalization is why eukaryotes cannot couple transcription and translation as bacteria do.

questions.q: What catalyzes peptide bond formation on the ribosome?
o: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase
This enzyme charges tRNAs; it does not form peptide bonds.
Elongation factor EF-Tu
EF-Tu delivers aminoacyl-tRNAs to the A site.
rRNA of the large ribosomal subunit
Correct: peptidyl transferase is a ribozyme activity of the large subunit rRNA.
A protein of the small ribosomal subunit
The small subunit decodes mRNA; catalysis is in the large subunit.
questions.x: Peptide bond formation is catalyzed by peptidyl transferase, an activity of the large subunit's rRNA (23S in bacteria, 28S in eukaryotes), making the ribosome a ribozyme. Ribosomal proteins mainly support structure. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge tRNAs, and elongation factors deliver tRNAs and drive translocation, but none of them forms the bond.

questions.q: Why does translational accuracy depend heavily on aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases?
o: They check codon–anticodon pairing in the A site
That decoding happens in the ribosome.
They attach each amino acid to the tRNAs with matching anticodons
Correct: once a tRNA is charged, the ribosome checks only the anticodon, not the amino acid.
They form peptide bonds between amino acids
Peptide bonds are formed by the ribosome.
They recognize stop codons
Stop codons are recognized by release factors.
questions.x: The ribosome checks only codon–anticodon pairing; it cannot tell which amino acid a tRNA carries. So accuracy depends on aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attaching the correct amino acid to each tRNA, and many have proofreading sites to remove wrong ones. A mischarged tRNA would insert the wrong amino acid without being caught.

questions.q: A cysteine already attached to tRNA^Cys is chemically converted to alanine. When this charged tRNA is used in translation, the alanine is inserted:
o: At alanine codons
The ribosome cannot detect which amino acid is attached.
Nowhere, because the ribosome rejects the mismatch
The ribosome does not proofread the attached amino acid.
At stop codons
Stop codons are read by release factors, not tRNAs.
At cysteine codons
Correct: the ribosome reads only the anticodon, so the tRNA identity decides placement.
questions.note: The tRNA is the adaptor: anticodon decides position, synthetase decides identity.
questions.x: The ribosome matches the tRNA's anticodon to the codon and ignores the amino acid attached. A tRNA^Cys still carries a cysteine anticodon, so the chemically altered alanine is inserted wherever cysteine codons appear. This classic experiment showed that tRNA is the adaptor and the synthetase's charging step determines amino acid identity.

questions.q: Counting tRNA charging, aminoacyl-tRNA delivery and translocation, how many high-energy phosphate bonds are used to add one amino acid to a growing chain?
o: Charging alone uses more than one high-energy bond.
This counts only charging (ATP → AMP + PPi).
Misses one of the steps; elongation uses two GTPs.
Correct: 2 for charging (ATP → AMP) plus 1 GTP for delivery and 1 GTP for translocation.
questions.x: Charging uses ATP → AMP + PPi, and PPi hydrolysis means two high-energy bonds are spent. Elongation then uses one GTP to deliver the aminoacyl-tRNA to the A site (EF-Tu/eEF1) and one GTP for translocation (EF-G/eEF2). Total: 4 high-energy bonds per amino acid added. The usual mistake is counting charging as a single bond.

questions.q: During elongation, an incoming aminoacyl-tRNA first binds to which ribosomal site?
o: The P site
The P site holds the tRNA carrying the growing chain.
The A site
Correct: the A (aminoacyl) site accepts each new charged tRNA.
The E site
The E site is where uncharged tRNAs exit.
The exit tunnel
The tunnel is where the growing polypeptide leaves.
questions.x: The ribosome has three tRNA sites: A (aminoacyl), P (peptidyl) and E (exit). Each incoming charged tRNA enters the A site, where its anticodon is checked against the codon. The P site holds the tRNA carrying the growing chain, and the E site is where uncharged tRNAs leave.

questions.q: After peptide bond formation, the ribosome translocates. Where does the now-uncharged tRNA that was in the P site go?
o: Back to the A site
Translocation moves tRNAs forward, never backward.
It stays in the P site
The peptidyl-tRNA from the A site moves into the P site.
To the E site, from which it leaves the ribosome
Correct: translocation shifts tRNAs from A→P and P→E.
Into the exit tunnel with the polypeptide
tRNAs exit through the E site; only the chain uses the tunnel.
questions.x: After peptidyl transfer, the growing chain sits on the tRNA in the A site and the P-site tRNA is now uncharged. Translocation moves the ribosome one codon toward the 3′ end, shifting the peptidyl-tRNA into the P site and the uncharged tRNA into the E site, from which it leaves. This empties the A site for the next aminoacyl-tRNA.

questions.q: In bacteria, how does the small ribosomal subunit locate the correct start codon?
o: It binds the 5′ cap and scans to the first AUG
Cap-dependent scanning is used in eukaryotes.
It binds the poly(A) tail and moves backward
Bacterial mRNAs lack stable poly(A) tails, and ribosomes do not scan backward.
It always starts at the first nucleotide of the mRNA
Start codons are usually some distance from the 5′ end.
Its 16S rRNA base-pairs with the Shine–Dalgarno sequence upstream of the start codon
Correct: this pairing places AUG in the P site.
questions.x: Bacterial mRNAs carry a Shine–Dalgarno sequence a few nucleotides upstream of the start codon. It base-pairs with the 3′ end of 16S rRNA in the small subunit, positioning the AUG in the P site. Because each gene has its own Shine–Dalgarno site, polycistronic mRNAs can start translation internally. Cap-dependent scanning is the eukaryotic mechanism.

questions.q: An extra AUG in strong sequence context is inserted into the 5′ UTR of a eukaryotic mRNA, out of frame with the normal start codon. What is the most likely effect?
o: No effect, because ribosomes start at the AUG closest to the poly(A) tail
Scanning begins at the 5′ cap, not the tail.
More of the normal protein is made, because two start codons are present
The new AUG is out of frame, so it competes rather than helps.
Less of the normal protein is made, because scanning ribosomes start at the new AUG
Correct: ribosomes scan from the cap and usually begin at the first good AUG.
The mRNA keeps its introns
Splicing is complete before translation begins.
questions.x: Eukaryotic ribosomes bind at the 5′ cap and scan 5′→3′, usually starting at the first AUG in a good sequence context (Kozak). An upstream out-of-frame AUG captures many scanning ribosomes, which then translate the wrong frame and usually hit a stop codon. Fewer ribosomes reach the normal start, so less of the normal protein is made.

questions.q: The initiator tRNA in bacteria carries which amino acid?
o: N-formylmethionine
Correct: bacteria begin proteins with fMet.
Unmodified methionine
Eukaryotic cytoplasmic translation starts with unmodified Met.
Tryptophan
Tryptophan is coded by UGG, not the start codon.
Selenocysteine
Selenocysteine is a rare amino acid inserted at certain UGA codons.
questions.x: Bacteria start translation with a special initiator tRNA carrying N-formylmethionine (fMet), which pairs with AUG in the P site. Eukaryotic cytoplasmic translation uses an initiator tRNA carrying ordinary methionine. Internal AUGs in both are read by a separate methionine tRNA.

questions.q: What happens when a stop codon enters the ribosome's A site?
o: A stop tRNA delivers a final amino acid
No standard tRNA reads stop codons.
A release factor binds and triggers release of the polypeptide from the tRNA
Correct: no tRNA matches stop codons, so release factors bind instead.
The ribosome stalls until the mRNA is degraded
Release factors end translation promptly.
The large subunit adds a final methionine
Methionine is added only at start codons (and internal AUGs).
questions.x: No standard tRNA has an anticodon for UAA, UAG or UGA. When a stop codon enters the A site, a release factor protein binds instead and causes peptidyl transferase to transfer the chain to water, hydrolyzing it from the P-site tRNA. The ribosome then dissociates, so no extra amino acid is added.

questions.q: In which directions are mRNA read and polypeptides built during translation?
o: mRNA is read 5′→3′; the protein grows from C-terminus to N-terminus
New amino acids are added to the C-terminus.
mRNA is read 3′→5′; the protein grows from N-terminus to C-terminus
Ribosomes move toward the mRNA's 3′ end.
mRNA is read 5′→3′; the protein grows from N-terminus to C-terminus
Correct: the first codon specifies the N-terminal amino acid.
mRNA is read 3′→5′; the protein grows from C-terminus to N-terminus
Both directions are reversed.
questions.x: Ribosomes read mRNA 5′→3′, and the first codon specifies the N-terminal amino acid. Each new amino acid is added to the C-terminus of the growing chain, so proteins grow N→C. These directions correspond: the 5′ end of the mRNA matches the protein's N-terminus.

questions.q: Bacterial 70S ribosomes are made of subunits of which sizes?
o: 40S and 60S
These are eukaryotic 80S ribosome subunits.
30S and 50S
Correct: S values reflect sedimentation and do not simply add.
35S and 35S
Ribosome subunits are unequal in size.
20S and 50S
The bacterial small subunit is 30S.
questions.x: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, built from a 30S small subunit and a 50S large subunit; eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, with 40S and 60S subunits. Svedberg units measure sedimentation rate, which depends on shape as well as mass, so subunit values do not add up to the whole.

questions.q: Why can antibiotics such as tetracycline block bacterial protein synthesis with little effect on human cytoplasmic translation?
o: Human cells have no ribosomes in the cytoplasm
Human cytoplasm is full of 80S ribosomes.
Bacterial ribosomes differ structurally from eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes
Correct: drugs bind sites unique to 70S ribosomes.
Bacteria do not use tRNA
Bacteria use tRNA just as eukaryotes do.
Bacteria use a different genetic code
The code is nearly universal.
questions.x: Bacterial 70S ribosomes differ in rRNA and protein structure from eukaryotic 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes. Antibiotics such as tetracycline, aminoglycosides and macrolides exploit these differences, binding sites present on bacterial ribosomes and largely absent from human cytoplasmic ones. The genetic code and tRNA use are the same in both, so they cannot explain selectivity.

questions.q: A patient receiving high doses of chloramphenicol, an inhibitor of bacterial 70S ribosomes, develops bone marrow suppression. Which explanation is most consistent with this?
o: The drug inhibits RNA polymerase II in marrow cells
Chloramphenicol targets ribosomes, not transcription.
The drug binds 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes more tightly than 70S
It is selective for bacterial-type ribosomes.
The drug also inhibits mitochondrial ribosomes, which resemble bacterial ribosomes
Correct: mitochondria descend from bacteria and have similar ribosomes.
The drug blocks nuclear DNA replication
Chloramphenicol does not target replication.
questions.x: Mitochondria descend from endosymbiotic bacteria and still have their own bacteria-like ribosomes. At high doses, chloramphenicol also inhibits mitochondrial protein synthesis, impairing rapidly dividing bone marrow cells and causing dose-related marrow suppression. Its selectivity for 70S-type ribosomes, not binding to cytoplasmic 80S ribosomes, is what produces this side effect.

questions.q: A secreted protein begins translation on a free ribosome. What happens next?
o: The protein is finished in the cytosol and imported into the Golgi
Secreted proteins enter the ER during translation.
A C-terminal signal sends the ribosome to the nucleus
Secretory signals are N-terminal and target the ER.
SRP binds the N-terminal signal sequence and brings the ribosome to the rough ER
Correct: translation continues into the ER lumen.
The ribosome moves into a mitochondrion
Mitochondrial import uses different signals and posttranslational import.
questions.x: All translation begins on free cytosolic ribosomes.
