For secreted proteins, an N-terminal signal sequence emerges and is bound by the signal recognition particle (SRP), which pauses translation and docks the ribosome on the rough ER via the SRP receptor. Translation resumes with the chain threading into the ER lumen, then the protein moves to the Golgi and out of the cell.

questions.q: A mutation deletes the signal sequence of a normally secreted protein. Where will the protein most likely end up?
o: In the cytosol
Correct: without a signal sequence, SRP cannot target it to the ER.
Outside the cell, secreted faster than normal
Secretion requires entry into the ER first.
In the ER lumen
The signal sequence is needed to enter the ER.
In the lysosome
Lysosomal proteins also pass through the ER.
questions.x: The N-terminal signal sequence is the ticket into the secretory pathway: SRP recognizes it and directs the ribosome to the rough ER. Without it, translation finishes on free ribosomes and the protein stays in the cytosol. Since secretion, lysosomal delivery and ER residence all require first entering the ER, none of those destinations is possible.

questions.q: Electron micrographs show many ribosomes spaced along a single mRNA. What does this structure allow?
o: Many copies of a protein to be made from one mRNA at the same time
Correct: polysomes translate one mRNA simultaneously.
Each ribosome to make a different protein from the same mRNA
All ribosomes on a monocistronic mRNA make the same protein.
The mRNA to be spliced while it is translated
Splicing is complete before translation in eukaryotes.
Ribosomes to read the mRNA in both directions
Ribosomes always move 5′→3′.
questions.x: A polysome (polyribosome) is one mRNA being translated by many ribosomes at once, each having started at the same start codon at a different time. Every ribosome makes a full copy of the same protein, greatly increasing output from a single mRNA. Ribosomes always move 5′→3′, and eukaryotic splicing is complete before translation.

questions.q: Which of the following is a post-translational modification rather than an RNA-processing step?
o: Phosphorylation of a serine residue
Correct: it modifies a protein after it is made.
Addition of a poly(A) tail
This modifies pre-mRNA.
Addition of a 5′ cap
This modifies pre-mRNA.
Removal of introns
Splicing processes pre-mRNA.
questions.x: Post-translational modifications change a protein after or during its synthesis, such as phosphorylation, glycosylation or proteolytic cleavage. Capping, polyadenylation and splicing modify pre-mRNA in the nucleus before translation, so they are RNA-processing steps. Ask whether the molecule being modified is RNA or protein.

questions.q: Insulin is made as one polypeptide that is later cut into two chains held together by disulfide bonds. This illustrates:
o: Post-translational proteolytic processing
Correct: cleavage after translation produces the active hormone.
Alternative splicing
Splicing acts on RNA, not on protein chains.
RNA editing
Editing changes RNA bases before translation.
Translation of two separate mRNAs
Both chains come from one precursor polypeptide.
questions.x: Insulin is synthesized as preproinsulin. The signal peptide is removed in the ER, disulfide bonds form, and proteases then excise the C-peptide, leaving A and B chains linked by disulfides. This is post-translational proteolytic processing of one polypeptide, not two separate translation products or RNA-level changes.

questions.q: What do heat-shock proteins acting as chaperones do?
o: Export mRNA from the nucleus
mRNA export uses other transport factors.
Form peptide bonds during translation
Peptide bonds are formed by the ribosome.
Add the 5′ cap to mRNA
Capping enzymes, not chaperones, do this.
Help new or stress-damaged proteins fold correctly
Correct: chaperones prevent misfolding and aggregation.
questions.x: Chaperones, many first identified as heat-shock proteins (such as Hsp70 and Hsp60), bind exposed hydrophobic regions of new or stress-damaged proteins. They prevent aggregation and help the proteins reach their native fold, often using ATP. Heat stress increases their expression because more proteins unfold at high temperature.

questions.q: A protein tagged with a chain of ubiquitin molecules is typically:
o: Secreted from the cell
Secretion depends on a signal sequence and the ER.
Degraded by the proteasome
Correct: polyubiquitin marks proteins for proteasomal destruction.
Imported into the nucleus
Nuclear import uses nuclear localization signals.
Stored in secretory vesicles
Ubiquitin chains do not signal storage.
questions.x: Ubiquitin ligases attach a chain of ubiquitin molecules to proteins that are damaged, misfolded or no longer needed. The 26S proteasome recognizes polyubiquitin, unfolds the protein and degrades it into short peptides. This regulated degradation controls the levels of key proteins such as cyclins.

questions.q: In the lac operon, what is the role of allolactose (derived from lactose)?
o: It is a corepressor that helps the repressor bind the operator
Corepressors act in repressible operons like trp.
It binds the CAP site to activate transcription
CAP binds cAMP, not lactose.
It binds RNA polymerase directly
Allolactose acts through the repressor.
It is an inducer that binds the repressor and prevents it from binding the operator
Correct: an inactive repressor lets RNA polymerase transcribe.
questions.x: The lac operon is inducible. With no lactose, the lac repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription. Allolactose, made from lactose, binds the repressor and changes its shape so it releases the operator, letting RNA polymerase transcribe lacZ, lacY and lacA. CAP is a separate activator controlled by cAMP, not by lactose.

questions.q: An E. coli strain has a lacI mutation that makes a repressor unable to bind DNA. With no glucose and no lactose present, the lac structural genes will be:
o: Not expressed
Nothing blocks the operator, and CAP–cAMP is active without glucose.
Expressed only after lactose is added
Induction is unnecessary when the repressor cannot bind.
Expressed only after glucose is added
Glucose lowers cAMP and would reduce expression.
Expressed at high levels
Correct: with no functional repressor, the operon is constitutive.
questions.x: If the repressor cannot bind DNA, nothing blocks the operator, so the operon no longer needs an inducer and becomes constitutive. With glucose absent, cAMP is high and CAP–cAMP also activates the promoter, so expression is high even without lactose. Adding glucose would lower cAMP and reduce expression, not raise it.

questions.q: A lacI⁻ E. coli strain (no functional repressor) receives a plasmid carrying a wild-type lacI gene. With no lactose present, the chromosomal lac genes will be:
o: Expressed constitutively, because the chromosomal mutation is dominant
lacI⁻ is recessive to lacI⁺.
Expressed, because the plasmid repressor binds only the plasmid
A protein product diffuses and acts on any operator.
Repressed, because the repressor is diffusible and acts in trans
Correct: repressor from the plasmid can bind the chromosomal operator.
Expressed at exactly half the uninduced level
One functional repressor gene is enough to repress.
questions.x: The lac repressor is a diffusible protein, so it acts in trans: repressor made from a plasmid can bind the operator on the chromosome. A wild-type lacI gene therefore restores repression of the chromosomal lac genes in the absence of lactose, making lacI⁻ recessive to lacI⁺. One functional lacI copy makes enough repressor to block both operators.

questions.q: A partial diploid E. coli carries lacI⁺ lacOᶜ lacZ⁻ on one DNA molecule and lacI⁺ lacO⁺ lacZ⁺ on the other. With glucose absent, β-galactosidase production will be:
o: Inducible, made only when lactose is present
Correct: lacOᶜ acts only in cis on the lacZ⁻ copy, and the lacZ⁺ copy is normally regulated.
Constitutive, because lacOᶜ is dominant
Operators act in cis, so lacOᶜ affects only the defective lacZ.
Absent under all conditions
The lacO⁺ lacZ⁺ copy can be induced.
Constitutive at half the normal level
The constitutive copy encodes nonfunctional enzyme.
questions.note: Proteins (lacI) act in trans; DNA sites (lacO) act in cis.
questions.x: Operators are DNA sites that act only in cis, controlling the genes on the same DNA molecule. The lacOᶜ copy is transcribed constitutively, but it carries lacZ⁻ and makes no functional enzyme. The functional lacZ⁺ copy has a normal operator, so it is repressed by lacI⁺ and turned on only when lactose is present. Overall β-galactosidase is inducible.

questions.q: Why is lac operon transcription low when both glucose and lactose are present?
o: The repressor remains bound to the operator
Lactose inactivates the repressor.
Glucose binds the repressor and locks it on the operator
Glucose acts through cAMP levels, not the repressor.
Lactose is degraded before it can act
Allolactose still forms and inactivates the repressor.
Low cAMP leaves CAP unable to stimulate RNA polymerase
Correct: glucose lowers cAMP, so the CAP activator is not bound.
questions.x: Full lac expression needs both repressor removal and activation by CAP. Lactose (via allolactose) inactivates the repressor, but glucose lowers cAMP, so CAP is not bound and RNA polymerase binds the weak lac promoter poorly. This catabolite repression ensures the cell uses glucose before lactose. Glucose does not act on the repressor itself.

questions.q: When tryptophan is abundant, the trp operon is shut off because tryptophan:
o: Binds RNA polymerase and blocks elongation
Tryptophan acts through the repressor.
Binds the trp repressor, allowing it to bind the operator
Correct: tryptophan is a corepressor.
Binds the repressor and releases it from the operator
That describes an inducer in an inducible system.
Binds CAP and blocks its activation
CAP regulates catabolic operons in response to cAMP.
questions.x: The trp operon is repressible. The trp repressor is made in an inactive form; when tryptophan is abundant, it binds the repressor as a corepressor, which then binds the operator and blocks transcription of the biosynthesis genes. This is the reverse of the lac system, where the small molecule removes the repressor from DNA.

questions.q: Attenuation of the trp operon depends on which feature of bacterial gene expression?
o: The trp mRNA is spliced in two alternative ways
Bacterial mRNAs are not spliced.
The trp repressor binds the mRNA leader
The repressor binds DNA; attenuation is a separate mechanism.
Ribosomes read the leader 3′→5′
Ribosomes read 5′→3′.
Translation of the leader sequence happens while transcription is still under way
Correct: ribosome speed on the leader decides which RNA hairpin forms.
questions.x: In bacteria, ribosomes translate the trp leader while RNA polymerase is still transcribing downstream. The leader contains Trp codons: when tryptophan is plentiful, the ribosome moves quickly and a terminator hairpin forms, ending transcription early; when it is scarce, the ribosome stalls and an antiterminator forms instead. This coupling is impossible in eukaryotes, where transcription and translation are separated.

questions.q: Operons for breaking down nutrients (like lac) and operons for building nutrients (like trp) are typically:
o: Repressible and inducible, respectively
This reverses the logic.
Both inducible
trp is turned off by its end product.
Inducible and repressible, respectively
Correct: catabolic genes turn on when substrate appears; anabolic genes turn off when product builds up.
Both constitutive
Both are regulated by nutrient levels.
questions.x: Catabolic operons such as lac are usually inducible: they switch on when the substrate to be broken down appears. Anabolic operons such as trp are usually repressible: they switch off when the end product accumulates. Both logics avoid making enzymes the cell does not currently need.

questions.q: Binding of the lac repressor to the operator is an example of:
o: Positive control of transcription
Positive control uses an activator, such as CAP.
Attenuation
Attenuation acts through leader RNA structure.
Negative control of transcription
Correct: a bound regulator blocks transcription.
Post-translational regulation
The repressor regulates transcription, not protein activity.
questions.x: Negative control means a regulatory protein turns transcription off by binding DNA, as the lac repressor does at the operator. Positive control means a bound protein turns transcription on, as CAP–cAMP does at the lac promoter. The lac operon is under both kinds of control at once.

questions.q: A mature microRNA loaded into RISC typically regulates gene expression by:
o: Pairing with target mRNAs, often in the 3′ UTR, to repress translation or trigger decay
Correct: miRNAs act after transcription.
Binding promoter DNA to block transcription
miRNAs target mRNA, not promoter DNA.
Being translated into a small regulatory peptide
miRNAs are noncoding.
Catalyzing splicing of pre-mRNA
Splicing uses snRNAs in the spliceosome.
questions.x: MicroRNAs are short noncoding RNAs processed by Drosha and Dicer and loaded into the RISC complex. The miRNA guides RISC to partly complementary sites, often in the 3′ UTR of target mRNAs, repressing translation and promoting mRNA decay. This is post-transcriptional regulation; miRNAs do not bind promoters or encode peptides.

questions.q: Double-stranded RNA matching a gene's coding sequence is introduced into cells. The encoded protein drops sharply, but the gene's transcription rate is unchanged. What is the most likely mechanism?
o: The dsRNA inserts into the genome and disrupts the gene
The gene is still transcribed normally.
The dsRNA methylates the promoter
Promoter silencing would lower transcription.
Dicer makes siRNAs that guide RISC to cleave the matching mRNA
Correct: RNA interference destroys the mRNA after it is made.
The dsRNA blocks all ribosomes in the cell
The effect is specific to one protein.
questions.x: Introduced dsRNA is cut by Dicer into short siRNAs, which are loaded into RISC. With perfect complementarity, the siRNA guides RISC (Argonaute) to cleave the matching mRNA, so the protein drops while transcription continues normally. The specificity and unchanged transcription rate rule out genome disruption and promoter silencing.

questions.q: In female mammals, one X chromosome is silenced as a Barr body mainly by:
o: Deleting most of its genes during development
The inactive X keeps its DNA and can be reactivated in germ cells.
Mutating its genes into nonfunctional pseudogenes
Silencing is epigenetic, not mutational.
Moving it out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm
The Barr body stays in the nucleus.
Coating by Xist RNA followed by heterochromatin formation
Correct: Xist triggers chromosome-wide silencing marks.
questions.x: In female mammals, one X is randomly inactivated early in development. The Xist long noncoding RNA is transcribed from the future inactive X and coats it in cis, recruiting histone modifiers and DNA methylation that convert it into compact heterochromatin, the Barr body. The genes are intact and silencing is epigenetic, which is why it can be reversed in germ cells.

questions.q: A gene is imprinted so that only the paternally inherited copy is expressed. Offspring inheriting a loss-of-function allele will show the mutant phenotype when the allele comes from:
o: The mother only
The maternal copy is not expressed, so its mutation has no effect.
The father only
Correct: the maternal copy is silenced anyway, so only a paternal mutant copy matters.
Either parent equally
Imprinting makes the effect depend on parental origin.
Both parents only
One mutant paternal copy is enough to cause the phenotype.
questions.x: Genomic imprinting silences one parental copy of a gene epigenetically, often by methylation. If only the paternal allele is expressed, the maternal copy is silent no matter what its sequence. So a loss-of-function allele causes the mutant phenotype only when inherited from the father; from the mother it has no effect because that copy was already off.

questions.q: How do steroid hormone receptors change gene expression?
o: They activate adenylyl cyclase at the cell membrane
That describes many G protein–coupled receptors.
They bind the hormone and then bind specific DNA response elements as transcription factors
Correct: hormone–receptor complexes regulate transcription directly.
They splice target pre-mRNAs directly
Receptors do not act as splicing machinery.
They phosphorylate ribosomal proteins
Steroid receptors are not kinases.
questions.x: Steroid hormones are lipophilic and cross the plasma membrane. They bind intracellular receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus, and the hormone–receptor complex binds hormone response elements in DNA, acting as a transcription factor that turns target genes on or off. Water-soluble hormones, by contrast, use surface receptors and second messengers such as cAMP.

questions.q: Which level of gene regulation is available to eukaryotes but generally not to bacteria?
o: Alternative splicing of pre-mRNA
Correct: bacterial genes generally lack introns to splice.
Control of transcription initiation
Bacteria regulate initiation extensively.
Control of mRNA degradation
Bacteria also regulate mRNA stability.
Control of protein degradation
Bacteria have regulated proteases as well.
questions.x: Bacteria regulate transcription initiation, mRNA stability and protein degradation, but their genes generally lack introns. Alternative splicing, which needs introns and a spliceosome, is therefore a eukaryotic layer of control. Other eukaryote-specific levels include chromatin remodeling and regulated nuclear export.

questions.q: Tumor cells resistant to methotrexate are found to carry many extra copies of the DHFR gene. This is an example of:
o: Alternative splicing
Splicing changes exon use, not gene copy number.
Gene amplification, which raises gene dosage
Correct: more copies make more DHFR enzyme.
Epigenetic silencing
Silencing would reduce expression.
RNA interference
RNAi reduces mRNA levels and does not add gene copies.
questions.x: Gene amplification is the repeated duplication of a chromosomal region, raising the number of copies of a gene. Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR); cells that amplify the DHFR gene make so much enzyme that the drug cannot inhibit it all, so they survive. Expression rises from added copies, not from changes in splicing or silencing.

questions.q: Two mRNAs are transcribed at the same rate. mRNA X has a half-life of 30 minutes; mRNA Y has a half-life of 10 hours. At steady state, how does the amount of Y compare with X?
o: About 20 times more abundant
Correct: steady-state level is proportional to half-life, and 10 h / 0.5 h = 20.
About 2 times more abundant
The ratio of half-lives is 20, not 2.
Equally abundant
Equal synthesis does not give equal levels when decay rates differ.
About 20 times less abundant
The longer-lived mRNA accumulates more, not less.
questions.x: At steady state, synthesis equals degradation, so the amount of mRNA equals synthesis rate divided by the decay rate constant, and the decay constant is inversely proportional to half-life. With equal synthesis, abundance is proportional to half-life: 10 h / 0.5 h = 20, so Y is about 20 times more abundant. This is why mRNA stability is a major control point.

questions.q: Liver cells and neurons from the same person have the same genome but make different proteins. What best explains this?
o: Neurons lose many genes as they differentiate
Most differentiated cells keep the full genome.
The two cell types use different genetic codes
The code is the same in all cells.
Liver cells contain extra chromosomes
Most somatic cells have the same chromosome set.
They contain different active transcription factors and chromatin states
Correct: differential gene expression, not different genes, defines cell types.
questions.x: Nearly all somatic cells in a person carry the same genome. Different cell types express different genes because they contain different combinations of active transcription factors and different chromatin and DNA-methylation states, which open some genes and silence others. Differentiation is differential gene expression, not loss of genes or a different code.

questions.q: Which enzyme lets retroviruses such as HIV copy their RNA genome into DNA, reversing the usual flow of genetic information?
o: Integrase
Integrase inserts viral DNA into the host genome after it is made.
DNA ligase
Ligase joins DNA fragments; it cannot copy RNA.
Reverse transcriptase
Correct: it is an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase.
RNA polymerase II
Pol II makes RNA from a DNA template, the usual direction.
questions.x: Retroviruses reverse the usual DNA → RNA flow with reverse transcriptase, an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase that copies the RNA genome into DNA. Integrase then inserts that DNA into the host chromosome, where host RNA polymerase II transcribes it. Reverse transcriptase lacks proofreading, contributing to HIV's high mutation rate.

questions.q: Restriction enzymes used in cloning typically recognize:
o: Random sequences anywhere along the DNA
Restriction enzymes are highly sequence specific.
Only methylated DNA sequences
Methylation usually protects a site from cutting.
Short, often palindromic, DNA sequences that they cut at defined sites
Correct: each enzyme cuts at its own specific recognition sequence.
Specific sequences in single-stranded RNA
Standard restriction enzymes cut double-stranded DNA.
questions.x: Restriction endonucleases recognize short specific DNA sequences, typically 4–8 bp and often palindromic (reading the same 5′→3′ on both strands), and cut both strands at defined positions. Many leave staggered sticky ends useful for cloning. Methylation of the site usually blocks cutting rather than being required for it.

questions.q: Why don't bacteria destroy their own chromosome with the restriction enzymes they make?
o: They methylate their own recognition sites, blocking cleavage
Correct: a matching methylase protects host DNA.
Their genomes contain no recognition sites
Bacterial genomes contain many such sites.
The enzymes are kept outside the cell
Restriction enzymes act inside the cell on invading DNA.
Their chromosome is single-stranded
Bacterial chromosomes are double-stranded DNA.
questions.x: Restriction–modification systems pair each restriction enzyme with a methyltransferase that methylates the same recognition sequence in the host's own DNA. Methylated sites are not cut, while unmethylated invading phage DNA is destroyed. The host genome still contains many recognition sites; it is the methylation that protects them.

questions.q: Why does cutting both a plasmid and a gene with the same restriction enzyme make cloning easier?
o: Both get blunt ends that can only join to each other
Same-enzyme cuts often leave sticky, not blunt, ends.
The restriction enzyme also joins the pieces together
Joining requires DNA ligase.
Both get complementary sticky ends that base-pair before ligase seals them
Correct: matching overhangs anneal, then ligase forms phosphodiester bonds.
The cut ends become methylated and stick together
Methylation does not join DNA ends.
questions.x: An enzyme that makes staggered cuts leaves single-stranded overhangs. Cutting the vector and insert with the same enzyme gives complementary sticky ends that anneal by base pairing, holding the pieces together until DNA ligase forms phosphodiester bonds to seal them. The restriction enzyme cuts; it never joins.

questions.q: A 10 kb linear DNA cut with EcoRI gives 3 kb and 7 kb fragments; cut with BamHI gives 4 kb and 6 kb. Cutting with both gives 3, 3 and 4 kb. How far apart are the EcoRI and BamHI sites?
o: 1 kb
A 1 kb spacing would give a double digest of 3, 1 and 6 kb.
3 kb
Correct: e.g., EcoRI at 3 kb and BamHI at 6 kb gives pieces of 3, 3 and 4 kb.
4 kb
4 kb is one end fragment, not the spacing between sites.
6 kb
The sites cannot be 6 kb apart if the middle fragment is 3 kb.
questions.note: Draw the line: place one site, then test both possible positions of the other.
questions.x: EcoRI cuts 3 kb from one end, and BamHI cuts 4 kb from one end (equivalently 6 kb from the other). If EcoRI is at 3 kb and BamHI at 6 kb, the double digest gives 3, 3 and 4 kb, matching the data; putting BamHI at 4 kb would give 3, 1 and 6 kb instead. The sites are 6 − 3 = 3 kb apart. Always test both possible orientations of the second site.

questions.q: After bacteria are transformed with a plasmid carrying an ampicillin-resistance gene, they are plated on ampicillin. What does this step do?
o: It selects only for cells whose plasmid contains the insert
Empty plasmids also carry the resistance gene.
It kills cells that contain the inserted gene
Cells with the plasmid survive whether or not it has an insert.
It induces expression of the cloned gene
Ampicillin is a selective agent, not an inducer.
It selects for cells that took up the plasmid
Correct: only plasmid-carrying cells survive the antibiotic.
questions.x: Antibiotic selection keeps only cells that took up the plasmid, because the plasmid carries the resistance gene. It cannot distinguish plasmids with an insert from empty ones, since both carry the resistance gene. A second screen, such as blue–white screening, is needed to find recombinants.

questions.q: A gene is cloned into a site within lacZ on an ampicillin-resistance plasmid. Transformed cells are plated on ampicillin plus X-gal. Which colonies most likely carry the insert?
o: Blue colonies
Blue means lacZ is intact, so no insert is present.
Colonies that grow only without ampicillin
Cells without plasmid cannot be screened this way and die on ampicillin.
Blue and white colonies equally
Color distinguishes recombinant from nonrecombinant plasmids.
White colonies
Correct: the insert disrupts lacZ, so X-gal is not cleaved to the blue product.
questions.x: Ampicillin selects for cells with the plasmid. If the insert lands within lacZ, β-galactosidase is not made, X-gal is not cleaved and the colony stays white. Plasmids without an insert keep lacZ intact, so their colonies turn blue. White colonies are therefore the likely recombinants.

questions.q: Why is cDNA rather than genomic DNA used to express a human gene in E. coli?
o: Bacteria cannot splice out introns, and cDNA lacks them
Correct: cDNA is copied from mature mRNA.
Genomic DNA is too unstable to clone in bacteria
Genomic DNA can be cloned; the problem is introns.
cDNA includes the human promoter needed in bacteria
cDNA lacks promoters, and human promoters do not work in bacteria.
Bacteria cannot read human codons
The genetic code is nearly universal.
questions.x: Bacteria have no spliceosome and cannot remove introns from eukaryotic genes. cDNA is made by reverse transcribing mature mRNA, so it contains only the exon-derived coding sequence. It must still be placed downstream of a bacterial promoter and ribosome-binding site, since cDNA lacks its gene's promoter.

questions.q: How does a cDNA library made from liver differ from a human genomic library?
o: It contains every gene, including introns
That describes a genomic library.
It contains promoters and enhancers of liver genes
Regulatory DNA is not part of mRNA.
It contains only sequences expressed as mRNA in liver, without introns
Correct: cDNA reflects the genes that tissue transcribed.
It is identical to a cDNA library from any other tissue
Different tissues express different genes.
questions.x: A cDNA library is made by reverse transcribing a tissue's mRNA, so it contains only genes expressed in that tissue, without introns, promoters or other noncoding DNA, and in proportion to their mRNA abundance. A genomic library contains the entire genome, including introns and regulatory sequences, and is the same for every tissue.

questions.q: What is the correct order of steps in one PCR cycle?
o: Annealing, denaturation, extension
Primers cannot bind until strands are separated.
Denaturation, annealing, extension
Correct: separate strands, bind primers, then extend them.
Extension, denaturation, annealing
Extension needs bound primers first.
Denaturation, extension, annealing
Polymerase needs annealed primers before it can extend.
questions.x: Each PCR cycle has three steps: denaturation at about 95 °C to separate the strands, annealing at a lower temperature so primers bind their complementary sites, and extension at about 72 °C as polymerase extends the primers. Primers cannot anneal to double-stranded DNA, and polymerase cannot extend without bound primers.

questions.q: Why is Taq polymerase used in PCR?
o: It has higher fidelity than any other polymerase
Taq lacks proofreading and is relatively error-prone.
It stays active through repeated heating to about 95 °C
Correct: it comes from a heat-loving bacterium.
It does not need primers
Like all DNA polymerases, it extends primers.
It copies RNA templates directly
Taq copies DNA; RNA must first be reverse transcribed.
questions.x: PCR heats the reaction to about 95 °C every cycle to separate strands, which would denature most enzymes. Taq polymerase, from the thermophile Thermus aquaticus, survives these cycles, so it need not be replaced after each round. Taq lacks 3′→5′ proofreading, so high-fidelity polymerases are used when accuracy matters.

questions.q: A PCR starts with 10 copies of a target sequence. Assuming perfect doubling, about how many copies exist after 10 cycles?
o: About 100
This assumes linear, not exponential, growth.
About 1,000
2¹⁰ is about 1,000; multiply by the starting 10 copies.
About 10,000
That would require about 17 cycles.
questions.x: Under ideal conditions each PCR cycle doubles the number of target copies, so copies = starting amount × 2ⁿ. After 10 cycles, 2¹⁰ = 1,024, about 1,000-fold. Starting from 10 copies gives about 10,000. Forgetting the starting copy number gives 1,000; treating growth as linear gives 100.

questions.q: A PCR produces the expected band plus many bands of unexpected sizes. Which change is most likely to remove the extra bands?
o: Raise the annealing temperature
Correct: higher stringency stops primers binding to partly matched sites.
Lower the annealing temperature
This lets primers bind even more mismatched sites.
Lower the denaturation temperature
Incomplete strand separation would reduce all products.
Add much more primer
Excess primer tends to increase nonspecific products.
questions.x: Extra PCR bands usually mean primers are annealing to partly matched sites. Raising the annealing temperature increases stringency, so only perfectly matched primer–template duplexes remain stable and nonspecific products disappear. Lowering the temperature or adding excess primer makes mispriming worse.

questions.q: Why does PCR require two different primers?
o: One primer is for the leading strand and one for the lagging strand
PCR has no replication fork, so no leading or lagging strands.
One primer copies DNA and the other copies RNA
Both primers prime DNA synthesis on DNA templates.
Two primers are needed to separate the strands
Strands are separated by heat.
Each primer anneals to a different strand at opposite ends of the target and they extend toward each other
Correct: this defines both ends of the amplified region.
questions.x: PCR uses a forward primer that anneals to one strand and a reverse primer that anneals to the opposite strand at the far end of the target, with their 3′ ends pointing toward each other. Each primer's extension product becomes a template for the other primer, defining both ends and allowing exponential amplification. Strand separation is done by heat, not primers.

questions.q: In agarose gel electrophoresis, toward which electrode do DNA fragments move, and which move fastest?
o: Toward the positive electrode; larger fragments move fastest
Large fragments are slowed more by the gel.
Toward the positive electrode; smaller fragments move fastest
Correct: negative DNA moves to the anode, and short pieces pass through the gel more easily.
Toward the negative electrode; smaller fragments move fastest
DNA is negatively charged, so it moves toward the positive electrode.
Toward the negative electrode; larger fragments move fastest
Both the direction and the size trend are reversed.
questions.x: DNA is negatively charged because of its phosphate backbone, so it migrates toward the positive electrode (anode). The agarose matrix acts as a sieve, so smaller fragments pass through more easily and travel farther, while larger fragments lag. On a gel, the bands nearest the wells are the largest.

questions.q: Why are DNA fragments separated by size, not by charge, in agarose gel electrophoresis?
o: Larger fragments carry more charge and so move faster
More charge is balanced by more mass and more drag.
All fragments have about the same charge per unit length, so the gel sieves them by size
Correct: every nucleotide carries one phosphate charge.
The gel neutralizes the DNA's charge
DNA stays negatively charged during the run.
DNA is uncharged at the buffer pH
Phosphates are ionized at typical buffer pH.
questions.x: Each nucleotide contributes one negative phosphate, so DNA has a nearly constant charge-to-mass ratio. Longer fragments have more charge but proportionally more mass and drag, so in free solution all sizes would move at about the same speed. The gel matrix then separates them by size, with smaller fragments moving faster.

questions.q: To test whether a gene's mRNA is present in muscle tissue, which technique is most appropriate?
o: Northern blot
Correct: Northern blots detect specific RNA.
Southern blot
Southern blots detect DNA, which is present in all cells.
Western blot
Western blots detect proteins.
Sanger sequencing of genomic DNA
Genomic DNA does not show whether the gene is transcribed.
questions.note: SNoW DRoP: Southern–DNA, Northern–RNA, Western–protein.
questions.x: Blots are named by molecule: Southern detects DNA, Northern detects RNA, and Western detects protein. To ask whether a gene's mRNA is present in muscle, use a Northern blot (or RT-PCR). Southern blotting would detect the gene in genomic DNA of every cell, saying nothing about expression.

questions.q: A Northern blot shows the same size and amount of a gene's mRNA in mutant and wild-type cells, but a Western blot shows no protein in the mutant. Where is the defect most likely?
o: Transcription initiation
Normal mRNA levels rule out a transcription defect.
Translation or protein stability
Correct: normal mRNA but no protein points to steps after transcription and processing.
Pre-mRNA splicing
A splicing defect would usually change mRNA size.
The gene's promoter
A promoter defect would lower mRNA levels.
questions.x: A normal Northern blot shows the mRNA is transcribed, spliced to the correct size and present in normal amounts. If the Western blot shows no protein, the defect lies after mRNA production: in translation (for example, a defective start codon) or in rapid protein degradation. Promoter, transcription or splicing defects would alter the mRNA itself.

questions.q: Why do dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs) stop DNA chain growth in Sanger sequencing?
o: They lack the 3′ hydroxyl needed to form the next phosphodiester bond
Correct: without a 3′ OH, no further nucleotide can be added.
They lack the 2′ hydroxyl group
DNA nucleotides already lack a 2′ OH; that does not stop synthesis.
They lack a nitrogenous base
ddNTPs carry normal bases and still pair.
They cannot base-pair with the template
They pair normally; they just cannot be extended.
questions.x: Chain elongation requires the 3′ OH of the last nucleotide to attack the next dNTP's α-phosphate. Dideoxynucleotides lack the 3′ OH (as well as the 2′ OH missing in all DNA nucleotides), so once one is incorporated, no further nucleotide can be added. Random incorporation produces fragments ending at every position of that base, which reveals the sequence.

questions.q: In a Sanger reaction, the terminated fragments, read from shortest to longest, end in ddA, ddC, ddC and ddT. What is the template strand sequence in that region, written 3′→5′?
o: 3′-ACCT-5′
This copies the new strand's bases instead of complementing them.
3′-AGGT-5′
This complements the new strand but in reversed order.
3′-TCCA-5′
This reverses the new strand without complementing it.
3′-TGGA-5′
Correct: the new strand is 5′-ACCT-3′, and its antiparallel complement is 3′-TGGA-5′.
questions.note: Shortest fragment = nucleotide nearest the primer = 5′ end of the new strand.
questions.x: In Sanger sequencing, the shortest fragment ends closest to the primer, so reading fragments from shortest to longest gives the new strand 5′→3′: 5′-ACCT-3′. The template is complementary and antiparallel: 3′-TGGA-5′. Distractors come from copying instead of complementing or from reversing the order.

questions.q: In CRISPR-Cas9 editing, how does Cas9 find its target site?
o: A protein domain recognizes the target sequence with no RNA
Cas9 depends on its guide RNA.
A guide RNA base-pairs with target DNA next to a PAM sequence
Correct: changing the guide RNA retargets Cas9.
It cuts at any palindromic restriction site
Cas9 targeting is set by the guide, not by palindromes.
An antibody directs it to the target gene
Antibodies are not part of the system.
questions.x: Cas9 is directed by a guide RNA whose roughly 20-nucleotide spacer base-pairs with the target DNA. Cas9 also requires a short PAM sequence (NGG for the common Cas9) right next to the target before it cuts. Changing only the guide RNA sequence retargets Cas9, which is why CRISPR is far easier to program than restriction enzymes.

questions.q: Cas9 makes a double-strand break in a gene and no repair template is provided. How is the gene most often disrupted?
o: Homologous recombination restores the exact original sequence
Without a supplied template, precise edits are uncommon and would not disrupt the gene.
Mismatch repair replaces the cut region
Mismatch repair fixes mispairs, not double-strand breaks.
Base excision repair removes the broken ends
BER repairs single damaged bases.
Error-prone nonhomologous end joining introduces small insertions or deletions
Correct: indels often cause frameshifts that knock out the gene.
questions.x: Without a repair template, cells usually fix Cas9-induced double-strand breaks by nonhomologous end joining, which ligates ends directly and often leaves small insertions or deletions. Indels in a coding exon frequently shift the reading frame and knock out the gene. Precise edits require homology-directed repair with a supplied template.

questions.q: To learn a gene's function by seeing what happens when it is missing, researchers would create:
o: A transgenic mouse that overexpresses the gene
Overexpression tests excess, not absence.
A cloned mouse with an identical genome
Cloning copies the genome without removing the gene.
A knockout mouse in which the gene is inactivated
Correct: loss-of-function reveals what the gene normally does.
A mouse injected with the gene's protein
Adding protein does not test the gene's absence.
questions.x: A knockout organism has a gene deliberately inactivated, so the resulting phenotype reveals what the gene normally does (loss-of-function analysis). A transgenic animal that overexpresses a gene tests the effect of excess (gain of function), and reproductive cloning copies the whole genome without removing anything.

questions.q: Why must DNA on a Southern blot membrane be single-stranded before it is probed?
o: So restriction enzymes can cut it on the membrane
Digestion is done before the gel is run.
So the single-stranded probe can base-pair with complementary target sequences
Correct: hybridization requires accessible bases.
So proteins are removed from the DNA
Denaturing does not remove proteins.
So the DNA can move through the gel faster
Denaturing on the membrane happens after electrophoresis.
questions.x: Southern blot detection depends on hybridization: a labeled single-stranded probe must base-pair with its complementary target sequence. The target DNA is denatured (typically with alkali) so its bases are exposed for the probe to bind. Restriction digestion and electrophoresis happen earlier, before transfer to the membrane.

questions.q: Why can short tandem repeat (STR) analysis distinguish between individuals?
o: Coding sequences differ greatly between people
Coding regions are highly conserved.
The number of repeats at each locus varies widely among people
Correct: many variable loci together give a near-unique profile.
Different people use different genetic codes
The code is nearly universal.
STRs are present in only some people
Everyone has these loci; repeat counts differ.
questions.x: Short tandem repeats are loci where a 2–6 bp unit is repeated, and the repeat number varies greatly between people. Each person inherits one allele per locus from each parent. Typing many independent STR loci gives a combined profile that is almost unique, except for identical twins. Coding sequences are too conserved to be useful.

questions.q: At one STR locus, a child has alleles of 12 and 15 repeats, and the mother has 12 and 14. Which man could be the biological father?
o: A man with 12 and 14 repeats
He lacks 15, which the mother cannot have given.
A man with 14 and 16 repeats
He lacks 15.
A man with 11 and 13 repeats
He lacks 15.
A man with 13 and 15 repeats
Correct: the child's 15 allele must come from the father.
questions.x: A child inherits one allele at each STR locus from each parent. The mother (12, 14) can only have given the 12, so the child's 15 must come from the biological father. Any man lacking a 15 allele at this locus is excluded, leaving the man with 13 and 15.

questions.q: To measure a gene's mRNA level by PCR, what must first be done to the RNA?
o: Translate it into protein
Protein cannot be amplified by PCR.
Methylate it to protect it
Methylation is not a PCR requirement.
Cut it with restriction enzymes
Restriction enzymes cut double-stranded DNA, not mRNA.
Convert it to cDNA with reverse transcriptase
Correct: Taq and other PCR polymerases need a DNA template.
questions.x: PCR polymerases such as Taq copy DNA, not RNA. To measure an mRNA, first convert it into complementary DNA with reverse transcriptase, an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase; this is RT-PCR, or RT-qPCR when quantified. The cDNA then serves as the template for amplification.

questions.q: In quantitative PCR with 100% efficiency, sample A reaches the detection threshold at cycle 20 and sample B at cycle 23. How did their starting amounts of template compare?
o: A had 3 times more than B
Each cycle doubles product, so 3 cycles is 2³, not 3.
A had 8 times more than B
Correct: A reached threshold 3 cycles earlier, so it started with 2³ = 8 times more.
A had 8 times less than B
Fewer cycles to threshold means more starting template.
A and B had equal amounts
Different threshold cycles mean different starting amounts.
questions.x: In qPCR, the threshold cycle (Ct) is when product crosses a detection threshold. With 100% efficiency, product doubles each cycle, so each cycle of difference means a twofold difference in starting template. A reached threshold 3 cycles earlier, so it started with 2³ = 8 times more template. A lower Ct always means more starting material.

questions.q: What does a DNA microarray experiment typically measure?
o: The amino acid sequence of thousands of proteins
Microarrays detect nucleic acids, not protein sequence.
The exact base sequence of one gene
Sequencing methods do that.
The rate of DNA replication in a cell
Microarrays measure abundance of sequences, not replication rate.
Expression of thousands of genes at once, by hybridizing labeled cDNA to spotted probes
Correct: spot intensity reflects each gene's mRNA level.
questions.x: A microarray carries thousands of DNA probes, each for a different gene. Labeled cDNA made from a sample's mRNA hybridizes to the matching spots, and signal intensity reflects how much of each mRNA was present. This gives a genome-wide snapshot of expression; it does not determine sequences or measure protein.

questions.q: To express a human cDNA in E. coli, the expression vector must place which element just upstream of the coding sequence?
o: A bacterial promoter and ribosome-binding site
Correct: E. coli machinery must recognize the start of transcription and translation.
A 5′ cap sequence
The cap is added enzymatically in eukaryotes; it is not a DNA sequence.
The gene's original introns
Bacteria cannot remove introns.
A eukaryotic TATA box
Bacterial RNA polymerase does not use TATA boxes.
questions.x: Bacterial RNA polymerase (with sigma factor) needs a bacterial promoter with −35 and −10 elements, and bacterial ribosomes need a ribosome-binding (Shine–Dalgarno) site just upstream of the start codon. Expression vectors provide both because cDNA lacks them. Eukaryotic elements such as a TATA box or cap are not recognized by bacteria.

questions.q: A human glycoprotein produced in E. coli has the correct amino acid sequence but is inactive. What is the most likely reason?
o: Bacteria use a different genetic code
The code is nearly universal, so the sequence is correct.
Bacteria cannot transcribe cDNA
The protein was made, so it was transcribed.
Bacteria lack the ER and Golgi machinery for glycosylation
Correct: the protein lacks needed sugar modifications.
Bacterial ribosomes cannot form peptide bonds with human amino acids
Amino acids are the same in all organisms.
questions.x: E. coli lacks an ER and Golgi, so it cannot carry out the glycosylation many human proteins need for proper folding, stability or activity. The amino acid sequence can be perfect yet the protein inactive. That is why some therapeutic glycoproteins are made in yeast or mammalian cells instead.

questions.q: What is a major safety concern with gene therapy using vectors that integrate into the host genome?
o: The vector cannot enter dividing cells
Integrating vectors infect dividing cells well.
The therapeutic gene is quickly lost when cells divide
Integration makes the gene permanent in daughter cells.
The vector changes the cell's genetic code
Vectors add genes; they do not change codon meanings.
Insertion near a proto-oncogene could activate it and cause cancer
Correct: this insertional mutagenesis has caused leukemia in some trials.
questions.x: Integrating vectors, such as retroviruses, insert the therapeutic gene into the host genome so it is passed to daughter cells. Insertion site is not fully controlled, so integration near a proto-oncogene can activate it (insertional mutagenesis), which caused leukemia in early gene therapy trials. Permanent integration is the benefit; uncontrolled placement is the risk.

questions.q: Which question is a Southern blot best suited to answer?
o: How much of a protein a tissue contains
Use a Western blot or ELISA.
Which tissues express a gene's mRNA
Use a Northern blot or RT-PCR.
Whether a gene is deleted or rearranged in a patient's genomic DNA
Correct: Southern blots detect specific DNA fragments.
How fast an enzyme catalyzes its reaction
Use an enzyme activity assay.
questions.x: A Southern blot detects specific DNA sequences in restriction-digested genomic DNA, so it can reveal deletions, rearrangements, copy number changes or restriction fragment length differences. It says nothing about expression: mRNA is assessed by Northern blot or RT-PCR, and protein by Western blot or ELISA.

questions.q: After a labeled probe hybridizes to a membrane, the wash temperature is raised. What is the main effect?
o: Imperfectly matched probe is removed, increasing specificity
Correct: higher stringency melts mismatched hybrids first.
More probe binds to mismatched sequences
Higher temperature does the opposite.
The membrane-bound DNA is cut into smaller pieces
Heat in a wash does not cleave DNA.
Perfectly matched probe is removed first
Perfect matches are the most stable and stay bound longest.
questions.x: Raising wash temperature (or lowering salt) increases stringency. Mismatched probe–target hybrids have fewer base pairs and melt at lower temperatures, so they wash off first, while perfectly matched hybrids stay bound. This removes nonspecific background and increases specificity.

questions.q: After the sticky ends of an insert and a vector anneal, which enzyme forms the covalent bonds that join them?
o: DNA ligase
Correct: ligase seals the sugar–phosphate backbone.
Restriction enzyme
Restriction enzymes cut DNA.
DNA polymerase
Polymerase adds nucleotides but does not seal nicks.
Reverse transcriptase
Reverse transcriptase copies RNA into DNA.
questions.x: After complementary sticky ends anneal, the pieces are held together only by hydrogen bonds, leaving nicks in each backbone. DNA ligase uses ATP (or NAD⁺ in bacteria) to form phosphodiester bonds between adjacent 3′ OH and 5′ phosphate groups, covalently sealing the recombinant molecule. Polymerases add nucleotides but cannot seal nicks.

questions.q: Treating E. coli with CaCl₂ and a brief heat shock before adding plasmid serves to:
o: Kill cells that do not take up plasmid
Selection is done later with an antibiotic.
Induce the lac operon
Induction uses lactose or IPTG.
Increase uptake of plasmid DNA
Correct: this makes cells competent for transformation.
Turn on the ampicillin-resistance gene
That gene is expressed only once the plasmid is inside.
questions.x: Most E. coli do not take up DNA efficiently. Treating cells with cold CaCl₂ neutralizes repulsion between DNA and the negatively charged cell surface, and a brief heat shock helps plasmid DNA enter: the cells become competent. Selection on antibiotic happens afterward and is a separate step.

questions.q: An uncut plasmid often shows two or more bands on an agarose gel even though it is a single sequence. What is the best explanation?
o: The plasmid has been degraded into random pieces
Degradation gives a smear, not discrete bands.
Each band contains a different plasmid sequence
The preparation contains one plasmid sequence.
The plasmid exists in different shapes, such as supercoiled and nicked circles, that migrate differently
Correct: compact supercoiled DNA runs faster than relaxed circles of the same length.
RNA bound to the plasmid creates the extra bands
Conformation, not bound RNA, explains distinct plasmid bands.
questions.x: An uncut plasmid prep contains one sequence in several conformations. Supercoiled DNA is compact and migrates fastest, nicked (relaxed) circles migrate slowest, and linear forms run in between. These give discrete bands despite identical length, whereas random degradation produces a smear. Fragment size can only be read from a gel after linearizing the plasmid.

questions.q: Phages with ³²P-labeled DNA infect bacteria. After blending and centrifugation, most radioactivity is in the bacterial pellet. What does this show?
o: Protein is the genetic material of phages
Protein labeled with ³⁵S stays outside the cells.
The phage genome is made of RNA
³²P labels DNA in these phages.
³²P labels the phage protein coat
Phosphorus is in DNA; sulfur is used to label protein.
DNA, not protein, enters the cell and carries the genetic information
Correct: the phage DNA label goes into the bacteria.
questions.x: Hershey and Chase labeled phage DNA with ³²P (phosphorus is in DNA, not protein) and phage protein with ³⁵S (sulfur is in protein). After infection and blending, ³²P went into the bacteria while ³⁵S stayed with the empty coats in the supernatant. Since only DNA entered and new phage were produced, DNA is the genetic material.

questions.q: A mutation makes a bacterial promoter's −10 box match the consensus sequence more closely. What is the most likely effect?
o: Transcription stops entirely
Improving the promoter strengthens binding.
Transcription initiation becomes more frequent
Correct: closer-to-consensus promoters bind sigma and RNA polymerase better.
The encoded protein's amino acid sequence changes
The promoter is not translated.
Termination occurs earlier
Promoters affect initiation, not termination.
questions.x: Bacterial promoter strength depends largely on how closely the −10 and −35 elements match the consensus sequences recognized by sigma factor. A closer match increases binding of RNA polymerase holoenzyme, so transcription starts more often. Promoters are not translated and do not affect the protein's sequence or where transcription ends.

questions.q: Raising the Na⁺ concentration of a DNA solution increases its melting temperature. Why?
o: Cations shield the negative phosphates, reducing repulsion between the strands
Correct: less repulsion stabilizes the duplex.
Na⁺ forms extra hydrogen bonds between bases
Ions do not create base-pair hydrogen bonds.
Na⁺ forms covalent cross-links between strands
Na⁺ binds electrostatically, not covalently.
Na⁺ lowers the pH and protonates the bases
Adding salt does not acidify the solution.
questions.x: The two strands of DNA each carry negative phosphate charges that repel each other. Cations such as Na⁺ cluster around the backbone and shield these charges, reducing repulsion and stabilizing the duplex, so a higher temperature is needed to melt it. At low salt, DNA melts more easily.

questions.q: A mutation in the lac promoter prevents RNA polymerase from binding. Which genes are affected?
o: All three structural genes: lacZ, lacY and lacA
Correct: one promoter drives the polycistronic operon.
Only lacZ, the first gene
The genes share one transcript, so all lose expression.
Only lacI, the repressor gene
lacI has its own separate promoter.
None, because CAP compensates
CAP helps polymerase bind; it cannot replace a dead promoter.
questions.x: In the lac operon, lacZ, lacY and lacA are transcribed together from a single promoter into one polycistronic mRNA. If RNA polymerase cannot bind that promoter, none of the three genes is transcribed. lacI has its own promoter and is unaffected, and CAP only helps polymerase bind a functional promoter.

questions.q: A gene's specific physical position on a chromosome is called its:
o: Locus
Correct: the locus is the gene's address on the chromosome.
Allele
An allele is a variant form of a gene, not its position.
Genotype
Genotype is the combination of alleles an individual carries.
Karyotype
A karyotype is the full set of chromosomes displayed, not one gene's site.
questions.x: A locus is a fixed address on a chromosome; every copy of that chromosome has the same locus, though the allele sitting there can differ. Alleles are the variant versions found at a locus, so 'allele' names the content, not the place. A karyotype is a picture of the whole chromosome set and cannot pinpoint a single gene.

questions.q: Mendel's law of segregation is best explained by which meiotic event?
o: Separation of sister chromatids in anaphase II
Sister chromatids are copies of one homolog; the allele pair splits when homologs separate.
Crossing over during prophase I
Crossing over recombines linked alleles; it does not separate an allele pair.
Cytokinesis after telophase II
Cytokinesis divides cytoplasm; the alleles were already separated earlier.
Separation of homologous chromosomes in anaphase I
Correct: each homolog carries one allele, so allele pairs part when homologs separate.
questions.note: Segregation = homologs part in meiosis I.
questions.x: Each homolog in a pair carries one allele of a gene, so when homologs are pulled to opposite poles in anaphase I, the two alleles end up in different cells. That is the physical basis of segregation. Sister chromatids are replicated copies of a single homolog and carry the same allele (barring crossing over), so splitting them in anaphase II does not separate an allele pair.

questions.q: Two plants heterozygous for two unlinked genes (AaBb × AaBb) are crossed. What fraction of offspring show both dominant phenotypes?
o: That is the fraction dominant for one trait and recessive for the other.
That is the double-recessive aabb fraction.
Considers only one gene; both must show the dominant phenotype.
questions.x: For unlinked genes, treat each gene as a separate monohybrid cross and multiply. Aa × Aa gives 3/4 dominant phenotype, and Bb × Bb also gives 3/4, so both dominant is 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16. The tempting 3/16 is a real class of the 9:3:3:1 ratio, but it counts offspring dominant for one trait and recessive for the other.

questions.q: A purple-flowered pea plant (purple dominant) is crossed with a white-flowered plant, and about half the offspring are white. What is the purple parent's genotype?
o: Homozygous dominant (PP)
PP × pp would give all purple offspring.
Homozygous recessive (pp)
A pp plant would be white, not purple.
PP or Pp, equally likely
The 1:1 testcross result identifies the parent as Pp.
Heterozygous (Pp)
Correct: Pp × pp gives 1/2 Pp purple and 1/2 pp white.
questions.note: A testcross with a recessive parent reveals the unknown genotype.
questions.x: Crossing an unknown dominant-phenotype individual to a homozygous recessive is a testcross: each offspring's phenotype directly shows which allele the unknown parent gave. A PP parent can only give P, so all offspring would be purple. Seeing about 50% white means the purple parent made p gametes half the time, so it must be Pp.

questions.q: Two carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder have three children. What is the probability that all three are unaffected?
o: That is (3/4)² for only two children.
Correct: each child is unaffected with probability 3/4; (3/4)³ = 27/64.
That is the probability for one child, not all three.
That is the probability that all three are affected.
questions.note: Independent births: multiply probabilities.
questions.x: Two carriers (Aa × Aa) have a 3/4 chance of an unaffected child each time, and each birth is an independent event. The probability that all three are unaffected is therefore 3/4 × 3/4 × 3/4 = 27/64. The choice 3/4 is the answer for one child; the past or future outcomes of siblings never change each child's own odds.

questions.q: Two carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder have two children. What is the probability that exactly one child is affected?
o: Correct: 2 birth orders × (1/4)(3/4) = 6/16 = 3/8.
Counts only one birth order; affected-first and affected-second both qualify.
That is the chance for a single child to be affected.
Treats affected and unaffected as equally likely outcomes.
questions.note: Exactly one of n: multiply by the number of orders.
questions.x: Each child is affected with probability 1/4 and unaffected with 3/4. 'Exactly one affected' can happen two ways (affected then unaffected, or unaffected then affected), each with probability 3/16, so the total is 2 × 3/16 = 3/8. Forgetting to count both orders gives 3/16, the most common error in binomial-type questions.

questions.q: A phenotypically normal woman has a brother with cystic fibrosis; both parents are unaffected. What is the probability that she is a carrier?
o: That is the carrier fraction among all offspring, ignoring that she is unaffected.
That is the chance of being affected (aa).
That is the chance of being unaffected, not of being a carrier.
Correct: parents are Aa × Aa; among unaffected offspring (AA, Aa, Aa), 2 of 3 are carriers.
questions.note: Trap: condition on what you know. She cannot be aa.
questions.x: An affected brother with unaffected parents shows both parents are carriers (Aa × Aa), giving AA : Aa : aa in a 1:2:1 ratio. Because the woman is unaffected, the aa class is excluded, leaving AA, Aa, Aa, so her chance of being a carrier is 2/3. The answer 1/2 comes from forgetting to remove the aa possibility from the denominator.

questions.q: An unaffected woman whose brother has an autosomal recessive disease (parents unaffected) has a child with a man who is a known carrier. What is the probability the child is affected?
o: Uses 1/2 as her carrier probability instead of 2/3.
Assumes she is definitely a carrier.
Correct: P(she is carrier) 2/3 × P(aa from two carriers) 1/4 = 1/6.
Adds an extra factor of 1/2; the 1/4 already includes both parents' transmission.
questions.x: First find her carrier probability: her parents must both be carriers, and since she is unaffected she is a carrier with probability 2/3. If she is a carrier, two carriers have an affected child 1/4 of the time. Multiply the independent steps: 2/3 × 1/4 = 1/6. Using 1/2 for her carrier status gives 1/8, the classic mistake.

questions.q: For unlinked genes, what is the probability that a cross of AaBbCc × aabbCc produces an AaBbcc offspring?
o: Uses 1/2 for cc; from Cc × Cc, cc is 1/4.
Correct: Aa 1/2 × Bb 1/2 × cc 1/4 = 1/16.
Uses 1/4 for Aa or Bb; from Aa × aa, Aa is 1/2.
That would apply to a trihybrid self-cross outcome, not this cross.
questions.note: Split multi-gene crosses into one gene at a time.
questions.x: Break the cross into one gene at a time. Aa × aa gives Aa with probability 1/2; Bb × bb gives Bb with probability 1/2; Cc × Cc gives cc with probability 1/4. Multiplying gives 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/16. The usual errors come from applying the heterozygote-cross fraction (1/4) to a testcross gene or vice versa.

questions.q: Mendel's law of independent assortment applies most strictly to genes that are:
o: Tightly linked on the same chromosome
Linked genes tend to be inherited together and violate independent assortment.
Alternative alleles of the same gene
Alleles of one gene segregate; assortment concerns different genes.
Found only on the X chromosome
Being X-linked does not make two genes assort independently.
Located on different nonhomologous chromosomes
Correct: nonhomologous chromosomes orient independently at metaphase I.
questions.x: Independent assortment arises because each pair of homologs lines up at metaphase I without regard to how other pairs line up. Genes on different chromosomes therefore sort independently, giving equal frequencies of all gamete combinations. Genes close together on one chromosome are physically tied and travel together unless a crossover separates them, so linkage violates this law.

questions.q: A dihybrid AaBb is testcrossed to aabb. If the genes are unlinked, what phenotypic ratio is expected?
o: That is the dihybrid self-cross (AaBb × AaBb) ratio.
That is a monohybrid cross between heterozygotes.
Correct: AaBb makes AB, Ab, aB and ab gametes equally, each revealed by aabb.
That is a monohybrid genotypic ratio.
questions.x: An unlinked AaBb individual makes four gamete types (AB, Ab, aB, ab) in equal proportions. The aabb tester contributes only recessive alleles, so each offspring's phenotype mirrors the dihybrid's gamete, giving 1:1:1:1. The 9:3:3:1 ratio requires both parents to be dihybrids, so dominant alleles from either parent can mask recessives.

questions.q: Red snapdragons crossed with white snapdragons give all pink F1 plants. What phenotypic ratio is expected in the F2?
o: 3 red : 1 white
Assumes complete dominance; heterozygotes here are pink.
All pink
That describes the F1, not the F2.
1 red : 2 pink : 1 white
Correct: with incomplete dominance each genotype has its own phenotype, so 1:2:1.
9 red : 3 pink : 3 white : 1 other
That ratio needs two genes; this is one gene.
questions.note: Incomplete dominance: phenotypic ratio = genotypic ratio.
questions.x: In incomplete dominance the heterozygote has an intermediate phenotype, so each genotype looks different. Selfing the pink F1 (Rr × Rr) gives 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr, which appears as 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white. The 3:1 ratio would require the red allele to fully mask white, which the pink F1 already rules out.

questions.q: A person with type AB blood expresses both A and B antigens on red cells. This is an example of:
o: Incomplete dominance
That produces an intermediate blend, not both full products.
Epistasis
Epistasis is one gene masking another gene.
Codominance
Correct: both alleles are fully and separately expressed in the heterozygote.
Pleiotropy
Pleiotropy is one gene affecting several traits.
questions.x: Codominance means both alleles in a heterozygote are fully expressed side by side, so an IᴬIᴮ person makes both A and B antigens. Incomplete dominance instead gives a single intermediate phenotype, like pink flowers, rather than two distinct products. The ABO system also shows multiple alleles, with i recessive to both Iᴬ and Iᴮ.

questions.q: A type A parent and a type B parent have a type O child. What are the parents' genotypes?
o: IᴬIᴬ and IᴮIᴮ
These parents could only have type AB children.
Iᴬi and Iᴮi
Correct: the type O child (ii) needs an i from each parent.
IᴬIᴮ and ii
Those parents would be type AB and type O, not A and B.
Iᴬi and IᴮIᴮ
An IᴮIᴮ parent cannot pass on i, so no ii child is possible.
questions.x: A type O child is ii and must receive an i allele from each parent. So the type A parent must be Iᴬi and the type B parent must be Iᴮi. Any homozygous parent (IᴬIᴬ or IᴮIᴮ) has no i to give, which rules out every choice containing one, even though such parents are perfectly consistent with their own blood types.

questions.q: A parent with type AB blood has children with a type O parent. Which blood types can the children have?
o: A or B only
Correct: children are Iᴬi or Iᴮi, so type A or type B.
A, B, AB, or O
That requires Iᴬi × Iᴮi parents.
AB or O only
The AB parent passes only one allele, and the O parent gives i.
A, B, or AB only
No child can receive both Iᴬ and Iᴮ, since one parent has only i.
questions.x: The AB parent (IᴬIᴮ) passes either Iᴬ or Iᴮ, and the O parent (ii) always passes i. Children are therefore Iᴬi (type A) or Iᴮi (type B), each with probability 1/2. No child can be AB, because that needs both Iᴬ and Iᴮ, and none can be O, because the AB parent has no i allele.

questions.q: In a dog breed, ee dogs are yellow regardless of the B gene; otherwise B_ is black and bb is brown. In a BbEe × BbEe cross, what fraction of puppies are yellow?
o: That is the brown fraction (bbE_).
Correct: any ee puppy is yellow, and ee occurs in 1/4 of offspring (9:3:4 overall).
Counts only bbee; all ee dogs are yellow.
That is the black fraction (B_E_).
questions.note: Recessive epistasis gives 9:3:4.
questions.x: This is recessive epistasis: the ee genotype masks the B gene entirely. Because the genes assort independently, ee occurs in 1/4 of puppies whatever their B genotype, and all of them are yellow, giving a 9 black : 3 brown : 4 yellow ratio. Counting only bbee (1/16) misses that BBee and Bbee dogs are also yellow.

questions.q: A mutation in a single connective-tissue gene affects the eye lens, the aorta and the skeleton. This illustrates:
o: Polygenic inheritance
That is many genes affecting one trait, the reverse.
Pleiotropy
Correct: one gene influencing multiple, seemingly unrelated traits.
Epistasis
Epistasis is an interaction where one gene masks another.
Incomplete penetrance
Penetrance concerns whether a genotype is expressed at all.
questions.x: Pleiotropy is when one gene affects several different traits, usually because its product is used in many tissues. A defect in a structural protein like fibrillin, as in Marfan syndrome, weakens connective tissue in the eye, the aorta and the bones at once. Polygenic inheritance is the reverse relationship: many genes each contributing to a single trait.

questions.q: Adult height in humans shows a continuous bell-shaped distribution mainly because it is:
o: Controlled by one gene with codominant alleles
One gene gives a few discrete classes, not a continuum.
Determined by mitochondrial DNA
Height is not mitochondrially inherited.
Caused by incomplete dominance of a single allele
One incompletely dominant gene gives three classes.
Influenced by many genes with small additive effects plus environment
Correct: polygenic, multifactorial traits produce continuous variation.
questions.x: When many genes each add a small effect, the number of possible allele combinations becomes large, and environmental effects blur the boundaries between them, producing a smooth bell-shaped curve. A single gene, whether codominant or incompletely dominant, can generate only a few distinct phenotypic classes. Continuous variation is the signature of polygenic, multifactorial inheritance.

questions.q: Of 100 people with a genotype for an autosomal dominant disease, 80 show signs of the disease and 20 show none. This describes:
o: 80% expressivity
Expressivity is the degree of severity among those who express it.
Codominance
Codominance concerns two alleles both being expressed in a heterozygote.
A 20% mutation rate
Carriers who show no signs still have the mutant genotype.
80% penetrance
Correct: penetrance is the fraction of carriers of a genotype who express the phenotype.
questions.note: Penetrance = whether; expressivity = how much.
questions.x: Penetrance is the percentage of individuals with a given genotype who show the phenotype at all; here 80 of 100 do, so penetrance is 80%. Expressivity is a different idea: it describes how severely the trait appears among those who do express it. The 20 unaffected people still carry the allele, so they are not explained by a lack of mutation.

questions.q: People carrying the same dominant mutation range from a few small skin spots to many large tumors. This variation in severity is called:
o: Variable expressivity
Correct: everyone expresses the trait, but to different degrees.
Incomplete penetrance
That would mean some carriers show no phenotype at all.
Incomplete dominance
That is a heterozygote intermediate between two homozygotes.
Genomic imprinting
Imprinting depends on parent of origin, not described here.
questions.x: Variable expressivity means everyone with the genotype shows the trait, but its severity differs from person to person, as in neurofibromatosis. Incomplete penetrance would mean some carriers show no signs at all, which is not what is described. Keep the two straight: penetrance asks whether the trait appears, expressivity asks how strongly.

questions.q: A woman who carries an X-linked recessive allele for hemophilia has children with an unaffected man. If they have a son, what is the probability he is affected?
o: That is the chance that any child is an affected son.
Correct: a son gets his X from his mother, who passes the mutant X half the time.
Sons inherit their X from the carrier mother.
The mother is heterozygous, so she passes the normal X half the time.
questions.note: Read carefully: 'given a son' vs 'an affected son'.
questions.x: A son receives his Y from his father and his only X from his mother. A carrier mother passes her mutant X half the time, so a son has a 1/2 chance of being affected. The answer 1/4 is the chance that a child of unknown sex is an affected son; once the child is known to be male, the sex factor of 1/2 drops out.

questions.q: A man with an X-linked recessive disorder has children with a homozygous normal woman. Which outcome is expected?
o: Half of the sons are affected
Sons inherit the father's Y, not his X.
All children are affected
Daughters are heterozygous carriers and sons get a normal X.
Half of the daughters are carriers
Every daughter receives the father's only X.
All daughters are carriers and no sons are affected
Correct: daughters get his mutant X; sons get his Y and a normal maternal X.
questions.x: A father passes his single X to every daughter and his Y to every son. So all daughters receive the mutant X and, with a normal X from their mother, become carriers, while sons get a normal maternal X and are unaffected. There is no father-to-son transmission of X-linked traits, which rules out any affected sons.

questions.q: A woman with normal vision has a color-blind father (X-linked recessive). She has a child with a man with normal vision. What is the probability their first child is a color-blind son?
o: That is the risk for a son once you know the child is male.
Correct: she is an obligate carrier; P(son) 1/2 × P(mutant X) 1/2 = 1/4.
Treats her carrier status as 1/2; her father gave her his mutant X for sure.
She must carry the allele from her father and can pass it on.
questions.x: Her color-blind father had only one X, carrying the mutant allele, and he must have given it to her, so she is an obligate carrier. A child is a son with probability 1/2, and a son gets her mutant X with probability 1/2, so a color-blind son has probability 1/4. Answering 1/2 answers a different question: the risk once you already know the child is a son.

questions.q: A man with an X-linked dominant disorder has children with an unaffected woman. What fraction of their daughters will be affected?
o: Half of them
That would apply if the mother were the heterozygous affected parent.
None of them
Daughters always receive the father's X.
Only those who also inherit a maternal mutant X
One copy of a dominant allele is enough.
All of them
Correct: every daughter receives his single X, which carries the dominant allele.
questions.x: An affected father has one X, carrying the dominant allele, and every daughter receives that X. Because one copy of a dominant allele is enough, all daughters are affected, while sons, who get his Y, are unaffected. The 'half of daughters' pattern applies only when the affected parent is a heterozygous mother.

questions.q: A disorder is transmitted from affected mothers to all of their children but never from affected fathers. The most likely cause is a mutation in:
o: An X-linked dominant gene
Affected fathers would then pass it to all daughters.
An autosomal dominant gene
Affected fathers would pass it to about half of their children.
Mitochondrial DNA
Correct: mitochondria are inherited through the egg cytoplasm.
A Y-linked gene
Y-linked traits pass from fathers to sons, never from mothers.
questions.x: Mitochondria in the zygote come almost entirely from the egg; sperm mitochondria are destroyed after fertilization. A mitochondrial mutation is therefore passed from an affected mother to all her children, and never from an affected father. X-linked dominant inheritance is the closest distractor, but there affected fathers transmit to all daughters.

questions.q: Siblings born to a mother with a mitochondrial DNA mutation vary widely in severity of the resulting disease. The best explanation is that:
o: Each oocyte received a different proportion of mutant mitochondria
Correct: heteroplasmy plus random partitioning gives each egg a different mutant load.
Paternal mitochondria compensate in some children
Paternal mitochondria are essentially not transmitted.
mtDNA recombines with nuclear DNA during meiosis
mtDNA does not cross over with nuclear chromosomes.
X-inactivation differs between siblings
X-inactivation is unrelated to mitochondrial genes.
questions.note: Heteroplasmy explains variable severity in mitochondrial disease.
questions.x: A cell can contain a mixture of normal and mutant mtDNA (heteroplasmy). When oocytes form, mitochondria are distributed randomly, so different eggs get different mutant fractions, and symptoms appear only above a threshold load. This explains why siblings from the same mother differ in severity; paternal mitochondria do not contribute to make up the difference.

questions.q: Deleting the same region of chromosome 15 causes one syndrome when inherited from the father and a different syndrome when inherited from the mother. This best illustrates:
o: X-inactivation
Chromosome 15 is an autosome; X-inactivation silences an X.
Mitochondrial inheritance
The defect is in a nuclear chromosome, passed by either parent.
Incomplete dominance
That concerns blending of allele effects, not parent of origin.
Genomic imprinting
Correct: some genes are silenced depending on parent of origin, so the active copy differs.
questions.x: In genomic imprinting, certain genes are epigenetically silenced depending on which parent transmitted them, so only one parental copy is active. Losing the 15q region from the father removes the active paternal genes (Prader-Willi syndrome), while losing it from the mother removes active maternal genes (Angelman syndrome). The key clue is that the outcome depends on parent of origin, not the DNA change itself.

questions.q: Female cats heterozygous for an X-linked coat-color gene show patches of orange and black fur. The best explanation is:
o: Codominant expression of both alleles in every cell
Each cell expresses only one X-linked allele, giving patches, not mixed hairs.
Random inactivation of one X in each cell early in development
Correct: each patch descends from a cell with a different active X.
Blending due to incomplete dominance
Blending would give one intermediate color, not patches.
Somatic mutations in skin cells
The pattern is regular in heterozygous females, not random mutation.
questions.x: Early in female mammalian development, each cell randomly inactivates one X, and all descendants of that cell keep the same X silenced. A heterozygous cat therefore becomes a mosaic of cell clones expressing either the orange or the black allele, producing patches. Codominance would show both alleles in every cell, which would not create a patchwork.

questions.q: How many Barr bodies are expected in the somatic cells of a person with a 47,XXY karyotype?
o: Barr bodies form whenever more than one X is present, even in males.
One X always remains active.
Correct: all X chromosomes beyond one are inactivated; 2 − 1 = 1.
Counts all sex chromosomes; the Y never forms a Barr body.
questions.note: Barr bodies = number of X − 1.
questions.x: Mammalian cells keep exactly one X active and condense every additional X into a Barr body, so the count is (number of X) − 1. A 47,XXY person has two X chromosomes and therefore one Barr body, even though phenotypically male. The Y chromosome is never inactivated, so it is not counted.

questions.q: In humans, development of the male phenotype is primarily triggered by:
o: Having only one X chromosome
45,X individuals develop as female.
The ratio of X chromosomes to autosomes
That system determines sex in fruit flies, not humans.
The SRY gene on the Y chromosome
Correct: SRY starts testis development, which drives male differentiation.
Maternal hormones during pregnancy
Sex is set by the embryo's own genes.
questions.x: In humans the SRY gene on the Y chromosome encodes a transcription factor that directs the bipotential gonad to become a testis. Testis hormones (testosterone and anti-Müllerian hormone) then drive the rest of male development. The X-to-autosome ratio decides sex in fruit flies, not humans; that is why 45,X people develop as female and 47,XXY people as male.

questions.q: Why are X-linked recessive traits expressed far more often in males than in females?
o: The Y chromosome carries a dominant suppressor
The Y has few genes and no matching allele for most X genes.
Males are hemizygous, so a single recessive allele is expressed
Correct: with one X, there is no second allele to mask it.
Males inherit their X from their father
Males inherit their X from their mother.
X-linked alleles mutate faster in males
Mutation rate does not explain the expression difference.
questions.x: Males have one X chromosome, so they are hemizygous for X-linked genes: a single recessive allele has no second allele to mask it and is expressed. Females need two copies of the recessive allele, which is much rarer. Note that males get their X from their mother, so a carrier mother is usually the source of the allele.

questions.q: Crossing two yellow mice (Yy × Yy) repeatedly gives yellow and non-yellow offspring in a 2:1 ratio. The best explanation is:
o: Yellow is incompletely dominant
That would give a 1:2:1 phenotypic ratio.
The yellow allele is X-linked
