X-linkage does not convert 3:1 to 2:1 in both sexes.
YY embryos die before birth
Correct: removing the 1/4 YY class leaves 2 Yy (yellow) : 1 yy.
Yellow shows incomplete penetrance
Non-expression would shift ratios toward non-yellow, not cause 2:1 regularly.
questions.note: A 2:1 ratio from a heterozygote cross signals a recessive lethal.
questions.x: Yy × Yy should give 1 YY : 2 Yy : 1 yy. If YY is lethal, the YY class disappears, leaving 2 Yy (yellow) : 1 yy, the 2:1 ratio. Here the Y allele is dominant for coat color but recessive for lethality. Incomplete dominance would leave all three genotypes alive and give a 1:2:1 ratio.

questions.q: A cross predicted to give 3:1 yields 290 dominant and 110 recessive offspring out of 400. What is the chi-square value?
o: Includes only the dominant class term.
Includes only the recessive class term.
Sums the deviations (10 + 10); they must be squared and divided by expected.
questions.note: χ² = Σ (observed − expected)² / expected.
questions.x: Chi-square compares observed counts with those expected under the hypothesis: χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E. A 3:1 ratio of 400 predicts 300 and 100; each class deviates by 10, giving 100/300 + 100/100 ≈ 0.33 + 1 = 1.33. Every class must contribute a term, and deviations must be squared, not simply added.

questions.q: Testing a 3:1 hypothesis gives χ² = 1.3 with 1 degree of freedom; the critical value at p = 0.05 is 3.84. What should be concluded?
o: The 3:1 hypothesis is rejected
Rejection requires χ² above 3.84.
The deviation from 3:1 is consistent with chance
Correct: χ² below the critical value means we fail to reject the hypothesis.
The data prove the ratio is exactly 3:1
Failing to reject is not proof.
The genes must be linked
This test concerns one gene's ratio, not linkage.
questions.x: If the computed χ² is smaller than the critical value, the observed deviation is the kind expected from random sampling more than 5% of the time, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis. Here 1.3 < 3.84, so the data fit a 3:1 ratio. Statistics never prove a hypothesis true; they only tell us whether the data are consistent with it.

questions.q: The term wild type refers to:
o: Any allele that is dominant
Wild-type alleles are often, but not necessarily, dominant.
A new mutation found in a wild population
New mutations are by definition not wild type.
The most common phenotype or allele in natural populations
Correct: wild type is the typical form, used as the reference.
The homozygous recessive genotype
Wild type is defined by frequency, not dominance.
questions.x: Wild type is the form of a gene or trait most commonly found in natural populations, used as the standard against which mutants are compared. It is defined by being typical, not by dominance. Many wild-type alleles happen to be dominant because they encode functional products, but that is a tendency, not part of the definition.

questions.q: The gene pool of a population is best defined as:
o: The two alleles carried by one individual
That is a genotype, not a population-level pool.
All alleles at all loci in all members of the population
Correct: the total collection of alleles available to the next generation.
Only the dominant alleles in the population
Recessive alleles are part of the pool too.
The genes expressed in gametes
The gene pool is defined by alleles present, not gamete expression.
questions.x: A gene pool is the sum of all alleles at all loci carried by all members of an interbreeding population. Population genetics tracks how allele frequencies in this pool change across generations. An individual carries only two alleles per locus (its genotype), which is a tiny sample of the pool, not the pool itself.

questions.q: In an Aa × Aa cross, what fraction of offspring with the dominant phenotype are homozygous?
o: That is AA as a fraction of all offspring.
That is the heterozygous fraction of all offspring.
Correct: dominant-phenotype offspring are 1 AA : 2 Aa, so 1/3 are AA.
That is the heterozygous fraction among dominant-phenotype offspring.
questions.x: Aa × Aa gives 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa. Restricting attention to dominant-phenotype offspring removes aa, leaving 1 AA : 2 Aa, so 1/3 are homozygous. This is conditional probability: the denominator becomes 3/4 instead of 1. Answering 1/4 forgets to remove the aa offspring from consideration.

questions.q: What is the probability that an offspring of Aa × Aa is homozygous (either AA or aa)?
o: Multiplies the two; 'either/or' for exclusive outcomes calls for adding.
Counts only one of the two homozygous classes.
Correct: mutually exclusive events add: 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.
That is the dominant phenotype fraction (AA + Aa).
questions.note: Or = add (exclusive events); and = multiply (independent events).
questions.x: An offspring can be AA (1/4) or aa (1/4), and these outcomes cannot both happen, so their probabilities add: 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2. Multiplication is for independent events that must both occur, such as two separate children. Using the product (1/16) confuses 'or' with 'and'.

questions.q: How many genetically different gametes can an AaBbCc individual produce if the three genes are unlinked?
o: Adds 2 + 2 + 2; combinations multiply.
Correct: 2 choices per gene, 2³ = 8.
Counts genes, not allele combinations.
That is 2⁴, for four heterozygous genes.
questions.note: Gamete types = 2ⁿ for n heterozygous unlinked genes.
questions.x: Each heterozygous, unlinked gene gives two choices of allele for a gamete, and choices for different genes are independent. The number of gamete types is therefore 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8. Adding the choices (6) undercounts, because each A choice can combine with every B and C choice.

questions.q: Mendel began his crosses with true-breeding plants. A true-breeding plant is one that is:
o: Homozygous for the trait, so selfing gives offspring identical for it
Correct: homozygotes make only one gamete type for that gene.
Heterozygous for the trait
Heterozygotes segregate and give variable offspring when selfed.
Always dominant for the trait
True-breeding recessive plants exist, such as white-flowered peas.
Produced by cross-pollination of two strains
Crossing strains creates hybrids, which are not true-breeding.
questions.x: A true-breeding plant is homozygous for the trait, so all its gametes carry the same allele and self-pollination yields offspring identical for that trait. Mendel needed such pure lines so the results of crossing them were interpretable. True breeding has nothing to do with dominance: a white-flowered (recessive) pea is also true-breeding.

questions.q: A testcross of AaBb × aabb gives 420 AB, 410 ab, 90 Ab and 80 aB offspring. What is the recombination frequency between the genes?
o: Counts only one recombinant class or halves the total.
That is the parental fraction.
Correct: recombinants (90 + 80) / 1000 = 0.17, so 17 map units.
Doubles the recombinant fraction; RF is recombinants over total.
questions.note: RF = recombinant offspring / total offspring; 1% = 1 cM.
questions.x: In a testcross, the dihybrid's gametes are read directly from offspring phenotypes. The two large classes (AB, ab) are parental and the two small ones (Ab, aB) are recombinant. Recombination frequency = recombinants / total = (90 + 80)/1000 = 17%, or 17 map units. Both recombinant classes must be included; using only one halves the answer.

questions.q: Two genes show a recombination frequency of 50% in testcrosses. This indicates that the genes:
o: Assort independently, as if unlinked
Correct: 50% recombinants is the maximum and matches independent assortment.
Are adjacent on the same chromosome
Adjacent genes would show near 0% recombination.
Are exactly 100 map units apart
Observed RF cannot exceed 50%, so it cannot measure 100 units.
Are linked in the repulsion phase
Phase changes which classes are recombinant, not the RF value.
questions.x: Recombination frequency maxes out at 50%, because even if a crossover always occurs between two loci, only half the chromatids involved are recombinant. An RF of 50% gives equal parental and recombinant classes, exactly as for genes on different chromosomes. Such genes may be far apart on one chromosome or on different chromosomes, but in either case they behave as unlinked.

questions.q: Map distances are A–B 12 cM, B–C 5 cM and A–C 7 cM. What is the gene order?
o: A–C–B
Correct: A–C (7) + C–B (5) = A–B (12), so C lies between A and B.
A–B–C
Then A–C would be 17, not 7.
B–A–C
Then B–C would be 19, not 5.
The order cannot be determined from these data
The additive distances fix the order uniquely.
questions.note: The two short distances add up to the longest one.
questions.x: To order three genes, find the pair separated by the largest distance; those genes are on the ends, and the third lies between them. Here A–B is 12, and A–C (7) plus C–B (5) equals 12, so C sits between A and B. Any other order would require one of the short distances to equal the sum of the other two.

questions.q: Genes are ordered A–B–C, with A–B 10 cM and B–C 20 cM. With no interference, what fraction of gametes is expected to be double crossovers?
o: Adds the two distances; independent events multiply.
Uses only the A–B interval.
Decimal error: 0.1 × 0.2 = 0.02, which is 2%.
questions.x: With no interference, crossovers in adjacent intervals are independent events, so the chance of both happening is the product of their frequencies. 0.10 × 0.20 = 0.02, or 2% of gametes. Adding the distances (30%) gives the distance from A to C, not the double-crossover frequency.

questions.q: In a three-point testcross, the parental classes are ABC and abc, and the two rarest classes are AbC and aBc. Which gene is in the middle?
o: A
A stays with C as in parentals in the rarest classes, so it is not in the middle.
C
C keeps its parental partner A in the rarest classes.
B
Correct: double crossovers swap only the middle gene relative to the parental arrangement.
It cannot be determined without map distances
The rarest (double crossover) class alone reveals the middle gene.
questions.note: Rarest class = double crossover; the swapped gene is in the middle.
questions.x: In a three-point testcross, the parental classes are the most common and the double-crossover classes are the rarest. A double crossover swaps only the middle gene relative to its flanking neighbors. Comparing ABC with AbC, only B has changed, so B is in the middle. No map distances are needed for this step.

questions.q: A dihybrid with genes linked in repulsion (Ab/aB) and little recombination is testcrossed to ab/ab. Which progeny classes are most frequent?
o: AB and ab (recombinant types)
Those are recombinant classes when the parent is in repulsion.
All four classes equally
That happens only with independent assortment.
AB only
A testcross reveals all gametes the dihybrid makes.
Ab and aB (parental types)
Correct: parental chromosomes are Ab and aB, so those classes dominate.
questions.x: The parental (non-recombinant) classes are always the allele combinations on the dihybrid's own chromosomes. In repulsion (Ab/aB), those are Ab and aB, so with little recombination they dominate the testcross. AB and ab arise only by crossing over here, so they are the rare recombinants. Which classes count as parental depends on phase.

questions.q: Genes A and B are 20 cM apart. Two dihybrids with coupling-phase chromosomes (AB/ab) are crossed. What fraction of offspring are ab/ab?
o: Correct: each parent makes ab gametes at (1 − 0.20)/2 = 0.40; 0.40 × 0.40 = 0.16.
That is 1/16, the value for unlinked genes.
Assumes complete linkage, so ab gametes would be 50%.
Squares a recombinant gamete frequency (0.10); ab is a parental gamete here.
questions.note: Linked genes: parental gametes = (1 − RF)/2 each; recombinant = RF/2 each.
questions.x: With 20% recombination, the dihybrid makes 80% parental gametes split equally (40% AB, 40% ab) and 20% recombinant gametes (10% Ab, 10% aB). An ab/ab offspring needs an ab gamete from each parent: 0.40 × 0.40 = 0.16. Treating ab as a recombinant gamete (0.10) would apply only to repulsion-phase parents.

questions.q: Why does recombination frequency between two linked genes increase with the physical distance between them?
o: Distant genes are on different chromatids
Linked genes lie on the same chromatid regardless of distance.
Crossing over occurs only near the centromere
Crossovers occur along the chromosome arms.
Distant genes replicate at different times
Replication timing does not set recombination frequency.
Crossovers occur roughly at random, so a longer stretch is more likely to contain one
Correct: more DNA between loci gives more chances for a crossover between them.
questions.x: Crossovers occur at roughly random positions along a chromosome, so the longer the stretch between two loci, the more likely at least one crossover falls between them. That is why recombination frequency can be used to build genetic maps. The relationship is only approximate, since crossover hotspots and interference make cM and physical distance differ locally.

questions.q: Recombination frequencies between distant genes underestimate their true map distance mainly because:
o: Distant genes are never separated by crossing over
Distant genes are separated most often.
Even numbers of crossovers between them restore parental combinations
Correct: double crossovers go undetected, so RF levels off near 50%.
Crossover frequency decreases toward chromosome ends
That is not the general reason RF saturates.
Recombinant gametes fail to fertilize eggs
Recombinant gametes are fully viable.
questions.note: Map from short intervals added together, not one long measurement.
questions.x: A single crossover between two loci produces a recombinant, but a second crossover in the same interval switches the alleles back to the parental arrangement. For distant genes, multiple crossovers are common and many go undetected, so the measured RF underestimates true distance and plateaus near 50%. Accurate maps add up distances measured over short intervals.

questions.q: The protein structure that holds paired homologous chromosomes closely together during prophase I is the:
o: Kinetochore
Kinetochores attach chromosomes to spindle microtubules.
Centrosome
Centrosomes organize spindle microtubules.
Nucleolus
The nucleolus is the site of rRNA synthesis.
Synaptonemal complex
Correct: it zips homologs together during synapsis, supporting crossing over.
questions.x: During prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair along their lengths (synapsis), held together by a protein scaffold called the synaptonemal complex. This close alignment supports crossing over between nonsister chromatids. Kinetochores and centrosomes work in spindle attachment and organization, not in holding homologs together.

questions.q: A tetrad (bivalent) seen in prophase I consists of:
o: Four homologous chromosomes
Diploid cells have only two homologs of each chromosome.
Two sister chromatids of one chromosome
That is one replicated chromosome, not a pair.
Two homologous chromosomes containing four chromatids
Correct: each replicated homolog has two sister chromatids.
Four nonhomologous chromosomes
Only homologs pair in synapsis.
questions.x: After S phase, each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids. When the two homologs pair during prophase I, the structure, called a bivalent or tetrad, contains two chromosomes and four chromatids. The name 'tetrad' refers to the four chromatids, not four chromosomes, which is the trap in choice A.

questions.q: The visible X-shaped point where nonsister chromatids have exchanged segments is called a:
o: Chiasma
Correct: chiasmata mark sites of crossing over.
Centromere
The centromere joins sister chromatids.
Telomere
Telomeres are protective chromosome ends.
Kinetochore
The kinetochore binds spindle microtubules.
questions.x: A chiasma is the visible cross-shaped connection where nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes have exchanged segments. Chiasmata also hold homologs together until anaphase I, helping them segregate correctly. The centromere instead joins the two sister chromatids of one chromosome and is the site where the kinetochore assembles.

questions.q: At the end of meiosis I in a human spermatocyte, each daughter cell contains:
o: 46 chromosomes, each with one chromatid
That describes a cell after mitosis, in G1.
23 chromosomes, each with one chromatid
That is the state after meiosis II.
23 chromosomes, each with two sister chromatids
Correct: homologs separated, but sister chromatids are still joined.
46 chromosomes, each with two chromatids
That is the cell before meiosis I divides.
questions.note: Meiosis I halves chromosome number; meiosis II splits chromatids.
questions.x: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, so the chromosome number halves from 46 to 23, but sister chromatids stay joined at their centromeres. Each daughter cell is therefore haploid with 23 double-chromatid chromosomes. Meiosis II then splits the sisters, producing cells with 23 single-chromatid chromosomes.

questions.q: Which event occurs in meiosis but not in mitosis?
o: Synapsis of homologous chromosomes
Correct: homolog pairing happens only in prophase I of meiosis.
Separation of sister chromatids
Occurs in mitotic anaphase and meiotic anaphase II.
DNA replication before division
S phase precedes both mitosis and meiosis.
Formation of a spindle
Both divisions use a spindle.
questions.x: Homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) only in prophase I of meiosis, which enables crossing over and the reductional separation of homologs. Mitosis never pairs homologs; each chromosome behaves independently. DNA replication, a spindle and sister chromatid separation all occur in both types of division.

questions.q: Independent assortment alone allows a human to produce about how many chromosomally distinct gametes?
o: 23², about 530
Squares the number of pairs instead of raising 2 to that power.
Counts chromosomes, not combinations.
2²³, about 8 million
Correct: each of 23 homolog pairs orients independently, 2 ways each.
2⁴⁶
Uses all 46 chromosomes; only the 23 pairs orient independently.
questions.x: At metaphase I, each homologous pair can orient with either the maternal or paternal homolog facing a given pole, and each pair orients independently. With 23 pairs and 2 orientations each, there are 2²³ ≈ 8.4 million possible chromosome combinations, before counting crossing over. Squaring 23 reverses base and exponent.

questions.q: If one pair of homologous chromosomes fails to separate in meiosis I, the four resulting gametes will be:
o: Two with an extra chromosome and two missing one
Correct: the whole pair goes to one cell, so both of its products are n+1.
Two normal, one n+1 and one n−1
That results from nondisjunction in meiosis II.
All normal
Nondisjunction always yields abnormal gametes from that cell.
All with an extra chromosome
Chromosomes are not created; one side must lack the pair.
questions.x: If homologs fail to separate in meiosis I, one cell gets both homologs and the other gets none. Meiosis II then splits sister chromatids normally, so the first cell yields two n+1 gametes and the second yields two n−1 gametes. Nondisjunction in meiosis II, by contrast, affects only one of the two cells, leaving two normal gametes.

questions.q: A child with trisomy 21 has two different maternal alleles at a marker very close to the chromosome 21 centromere. Nondisjunction most likely occurred in:
o: Maternal meiosis II
Sister chromatids would give two identical maternal alleles near the centromere.
Paternal meiosis I
The extra copies are maternal in origin.
Maternal meiosis I
Correct: two different maternal alleles means both homologs entered the egg.
Mitosis after fertilization
Post-zygotic error would duplicate one existing allele, not add a second different one.
questions.note: Different homologs = MI error; identical copies = MII error.
questions.x: Near the centromere, crossing over rarely separates the alleles, so markers there reflect which centromeres went into the egg. Two different maternal alleles mean both maternal homologs entered the egg, which happens when homologs fail to separate in meiosis I. In a meiosis II error, the egg would get two sister chromatids carrying identical alleles near the centromere.

questions.q: A normal egg is fertilized by sperm produced after nondisjunction of the sex chromosomes in paternal meiosis I. What karyotypes can result?
o: 47,XYY or 45,X
YY sperm come from nondisjunction in meiosis II.
47,XXY or 45,X
Correct: MI nondisjunction gives XY or no-sex-chromosome sperm.
47,XXX or 45,X
XX sperm come from meiosis II nondisjunction.
47,XXY only
The other daughter cell lacks a sex chromosome, giving 45,X.
questions.x: In the father, meiosis I normally separates X from Y. If they fail to separate, one secondary spermatocyte gets both X and Y and the other gets neither, so sperm are XY or carry no sex chromosome. Fertilizing a normal X egg gives 47,XXY or 45,X. XX or YY sperm arise only from meiosis II nondisjunction, after X and Y have already separated.

questions.q: The risk of trisomy in offspring rises sharply with maternal age mainly because:
o: Older women make more oocytes per cycle
Oocyte number declines with age.
Spermatogenesis slows in the partners of older women
Paternal factors are not the main driver.
Mitochondrial mutations accumulate in older eggs
mtDNA defects do not cause chromosome trisomy.
Oocytes remain arrested in prophase I for decades and homolog cohesion weakens
Correct: aging oocytes are prone to nondisjunction when meiosis resumes.
questions.x: Human oocytes enter meiosis I before birth and stay arrested in prophase I until ovulation, which can be 40 or more years later. Over that time the cohesin that holds homologs and sister chromatids together deteriorates, making nondisjunction more likely when meiosis resumes. Oocyte number declines with age, and mitochondrial changes do not produce extra whole chromosomes.

questions.q: Crossing over during meiosis exchanges segments between:
o: Sister chromatids of one chromosome
Sister exchange swaps identical DNA, producing no new combinations.
Nonhomologous chromosomes
That would be a translocation, not normal crossing over.
Nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
Correct: this creates new allele combinations on each chromatid.
Mitochondrial and nuclear chromosomes
mtDNA does not undergo meiotic crossing over.
questions.x: Crossing over occurs between nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes during prophase I, creating chromatids with new combinations of maternal and paternal alleles. Exchange between sister chromatids swaps identical sequences and creates no new combinations. Exchange between nonhomologous chromosomes is an abnormal rearrangement, a translocation.

questions.q: Which process does NOT generate genetic differences among offspring of the same two parents?
o: Separation of sister chromatids in mitosis
Correct: mitosis produces genetically identical daughter cells.
Crossing over in prophase I
Recombination creates new allele combinations.
Independent assortment in metaphase I
Random homolog orientation mixes maternal and paternal chromosomes.
Random fertilization
Any sperm can fuse with any egg, multiplying combinations.
questions.x: Genetic variety among siblings comes from meiosis and fertilization: crossing over reshuffles alleles along chromosomes, independent assortment mixes whole chromosomes, and random fertilization combines any sperm with any egg. Mitosis copies the genome and divides it equally, giving genetically identical daughter cells, so it adds no variation between offspring.

questions.q: A phenotypically normal man with a balanced reciprocal translocation has a partner with several miscarriages. The most likely reason is that:
o: His somatic cells are missing genes
A balanced translocation retains all genetic material.
His meiosis often produces gametes with unbalanced chromosome segments
Correct: segregation of translocated chromosomes can give gametes with duplications and deletions.
Translocations block crossing over entirely
Pairing is altered, but the key issue is unbalanced gametes.
His sperm carry extra mitochondria
Translocations do not affect mitochondrial number.
questions.x: A balanced translocation carrier has all the genetic material, just rearranged, so he is healthy. At meiosis the translocated and normal chromosomes pair in an unusual configuration, and several segregation patterns give gametes with extra copies of some segments and missing copies of others. Embryos from these unbalanced gametes often miscarry.

questions.q: A healthy person has 45 chromosomes because the long arms of chromosomes 14 and 21 are fused into one chromosome. This is a:
o: Monosomy 21
Chromosome 21's long arm is still present, so no essential material is lost.
Paracentric inversion
An inversion flips a segment within one chromosome.
Reciprocal translocation
A reciprocal swap keeps 46 chromosomes.
Robertsonian translocation
Correct: two acrocentric chromosomes fuse at their centromeres.
questions.x: A Robertsonian translocation fuses the long arms of two acrocentric chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21 or 22) at the centromere, and the tiny short arms, which hold repeated rRNA genes, are lost without harm. The carrier has 45 chromosomes but a balanced genome. Carriers can produce gametes with extra 21q material, a cause of familial Down syndrome.

questions.q: A codon in the coding strand changes from GAA to GAG; both encode glutamate. This is a:
o: Missense mutation
Missense changes the amino acid.
Nonsense mutation
Nonsense creates a stop codon.
Silent mutation
Correct: the amino acid is unchanged because of code degeneracy.
Frameshift mutation
A substitution does not shift the reading frame.
questions.x: The genetic code is degenerate: most amino acids are encoded by more than one codon, often differing at the third position. GAA and GAG both encode glutamate, so this base substitution does not change the protein and is a silent mutation. A missense mutation would change the amino acid, and a nonsense mutation would create a stop codon.

questions.q: An mRNA codon changes from UAC (tyrosine) to UAA. This is a:
o: Nonsense mutation
Correct: UAA is a stop codon, truncating the protein.
Silent mutation
The codon no longer encodes tyrosine.
Missense mutation
No amino acid replaces tyrosine; translation stops.
Frameshift mutation
A single substitution keeps the frame.
questions.x: UAA is one of the three stop codons (along with UAG and UGA). Changing a sense codon into a stop codon is a nonsense mutation, which causes translation to end early and usually yields a truncated, nonfunctional protein. It is not missense, because no new amino acid is inserted at that position.

questions.q: Which mutation near the start of a coding sequence is most likely to destroy protein function?
o: Insertion of three nucleotides
Adds one amino acid while keeping the frame.
A silent substitution
No amino acid changes.
Insertion of one nucleotide
Correct: a frameshift changes every downstream codon and often creates an early stop.
A conservative missense substitution
Swapping a similar amino acid often preserves function.
questions.x: Inserting a single nucleotide shifts the reading frame, so every codon downstream is read differently, and a premature stop codon usually appears soon after. Near the start of a gene, nearly the whole protein is lost. Inserting three nucleotides adds one amino acid without shifting the frame, which is often tolerated.

questions.q: Deletion of three consecutive nucleotides within an exon usually results in a protein that:
o: Is entirely different after the deletion
That results from deletions that are not multiples of three.
Is unchanged
A codon's worth of sequence is gone.
Is always truncated by a stop codon
A stop is possible only if the junction happens to form one.
Lacks one amino acid but is otherwise in frame
Correct: 3 nt = one codon, so the reading frame is preserved.
questions.x: Because codons are three nucleotides long, deleting exactly three nucleotides removes one codon's worth of sequence and keeps the downstream reading frame intact. The protein is missing one amino acid (sometimes with one adjacent amino acid altered), but the rest is normal. Deletions not divisible by three cause frameshifts.

questions.q: Which missense substitution is least likely to affect a protein's function?
o: Active-site histidine → alanine
Removes a catalytic side chain.
Cysteine → serine at a disulfide bond
Serine cannot form the disulfide bridge.
Glycine → proline in the middle of an α-helix
Proline is rigid and disrupts helices.
Leucine → isoleucine on a surface loop
Correct: both are similar nonpolar residues, in a non-critical location.
questions.x: A missense change is least harmful when it swaps chemically similar amino acids at a position that is not structurally or catalytically critical. Leucine and isoleucine are both bulky nonpolar residues, and a surface loop is usually tolerant of change. The other choices remove a catalytic residue, break a disulfide bond, or put a helix-breaking proline inside a helix.

questions.q: A chromosome segment breaks out, flips 180°, and reinserts in the same place. This is a(n):
o: Translocation
A translocation moves material to a nonhomologous chromosome.
Inversion
Correct: the segment's orientation is reversed.
Duplication
A duplication repeats a segment.
Deletion
No material is lost here.
questions.x: An inversion occurs when a chromosome segment breaks out, flips 180°, and reinserts in the same location, so the gene order in that segment is reversed. No genetic material is gained or lost, and carriers are often healthy, though crossing over within the inversion can yield unbalanced gametes. A translocation moves material to a different, nonhomologous chromosome.

questions.q: When homologous chromosomes misalign and cross over unequally, the products are:
o: Two chromatids with inversions
Unequal exchange changes copy number, not orientation.
Two normal recombinant chromatids
Misalignment yields unequal segment lengths.
One chromatid with a duplication and one with a deletion
Correct: one partner gains what the other loses.
A reciprocal translocation
Exchange is between homologs, not nonhomologous chromosomes.
questions.note: Unequal crossing over drives gene family expansion.
questions.x: When homologs pair out of register, often because of repeated sequences, a crossover between them gives unequal products: one chromatid gains an extra copy of a segment (duplication) while the other loses it (deletion). This is a major way gene families, like the globin genes, expand. No orientation changes, so it does not create inversions.

questions.q: Transposable elements contribute to genetic diversity mainly by:
o: Replacing the genome during each meiosis
Transposition is occasional and local.
Increasing the rate of independent assortment
Assortment depends on chromosome number, not transposons.
Moving within the genome and disrupting or altering genes they insert near
Correct: insertions create new mutations and regulatory changes.
Transferring mitochondria between cells
Transposons move DNA within a genome.
questions.x: Transposable elements are DNA sequences that can move or copy themselves to new locations in the genome. Insertion into a gene can disrupt it, and insertion near a gene can alter its regulation; transposons also promote rearrangements between copies. They are a source of new mutations, not a mechanism of independent assortment or organelle transfer.

questions.q: In the Ames test, a compound greatly increases the number of colonies of histidine-requiring bacteria that grow on histidine-free medium. This suggests the compound is:
o: A mutagen and a potential carcinogen
Correct: more revertants means more mutations restoring histidine synthesis.
A source of histidine
Revertant colonies reflect new mutations, not a supplied nutrient.
An antibiotic
An antibiotic would reduce colony growth.
Harmless, because bacteria thrived
Growth here reflects mutation, not health.
questions.x: The Ames test uses Salmonella strains that cannot make histidine because of a mutation. Only bacteria that acquire a new, reversing mutation can grow on histidine-free medium. A compound that greatly increases revertant colonies is causing mutations, and because most carcinogens are mutagens, it is a likely carcinogen. Growth here is a readout of mutation, not a sign of safety.

questions.q: A compound causes reversion in the Ames test only when rat liver extract is added; extract alone causes no reversion. The best interpretation is:
o: Liver extract itself is the mutagen
Extract alone caused no reversion, so it is not the mutagen.
The compound is mutagenic only to mammals
The bacteria do mutate once the compound is activated.
Liver enzymes convert it into a mutagenic metabolite
Correct: metabolic activation makes some procarcinogens mutagenic.
Liver enzymes repair the bacterial DNA
Repair would reduce, not increase, revertants.
questions.x: Many compounds are not mutagenic themselves but are converted by liver enzymes such as cytochrome P450s into reactive, DNA-damaging metabolites. Adding rat liver extract to the Ames test mimics this metabolic activation. Since the extract alone causes no reversion, the extract is not the mutagen; the activated compound is.

questions.q: The most common DNA lesion caused by ultraviolet light is:
o: Deamination of cytosine to uracil
That is mostly spontaneous or chemical, not the hallmark of UV.
Covalently linked adjacent pyrimidines (such as thymine dimers)
Correct: UV joins neighboring pyrimidines, distorting the helix.
Loss of purine bases
Depurination is mainly spontaneous hydrolysis.
Methylation of guanine
That is caused by alkylating agents.
questions.x: UV light causes covalent bonds to form between adjacent pyrimidines on the same strand, most often thymine dimers. These dimers distort the helix and block replication and transcription, and they are repaired by nucleotide excision repair; defects in this repair cause xeroderma pigmentosum. Cytosine deamination and depurination happen mostly spontaneously, not specifically from UV.

questions.q: Most inborn errors of metabolism caused by enzyme loss are inherited as recessive traits because:
o: Enzyme genes are found only on the X chromosome
Most metabolic enzyme genes are autosomal.
One functional allele usually makes enough enzyme for normal metabolism
Correct: heterozygotes have about half activity, which is usually sufficient.
Mutant enzymes are always toxic
Toxic gain of function would act dominantly.
Recessive alleles mutate more often
Mutation rate does not determine dominance.
questions.x: Most enzymes are present in excess, so a heterozygote producing about half the normal amount usually still has enough activity for normal metabolism. Disease appears only when both alleles are nonfunctional, making the trait recessive. A mutant protein that is toxic or overactive would act dominantly, which is the opposite of what is seen in most enzyme deficiencies.

questions.q: A mutation makes a growth-factor receptor signal constantly even without its ligand. Such a mutation is most likely to act as:
o: Dominant, since the overactive protein signals even with a normal allele present
Correct: gain-of-function alleles typically act dominantly.
Recessive, since the normal allele compensates
A normal allele cannot switch off a constitutively active receptor.
Silent, since the protein still exists
Its activity is changed.
X-linked, since growth genes are on X
Mode of action, not chromosome location, is in question.
questions.x: A gain-of-function mutation gives a protein new or excessive activity. A receptor that signals without ligand keeps sending signals no matter what the normal allele does, so one mutant copy is enough to cause the effect, making it dominant. This is how many proto-oncogenes become oncogenes. A normal allele can compensate only for a loss of function.

questions.q: A mutant subunit of a dimeric protein binds normal subunits and blocks their function, so heterozygotes are severely affected. This is a:
o: Silent mutation
Function is clearly altered.
Dominant-negative mutation
Correct: the mutant product interferes with the normal product.
Loss-of-function recessive mutation
Heterozygotes would be near normal if the mutant were just inactive.
Gain-of-function mutation
The protein loses function; it gains no new activity.
questions.x: In a dominant-negative mutation, the mutant protein is not just inactive; it binds to and inhibits the normal product, often within a multi-subunit complex. Heterozygotes therefore lose much more than half of the protein's function and are strongly affected. A simple loss-of-function allele would leave the normal half working, so it would usually be recessive.

questions.q: A heterozygote makes equal amounts of normal and mutant subunits of a tetrameric protein; any tetramer with one or more mutant subunits is inactive. What fraction of tetramers is active?
o: Assumes subunits act alone, not in tetramers.
Uses (1/2)², as for a dimer.
Uses (1/2)³; there are four subunits.
Correct: all four must be normal: (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.
questions.note: Dominant negatives hit multimeric proteins hardest.
questions.x: Subunits assemble randomly, and each is normal with probability 1/2. A tetramer is active only if all four subunits are normal: (1/2)⁴ = 1/16, so a heterozygote keeps just about 6% activity. This is why dominant-negative mutations are especially damaging for proteins built from many subunits; for a dimer, the active fraction would be 1/4.

questions.q: A mutation arises in a skin cell of an adult. Which statement is correct?
o: It cannot be passed to the person's offspring
Correct: only germline mutations are inherited.
It will be present in all of the person's cells
Only descendants of that one skin cell carry it.
It will appear in half of the person's children
Somatic mutations are not in gametes.
It must be harmless
Somatic mutations can cause cancer.
questions.x: Somatic mutations arise in body cells and are passed only to that cell's descendants by mitosis. Because gametes come from the germline, a mutation in a skin cell cannot be inherited by children. Somatic mutations can still be harmful, since an accumulation of them in one cell lineage can cause cancer.

questions.q: A cytosine in a C–G base pair is deaminated to uracil and not repaired. After two rounds of replication, one descendant DNA molecule will carry what at that site?
o: A G–C pair, no change
The original G strand gives normal products, but the U strand does not.
A T–A pair, a C→T transition
Correct: U pairs with A, and A then pairs with T.
A G–T mismatch
Mismatches are resolved by replication into full base pairs.
An A–T transversion from purine to pyrimidine
C→T is pyrimidine to pyrimidine, a transition.
questions.x: Uracil pairs with adenine. In the first replication, the U strand templates an A, giving a U–A pair; in the next round, that A templates a T, giving a T–A pair. The net effect is C–G → T–A, a transition (pyrimidine to pyrimidine). This is why cells remove uracil from DNA with uracil-DNA glycosylase before replication.

questions.q: In a population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, 4% of individuals show a recessive phenotype. What is the frequency of the dominant allele?
o: That is the dominant phenotype frequency (1 − q²), not an allele frequency.
That is q, the recessive allele frequency.
That is p², the homozygous dominant genotype frequency.
Correct: q² = 0.04, so q = 0.2 and p = 1 − 0.2 = 0.8.
questions.note: Always start from q² = recessive phenotype frequency.
questions.x: In Hardy–Weinberg problems, the recessive phenotype frequency equals q², the only class whose genotype is known from phenotype. Here q² = 0.04, so q = 0.2 and p = 1 − q = 0.8. The tempting 0.96 is the frequency of people showing the dominant phenotype (p² + 2pq), not the frequency of the dominant allele.

questions.q: In a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the frequency of allele A is 0.7. What fraction of the population is AA?
o: That is the allele frequency, not the genotype frequency.
That is 2pq, the heterozygote frequency.
Correct: p² = 0.7² = 0.49.
That is q², the aa frequency.
questions.x: At equilibrium, genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q². With p = 0.7 and q = 0.3, AA = 0.7² = 0.49, Aa = 2(0.7)(0.3) = 0.42 and aa = 0.09, which sum to 1. Answering 0.7 confuses the frequency of an allele with the frequency of a genotype that needs two copies of it.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a condition for Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium?
o: No migration into or out of the population
Gene flow would change allele frequencies.
Random mating
Nonrandom mating changes genotype frequencies.
The two alleles must have equal frequencies
Correct: equilibrium can hold at any allele frequencies.
No natural selection
Selection changes allele frequencies.
questions.note: HW: large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration, no selection.
questions.x: Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium requires a large population, random mating, and no mutation, migration or selection. Under these conditions allele and genotype frequencies stay constant at any starting values; p = 0.9 is just as stable as p = 0.5. Each listed force, if present, would change allele or genotype frequencies.

questions.q: A population sample contains 50 AA, 20 Aa and 30 aa individuals. What is the frequency of allele A?
o: Counts AA individuals as a fraction of people, not alleles.
Counts AA plus Aa individuals as if each contributed one A.
That would be the expected AA frequency if p were 0.6.
questions.note: Count alleles: homozygotes give 2, heterozygotes 1.
questions.x: Allele frequency is calculated by counting alleles, not individuals. 100 people carry 200 alleles; each AA contributes two A alleles and each Aa contributes one, so A = (2 × 50 + 20)/200 = 120/200 = 0.6. Counting each person who carries A as one (0.7) or counting only AA individuals (0.5) mixes up people and alleles.

questions.q: A sample of 100 individuals has 50 AA, 20 Aa and 30 aa (p = 0.6). Compared with Hardy–Weinberg expectations, this population has:
o: More heterozygotes than expected
Observed 20 is well below the expected 48.
Far fewer heterozygotes than expected
Correct: expected Aa = 2(0.6)(0.4)(100) = 48, but only 20 are observed.
Genotype frequencies matching expectations
Expected AA 36, Aa 48, aa 16 differ greatly from what was observed.
Fewer AA homozygotes than expected
Observed AA (50) exceeds the expected 36.
questions.note: A heterozygote deficit suggests inbreeding, assortative mating or population structure.
questions.x: With p = 0.6 and q = 0.4, Hardy–Weinberg predicts 36 AA, 48 Aa and 16 aa per 100. The sample has 50 AA, 20 Aa and 30 aa: too many homozygotes and far too few heterozygotes. A heterozygote deficit is the signature of nonrandom mating such as inbreeding, or of hidden population subdivision.

questions.q: An X-linked recessive trait affects 1 in 10 males in a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. What fraction of females is expected to be affected?
o: That is the male frequency, equal to q.
Correct: male frequency gives q = 0.1, and affected females need two copies: q² = 0.01.
That is 2pq, the carrier frequency in females.
Halving the male frequency has no genetic basis.
questions.note: For X-linked traits, frequency in males = q.
questions.x: Males have one X, so the fraction of affected males equals the allele frequency: q = 0.1. Females need two copies, so their affected frequency is q² = 0.01, or 1%. This is why X-linked recessive traits are much more common in males; 18% (2pq) is the expected fraction of carrier females.

questions.q: In a population at equilibrium, ABO allele frequencies are Iᴬ = 0.3, Iᴮ = 0.1 and i = 0.6. What fraction of people have type A blood?
o: Counts only IᴬIᴬ; Iᴬi people are type A too.
Counts only Iᴬi (or confuses with type O, i² = 0.36).
That is the allele frequency, not the phenotype frequency.
questions.x: Type A blood comes from two genotypes, IᴬIᴬ and Iᴬi, because Iᴬ is dominant to i. Their frequencies are 0.3² = 0.09 and 2(0.3)(0.6) = 0.36, totaling 0.45. With multiple alleles, Hardy–Weinberg still applies: each homozygote is the allele frequency squared and each heterozygote is twice the product of the two allele frequencies.

questions.q: A population consists of 50% AA and 50% aa individuals with no heterozygotes. If it then mates randomly with no other evolutionary forces, what are the genotype frequencies in the next generation?
o: Random mating between AA and aa produces heterozygotes.
Correct: p = q = 0.5, and one round of random mating gives p², 2pq, q².
0 AA, 1.00 Aa, 0 aa
That would require every mating to be AA × aa.
HW frequencies follow p², 2pq, q², not equal thirds.
questions.note: One generation of random mating restores HW genotype proportions.
questions.x: The population's allele frequencies are p = q = 0.5, even though it has no heterozygotes. Random mating combines gametes at random, so one generation produces p² = 0.25 AA, 2pq = 0.50 Aa and q² = 0.25 aa. Hardy–Weinberg genotype proportions are restored after a single round of random mating, regardless of the starting genotype mix.

questions.q: A small group of settlers founds an island population, and their descendants have a high frequency of an allele rare on the mainland. This is best explained by:
o: Gene flow
Gene flow would make island and mainland frequencies more similar.
Directional selection
Nothing indicates the allele is favored.
A high mutation rate
Mutation is too slow to explain a sudden difference.
The founder effect
Correct: the founders' allele frequencies happened to differ from the source population.
questions.x: When a small group starts a new population, its allele frequencies are a random sample of the source population and can differ by chance. That founder effect is a form of genetic drift, and rare alleles can become common in the descendants. Gene flow would act in the opposite direction, making island and mainland populations more similar.

questions.q: Hunting reduces a species to a few dozen individuals; it later recovers to thousands but shows very low heterozygosity. This mainly reflects:
o: Stabilizing selection
Selection on one trait would not reduce variation across the genome.
Gene flow from other populations
Gene flow would add variation.
A population bottleneck
Correct: drift during the small-population phase removed much of the variation.
Increased mutation after recovery
Mutation adds variation, slowly.
questions.x: In a bottleneck, a population shrinks drastically, and the few survivors carry only a subset of the original alleles; drift in the small population then removes more. Even after numbers recover, the lost variation stays low because new mutations accumulate slowly. Northern elephant seals are a classic example. Selection on one trait would not reduce diversity across the whole genome.

questions.q: Regular migration of individuals between two populations tends to:
o: Increase genetic differences between them
That is the effect of isolation, not migration.
Make their allele frequencies more similar
Correct: gene flow homogenizes populations.
Cause immediate speciation
Gene flow works against speciation.
Stop all evolution in both populations
Gene flow is itself an evolutionary force.
questions.x: Gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations through migration and breeding. Regular exchange mixes the gene pools, so allele frequencies converge and the populations become genetically similar. This works against divergence and speciation; geographic isolation, which blocks gene flow, is what allows populations to drift apart.

questions.q: Inbreeding increases the incidence of recessive genetic disorders mainly because it:
o: Raises the mutation rate
Inbreeding does not create new mutations.
Increases homozygosity, exposing recessive alleles
Correct: relatives share alleles, so offspring are more often homozygous.
Converts dominant alleles into recessive ones
Alleles are not converted by mating patterns.
Directly increases the recessive allele frequency
Inbreeding by itself changes genotype, not allele, frequencies.
questions.x: Relatives share alleles inherited from common ancestors, so their offspring are more likely to receive two identical copies of an allele. That raises the frequency of homozygotes, including homozygotes for rare harmful recessive alleles that would otherwise stay hidden in carriers. Inbreeding changes genotype frequencies; on its own it does not change allele frequencies.

questions.q: Crossing two inbred lines of corn produces F1 hybrids more vigorous than either parent. This is mainly because the hybrids:
o: Have higher mutation rates
Mutation is not the source of hybrid vigor.
Are polyploid
A cross between diploid lines gives diploid offspring.
Receive mitochondria from both parents
Mitochondria come from the maternal parent.
Are heterozygous at many loci, masking each line's harmful recessive alleles
Correct: outbreeding restores heterozygosity (hybrid vigor).
questions.x: Inbred lines are homozygous at many loci, including some harmful recessive alleles, which lowers their vigor. Crossing two different inbred lines makes F1 offspring heterozygous at many loci, so each line's harmful recessives are masked by the other's functional alleles. This is hybrid vigor (heterosis), the reverse of inbreeding depression.

questions.q: Which evolutionary process is the ultimate source of new alleles in a population?
o: Natural selection
Selection sorts existing variation.
Genetic drift
Drift changes frequencies of existing alleles.
Independent assortment
Assortment reshuffles existing alleles.
Mutation
Correct: only mutation creates new alleles; other forces shuffle or sort them.
questions.x: Mutation is the only process that creates genuinely new alleles by changing DNA sequence. Natural selection and genetic drift change the frequencies of alleles already present, and independent assortment and crossing over reshuffle existing alleles into new combinations. Without mutation, there would eventually be no new variation for evolution to act on.

questions.q: In a population with strong positive assortative mating for a trait controlled by one gene, what happens over generations without other forces?
o: Allele frequencies shift toward the dominant allele
Mating pattern alone does not change allele frequencies.
Homozygotes increase and heterozygotes decrease, with allele frequencies unchanged
Correct: like-with-like mating shifts genotypes, not allele counts.
Heterozygotes increase
Similar mates produce more homozygotes.
Genotype frequencies remain at Hardy–Weinberg values
Nonrandom mating violates HW.
questions.x: In positive assortative mating, individuals choose mates with the same phenotype, so like genotypes tend to mate together. This raises the proportion of homozygotes and reduces heterozygotes each generation. Because no alleles are added or removed, allele frequencies stay the same; only genotype frequencies depart from Hardy–Weinberg proportions.

questions.q: Even when affected homozygotes die before reproducing, a rare recessive lethal allele is eliminated very slowly from a large population because:
o: Recessive alleles cannot be affected by selection
Selection does act on aa individuals.
Most copies are carried by heterozygotes, which are not selected against
Correct: when q is small, nearly all copies hide in carriers.
Lethal alleles mutate back to normal
Back mutation is far too rare to matter.
Heterozygotes always have higher fitness
Heterozygote advantage is not required for this pattern.
questions.x: When a recessive allele is rare, almost all copies are in heterozygotes: with q = 0.01, carriers (≈2q) outnumber affected homozygotes (q²) about 200 to 1. Selection acts only on the affected aa individuals, so each generation removes only a small fraction of the allele's copies. The allele declines, but very slowly.

questions.q: An autosomal recessive disease affects 1 in 10,000 people in a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium. About what fraction of people are carriers?
o: That is q, the allele frequency.
Doubles the disease frequency instead of q.
That is q², the affected frequency.
questions.note: For rare alleles, carriers ≈ 2q, far more common than affected people.
questions.x: Start with q² = 1/10,000, so q = 0.01 and p ≈ 0.99. The carrier frequency is 2pq ≈ 2(0.99)(0.01) ≈ 0.02, or about 1 in 50. Carriers are about 200 times more common than affected people, which is why rare recessive alleles persist. The answer 1/100 is the allele frequency itself, not a genotype frequency.

questions.q: Darwinian fitness of an individual is best measured by:
o: Its physical strength
Strength matters only if it raises reproduction.
Its lifespan
Long life without reproduction gives zero fitness.
Its body size
Size is a trait, not a measure of fitness.
Its number of surviving, fertile offspring relative to others
Correct: fitness is reproductive success.
questions.x: In evolutionary terms, fitness is reproductive success: the number of offspring an individual leaves that survive and reproduce, relative to other individuals. Traits like strength, size or longevity increase fitness only if they translate into more surviving offspring. An individual that lives long but never reproduces has zero fitness.

questions.q: A pedigree shows a trait in every generation, about equal numbers of affected males and females, and an affected father with an affected son. The most likely mode of inheritance is:
o: X-linked dominant
Fathers cannot pass an X-linked trait to sons.
Autosomal dominant
Correct: vertical transmission, both sexes, and male-to-male transmission fit.
Autosomal recessive
Recessive traits usually skip generations.
Mitochondrial
Fathers do not transmit mitochondrial traits.
questions.x: Autosomal dominant traits appear in every generation, affect males and females about equally, and can pass from father to son. Male-to-male transmission is the key clue: a father gives his son a Y, not an X, so X-linked inheritance is ruled out, and fathers do not pass mitochondria. Recessive traits typically skip generations.

questions.q: Two unaffected parents have a daughter affected by a rare disorder. Assuming full penetrance, the most likely mode of inheritance is:
o: X-linked recessive
An affected daughter would need an affected father.
Autosomal recessive
Correct: both parents are carriers and the daughter received two recessive alleles.
Autosomal dominant
An affected child would need an affected parent.
Y-linked
Daughters do not receive a Y chromosome.
questions.x: Unaffected parents with an affected child point to recessive inheritance, with both parents carriers. An affected daughter rules out X-linked recessive inheritance, which would require her father to be affected because she gets his only X. Dominant inheritance with full penetrance would require an affected parent. Autosomal recessive is the only fit.

questions.q: A trait skips generations, affects almost only males, and is often seen in sons of unaffected daughters of affected men. The most likely mode of inheritance is:
o: Autosomal recessive
Males and females would be equally affected.
Y-linked
Y-linked traits pass father to son directly and never via daughters.
X-linked recessive
Correct: affected men pass the allele to carrier daughters, who pass it to sons.
X-linked dominant
Daughters of affected men would all be affected.
questions.x: In X-linked recessive inheritance, affected men pass their mutant X to all daughters, who are usually unaffected carriers, and each carrier daughter passes it to half her sons. The trait therefore skips a generation and shows up mostly in males, through their mothers. Y-linked traits go straight from father to son and never pass through daughters.

questions.q: Which pedigree observation rules out X-linked recessive inheritance (with full penetrance)?
o: Unaffected parents have an affected son
Fits a carrier mother.
More males than females are affected
This is typical of X-linked recessive traits.
An affected woman has an unaffected son
Correct: an affected mother has two mutant X's, so every son would be affected.
An affected man has only unaffected children
His daughters are carriers and sons get his Y, so this fits.
questions.x: An affected woman with an X-linked recessive trait must have two mutant X chromosomes, so every son receives a mutant X from her and must be affected. An unaffected son of an affected mother is therefore incompatible with this mode. Unaffected parents having an affected son and an excess of affected males are both typical of X-linked recessive traits.

questions.q: Which pedigree observation rules out X-linked dominant inheritance (with full penetrance)?
o: An affected woman has an unaffected son
A heterozygous mother passes the normal X half the time.
Affected women outnumber affected men
This is typical of X-linked dominant traits.
An affected man has an unaffected daughter
Correct: every daughter receives her father's X.
An affected man has unaffected sons
Sons receive his Y, so this fits.
questions.x: A father passes his only X to every daughter. In X-linked dominant inheritance, that X carries the dominant allele, so all daughters of an affected man must be affected. An unaffected daughter of an affected father rules this mode out. An affected woman can have unaffected sons, because she is usually heterozygous and passes her normal X half the time.

questions.q: A trait is passed from affected fathers to all of their sons and never to daughters. The most likely mode of inheritance is:
o: Y-linked
Correct: only sons receive the father's Y chromosome.
X-linked recessive
Fathers give their X to daughters, not sons.
Mitochondrial
Mitochondrial traits pass through mothers.
Autosomal dominant
Daughters would be affected about half the time.
questions.x: The Y chromosome passes only from father to son, so a Y-linked trait goes from an affected father to all of his sons and never to daughters. X-linked traits cannot pass from father to son, mitochondrial traits come from mothers, and autosomal dominant traits would affect about half of both sons and daughters.

questions.q: A man heterozygous for a fully penetrant autosomal dominant disorder has children with an unaffected woman. What is the probability that their first two children are both unaffected?
o: That is the probability for one child.
Uses the recessive 3/4 unaffected figure, which does not apply here.
Correct: each child is unaffected with probability 1/2; (1/2)² = 1/4.
Uses (1/4)², as if each child had a 1/4 chance.
questions.x: A heterozygous affected parent (Aa) mated with aa passes the dominant allele half the time, so each child has a 1/2 chance of being unaffected. Births are independent, so both children unaffected is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. The 3/4 figure belongs to two carriers of a recessive trait, not to a dominant cross with one heterozygous parent.

questions.q: An unaffected man whose sister has an autosomal recessive disease (parents unaffected) has a child with an unaffected woman whose carrier risk is 1/50. What is the probability the child is affected?
o: Assumes the man is definitely a carrier.
Uses 1/2 instead of 1/4 for two carriers having an affected child.
Uses 1/3 as his carrier probability; it is 2/3.
questions.x: Multiply three independent probabilities. The man has an affected sister and unaffected parents, so his parents are carriers; being unaffected, he is a carrier with probability 2/3. The woman is a carrier with probability 1/50. If both are carriers, a child is affected with probability 1/4. Overall 2/3 × 1/50 × 1/4 = 1/300.

questions.q: A rare disorder appears repeatedly in children of first-cousin marriages but not in their parents. The most likely mode of inheritance is:
o: Autosomal dominant
A parent would usually be affected.
Autosomal recessive
Correct: consanguinity raises the chance both parents carry the same rare recessive allele.
Y-linked
Affected fathers would be expected.
X-linked dominant
An affected parent would be expected.
questions.x: First cousins share a set of grandparents, so they are more likely than unrelated people to carry the same rare recessive allele inherited from a common ancestor. Their children then have a raised chance of being homozygous. A rare disorder that shows up in children of consanguineous unions but not in their parents points to autosomal recessive inheritance.

questions.q: In a pedigree of an autosomal dominant disorder, an unaffected man has an affected father and an affected daughter whose mother has no family history. The best explanation is:
o: Variable expressivity in the daughter
Expressivity concerns severity, not the father's lack of any phenotype.
X-linked inheritance
He got the allele from his father, and fathers never pass X-linked alleles to sons.
Genetic anticipation
Anticipation concerns increasing severity, not a skipped carrier.
Incomplete penetrance in the man
Correct: he carries the allele but does not express it.
questions.x: The man must carry the dominant allele: he got it from his affected father and passed it to his affected daughter, whose mother has no history. Since he shows no signs, the allele is not penetrant in him. That is incomplete penetrance. Variable expressivity would apply only if he showed some degree of the phenotype, however mild.

questions.q: Two unaffected parents with no family history have two children with the same fully penetrant autosomal dominant disorder. The best explanation is:
o: Two independent new mutations
Possible but extremely unlikely in the same gene twice.
Both parents are carriers of a recessive allele
The disorder is dominant with full penetrance.
Incomplete penetrance in both children
The children are affected; penetrance is full.
Germline mosaicism in one parent
Correct: a mutation in part of one parent's germline can reach several children.
questions.x: Germline mosaicism occurs when a mutation arises in a parent's germ-cell lineage during development, so some of that parent's gametes carry it while their body cells do not. The parent is unaffected yet can pass the dominant allele to more than one child. Two separate new mutations in the same gene in one family would be extremely improbable.

questions.q: A dominant neurological disorder appears earlier and more severely in each successive generation of a family. This pattern is most often caused by:
o: Expansion of a trinucleotide repeat
Correct: repeats lengthen when transmitted, producing anticipation.
A silent point mutation
Silent mutations do not cause progressive disease.
Mitochondrial heteroplasmy
That causes variable severity but not consistent worsening.
Independent assortment
Assortment does not worsen a trait over generations.
questions.x: Anticipation, earlier onset and greater severity in successive generations, is characteristic of trinucleotide repeat expansion disorders such as Huntington disease and myotonic dystrophy. These repeats are unstable and tend to lengthen when passed on, and longer repeats cause more severe, earlier disease. Mitochondrial heteroplasmy causes variability, but not a consistent worsening trend.

questions.q: A phenotypically normal woman's brother has hemophilia A (X-linked recessive); her parents are unaffected. If she has a son with an unaffected man, what is the probability the son has hemophilia?
o: Assumes she is definitely a carrier.
Multiplies an extra 1/2 for the child's sex; the child is known to be a son.
Correct: her mother is a carrier, so she is a carrier with 1/2; then 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
Uses the autosomal 2/3 carrier logic, which does not apply to X-linked traits.
questions.x: An affected brother with unaffected parents means their mother is a carrier (X-linked recessive alleles in sons come from the mother). So the woman inherited the mutant X from her mother with probability 1/2. If she is a carrier, a son has a 1/2 chance of getting her mutant X: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. The 2/3 rule is for autosomal recessive cases, not X-linked.

questions.q: Why do pedigrees of X-linked recessive traits show no father-to-son transmission?
o: The trait is lethal in sons
Affected males are common in X-linked recessive pedigrees.
Fathers are never affected
Affected fathers are possible; they just pass the allele to daughters.
Fathers pass a Y chromosome, not their X, to sons
Correct: sons inherit their X from their mother.
The Y chromosome masks the allele
The Y carries no matching allele for most X genes.
questions.x: A son always receives his father's Y chromosome and his mother's X. Since X-linked alleles travel on the X, a father cannot transmit an X-linked trait to his sons; he passes his X only to daughters. This absence of male-to-male transmission is a key feature for distinguishing X-linked from autosomal inheritance in pedigrees.

questions.q: For a gene with two alleles at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, the heterozygote frequency is highest when:
o: p = q = 0.5, giving 2pq = 0.5
Correct: 2pq is maximized when the alleles are equally common.
Then everyone is AA and 2pq = 0.
questions.x: The heterozygote frequency 2pq is a product of two numbers that add to 1, and such a product is largest when the two are equal. At p = q = 0.5, 2pq = 0.5, so half the population is heterozygous; as either allele becomes rarer, heterozygotes decline toward zero. No two-allele locus at equilibrium can have more than 50% heterozygotes.

questions.q: In a population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, 9% of people show a recessive phenotype. What fraction of people with the dominant phenotype are heterozygous?
o: That is heterozygotes as a fraction of the whole population.
That is p², the homozygous dominant fraction.
That is pq without the factor of 2.
Correct: q = 0.3, 2pq = 0.42, dominant phenotype = 0.91; 0.42/0.91 = 6/13.
questions.note: Conditional: divide by the dominant phenotype frequency, 1 − q².
questions.x: q² = 0.09, so q = 0.3 and p = 0.7. Heterozygotes make up 2pq = 0.42 of the population, and the dominant phenotype is 1 − q² = 0.91. Among dominant-phenotype people, the heterozygous fraction is 0.42/0.91 = 6/13 ≈ 0.46. The trap is answering 0.42, which forgets to restrict the denominator to dominant-phenotype individuals.

questions.q: If individuals with genotype aa are infertile, which Hardy–Weinberg assumption is violated?
o: Random mating
Mate choice is not described as changing.
No natural selection
Correct: genotypes now differ in reproductive success.
No migration
No one is entering or leaving.
No mutation
No new alleles are being created.
questions.x: Natural selection means genotypes differ in survival or reproductive success. If aa individuals cannot reproduce, their alleles are not passed on, so the a allele is removed from the gene pool faster than under equilibrium. This violates the no-selection assumption; nothing in the scenario changes mate choice, migration or mutation.

questions.q: In a diploid population of N individuals, what is the probability that a single new neutral mutation will eventually become fixed by genetic drift?
o: A single copy among 2N is far more likely to be lost.
Zero, since neutral alleles never fix
Drift can fix neutral alleles by chance.
1/(2N), its starting frequency
Correct: a neutral allele's fixation probability equals its initial frequency.
1/N²
The starting frequency is 1/(2N), not 1/N².
questions.x: A diploid population of N individuals has 2N copies of each gene, so a new mutation starts at a frequency of 1/(2N). For a neutral allele, drift is equally likely to favor any copy, so the chance that this particular copy's descendants eventually replace all the others equals its starting frequency, 1/(2N). Most new neutral mutations are lost.

questions.q: Adult height in a population is normally distributed with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 10 cm. About what percentage are taller than 190 cm?
o: Correct: 190 is 2 SD above the mean; about 95% lie within ±2 SD, leaving 2.5% in each tail.
That is both tails combined.
That is the fraction above 1 SD (180 cm).
That is roughly the fraction above 3 SD.
questions.x: For a normal distribution, about 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean, 95% within 2 SD and 99.7% within 3 SD. 190 cm is (190 − 170)/10 = 2 SD above the mean. The 5% outside ±2 SD is split equally between the two tails, so about 2.5% are taller than 190 cm.

questions.q: A locus at which two or more alleles are each present at appreciable frequency in a population is described as:
o: Polymorphic
Correct: polymorphism means multiple common variants at a locus.
Hemizygous
Hemizygous refers to having one copy, as with X genes in males.
Fixed
A fixed locus has only one allele.
Pleiotropic
Pleiotropy is one gene affecting many traits.
questions.x: A polymorphic locus has two or more alleles each at appreciable frequency in a population (a common rule of thumb: the rarest allele above 1%). The ABO blood group gene is a classic example. A fixed locus has only one allele in the population, and hemizygous describes a single gene copy in an individual, not population variation.

questions.q: The sickle-cell allele remains common in regions with malaria despite causing disease in homozygotes. This is because:
o: The allele is continually reintroduced by mutation
Mutation is far too rare to explain high frequency.
Homozygotes have the highest fitness
Sickle homozygotes have severe disease.
Genetic drift fixed the allele
The allele is common but not fixed, and selection is involved.
Heterozygotes are more resistant to malaria than either homozygote
Correct: heterozygote advantage maintains both alleles (balanced polymorphism).
questions.x: Sickle-cell heterozygotes (HbA/HbS) are resistant to severe malaria while having only mild effects, so they have higher fitness than HbA/HbA (malaria-susceptible) and HbS/HbS (sickle-cell disease) individuals. Selection therefore keeps both alleles in the population, a balanced polymorphism. The homozygotes are not the fittest; the heterozygote is.

questions.q: If malaria were permanently eliminated from a region, what would be expected to happen over many generations to the sickle-cell allele there?
o: Its frequency would decline
Correct: without heterozygote advantage, selection acts only against affected homozygotes.
Its frequency would rise
It would lose its only advantage.
Its frequency would be unchanged forever
Selection against homozygotes would still act.
It would disappear in one generation
Most copies are in carriers, so decline is gradual.
questions.x: The sickle allele is maintained by the malaria resistance it gives heterozygotes. Without malaria, heterozygotes have no advantage, and selection acts only against HbS/HbS individuals, so the allele frequency declines. The decline is slow, because most copies sit in unaffected carriers, which hides them from selection.

questions.q: After a drought leaves only large, hard seeds, the average beak depth in a finch population increases over several generations. This is an example of:
o: Stabilizing selection
That favors the mean and reduces variance.
Disruptive selection
That favors both extremes.
Genetic drift
The change tracks an environmental pressure, not chance.
Directional selection
Correct: one extreme of the trait is favored, shifting the mean.
questions.x: Directional selection favors individuals at one end of a trait's range, so the population mean shifts in that direction over generations. When only large, hard seeds were available, finches with deeper beaks cracked them better and left more offspring, so average beak depth increased. Stabilizing selection would instead favor the existing mean.

questions.q: Newborns of intermediate birth weight have the highest survival, while very small and very large babies have lower survival. This illustrates:
o: Directional selection
No single extreme is favored.
Disruptive selection
Both extremes are disfavored, not favored.
Sexual selection
The pressure is survival, not mate choice.
Stabilizing selection
Correct: intermediates are favored, narrowing the distribution.
questions.x: Stabilizing selection favors intermediate phenotypes and works against both extremes, so the mean stays the same while variation narrows. Human birth weight is a classic case: very small babies and very large babies (with delivery complications) historically had lower survival. Disruptive selection is the opposite, favoring both extremes over the middle.

questions.q: In a population, both small and large individuals survive better than intermediate ones, and over time the size distribution becomes bimodal. This is:
o: Stabilizing selection
That would favor intermediates.
Disruptive selection
Correct: both extremes are favored over the mean.
Directional selection
That shifts the whole curve toward one extreme.
A population bottleneck
A bottleneck reduces variation by chance.
questions.note: Disruptive selection can be a step toward sympatric speciation.
questions.x: Disruptive (diversifying) selection favors individuals at both extremes over intermediates, splitting the distribution into two peaks. It can arise when two different resources or niches favor different forms. Stabilizing selection is the opposite, and directional selection moves the whole distribution toward one extreme rather than splitting it.

questions.q: Males of a bird species have long, conspicuous tails that make them easier for predators to catch, yet the trait persists. The most likely explanation is that:
o: Females preferentially mate with long-tailed males
Correct: sexual selection can outweigh survival costs.
Long tails improve survival in all conditions
The stem says the tails increase predation.
The trait is neutral and maintained by drift
A costly trait would be removed unless something favors it.
Males acquired long tails by using them more
Use and disuse do not change inherited traits.
questions.x: Sexual selection favors traits that improve mating success, even if they reduce survival. If females prefer long-tailed males, those males father more offspring, and the extra reproduction can outweigh the cost of higher predation. Fitness is about reproduction, not survival alone. Use-and-disuse explanations are Lamarckian and do not explain inherited traits.

questions.q: Sterile worker bees spend their lives helping the queen reproduce. This behavior is best explained by:
o: Directional selection on worker body size
Body size does not explain the reproductive sacrifice.
Lamarckian inheritance of behavior
Acquired traits are not inherited.
Mutualism between unrelated species
Workers and queen are close relatives of one species.
Kin selection, since helping close relatives passes on shared alleles
Correct: inclusive fitness counts copies of alleles in relatives' offspring.
questions.x: Kin selection explains altruism toward relatives: an individual can pass on its alleles by helping relatives that carry copies of them reproduce. Worker bees are closely related to the queen's offspring, so helping her raise them increases the workers' inclusive fitness. Lamarckian inheritance and mutualism between species do not apply to sterile helpers within one colony.

questions.q: By Hamilton's rule (rB > C), which altruistic act is favored, where B and C are offspring gained by the recipient and lost by the actor?
o: Cost 1, benefit 3 to a first cousin (r = 1/8)
rB = 0.375, less than C = 1.
Cost 2, benefit 3 to a half sibling (r = 1/4)
rB = 0.75, less than C = 2.
Cost 1, benefit 1.5 to a nephew (r = 1/4)
rB = 0.375, less than C = 1.
Cost 1, benefit 3 to a full sibling (r = 1/2)
Correct: rB = 1.5, which exceeds C = 1.
questions.x: Hamilton's rule says an altruistic act is favored when the benefit to the recipient, weighted by relatedness (rB), exceeds the cost to the actor (C). For a full sibling, rB = 1/2 × 3 = 1.5, which is greater than 1. Each other option gives rB below its cost, so selection would not favor those acts.

questions.q: Two frog species share a pond, but one breeds in early spring and the other in late summer. This reproductive barrier is:
o: Temporal isolation
Correct: different breeding times prevent mating, a prezygotic barrier.
Habitat isolation
They share the same habitat.
Hybrid sterility
That is postzygotic; here no hybrids form.
Hybrid breakdown
That affects later hybrid generations.
questions.x: Temporal isolation is a prezygotic barrier in which species breed at different times of day or year, so they never mate even when they share a habitat. Breeding in spring versus late summer keeps the frogs apart. Hybrid sterility and hybrid breakdown are postzygotic barriers, which act only after a hybrid zygote forms.

questions.q: A horse and a donkey can mate and produce a healthy but sterile mule. The barrier keeping horses and donkeys separate species is:
o: Postzygotic, through reduced hybrid fertility
Correct: a zygote forms and develops, but the hybrid cannot reproduce.
Prezygotic, through mechanical isolation
Mating and fertilization do occur.
Prezygotic, through gametic isolation
Gametes do fuse, since a mule is born.
Postzygotic, through hybrid inviability
The mule is viable, only sterile.
questions.x: Prezygotic barriers stop fertilization; postzygotic barriers act after a zygote forms. A mule shows that mating and fertilization succeed and the hybrid develops normally, but it cannot produce functional gametes, so the barrier is postzygotic hybrid sterility. Hybrid inviability would mean the hybrid dies before reaching maturity, which mules do not.

questions.q: A river changes course and splits a population of beetles; over many generations the two groups diverge until they can no longer interbreed. This is:
o: Sympatric speciation
Sympatric speciation happens without geographic separation.
Convergent evolution
Convergence is unrelated lineages becoming similar.
Allopatric speciation
Correct: speciation following geographic separation.
Gene flow
The river blocks gene flow.
questions.x: Allopatric speciation occurs when a physical barrier divides a population and blocks gene flow. The isolated groups then diverge through mutation, drift and different selection pressures until they can no longer interbreed. Sympatric speciation happens without geographic separation, for example through polyploidy or disruptive selection.

questions.q: A tetraploid plant arises from a diploid ancestor. It cannot produce fertile offspring with the diploid because:
o: Tetraploid pollen cannot fertilize diploid ovules
Fertilization can occur; hybrid sterility is the barrier.
The tetraploid has different genes than the diploid
It has the same genes, just doubled.
Their triploid hybrids have unpaired chromosomes in meiosis and are sterile
Correct: odd ploidy disrupts homolog pairing, so few balanced gametes form.
Tetraploids reproduce only asexually
Many polyploid plants reproduce sexually.
questions.note: Polyploidy can create a new species in a single generation.
questions.x: A tetraploid makes diploid gametes and a diploid makes haploid gametes, so their hybrid is triploid. In triploid meiosis, three copies of each chromosome cannot pair evenly, so most gametes get unbalanced chromosome sets and are not viable. This hybrid sterility isolates the tetraploid reproductively from its parent species in a single generation, a common way plants speciate.

questions.q: Under the biological species concept, two populations are different species if they:
o: Cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring in nature
