Correct: reproductive isolation defines a biological species.
Look different
Physically different populations can still interbreed.
Live in different habitats
Separate habitats alone do not define species.
Differ at any genetic locus
Individuals within a species differ at many loci.
questions.x: The biological species concept defines a species as a group of populations whose members can interbreed in nature and produce fertile offspring, and which are reproductively isolated from other such groups. Appearance, habitat and genetic differences can vary within a species. The concept's weakness is that it cannot be applied to asexual organisms or fossils.

questions.q: Sharks and dolphins both have streamlined bodies and dorsal fins despite being only distantly related. This is an example of:
o: Divergent evolution
That is related lineages becoming different.
Homologous structures from a recent common ancestor
Their last common ancestor lacked these features.
Genetic drift
Repeated, adaptive similarity reflects selection.
Convergent evolution
Correct: similar pressures produce similar (analogous) traits in unrelated lineages.
questions.x: Convergent evolution occurs when unrelated lineages evolve similar traits because they face similar selective pressures, such as moving fast through water. The resulting features are analogous: similar in form and function but not inherited from a common ancestor with that trait. Sharks are fish, dolphins are mammals, and their shared ancestor had neither feature.

questions.q: The human arm, bat wing and whale flipper share the same basic bone arrangement. These are:
o: Analogous structures from convergence
Analogous structures share function, not ancestry.
Vestigial structures
These limbs are fully functional.
Products of genetic drift
Shared anatomy reflects descent, not chance.
Homologous structures reflecting common ancestry
Correct: shared structure inherited from a common ancestor, now used differently.
questions.x: Homologous structures share an underlying anatomy because they were inherited from a common ancestor, even if they now serve different functions. The forelimbs of humans, bats and whales all contain the same set of bones (humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, phalanges). Analogous structures share function but not ancestry, like insect and bird wings.

questions.q: A single ancestral bird species colonizes an island chain and gives rise to many species, each specialized for a different food source. This is:
o: Convergent evolution
The species are diverging from one ancestor, not converging.
Adaptive radiation
Correct: rapid diversification into many niches from one ancestor.
Stabilizing selection
That would maintain one form.
Coevolution
Coevolution is reciprocal change between interacting species.
questions.x: Adaptive radiation is the rapid diversification of one ancestral lineage into many species, each adapted to a different ecological niche. It often follows colonization of new environments with open niches, as with Darwin's finches in the Galápagos. Convergent evolution is the opposite pattern: unrelated lineages becoming similar.

questions.q: Certain flowers and their specific pollinators show matching adaptations, each having evolved in response to the other. This is:
o: Convergent evolution
That involves unrelated species independently evolving similar traits.
Coevolution
Correct: reciprocal evolutionary change between interacting species.
Genetic drift
The matching traits are adaptive.
Allopatric speciation
No geographic separation or speciation is described.
questions.x: Coevolution is reciprocal evolutionary change between interacting species, where adaptations in one create selective pressure on the other. Flower shapes that fit specific pollinators, and pollinator mouthparts that fit specific flowers, are classic examples, as are predator–prey and host–parasite arms races. Convergence involves unrelated species evolving similar traits independently, not in response to each other.

questions.q: Two species differ at 30 sites in a neutral DNA sequence. If differences accumulate between two lineages at a combined rate of 2 per million years, about how long ago did they diverge?
o: 30 million years
Ignores the rate of 2 differences per million years.
15 million years
Correct: 30 differences ÷ 2 per million years = 15 million years.
60 million years
Multiplies by the rate instead of dividing.
7.5 million years
Halves the answer again; the rate is already the combined rate.
questions.x: A molecular clock converts sequence differences into time by dividing by the rate at which differences accumulate. Here, 30 differences ÷ 2 differences per million years = 15 million years. Because the rate given is already the combined rate for both lineages, no further halving is needed; halving would be required only if the rate were given per lineage.

questions.q: Molecular clock estimates of divergence time rely on the assumption that:
o: Neutral mutations accumulate at a roughly constant rate
Correct: steady accumulation lets sequence differences track time.
Natural selection acts on every base
Selection would make rates uneven.
Mutation rates speed up during speciation
A changing rate undermines the clock.
All species have identical genomes
Clocks measure differences that build up over time.
questions.x: A molecular clock assumes that neutral mutations accumulate at a roughly constant rate over time, so the number of sequence differences between two lineages is proportional to the time since they split. Neutral sites are used because selection would speed up or slow down change unpredictably. Clocks must be calibrated with fossils or other dated events.

questions.q: Natural selection acts most directly on:
o: Phenotypes of individuals
Correct: selection 'sees' traits that affect survival and reproduction.
Genotypes, independent of phenotype
Genotypes are selected only through the phenotypes they produce.
Mutation rates of genes
Selection sorts variation rather than causing mutations.
Unexpressed recessive alleles in carriers
Hidden alleles are largely shielded from selection.
questions.note: Selection acts on individuals; populations are what evolve.
questions.x: Natural selection acts on phenotypes, the observable traits that affect survival and reproduction. Genotypes are affected only indirectly, through the phenotypes they produce. That is why recessive alleles hidden in heterozygous carriers are largely shielded from selection, and why individuals are selected while populations evolve.

questions.q: Which explanation for the long necks of giraffes is consistent with natural selection?
o: Giraffes stretched their necks and passed on the result
That is Lamarckian inheritance of acquired traits.
Giraffes with heritably longer necks left more offspring
Correct: heritable variation plus differential reproduction changes the population.
Mutations for long necks arose because giraffes needed them
Mutations are random with respect to need.
Each giraffe evolved a longer neck during its lifetime
Individuals do not evolve; populations do.
questions.x: Darwin's natural selection requires heritable variation and differential reproduction: giraffes that inherited longer necks reached more food and left more offspring, so the trait became more common. Lamarck's idea, that traits acquired by use are inherited, is wrong because changes to the body during life do not alter gametes. Mutations arise randomly, not because they are needed.

questions.q: Replica plating shows that antibiotic-resistant colonies were already present on the original plate before any bacteria were exposed to the antibiotic. This demonstrates that:
o: The antibiotic causes resistance mutations
Resistant colonies existed before exposure.
Resistance is acquired through use and disuse
This is a Lamarckian idea the result refutes.
All bacteria on the plate were resistant
Only a few colonies were resistant.
Resistance mutations arise randomly before selection
Correct: the antibiotic selects pre-existing mutants rather than inducing them.
questions.x: Replica plating (Lederberg) copied the same colony pattern onto plates with and without antibiotic. Resistant colonies appeared at matching positions, showing they were already resistant before exposure. So mutations occur randomly and the antibiotic only selects pre-existing resistant cells; it does not induce resistance, contrary to Lamarckian ideas.

questions.q: AA and Aa individuals each leave 100 offspring on average, while aa individuals leave 50. What is the selection coefficient against aa?
o: Squares the fitness ratio.
Inverts the ratio; s is between 0 and 1.
Uses offspring difference, not a relative measure.
Correct: relative fitness of aa = 50/100 = 0.5, and s = 1 − 0.5 = 0.5.
questions.note: Relative fitness w = offspring / best offspring; s = 1 − w.
questions.x: Relative fitness (w) compares each genotype's reproductive output to the best genotype's: w(aa) = 50/100 = 0.5. The selection coefficient measures the reduction in fitness: s = 1 − w = 0.5. Both w and s are fractions between 0 and 1; raw offspring differences such as 50 are not a selection coefficient.

questions.q: In population genetics terms, the evolutionary success of an allele is best measured by:
o: How dominant it is
Dominance does not determine whether an allele spreads.
How long its carriers live
Survival matters only through reproduction.
How old the allele is
Age alone says nothing about spread.
An increase in its frequency in the gene pool over generations
Correct: success means growing representation in future generations.
questions.x: From a population genetics perspective, an allele is evolutionarily successful if its frequency in the gene pool increases over generations. Evolution itself is defined as a change in allele frequencies. Dominance, age and carrier lifespan do not matter unless they cause more copies of the allele to be passed on.

questions.q: The concept of group selection proposes that a trait can spread because:
o: Groups with the trait outcompete other groups, even if it is costly to individuals
Correct: selection between groups can favor traits that benefit the group.
Individuals always act for their own survival
That is individual selection.
Relatives share alleles
That is kin selection.
The trait arises in many individuals at once
Group selection concerns differential success of groups.
questions.x: Group selection proposes that some traits spread because groups possessing them outcompete or outlast other groups, even if the trait costs the individual who has it. It differs from kin selection, which explains altruism through shared alleles in relatives. Most biologists consider group selection a weak force compared with individual and kin selection.

questions.q: Whales retain small pelvic bones that do not support walking. These bones are best described as:
o: Analogous structures
Analogy refers to similar function from separate origins.
Newly evolved adaptations
They are remnants, not new structures.
Vestigial structures
Correct: reduced remnants of structures functional in ancestors.
Acquired characteristics
They are inherited, not acquired during life.
questions.x: Vestigial structures are reduced or nonfunctional remnants of features that served a purpose in an organism's ancestors. Whale pelvic bones are leftovers from four-legged land-dwelling ancestors and are evidence of common descent. They are inherited, not acquired during life, and they are homologous to the pelvis of land mammals rather than analogous.

questions.q: The fossil record of a lineage shows long periods of little change interrupted by brief bursts of rapid speciation. This pattern is called:
o: Gradualism
Gradualism predicts slow, steady change.
Punctuated equilibrium
Correct: stasis broken by rapid change.
Stabilizing selection
That describes selection on a trait, not a fossil pattern of bursts.
Adaptive radiation only
Radiation may occur during bursts but does not name the overall pattern.
questions.x: Punctuated equilibrium describes long periods of stasis, with little evolutionary change, interrupted by short bursts of rapid change and speciation. This pattern often appears in the fossil record. Gradualism is the alternative model, in which species change slowly and steadily over long periods.

questions.q: A species that feeds on only one plant in a single habitat is most at risk of extinction when:
o: Its food plant or habitat changes rapidly
Correct: specialization brings efficiency but little flexibility.
Competitors in other habitats decline
That would not harm it.
Its population is large and stable
Large, stable populations are less at risk.
Mutation produces new variants
New variation can aid adaptation.
questions.x: Specialists depend on a narrow set of resources, so they are efficient in a stable environment but vulnerable when that environment changes. If the only food plant or habitat disappears, a specialist has nowhere else to go. Generalists, which can use many resources, are more resilient to environmental change.

questions.q: A population with very low genetic diversity is at higher risk of extinction mainly because:
o: It has little variation for selection to act on when the environment changes
Correct: low diversity limits adaptation to new pressures and diseases.
Its mutation rate is higher
Diversity and mutation rate are not linked this way.
It cannot reproduce sexually
Low diversity does not prevent sexual reproduction.
Its alleles are all dominant
Diversity is about variety, not dominance.
questions.x: Genetic diversity is the raw material for adaptation. When a population has little variation, it is less likely to contain individuals able to survive a new disease, climate shift or predator, so it cannot adapt and may decline. Low diversity also increases inbreeding depression. Diversity is about the variety of alleles, not their dominance or the mutation rate.

questions.q: Guppies moved from a stream with many predators to a stream with few predators evolve brighter-colored males over several generations. The best interpretation is that:
o: Bright color was caused by the new stream's diet in each fish
Change over generations indicates heritable evolution.
Reduced predation let sexual selection for bright males outweigh natural selection against them
Correct: the balance of selective pressures shifted once predators were rare.
Predators prefer bright guppies, so color increased
Fewer predators means less selection against bright males, not more.
Genetic drift produced the same change by chance
A consistent, directional change matches altered selection.
questions.x: Male guppy coloration is under two opposing pressures: sexual selection (females prefer bright males) and natural selection (predators spot bright males). Where predators are rare, the cost of brightness falls, so sexual selection dominates and brighter males leave more offspring. A consistent, directional change over generations points to selection, not drift or diet.

questions.q: A moth's dark form rose from 10% to 90% of the population as tree bark darkened from soot, then declined after pollution controls cleaned the bark. This best shows:
o: Stabilizing selection on wing color
No intermediate is favored.
Mutation responding to pollution
Selection, not induced mutation, shifted the frequencies.
Directional selection whose direction tracks the environment
Correct: the favored form changed when the background changed.
Genetic drift in a small population
Parallel, reversible tracking of the environment points to selection.
questions.x: In the peppered moth, dark moths were better camouflaged on soot-darkened bark and survived bird predation better, so their frequency rose. When pollution controls lightened the bark, the light form regained the advantage and the dark form declined. The direction of selection simply followed the environment. Mutation did not respond to pollution; selection acted on existing variation.

questions.q: A point mutation in an intron that does not alter splicing or gene regulation will most likely change in frequency through:
o: Strong positive selection
It has no effect on phenotype to select.
Strong negative selection
It is not harmful.
Genetic drift, since it is selectively neutral
Correct: neutral variants are not selected and drift randomly.
Heterozygote advantage
No fitness difference among genotypes exists.
questions.x: A mutation that does not change protein sequence, splicing or regulation has no effect on phenotype, so it is selectively neutral. Its frequency changes only through genetic drift, the random sampling of alleles each generation. Selection, whether positive, negative or balancing, requires a fitness difference among genotypes.

questions.q: Where two closely related species meet, their hybrids have low fitness, and over time mating preferences that avoid hybridization become stronger. This process is called:
o: Reinforcement
Correct: selection against hybrids strengthens prezygotic isolation.
Gene flow
Gene flow would blend the species.
Hybrid vigor
Here the hybrids are less fit, not more.
Genetic drift
The change is driven by selection against hybrids.
questions.x: Reinforcement occurs when two diverging populations meet again and their hybrids have low fitness. Individuals who mate with their own type leave more fit offspring, so selection strengthens prezygotic isolating mechanisms such as mating preferences. This completes speciation. Gene flow, by contrast, would merge the two populations.

questions.q: Two insect species cannot mate because their reproductive structures are physically incompatible. This barrier is:
o: Behavioral isolation
That involves courtship or mate recognition.
Gametic isolation
That involves sperm and egg failing to fuse.
Hybrid inviability
No hybrid zygote is formed.
Mechanical isolation
Correct: a prezygotic barrier based on anatomy.
questions.x: Mechanical isolation is a prezygotic barrier in which differences in reproductive anatomy prevent mating or sperm transfer. Behavioral isolation involves differences in courtship or mate recognition, and gametic isolation involves sperm and egg that meet but cannot fuse. Since no zygote forms, postzygotic barriers like hybrid inviability do not apply.

questions.q: First-generation hybrids between two plant populations are fertile, but their offspring are weak and largely sterile. This barrier is:
o: Hybrid sterility
The F1 hybrids here are fertile.
Temporal isolation
The populations clearly interbreed.
Hybrid vigor
The F2 are weaker, not stronger.
Hybrid breakdown
Correct: postzygotic failure appearing in later hybrid generations.
questions.x: Hybrid breakdown is a postzygotic barrier in which first-generation hybrids are viable and fertile, but their offspring (F2 or backcrosses) are weak or sterile. It is distinct from hybrid sterility, where the F1 itself cannot reproduce. Because the populations do mate and produce F1 hybrids, prezygotic barriers like temporal isolation are not at work.

questions.q: Which observation provides the strongest evidence that two species share a recent common ancestor?
o: Both species have wings
Wings evolved independently in several lineages.
Both species live in the same habitat
Habitat sharing does not indicate ancestry.
High DNA sequence similarity at many neutral loci
Correct: shared neutral sequence reflects shared descent, not shared function.
Both species are the same body size
Size can converge in unrelated species.
questions.x: Neutral DNA sequences are not shaped by function or environment, so similarities between species at many such loci are best explained by inheritance from a recent common ancestor. Traits like wings or body size can evolve independently through convergence, so they are weaker evidence of relatedness. Molecular data underlie modern phylogenies for this reason.

questions.q: In a fish species, individuals with the rarer of two mouth shapes always have higher feeding success. Over many generations this will most likely:
o: Fix the more common form
The common form is at a disadvantage.
Eliminate both forms
Selection favors one or the other, not neither.
Fix whichever form is rare now
As it becomes common it loses its advantage.
Keep both forms present near a stable intermediate frequency
Correct: negative frequency-dependent selection favors whichever is rare.
questions.x: In negative frequency-dependent selection, a phenotype's fitness is higher when it is rare. As the rare form becomes common it loses its advantage, while the formerly common form becomes rare and gains it. This pushes both forms toward a stable balance, maintaining polymorphism. Neither form can become fixed, because each is disfavored once it predominates.

questions.q: An allele that causes a fatal disease only after age 70 is under weak selection mainly because:
o: It is recessive
Even dominant late-onset alleles persist.
Its effects appear after most reproduction is complete
Correct: late-acting alleles barely change reproductive output.
It mutates back to normal
Back mutation is very rare.
Older people are not part of the gene pool
They are part of it but contribute few new offspring.
questions.x: Selection acts through reproductive success. An allele whose harmful effects appear only after age 70 has little impact on how many offspring carriers produce, since most reproduction has already happened. Therefore selection against it is weak, and the allele can persist even if dominant, as with Huntington disease, whose onset usually comes after reproduction has begun.

questions.q: The main evolutionary advantage of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction is that it:
o: Produces genetically varied offspring that may adapt to changing conditions
Correct: meiosis and fertilization generate new allele combinations.
Produces more offspring per parent
Asexual reproduction usually produces offspring faster.
Avoids all mutations
Sexual organisms still mutate.
Creates offspring identical to the parents
That describes asexual reproduction.
questions.x: Sexual reproduction creates new allele combinations through crossing over, independent assortment and random fertilization. This variation improves the chance that some offspring will survive in changing environments or resist evolving parasites. Asexual reproduction is usually faster and more efficient but produces genetically identical offspring.

questions.q: A neutral allele tightly linked to a strongly favored allele rises in frequency along with it. The best explanation is:
o: The neutral allele is itself favored
By definition it has no fitness effect.
Independent assortment
Tightly linked genes do not assort independently.
Mutation repeatedly creates the neutral allele
Mutation is far too slow to cause this rise.
Genetic hitchhiking, since linkage keeps the two alleles together
Correct: little recombination lets the neutral allele ride the selective sweep.
questions.x: Genetic hitchhiking occurs when a neutral allele rises in frequency because it is tightly linked to a beneficial allele under strong selection. With little recombination between them, the neutral allele is carried along during the selective sweep. This reduces variation near selected genes. The neutral allele itself has no fitness effect; linkage, not selection on it, drives its rise.

questions.q: Bacteria grown at 42 °C for 2000 generations become more fit at 42 °C but less fit at 32 °C than their ancestors. The best conclusion is that:
o: Adaptation to one environment can carry trade-offs in another
Correct: changes favored at 42 °C were costly at 32 °C.
The bacteria failed to evolve
Fitness changed in both environments.
High temperature induced directed mutations
Selection on random mutations explains the result.
The 32 °C fitness drop was caused by contamination
Nothing suggests contamination; trade-offs are expected.
questions.x: Adaptation is specific to the environment that does the selecting. Mutations favored at 42 °C improved fitness there but had side effects that lowered fitness at 32 °C, an evolutionary trade-off. This shows evolution does not produce universally better organisms, only organisms better suited to their current conditions.

questions.q: A population has 10 breeding males and 90 breeding females. Using Nₑ = 4(Nm)(Nf)/(Nm + Nf), what is its effective population size?
o: That is the census number of breeders, not Nₑ.
Averages the two sexes; Nₑ depends on their product, so the rarer sex dominates.
Uses twice the number of males.
questions.note: A skewed sex ratio lowers Nₑ and strengthens drift.
questions.x: Effective population size (Nₑ) is the size of an idealized population that would show the same amount of drift. With unequal sex ratios, Nₑ is dominated by the rarer sex because half of each offspring's genes come from it: 4(10)(90)/(10 + 90) = 3600/100 = 36. That is far below the census count of 100, so drift is stronger than headcount suggests.

questions.q: Which structure is present in every prokaryotic cell?
o: A nuclear envelope
Prokaryotes have a nucleoid region with no surrounding membrane.
Mitochondria
Membrane-bound organelles like mitochondria are eukaryotic.
A peptidoglycan cell wall
Most bacteria have one, but Mycoplasma and archaea lack peptidoglycan.
Ribosomes
Correct: all cells, including prokaryotes, need ribosomes to make proteins.
questions.note: Prokaryote = no membrane-bound organelles, but ribosomes are universal.
questions.x: Ribosomes are universal because every cell must translate mRNA into protein. Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles and a nuclear envelope. The tempting wrong answer is the peptidoglycan wall: most bacteria have one, but Mycoplasma has no wall at all and archaea build walls from other materials, so it is not universal.

questions.q: Which describes the ribosomes of a bacterium such as E. coli?
o: 80S, built from 40S and 60S subunits
These are eukaryotic cytosolic ribosomes.
80S, built from 30S and 50S subunits
Assumes Svedberg values add; they depend on shape, not just mass.
60S, built from two 30S subunits
Bacterial subunits differ in size; the small is 30S, the large 50S.
70S, built from 30S and 50S subunits
Correct: bacterial ribosomes are 70S with 30S small and 50S large subunits.
questions.note: Svedberg units are not additive: 30S + 50S = 70S.
questions.x: Bacterial ribosomes are 70S, made of a 30S small subunit (16S rRNA) and a 50S large subunit. Svedberg units measure sedimentation rate, which depends on mass and shape, so they do not add: 30S plus 50S gives 70S, not 80S. The 80S ribosome with 40S and 60S subunits is the eukaryotic cytosolic type, which is why ribosome-targeting antibiotics can be selective.

questions.q: The glycan backbone of bacterial peptidoglycan is made of alternating units of:
o: Glucose and galactose
These two sugars form lactose, not peptidoglycan.
N-acetylglucosamine and N-acetylmuramic acid
Correct: NAG–NAM chains are cross-linked by short peptides.
N-acetylglucosamine alone
A polymer of only NAG is chitin, found in fungal walls.
Lipid A and O-antigen
These are parts of lipopolysaccharide in the Gram-negative outer membrane.
questions.x: Peptidoglycan is a mesh of glycan strands made of alternating N-acetylglucosamine (NAG) and N-acetylmuramic acid (NAM), with short peptides on NAM cross-linking neighboring strands. That cross-linked mesh gives the wall its strength. A polymer of NAG alone is chitin, found in fungal walls and arthropod exoskeletons, not bacteria.

questions.q: Septic shock during a Gram-negative bloodstream infection is triggered mainly by which bacterial component?
o: Teichoic acids
Teichoic acids belong to Gram-positive walls.
Secreted protein exotoxins
Endotoxin is a structural membrane component, not a secreted protein.
Lipid A of outer-membrane lipopolysaccharide
Correct: lipid A (endotoxin) strongly activates innate immune signaling, causing fever and shock.
Dipicolinic acid
Dipicolinic acid is found in endospores, not Gram-negative envelopes.
questions.note: Endotoxin = LPS (lipid A), only in Gram-negatives.
questions.x: Endotoxin is lipid A, the membrane anchor of lipopolysaccharide in the Gram-negative outer membrane. When bacteria in the blood die or shed it, lipid A strongly triggers innate immune signaling (TLR4), driving cytokine release, fever, vasodilation and shock. Exotoxins are secreted proteins with specific actions and are not the defining trigger of Gram-negative septic shock.

questions.q: During Gram staining, why do Gram-positive cells remain purple after the alcohol wash?
o: Their thick peptidoglycan layer traps the crystal violet–iodine complex
Correct: alcohol dehydrates the thick wall, locking the dye complex inside.
Their outer membrane binds the crystal violet tightly
Gram-positives lack an outer membrane; alcohol dissolves Gram-negative outer membranes.
They lack peptidoglycan entirely
Gram-positives have the thickest peptidoglycan of all bacteria.
Safranin binds them more strongly than crystal violet
Safranin is applied after decolorizing and stains cells left colorless.
questions.x: In the Gram stain, crystal violet and iodine form a large complex inside all cells. Alcohol dehydrates and tightens the thick peptidoglycan of Gram-positive cells, trapping the complex, while it disrupts the Gram-negative outer membrane and the thin wall lets the dye wash out. Gram-positives have no outer membrane, so the dye retention comes from the thick wall.

questions.q: A technician Gram stains E. coli (Gram-negative) but forgets the alcohol decolorizing step. How will the cells appear?
o: Pink
Pink requires removing crystal violet so safranin shows.
Purple
Correct: without decolorizing, crystal violet is never washed out of the thin wall.
Colorless
Cells keep the primary stain when alcohol is skipped.
Green
No green dye is used in a Gram stain.
questions.note: Skip decolorizer: everything looks Gram-positive.
questions.x: The decolorizing alcohol step is the only step that tells Gram-positive and Gram-negative cells apart. If it is skipped, crystal violet–iodine stays in every cell, and the later safranin is hidden by the dark purple. So Gram-negative E. coli would wrongly look purple, like a Gram-positive.

questions.q: If the safranin counterstain is omitted, how will a smear of Staphylococcus (Gram-positive) mixed with E. coli (Gram-negative) appear?
o: Both purple
That would happen if the alcohol step, not safranin, were skipped.
Staphylococcus purple; E. coli colorless
Correct: E. coli loses crystal violet in alcohol and nothing restains it.
Both pink
Pink comes from safranin, which was left out.
Staphylococcus colorless; E. coli pink
This reverses retention and still assumes safranin was applied.
questions.x: Alcohol still removes crystal violet from the Gram-negative E. coli, while Gram-positive Staphylococcus keeps it and stays purple. Safranin is the step that would turn the decolorized cells pink, so without it E. coli is left colorless. Both purple would be the result of skipping the alcohol step instead.

questions.q: In Gram-negative bacteria, the compartment between the plasma membrane and the outer membrane, which holds a thin peptidoglycan layer, is the:
o: Nucleoid
The nucleoid is the DNA region inside the cytoplasm.
Capsule
The capsule lies outside the outer membrane.
Periplasmic space
Correct: the periplasm lies between the inner and outer membranes.
Cytosol
The cytosol is inside the plasma membrane.
questions.x: The Gram-negative envelope has an inner (plasma) membrane, a thin peptidoglycan layer, and an outer membrane. The space between the two membranes is the periplasm, which holds the peptidoglycan and many binding proteins and enzymes such as β-lactamases. A capsule, if present, lies outside the outer membrane.

questions.q: Mycoplasma species are naturally unaffected by penicillin and cannot be classified by Gram staining. Which feature explains both?
o: They have a thick polysaccharide capsule
A capsule does not remove the penicillin target or block Gram classification.
They have no peptidoglycan cell wall
Correct: no wall means no penicillin target and nothing for the Gram stain to assess.
They have an LPS-containing outer membrane
Such cells stain Gram-negative, so they can be classified.
They form endospores
Mycoplasma do not form spores, and spores would not explain both traits.
questions.x: Mycoplasma has no cell wall, only a plasma membrane stiffened by sterols. Penicillin acts by blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking, so with no wall there is no target. The Gram stain classifies cells by wall structure, so a wall-less cell cannot be meaningfully called Gram-positive or Gram-negative.

questions.q: What directly powers the rotation of a bacterial flagellum?
o: ATP hydrolysis by dynein arms
Dynein drives the whiplike beating of eukaryotic flagella.
GTP hydrolysis by tubulin
Bacterial flagella are made of flagellin, not microtubules.
Proton flow across the plasma membrane
Correct: the flagellar motor is driven by the proton motive force.
Myosin sliding along actin filaments
Actomyosin is a eukaryotic motility system.
questions.note: Bacterial flagellum: flagellin + rotary motor + H⁺ gradient.
questions.x: The bacterial flagellum is a rigid helical filament of flagellin turned by a rotary motor at its base. In E. coli the motor is powered by protons flowing back into the cell down the proton motive force, not by ATP. Eukaryotic flagella are completely different: microtubules that bend because dynein hydrolyzes ATP.

questions.q: As a peritrichous E. coli cell swims up a gradient of an attractant, how does its behavior change?
o: Tumbles become less frequent, so runs last longer
Correct: a biased random walk lengthens runs in favorable directions.
Tumbles become more frequent, so it turns more often
More tumbling occurs when moving toward lower attractant.
Its flagella switch to whiplike beating
Bacterial flagella rotate; they do not beat.
It steers by turning a flagellum like a rudder
E. coli cannot steer; it changes run length instead.
questions.note: Counterclockwise rotation = run; clockwise = tumble.
questions.x: E. coli alternates runs (counterclockwise rotation, flagella bundled) with tumbles (clockwise rotation, random reorientation). It cannot steer, so it senses whether attractant is rising over time and suppresses tumbling when things improve. Runs up the gradient last longer, giving a biased random walk toward the attractant; more frequent tumbling happens when moving the wrong way.

questions.q: Short, numerous hairlike fimbriae on a bacterial surface mainly help the cell:
o: Swim toward nutrients
Swimming uses flagella, not fimbriae.
Adhere to host cells and other surfaces
Correct: fimbriae are attachment structures important for colonization.
Survive boiling temperatures
Heat resistance comes from endospores.
Store extra copies of the genome
Fimbriae are protein appendages, not genetic storage.
questions.x: Fimbriae are many short protein hairs that let bacteria stick to host tissues and surfaces, a key early step in colonization and infection. They do not drive movement; swimming uses flagella. Sex pili are a separate, longer structure used in conjugation.

questions.q: A wild-type bacterial strain with a polysaccharide capsule is lethal to mice, but a capsule-deficient mutant is cleared quickly. The best explanation is that the capsule:
o: Is required for conjugation
Conjugation uses sex pili, not capsules.
Is itself a secreted protein toxin
Capsules are usually polysaccharide coats, not toxins.
Makes the bacterium resistant to every antibiotic
Capsules do not confer broad antibiotic resistance.
Hinders phagocytosis by host immune cells
Correct: capsules make bacteria hard for phagocytes to engulf.
questions.x: A polysaccharide capsule is slippery and hides surface molecules, so phagocytes and complement have trouble grabbing and engulfing the bacterium. That lets encapsulated strains multiply and cause disease, while capsule-less mutants are quickly cleared. The capsule is a virulence factor through immune evasion, not a toxin.

questions.q: Why is boiling for a few minutes often insufficient to sterilize material contaminated with Clostridium?
o: Clostridium cells divide faster than heat kills them
Vegetative cells die quickly at 100 °C.
Its endospores have a dehydrated core that resists heat
Correct: spores with low water and Ca²⁺–dipicolinic acid survive boiling.
Its capsule insulates the cell from heat
Capsules do not provide meaningful heat resistance.
Clostridium grows best at 100 °C
Clostridium species are not hyperthermophiles.
questions.note: Spores, not capsules, explain heat resistance: autoclave at 121 °C.
questions.x: Clostridium and Bacillus form endospores, dormant structures with a dehydrated core, protective coats, and calcium–dipicolinic acid that stabilize DNA and proteins. Spores survive boiling, so sterilization needs autoclaving at 121 °C under pressure. Vegetative cells die quickly at 100 °C, and capsules give no real heat protection.

questions.q: A single vegetative Bacillus cell forms one endospore, which later germinates under good conditions. How many vegetative cells result from that one spore?
o: Correct: sporulation is a survival strategy, not reproduction; one cell becomes one spore becomes one cell.
Confuses sporulation with binary fission.
Confuses sporulation with meiosis producing four products.
Bacterial endospores do not multiply inside the mother cell.
questions.note: Trap: endospores are not reproductive.
questions.x: Endospore formation is a survival response to starvation, not a way to reproduce. One vegetative cell builds one spore inside itself, and when that spore germinates it gives back one vegetative cell. The population grows only afterward, by binary fission.

questions.q: Spherical bacteria arranged in grapelike clusters are described as:
o: Streptococci
Streptococci are cocci in chains.
Staphylococci
Correct: 'staphylo' means cluster; 'coccus' means sphere.
Bacilli
Bacilli are rod-shaped.
Spirochetes
Spirochetes are flexible spiral cells.
questions.x: Bacterial names combine shape and arrangement: cocci are spheres, bacilli rods, spirilla and spirochetes spirals. Staphylococci form grapelike clusters because they divide in multiple planes, while streptococci form chains because they divide in one plane.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes archaeal plasma membranes from bacterial ones?
o: Ester bonds link glycerol to straight fatty acids
That describes bacterial and eukaryotic membranes.
They contain large amounts of cholesterol
Cholesterol is characteristic of animal cell membranes.
Peptidoglycan is embedded within the bilayer
Archaea lack peptidoglycan entirely.
Ether bonds link glycerol to branched isoprenoid chains
Correct: archaeal lipids are ether-linked isoprenoids, which are chemically sturdy.
questions.x: Archaeal membrane lipids attach glycerol to branched isoprenoid chains by ether bonds, while bacteria and eukaryotes use ester bonds to straight fatty acids. Ether bonds resist heat and chemical attack, which helps extremophiles. Some archaea even form monolayers of lipids that span the whole membrane.

questions.q: A newly discovered single-celled organism has no nucleus, wraps its DNA around histones, and starts translation with unmodified methionine. It most likely belongs to:
o: Bacteria
Bacteria initiate with N-formylmethionine and generally lack histones.
Eukarya
Eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus.
Archaea
Correct: archaea are prokaryotic yet share histones and Met initiation with eukaryotes.
Viruses
Viruses are not cells and lack their own ribosomes.
questions.x: Archaea are prokaryotes with no nucleus, but in their information-processing machinery they look like eukaryotes. Many package DNA with histones and start translation with plain methionine, while bacteria use N-formylmethionine and generally lack histones. Eukarya is ruled out because those cells have a membrane-bound nucleus.

questions.q: In a batch culture, during which phase do new cell divisions roughly balance cell deaths?
o: Lag phase
In lag phase cells adapt and make enzymes; little division or death occurs.
Stationary phase
Correct: nutrient depletion and waste buildup make growth equal death.
Exponential phase
Divisions far outpace deaths during log growth.
Death phase
Deaths exceed divisions in the death phase.
questions.x: In batch culture, stationary phase comes when nutrients run low and wastes build up, so the rate of new divisions roughly equals the rate of cell death and the viable count levels off. In lag phase cells adapt without much division; in log phase divisions far exceed deaths; in death phase deaths win.

questions.q: Cells moved from a rich broth into a minimal glucose–salts medium show a longer lag phase than cells moved into fresh rich broth. Why?
o: They must conjugate before they can divide
Conjugation is not required for growth.
Minimal medium kills most of the transferred cells
Minimal medium supports growth of prototrophs after adaptation.
They must first make enzymes to synthesize amino acids and other building blocks
Correct: lag reflects time to induce biosynthetic pathways before dividing.
Minimal medium causes immediate sporulation
Sporulation is not the reason for a longer lag.
questions.x: Lag phase is the time cells spend adjusting to a new environment before dividing. Cells moved from rich broth to minimal medium must turn on and make enzymes to synthesize amino acids, nucleotides and vitamins that the broth used to supply. Cells moved into the same rich broth need little adjustment, so their lag is short.

questions.q: A bacterium doubles every 20 minutes. If 5 × 10³ cells enter exponential growth, about how many cells are present 2 hours later?
o: Multiplies by 6, the number of generations, instead of by 2⁶.
Uses 5 generations (2⁵ = 32); 120 min ÷ 20 min = 6.
Correct: 6 generations, 2⁶ = 64, and 64 × 5 × 10³ = 3.2 × 10⁵.
Uses 7 generations (2⁷ = 128).
questions.note: N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, with n = time ÷ doubling time.
questions.x: Exponential growth follows N = N₀ × 2ⁿ, where n is the number of doublings. In 120 minutes with a 20-minute doubling time, n = 6, so the population rises 2⁶ = 64-fold: 64 × 5 × 10³ = 3.2 × 10⁵ cells. The common error is multiplying by n (6) instead of raising 2 to the n.

questions.q: During exponential growth, a culture rises from 2 × 10⁶ to 1.6 × 10⁷ cells/mL in 90 minutes. What is the doubling time?
o: About 11 min
Divides 90 min by 8, the fold change, rather than by the number of doublings.
30 min
Correct: an 8-fold rise is 3 doublings (2³), so 90 ÷ 3 = 30 min.
45 min
That would give only a 4-fold rise in 90 min.
90 min
That would give only a 2-fold rise.
questions.x: To find doubling time, convert the fold change into a number of doublings. A rise from 2 × 10⁶ to 1.6 × 10⁷ is 8-fold, which is 2³, so three doublings took 90 minutes, or 30 minutes each. Dividing 90 by 8 confuses fold change with the number of doublings.

questions.q: Penicillin kills a culture most effectively during which situation?
o: Exponential phase, when cells are actively building new cell wall
Correct: β-lactams block wall synthesis, which matters most in dividing cells.
Lag phase, when cells are not yet dividing
Little new wall is being assembled before division resumes.
Stationary phase, when nutrients are exhausted
Non-growing cells make little new peptidoglycan, so they tolerate penicillin.
Equally in every phase, since all cells have walls
Penicillin blocks synthesis of new wall, not existing wall.
questions.x: β-lactams such as penicillin block transpeptidases that cross-link new peptidoglycan. Only cells actively growing and dividing are assembling new wall, so exponential-phase cells are weakened and lyse osmotically. Non-growing cells in lag or stationary phase make little new wall and tolerate the drug, even though they still have walls.

questions.q: E. coli grown in a medium containing both glucose and lactose shows two exponential phases separated by a brief plateau. What happens during the plateau?
o: Glucose runs out, cAMP rises, and the lac operon is induced
Correct: cells pause while making lactose-metabolizing enzymes such as β-galactosidase.
Cells conjugate to acquire lactose-utilization genes
E. coli already carries the lac operon on its chromosome.
Lactose becomes toxic and kills part of the population
Lactose is a usable carbon source, not a toxin.
Cells enter the death phase and then recover
The plateau is a metabolic switch, not death.
questions.note: Diauxie: glucose first, then lac induction once glucose is gone.
questions.x: This is diauxic growth. E. coli uses glucose first because glucose keeps cAMP low and blocks lac operon induction. When glucose runs out, cAMP rises, cAMP–CAP plus the lactose inducer switch on the lac operon, and growth pauses until enough β-galactosidase and permease are made to use lactose. The genes are already on the chromosome; no new DNA is needed.

questions.q: In a tube of thioglycolate broth (oxygen high at the top, absent at the bottom), an organism grows only in a band at the very bottom. It is most likely:
o: An obligate aerobe
Obligate aerobes grow only at the oxygen-rich top.
An obligate anaerobe
Correct: it grows only where oxygen is absent.
A facultative anaerobe
Facultative anaerobes grow throughout, densest at the top.
An aerotolerant anaerobe
Aerotolerant organisms grow evenly throughout the tube.
questions.x: Thioglycolate broth sets up an oxygen gradient, so where organisms grow reveals their oxygen needs. Obligate anaerobes are harmed by oxygen and grow only at the oxygen-free bottom. Facultative anaerobes grow throughout but best at the top, and aerotolerant anaerobes grow evenly because they ignore oxygen.

questions.q: In thioglycolate broth, a bacterium grows throughout the tube but most densely near the top. It is best classified as:
o: An aerotolerant anaerobe
Aerotolerant cells do not use O₂, so growth is uniform.
A facultative anaerobe
Correct: it uses O₂ when available (more growth) but can also grow without it.
A microaerophile
Microaerophiles grow in a narrow band just below the surface.
An obligate aerobe
Obligate aerobes cannot grow in the oxygen-free lower region.
questions.x: Facultative anaerobes can respire with oxygen or ferment without it. They grow throughout the tube, but densest at the top because aerobic respiration yields far more ATP. Aerotolerant anaerobes also grow throughout, but evenly, since they never use oxygen.

questions.q: Why does a facultative anaerobe grow faster with oxygen than without it?
o: O₂ is required for glycolysis to proceed
Glycolysis is anaerobic and runs without O₂.
Fermentation generates reactive oxygen species
Fermentation does not need O₂ and does not produce ROS as its main limit.
O₂ is incorporated directly into peptidoglycan
O₂ is not a structural component of the cell wall.
O₂ acts as the final electron acceptor, allowing oxidative phosphorylation and far more ATP per glucose
Correct: aerobic respiration yields much more ATP than fermentation.
questions.x: With oxygen as the final electron acceptor, a facultative anaerobe can run the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation, making many more ATP per glucose than fermentation. Fermentation gives only the 2 ATP of glycolysis. Glycolysis itself does not require oxygen, so that is not the reason for faster growth.

questions.q: Why is oxygen toxic to many obligate anaerobes?
o: O₂ binds and permanently blocks their ribosomes
O₂ is not a ribosome inhibitor.
O₂ dissolves their peptidoglycan
O₂ does not degrade cell walls.
O₂ forces glycolysis to run in reverse
O₂ does not reverse glycolysis.
They lack enzymes such as superoxide dismutase and catalase that detoxify reactive oxygen species
Correct: without these enzymes, superoxide and peroxide damage the cell.
questions.x: Oxygen metabolism produces reactive oxygen species such as superoxide and hydrogen peroxide. Aerobes and many facultative organisms destroy these with superoxide dismutase and catalase or peroxidase. Many obligate anaerobes lack enough of these enzymes, so oxygen exposure leads to oxidative damage to their proteins, lipids and DNA.

questions.q: Where is the electron transport chain located in an aerobic bacterium?
o: In the inner mitochondrial membrane
Bacteria have no mitochondria.
Free in the cytosol
An ETC must be membrane-bound to build a proton gradient.
In the plasma membrane
Correct: bacteria lack mitochondria, so respiration occurs at the plasma membrane.
In the peptidoglycan cell wall
The porous wall cannot hold a proton gradient.
questions.x: Bacteria have no mitochondria, so they place the electron transport chain and ATP synthase in the plasma membrane and pump protons out to the periplasm or outside. This matches the idea that mitochondria descend from bacteria, whose inner membrane carries the same machinery. A chain floating in the cytosol could not build a proton gradient.

questions.q: A protonophore that makes the bacterial plasma membrane freely permeable to H⁺ is added to motile E. coli. Which outcome is expected?
o: ATP synthesis declines, but motility is unaffected because flagella run on ATP
Bacterial flagella are powered by H⁺ flow, not ATP.
Both ATP synthase activity and flagellar rotation decline
Correct: both depend on the proton motive force that the drug dissipates.
Motility declines, but ATP synthesis rises
ATP synthase also needs the H⁺ gradient, so it falls.
Glycolysis stops completely
Glycolysis makes ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation without a gradient.
questions.x: In bacteria the proton motive force across the plasma membrane powers both ATP synthase and the flagellar motor. A protonophore lets H⁺ leak freely across the membrane, collapsing the gradient, so ATP synthesis and swimming both decline. Glycolysis continues because it makes ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation, which does not need a gradient.

questions.q: A soil bacterium gets its carbon from CO₂ and its energy by oxidizing ammonia. It is best classified as a:
o: Photoautotroph
Photoautotrophs get energy from light.
Chemoautotroph
Correct: energy from inorganic chemicals (chemo) and carbon from CO₂ (auto).
Chemoheterotroph
Chemoheterotrophs get carbon from organic compounds.
Photoheterotroph
Photoheterotrophs use light and organic carbon.
questions.x: Nutritional types combine an energy source with a carbon source. Energy from light is photo-, from chemical oxidation is chemo-; carbon from CO₂ is auto-, from organic molecules is hetero-. Oxidizing ammonia for energy and fixing CO₂ for carbon makes this nitrifying bacterium a chemoautotroph.

questions.q: Which statement about bacterial binary fission is correct?
o: Spindle microtubules pull sister chromatids to opposite poles
Bacteria do not form mitotic spindles.
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes occurs first
Bacteria are haploid and do not undergo meiotic crossing over.
It begins with breakdown of the nuclear envelope
Bacteria have no nuclear envelope.
Replicated chromosomes separate without a mitotic spindle, giving two identical cells
Correct: chromosomes are partitioned as the cell elongates and divides.
questions.x: Binary fission is a simple asexual division: the circular chromosome is replicated, the copies are moved apart as the cell elongates, and a septum forms between them. There is no nucleus, no mitotic spindle and no crossing over, so the two daughter cells are genetically identical apart from rare mutations.

questions.q: A temperature-sensitive E. coli mutant has an FtsZ protein that cannot form the division ring at 42 °C. What is seen when the mutant grows at 42 °C?
o: Normal division, but daughter cells lack DNA
FtsZ is needed for division itself, not chromosome inheritance.
Immediate lysis of every cell
Loss of FtsZ blocks division; it does not directly lyse cells.
Long filaments that keep replicating DNA but fail to divide
Correct: growth and replication continue, but septum formation fails.
Formation of endospores
E. coli does not form endospores.
questions.x: FtsZ, a tubulin-like protein, forms the Z ring at mid-cell that recruits the division machinery and pinches the cell in two. If FtsZ fails, cells keep growing and copying their DNA but cannot divide, so they form long filaments containing many chromosomes. Lack of FtsZ blocks division; it does not by itself make cells lyse.

questions.q: A typical bacterial chromosome is best described as:
o: Several linear DNA molecules with many origins
This describes eukaryotic chromosomes.
One circular double-stranded DNA molecule with a single origin of replication
Correct: e.g. the E. coli chromosome has one origin, oriC.
A circular single-stranded RNA molecule
Cellular genomes are double-stranded DNA.
A linear double-stranded DNA molecule capped by telomeres
Telomeres solve an end-replication problem that circular DNA lacks.
questions.x: Most bacteria carry a single circular, double-stranded DNA chromosome with one origin of replication (oriC in E. coli), packed in the nucleoid region. Circular DNA has no ends, so bacteria do not need telomeres. Several linear chromosomes with many origins describes eukaryotes.

questions.q: An E. coli chromosome has about 4.6 × 10⁶ bp. If each replication fork moves about 1000 bp/s, roughly how long does it take to replicate the whole chromosome from its single origin?
o: About 4 min
Off by a factor of 10 in the arithmetic.
About 19 min
Assumes four forks; one origin gives only two.
About 38 min
Correct: two forks move bidirectionally, so 4.6 × 10⁶ ÷ 2000 bp/s = 2300 s ≈ 38 min.
About 77 min
Assumes a single fork; replication from oriC is bidirectional.
questions.note: One origin, two forks moving in opposite directions.
questions.x: From one origin, replication proceeds in both directions, so two forks work at once. Two forks at 1000 bp/s copy 2000 bp/s, so 4.6 × 10⁶ ÷ 2000 = 2300 s, about 38 minutes. Forgetting that replication is bidirectional doubles the answer to about 77 minutes.

questions.q: Which statement about bacterial plasmids is correct?
o: They carry genes required for survival under all conditions
Essential genes are on the chromosome; plasmids are usually dispensable.
They replicate independently of the chromosome and often carry nonessential genes such as antibiotic resistance
Correct: plasmids are extrachromosomal DNA that can confer useful traits.
They are made of single-stranded RNA
Plasmids are typically circular double-stranded DNA.
They occur only in eukaryotic cells
Plasmids are most common in bacteria (yeast has a few).
questions.x: Plasmids are small, usually circular double-stranded DNA molecules that replicate independently of the chromosome. They often carry genes useful only in certain conditions, such as antibiotic resistance, toxins or the F factor for conjugation. Genes needed under all conditions are normally on the chromosome, so plasmids are usually dispensable.

questions.q: A plasmid that can either replicate on its own or integrate into the bacterial chromosome is called:
o: An episome
Correct: an episome (e.g. the F factor) can exist free or integrated.
A prophage
A prophage is an integrated phage genome, not a plasmid.
A transposon
Transposons move between sites but do not replicate as independent plasmids.
A provirus
A provirus is integrated retroviral DNA in a eukaryotic genome.
questions.x: An episome is a plasmid that can either replicate on its own in the cytoplasm or integrate into the chromosome. The F factor is the classic case: free it makes an F⁺ cell, integrated it makes an Hfr cell. A prophage is an integrated phage genome, not a plasmid.

questions.q: After conjugation between an F⁺ and an F⁻ E. coli cell, what is the F status of each cell?
o: Both are F⁺
Correct: one strand is transferred while the donor replicates its copy, so both end up with F.
Both are F⁻
The donor keeps a copy of the F plasmid.
The donor becomes F⁻ and the recipient F⁺
Rolling-circle replication means the donor never gives up its F plasmid.
Both become Hfr
Hfr requires the F factor to integrate into the chromosome, which is rare.
questions.x: During F⁺ × F⁻ conjugation, one strand of the F plasmid is nicked and passed into the recipient while the donor rebuilds its copy by rolling-circle replication. The recipient then makes the complementary strand. Both cells end up with a full F plasmid, so both are F⁺; the donor never gives up its copy.

questions.q: An Hfr × F⁻ mating is interrupted after 10 minutes. The recipient most likely:
o: Becomes F⁺ because the F factor transfers first
In Hfr cells, most of the F factor is transferred at the very end.
Becomes Hfr
That would require the whole chromosome plus F to transfer, which almost never happens.
Receives the entire donor chromosome
Full transfer takes about 100 minutes.
Gains a few donor genes near the origin of transfer but remains F⁻
Correct: most F sequences enter last, so short matings rarely transfer them.
questions.x: In an Hfr cell, the F factor is integrated into the chromosome. Transfer starts in the middle of F, so donor genes near the origin of transfer go first and the rest of F would come last, after about 100 minutes. Matings usually break off early, so the recipient gains some donor genes but stays F⁻.

questions.q: In interrupted-mating experiments with an Hfr strain, the thr gene first enters recipients at 8 minutes and the lac gene at 17 minutes. What does this indicate?
o: thr lies closer to the origin of transfer than lac
Correct: genes enter in order of their distance from the origin of transfer.
lac lies closer to the origin of transfer than thr
Closer genes enter earlier, so lac is farther.
lac mutates more often than thr
Entry time reflects map position, not mutation rate.
thr is carried on a separate plasmid
Both genes are transferred as part of the Hfr chromosome.
questions.x: In interrupted mating, an Hfr strain transfers its chromosome in a fixed linear order starting at the origin of transfer. The time a gene first appears in recipients measures its distance from that origin. thr entering at 8 minutes and lac at 17 minutes means thr is closer to the origin, and the 9-minute gap is a map distance.

questions.q: Two auxotrophic strains are placed on opposite sides of a filter that lets medium and free DNA pass but blocks cells. No recombinant prototrophs appear, though mixing the strains directly yields many. The gene transfer requires:
o: Conjugation, which needs direct cell-to-cell contact
Correct: blocking contact abolished transfer, the hallmark of conjugation.
Transformation by free DNA
Free DNA could cross the filter, yet no transfer occurred.
Transduction by phage
Phage particles are small enough to pass such a filter.
Transposition within one cell
Transposition alone cannot combine genes from two strains.
questions.x: Conjugation needs direct contact between living donor and recipient cells through a pilus and mating bridge. A filter that blocks cells but passes medium, free DNA and small particles separates the three transfer routes. Since no recombinants formed, transfer could not have been by free DNA (transformation) or phage (transduction), which would cross the filter, so it requires contact.

questions.q: Gene transfer between two strains in a mixed culture is abolished when DNase is added to the medium. The transfer mechanism is most likely:
o: Transformation
Correct: only transformation exposes naked DNA to extracellular DNase.
Conjugation
DNA moves through a mating bridge, protected from DNase.
Transduction
DNA is protected inside the phage capsid.
Lysogenic conversion
Phage DNA is delivered inside capsids, safe from DNase.
questions.note: DNase-sensitive = transformation.
questions.x: The three gene-transfer routes differ in how the DNA travels. In transformation, naked DNA sits in the medium where DNase can destroy it. In conjugation the DNA passes through a protected cell-to-cell bridge, and in transduction it rides inside a phage capsid, so DNase does not block either of those.

questions.q: When heat-killed encapsulated bacteria are mixed with live nonencapsulated bacteria, some live cells become encapsulated and pass the trait on. This results from:
o: Conjugation through a sex pilus
Heat-killed cells cannot conjugate.
Uptake of free DNA from the environment
Correct: this is transformation by DNA released from the killed cells.
Transduction by a bacteriophage
No phage is involved in this setup.
Spontaneous mutation in each live cell
Mutation would not occur at this rate or depend on the dead cells.
questions.x: This is Griffith's transformation experiment. Heat killed the encapsulated cells but left their DNA intact; live non-encapsulated cells took up the capsule gene from the medium, recombined it into their chromosome, and passed the trait to their descendants. Dead cells cannot conjugate, and no phage was involved.

questions.q: A temperate phage that always integrates at one specific chromosomal site can transfer only bacterial genes adjacent to that site. This process is:
o: Generalized transduction
Generalized transduction can carry almost any host gene.
Transformation
Transformation involves free DNA, not phages.
Specialized transduction
Correct: imprecise prophage excision carries neighboring host genes.
Hfr conjugation
Hfr transfer needs a mating bridge, not a phage.
questions.x: In specialized transduction, a temperate phage integrates at one fixed chromosomal site. When the prophage occasionally excises imprecisely, it takes along host genes right next to that site, so only those neighboring genes can be moved. Generalized transduction, by contrast, packages random host DNA and can move almost any gene.

questions.q: In generalized transduction, how does a random fragment of bacterial DNA end up inside a phage particle?
o: Host chromosome fragments made during lytic infection are mistakenly packaged into capsids
Correct: the packaging machinery occasionally fills a head with host DNA.
The prophage excises imprecisely and takes neighboring genes
This describes specialized transduction, which moves only nearby genes.
A conjugative plasmid transfers into the phage head
Plasmids do not conjugate into phages.
Phage reverse transcriptase copies host mRNA into DNA
Bacteriophages used in transduction do not reverse transcribe host mRNA.
questions.x: Generalized transduction happens during the lytic cycle. The phage breaks up the host chromosome, and its packaging machinery sometimes fills a capsid with a host DNA fragment instead of phage DNA. That particle can inject the host DNA into a new cell, where it may recombine, so any gene can be carried. Imprecise prophage excision is the specialized mechanism, limited to neighboring genes.

questions.q: Insertion of a transposon into the middle of a bacterial gene most likely:
o: Always increases that gene's expression
Interrupting a coding region usually destroys function.
Disrupts the gene, often abolishing its function
Correct: insertional mutagenesis breaks up the coding sequence.
Converts the bacterium into an F⁺ donor
F status depends on the F plasmid, not transposition.
Has no effect, because transposons insert only into plasmids
Transposons can insert into chromosomes and plasmids.
questions.x: A transposon that lands inside a coding sequence interrupts it, usually causing a frameshift, premature stop codon or disrupted protein, so the gene loses function. This insertional mutagenesis is widely used to knock out genes on purpose. Insertion can sometimes alter nearby expression, but it does not always increase it.

questions.q: A bacterial insertion sequence (IS element) moves within the genome. Which enzyme does it encode to catalyze this movement?
o: Reverse transcriptase
Bacterial IS elements move as DNA, without an RNA intermediate.
Restriction endonuclease
Restriction enzymes defend against foreign DNA.
Transposase
Correct: IS elements encode transposase flanked by inverted repeats.
Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase
This enzyme charges tRNAs for translation.
questions.x: An insertion sequence is the simplest transposon: a transposase gene flanked by inverted repeats. Transposase recognizes the repeats, cuts the element out or copies it, and inserts it at a new DNA site. Bacterial IS elements move as DNA; reverse transcriptase is used by retrotransposons and retroviruses, which go through an RNA intermediate.

questions.q: A gene for tetracycline resistance flanked by two identical insertion sequences is found on a plasmid in one strain and on the chromosome in its descendant. The best explanation is:
o: The antibiotic induced the same mutation in the chromosome
Antibiotics select mutants; they do not create matching genes.
The descendant took up the gene by transformation from the medium
The gene moved within the same lineage, and IS flanks point to transposition.
The gene is part of a composite transposon that jumped from the plasmid to the chromosome
Correct: two IS elements flanking a gene can move it as a unit.
The chromosome was converted into a plasmid
Chromosomes do not convert into plasmids.
questions.x: A composite transposon is a gene, such as an antibiotic-resistance gene, flanked by two IS elements. The pair of IS elements' transposases can move the whole unit, so the resistance gene can jump from a plasmid to the chromosome or between plasmids. This is how resistance genes spread so widely; antibiotics select for resistance but do not create it.

questions.q: Under which condition is transcription of the E. coli lac operon highest?
o: Glucose high, lactose present
Repressor is off, but low cAMP leaves CAP inactive, so expression is low.
Glucose high, lactose absent
Repressor binds the operator and CAP is inactive.
Glucose low, lactose absent
CAP is active, but the repressor still blocks the operator.
Glucose low, lactose present
Correct: repressor is released and cAMP–CAP activates transcription.
questions.x: The lac operon is controlled by two signals. Lactose (as allolactose) removes the repressor from the operator, and low glucose raises cAMP, which activates CAP to boost RNA polymerase binding. Expression is highest only when both conditions are met: lactose present and glucose low. With glucose high, CAP is inactive and expression stays low even with lactose.

questions.q: When lactose is available, allolactose binds the lac repressor. What happens next?
o: The repressor binds the promoter to recruit RNA polymerase
The repressor blocks transcription; it does not recruit polymerase.
The repressor becomes active and binds the operator more tightly
That describes a corepressor such as tryptophan in the trp operon.
The repressor degrades lacZ mRNA
The repressor is a DNA-binding protein, not a nuclease.
The repressor changes shape and releases the operator
Correct: an inducer inactivates the repressor so RNA polymerase can transcribe.
questions.x: The lac repressor binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. Allolactose, the inducer, binds the repressor and changes its shape (allosteric change), so it can no longer bind the operator and transcription can proceed. The opposite logic, where a small molecule activates a repressor, is the corepressor system of the trp operon.

questions.q: When glucose is scarce, rising cAMP increases lac operon transcription because cAMP:
o: Binds CAP, which binds near the promoter and helps recruit RNA polymerase
Correct: cAMP–CAP is a positive regulator.
Binds the lac repressor and removes it from the operator
Allolactose, not cAMP, inactivates the repressor.
Inactivates the sigma factor
Inactivating sigma would reduce transcription.
Is broken down by β-galactosidase to release energy
β-galactosidase cleaves lactose, not cAMP.
questions.x: CAP is a positive regulator. When glucose is low, cAMP rises and binds CAP; the cAMP–CAP complex binds a site near the lac promoter and helps RNA polymerase bind and start transcription. cAMP does not touch the repressor; inactivating the repressor is the job of allolactose.

questions.q: An E. coli strain with a nonfunctional lacI gene (no repressor) is grown on glycerol with no glucose or lactose. Its lac operon expression is:
o: Absent, because no inducer is present
No inducer is needed when the repressor is missing.
Present only after lactose is added
That is wild-type inducible behavior.
Low, because cAMP levels are low
With no glucose, cAMP is high.
High, even without lactose
Correct: with no repressor and active cAMP–CAP, the operon is constitutive.
questions.x: Without a functional lacI repressor, nothing blocks the operator, so the operon no longer needs an inducer and is expressed constitutively. On glycerol with no glucose, cAMP is high and CAP is active, so expression is high even without lactose. The idea that an inducer is still needed is the trap: the inducer only matters because it removes the repressor.

questions.q: A partial diploid carries lacI⁺ lacOᶜ lacZ⁻ on an F′ plasmid and lacI⁺ lacO⁺ lacZ⁺ on the chromosome. When is functional β-galactosidase made?
o: Only when lactose is present
Correct: Oᶜ acts only in cis on its own mutant lacZ; the working lacZ stays under normal repressor control.
Constitutively, with or without lactose
The constitutive operator drives only the nonfunctional lacZ beside it.
Never
The chromosomal lacZ⁺ is inducible.
Only when glucose is present
Glucose lowers lac expression via low cAMP.
questions.note: Operator mutations are cis-acting; lacI mutations can act in trans.
questions.x: In a partial diploid, a lacOᶜ operator acts only in cis: it controls only the genes on the same DNA molecule. Here the constitutive operator sits next to a broken lacZ, so it makes no working enzyme. The working lacZ⁺ is next to a normal operator and remains under repressor control, so functional β-galactosidase is made only when inducer is present.

questions.q: When tryptophan is abundant, trp operon transcription falls because tryptophan:
o: Binds the trp repressor and releases it from the operator
That is inducer behavior, as in the lac operon.
Binds CAP and blocks its activity
CAP regulation is tied to cAMP and catabolite repression.
Binds the trp repressor, enabling it to bind the operator
Correct: tryptophan is a corepressor that activates the repressor.
Degrades RNA polymerase
Tryptophan does not destroy enzymes.
questions.note: Repressible operon: product turns its own synthesis off.
questions.x: The trp operon is repressible. The trp repressor is inactive alone; when tryptophan is plentiful, it acts as a corepressor, binds the repressor, and lets it bind the operator to shut off the genes for making tryptophan. This is the reverse of the lac inducer, which removes a repressor from the operator.

questions.q: A single bacterial mRNA that encodes three enzymes of the same metabolic pathway is described as:
o: Polycistronic
Correct: one transcript carries several coding sequences, typical of operons.
Monocistronic
Monocistronic mRNAs encode one protein, as in most eukaryotes.
Spliced
Bacterial mRNAs generally are not spliced.
Polyadenylated
A poly-A tail is a eukaryotic mRNA feature.
questions.x: Bacterial operons are transcribed as a single polycistronic mRNA that carries several coding sequences, each with its own ribosome-binding site and start codon. This lets a cell turn on all enzymes of a pathway together. Most eukaryotic mRNAs are monocistronic, encoding one protein each.

questions.q: Why can ribosomes begin translating a bacterial mRNA before its transcription is finished?
o: Bacterial mRNA is spliced faster than eukaryotic mRNA
Bacterial mRNAs are generally not spliced.
Ribosomes start at the 3′ end, which is made first
The 5′ end is made first, and translation also starts near the 5′ end.
Bacterial RNA polymerase also forms peptide bonds
Only ribosomes form peptide bonds.
No nuclear envelope separates transcription from translation
Correct: both occur in the cytoplasm, so they can be coupled.
questions.x: In bacteria there is no nuclear envelope, so transcription and translation happen in the same compartment. Since mRNA is made 5′ to 3′ and ribosomes start near the 5′ end, ribosomes can begin translating while RNA polymerase is still making the rest of the transcript. In eukaryotes, mRNA must be processed and exported from the nucleus first.

questions.q: In bacteria, the small ribosomal subunit finds the start codon by base pairing its 16S rRNA with:
o: The Shine–Dalgarno sequence upstream of the start codon
Correct: this purine-rich sequence positions the ribosome at AUG.
The 5′ methylguanosine cap
The 5′ cap is used by eukaryotic ribosomes.
The poly-A tail
Bacterial mRNAs lack the stable poly-A tails used in eukaryotes.
The TATA box
The TATA box is a eukaryotic promoter element in DNA, not mRNA.
questions.x: Bacterial ribosomes find the start codon by base pairing between the 3′ end of 16S rRNA in the 30S subunit and the Shine–Dalgarno sequence, a purine-rich site a few bases upstream of AUG. This lets bacteria start translation at several internal sites on a polycistronic mRNA. Eukaryotic ribosomes instead bind the 5′ cap and scan for the first AUG.

questions.q: Bacterial translation begins with which initiator amino acid?
o: Unmodified methionine
Eukaryotes and archaea initiate with methionine.
N-formylmethionine
Correct: bacterial initiator tRNA carries fMet.
Formylglycine
Glycine is not the initiator amino acid.
Valine
Valine is not used to start translation.
questions.x: Bacteria begin every protein with N-formylmethionine carried by a special initiator tRNA. The formyl group is often removed afterward. Eukaryotes and archaea start with unmodified methionine, and fMet peptides act as a danger signal that attracts human neutrophils to bacterial infections.

questions.q: Which component allows bacterial RNA polymerase to recognize promoter sequences?
o: The sigma factor
Correct: sigma directs the core enzyme to the −10 and −35 promoter regions.
The rho factor
Rho helps terminate transcription.
TFIID
TFIID is a eukaryotic general transcription factor.
DNA gyrase
Gyrase relieves supercoiling; it does not read promoters.
questions.x: Bacterial RNA polymerase core enzyme can make RNA but cannot find promoters on its own. The sigma factor binds the core to form the holoenzyme and recognizes the −35 and −10 promoter elements, then is released after transcription begins. Different sigma factors let bacteria turn on different sets of genes, while rho helps end transcription.

questions.q: Rifampin binds the β subunit of bacterial RNA polymerase. Which process does it directly block?
o: DNA replication
Replication uses DNA polymerase.
Peptide bond formation
That is the ribosome's job.
RNA synthesis (transcription)
Correct: inhibiting RNA polymerase stops mRNA production.
Peptidoglycan cross-linking
That is blocked by β-lactams.
questions.x: Rifampin binds the β subunit of bacterial RNA polymerase and blocks RNA chain elongation, stopping transcription. Because bacterial RNA polymerase differs from the eukaryotic enzymes, the drug is selective. DNA replication uses DNA polymerase and is not the direct target.

questions.q: Penicillin kills growing bacteria mainly by:
o: Binding the 30S ribosomal subunit
That is how aminoglycosides and tetracyclines act.
Inhibiting transpeptidases that cross-link peptidoglycan, so cells lyse osmotically
Correct: penicillin binds penicillin-binding proteins and weakens new wall.
Inhibiting DNA gyrase
That is how fluoroquinolones act.
Dissolving the plasma membrane
That is closer to polymyxin action.
questions.x: Penicillin and other β-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins, the transpeptidases that cross-link the peptide chains of peptidoglycan. Without cross-links, the new wall is weak, and the cell bursts from internal osmotic pressure. Blocking the 30S subunit is how aminoglycosides and tetracyclines work, not β-lactams.

questions.q: E. coli grown with penicillin in a medium made isotonic with sucrose become round cells that survive. Why don't they lyse?
o: With no osmotic gradient, the wall-deficient cells do not take in enough water to burst
Correct: the wall prevents osmotic lysis, which isotonic medium avoids.
Sucrose inactivates penicillin
Penicillin still acts; that is why the cells lose wall and become round.
Sucrose provides building blocks to repair the wall
Sucrose is not a peptidoglycan precursor.
The cells convert into endospores
E. coli does not sporulate.
questions.x: The cell wall protects bacteria from bursting because their cytoplasm is hypertonic to most surroundings, so water rushes in. Penicillin still removes the wall, producing round wall-deficient cells, but in an isotonic sucrose medium there is no net water influx, so they survive. This shows the wall's main job is resisting osmotic lysis.

questions.q: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci change the D-Ala-D-Ala end of their peptidoglycan precursors to D-Ala-D-lactate. Why does this confer resistance?
o: D-lactate enzymatically destroys vancomycin
The change modifies the target, not the drug.
Vancomycin binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus, and the altered end binds it poorly
Correct: changing the target reduces vancomycin binding.
The change closes outer-membrane porins
Enterococci are Gram-positive and have no outer membrane.
The change alters the 50S ribosomal subunit
Vancomycin acts on wall synthesis, not ribosomes.
questions.x: Vancomycin works by binding the D-Ala-D-Ala end of peptidoglycan precursors, physically blocking cross-linking. Swapping the terminal D-Ala for D-lactate removes a key hydrogen bond and reduces vancomycin binding about a thousandfold, so the wall can still be built. This is target modification, not destruction of the drug.

questions.q: Lysozyme in tears cleaves the glycosidic bonds of the peptidoglycan backbone. Which bacteria are most directly susceptible?
o: Gram-negative bacteria, because their wall is thin
Their outer membrane largely blocks lysozyme from reaching the wall.
Gram-positive bacteria, whose peptidoglycan is exposed
Correct: no outer membrane shields their wall.
Mycoplasma, because they lack a wall
No wall means no lysozyme target.
Archaea, because their walls are made of peptidoglycan
Archaea lack peptidoglycan.
questions.x: Lysozyme cuts the β(1→4) bonds between NAM and NAG in the peptidoglycan backbone. In Gram-positive bacteria this thick wall is exposed on the surface, so lysozyme reaches it directly. Gram-negative bacteria have a thinner wall, but their outer membrane largely keeps lysozyme from reaching it, so thinness alone does not make them more susceptible.

questions.q: Tetracycline blocks aminoacyl-tRNA binding to the bacterial 30S subunit. Why does it affect human cytosolic translation very little?
o: Human ribosomes lack an A site
Eukaryotic ribosomes also have A, P and E sites.
Human cells make proteins without ribosomes
All cells use ribosomes.
Human cytosolic ribosomes are 80S, with 40S and 60S subunits that bind it poorly
Correct: structural differences give selective toxicity.
Human cytosolic ribosomes are 70S
Human cytosolic ribosomes are 80S; only mitochondrial ones resemble 70S.
questions.x: Selective toxicity comes from differences between bacterial and human targets. Bacteria use 70S ribosomes (30S and 50S), while human cytosolic ribosomes are 80S (40S and 60S) and bind tetracycline poorly. Human mitochondrial ribosomes resemble bacterial ones, which explains some side effects of ribosome-targeting antibiotics.

questions.q: Chloramphenicol inhibits the peptidyl transferase center of the bacterial 50S subunit. Which step of protein synthesis does it block?
o: Binding of the small subunit to the Shine–Dalgarno sequence
That initiation step involves the 30S subunit.
Transcription of mRNA
