Transcription is done by RNA polymerase.
Charging of tRNAs with amino acids
Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge tRNAs.
Peptide bond formation between amino acids in the P and A sites
Correct: peptidyl transferase links the growing chain to the incoming amino acid.
questions.x: Peptidyl transferase, an activity of the rRNA in the 50S subunit, forms the peptide bond between the growing chain in the P site and the amino acid on the tRNA in the A site. Chloramphenicol blocks this step, stopping elongation. Initiation at the Shine–Dalgarno sequence is a 30S event and is not directly blocked.

questions.q: Ciprofloxacin inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase. What is the most direct consequence?
o: Ribosomes stall at stop codons
Gyrase is not part of translation.
Supercoils build up ahead of replication forks, halting DNA replication
Correct: gyrase (a type II topoisomerase) relieves positive supercoiling.
Peptidoglycan cross-links fail to form
That is the β-lactam mechanism.
Folic acid synthesis stops
That is the sulfonamide mechanism.
questions.x: DNA gyrase is a bacterial type II topoisomerase that cuts both strands to remove positive supercoils building up ahead of replication forks and adds negative supercoils. Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin inhibit gyrase, so torsional strain builds and replication stalls, with broken DNA left behind. Folate synthesis and wall cross-linking are the targets of sulfonamides and β-lactams.

questions.q: Sulfonamides block the bacterial pathway that makes folic acid from PABA. Why are human cells largely unaffected?
o: Human cells contain no DNA to synthesize
Human cells need folate for DNA synthesis too.
Human dihydrofolate reductase degrades sulfonamides
DHFR is not a sulfonamide-degrading enzyme.
Cholesterol in human membranes blocks sulfonamide entry
Selectivity comes from the missing target, not drug exclusion.
Humans obtain folate from the diet and lack this synthetic pathway
Correct: the drug's target enzyme does not exist in human cells.
questions.x: Sulfonamides mimic PABA and block dihydropteroate synthase, an enzyme bacteria need to make folate from scratch. Humans lack this pathway and absorb ready-made folate from food, so the drug has no human target. Humans do need folate for DNA synthesis, so selectivity comes from the missing enzyme, not a lack of need.

questions.q: Polymyxins bind lipopolysaccharide and disrupt bacterial membranes. Their activity is mostly limited to:
o: Gram-positive bacteria
Gram-positives have no LPS for polymyxins to bind.
Fungi
Fungi lack LPS.
Viruses
Viruses lack LPS and have no metabolism to disrupt.
Gram-negative bacteria
Correct: LPS is found only in Gram-negative outer membranes.
questions.x: Polymyxins are cationic peptides that bind the negatively charged lipid A of lipopolysaccharide and disrupt the outer membrane and then the inner membrane. LPS is found only in the Gram-negative outer membrane. Gram-positives, fungi and viruses lack LPS, so polymyxins have little effect on them.

questions.q: Amoxicillin is combined with clavulanic acid to treat infections caused by β-lactamase–producing bacteria. What does clavulanic acid do?
o: Blocks the 30S ribosomal subunit
Clavulanic acid does not target ribosomes.
Inhibits β-lactamase, protecting amoxicillin from destruction
Correct: it is a β-lactamase inhibitor.
Makes the outer membrane permeable to all drugs
That is not its mechanism.
Binds D-Ala-D-Ala like vancomycin
That describes glycopeptide antibiotics.
questions.x: Many resistant bacteria make β-lactamases, enzymes that break the β-lactam ring and inactivate penicillins like amoxicillin. Clavulanic acid has a β-lactam structure that binds and irreversibly inactivates β-lactamase while having little antibacterial activity itself. Pairing it with amoxicillin protects the antibiotic so it can reach its real target, the transpeptidases.

questions.q: A patient stops an antibiotic course early, and a resistant population later takes over the infection. The best explanation is that the antibiotic:
o: Caused the bacteria to mutate in order to survive
Mutations arise randomly, not in response to need.
Killed susceptible cells, leaving pre-existing resistant cells to multiply
Correct: antibiotics select for resistance that is already present.
Taught surviving bacteria to avoid the drug
Bacteria do not learn; resistance is genetic.
Changed into a weaker compound inside the body
Drug breakdown does not create resistant genotypes.
questions.x: Antibiotics act as a selective pressure, not a mutagen that creates resistance on demand. Resistant cells already exist in a large population because of random mutation or acquired genes. The drug kills susceptible cells, and if treatment stops early the surviving resistant cells grow back and dominate.

questions.q: Many small parallel cultures plated on phage give wildly different numbers of resistant colonies (many zero, a few hundreds), while repeated samples from one large culture give similar counts. This supports the idea that:
o: Resistance mutations arise randomly before exposure to the phage
Correct: early random mutations produce 'jackpot' cultures.
The phage induces resistance on contact
Induced resistance would give similar counts in every culture.
Resistance spreads mainly by conjugation
Conjugation does not explain the variance pattern.
Plating errors are larger for small cultures
Sampling error is what the large-culture control measures, and it was small.
questions.x: This is the Luria–Delbrück fluctuation test. If resistance arose randomly before exposure, a mutation early in one culture's growth would leave many resistant descendants (a jackpot), while most cultures would have few or none, producing huge variation. If phage induced resistance on contact, every culture would show similar counts, like the samples from a single large culture.

questions.q: Colonies on a complete-medium master plate are replica plated onto minimal medium. Colonies that grow on the master plate but not on minimal medium are:
o: Prototrophs
Prototrophs grow on minimal medium.
Lysogens
Lysogeny is unrelated to nutritional requirements.
F⁻ cells
F status does not determine growth on minimal medium.
Auxotrophs
Correct: they cannot synthesize some nutrient that minimal medium lacks.
questions.x: Replica plating copies the colony pattern from a complete-medium master plate onto minimal medium. Prototrophs can make all their own building blocks and grow on both. Colonies missing on minimal medium are auxotrophs, which lack a biosynthetic enzyme and need a nutrient that only complete medium supplies.

questions.q: Why are antibiotics such as penicillin ineffective against influenza virus?
o: The influenza capsid is made of resistant peptidoglycan
Viral capsids are protein, not peptidoglycan.
Influenza produces β-lactamase
Viruses do not make β-lactamase, and they have no wall for penicillin to act on anyway.
Viruses lack the cell walls, ribosomes and metabolism that antibiotics target
Correct: antibacterial drugs act on bacterial structures viruses do not have.
Viruses are too large for antibiotics to reach
Viruses are much smaller than bacteria.
questions.x: Antibiotics target bacterial structures and processes: peptidoglycan walls, 70S ribosomes, bacterial enzymes such as DNA gyrase and folate synthesis. Viruses have none of these, since they use the host's ribosomes and metabolism, so penicillin has nothing to act on. Influenza must be treated with antivirals that target viral proteins such as neuraminidase.

questions.q: Every virus particle contains:
o: A DNA or RNA genome enclosed in a protein capsid
Correct: genome plus capsid is the minimal virion.
Both DNA and RNA genomes
A virion carries either DNA or RNA as its genome.
A lipid envelope
Many viruses are naked, with no envelope.
Ribosomes for protein synthesis
Viruses rely on host ribosomes.
questions.x: The minimum virion is a nucleic acid genome, either DNA or RNA but not both, inside a protein capsid. Some viruses add a lipid envelope taken from the host, but many are naked, so the envelope is not universal. Viruses never carry ribosomes; they depend on the host for translation.

questions.q: A mild detergent destroys the infectivity of one virus but not another. The detergent-sensitive virus most likely:
o: Has a DNA genome
Genome type does not determine detergent sensitivity.
Has an icosahedral capsid
Capsid shape does not make a virus detergent-sensitive.
Lacks a capsid
All viruses have a capsid.
Has a lipid envelope
Correct: detergents dissolve lipid membranes, removing the attachment proteins.
questions.x: Envelope lipid comes from host membranes and is studded with the viral glycoproteins needed to attach and enter cells. Detergents dissolve lipid bilayers, destroying the envelope and its attachment proteins, so enveloped viruses lose infectivity. Naked viruses have only a protein capsid and are usually much more resistant to detergents, alcohol and drying.

questions.q: The lipid envelope of an influenza virion comes from:
o: Lipids made by viral enzymes
Viruses do not encode lipid-synthesis pathways for their envelope.
Folded capsid proteins
Capsid proteins are protein, not lipid.
A bacterial outer membrane
Influenza infects animal cells, not bacteria.
Host cell membrane acquired as the virus buds
Correct: the envelope is host membrane studded with viral glycoproteins.
questions.x: Enveloped viruses such as influenza insert their glycoproteins into a host membrane, here the plasma membrane, then bud out wrapped in that patch. So the envelope's lipids come from the host, while the embedded spike proteins (hemagglutinin and neuraminidase) are viral. Viruses do not have their own lipid-synthesis pathways for building an envelope.

questions.q: Viruses cannot replicate outside host cells mainly because they lack:
o: Ribosomes and the metabolic machinery to make proteins and ATP
Correct: they are obligate intracellular parasites.
Genetic material
Every virus carries DNA or RNA.
A protein capsid
Every virion has a capsid.
The ability to mutate
Viruses mutate, often rapidly.
questions.x: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites. They carry a genome but no ribosomes, no ATP-producing metabolism and no machinery to build their parts, so they must hijack a host cell to make new virions. Outside a cell they are inert particles, even though they do carry genetic material and can mutate.

questions.q: Phages labeled with ³²P or with ³⁵S infect bacteria in separate tubes. After blending and centrifuging, the bacterial pellet contains mostly ³²P. This shows that:
o: Protein enters the cell and carries the genetic information
³⁵S-labeled protein stayed in the supernatant.
DNA, not protein, enters the cell and directs phage production
Correct: ³²P labels DNA, ³⁵S labels protein, which stays outside.
The capsid stays attached and serves as the genome
The capsid is protein, and protein did not enter.
Phage DNA contains sulfur
DNA has phosphorus but no sulfur.
questions.x: In the Hershey–Chase experiment, ³²P labels DNA (phosphate backbone) and ³⁵S labels protein (cysteine and methionine); DNA has no sulfur. After blending knocked empty phage coats off, the ³²P was found with the bacteria while the ³⁵S stayed outside. So DNA is the material that enters the cell and directs production of new phages.

questions.q: In the lytic cycle, a bacteriophage:
o: Uses host machinery to make many progeny and then bursts the cell
Correct: lytic infection ends in host lysis.
Integrates into the host chromosome and stays dormant
That describes lysogeny.
Transfers plasmids between bacteria
Plasmid transfer occurs by conjugation.
Forms a spore that survives harsh conditions
Phages do not form spores.
questions.x: In the lytic cycle, a phage injects its genome, takes over host transcription and translation to make many copies of phage parts, assembles new virions, and then lyses the cell to release them. The lysogenic cycle is the alternative: the genome integrates as a prophage and is copied quietly with the host chromosome.

questions.q: A lysogenic bacterial culture is exposed to UV light and soon lyses, releasing phages. What is the best explanation?
o: DNA damage triggers the SOS response, inactivating the phage repressor so the prophage enters the lytic cycle
Correct: this is prophage induction.
UV kills the bacteria, releasing phages that were already assembled
Lysogens contain no assembled phages until induction.
UV mutates the prophage into a virulent strain in every cell
Induction is a regulated switch, not mass mutation.
UV breaks down capsids, freeing phage DNA
This would reduce, not increase, phage release.
questions.x: A prophage such as λ stays dormant because a phage repressor blocks its lytic genes. UV damages host DNA and activates RecA in the SOS response, which triggers cleavage of the repressor, so the prophage excises and enters the lytic cycle. Lysogens hold no finished phages before induction, so the phages released were made after the UV exposure.

questions.q: Corynebacterium diphtheriae makes diphtheria toxin only when it carries a particular prophage. This is an example of:
o: Transformation
No free DNA is taken up.
Generalized transduction
The toxin gene is part of the phage genome, not a packaged host fragment.
Conjugation
No mating bridge is involved.
Lysogenic conversion
Correct: genes on the prophage give the host a new trait.
questions.x: In lysogenic conversion, genes carried on a prophage change the host's phenotype. The diphtheria toxin gene belongs to the phage genome, so only C. diphtheriae lysogenized by that phage can make toxin. Transduction moves host genes between bacteria, whereas here the new trait is encoded by the phage itself.

questions.q: A bacterium lysogenic for phage λ cannot be productively infected by more λ phages but is still killed by unrelated phages. What best explains this?
o: The bacterium makes antibodies against λ
Bacteria do not make antibodies.
The prophage makes the cell wall impermeable to all phage DNA
Unrelated phages still infect, so entry is not blocked.
The prophage-encoded repressor also blocks lytic genes of incoming λ genomes
Correct: superinfection immunity is specific to phages controlled by that repressor.
The lysogen has stopped transcribing all of its genes
Lysogens grow and express their genes normally.
questions.x: A λ prophage stays dormant because it constantly makes the λ repressor. That repressor also binds the operators of any new λ genome that enters, so incoming λ cannot start its lytic program, a state called superinfection immunity. Unrelated phages use different regulatory sequences the repressor does not recognize, so they can still infect and kill the cell.

questions.q: During lysogeny, the phage genome:
o: Is rapidly transcribed to produce progeny phages
That describes the lytic cycle.
Is destroyed by host enzymes
The genome persists as a prophage.
Is integrated into the host chromosome and copied along with it
Correct: the integrated prophage is passed to daughter cells.
Is converted into RNA for storage
The prophage remains DNA.
questions.x: In lysogeny, a temperate phage integrates its DNA into the host chromosome as a prophage. Most phage genes are kept silent, and the prophage is copied and passed to daughter cells each time the bacterium divides. Under stress it can later excise and switch to the lytic cycle.

questions.q: Purified genomic RNA from a polio-like virus is injected into cells and produces infectious virions, but purified genomic RNA from an influenza-like virus does not. Why?
o: Influenza viruses have DNA genomes
Influenza has a segmented negative-sense RNA genome.
The polio-like RNA encodes reverse transcriptase
Polio-like viruses do not use reverse transcription.
The first genome is positive-sense and translated directly; the negative-sense genome needs a polymerase packaged in the virion
Correct: negative-sense RNA must first be copied by viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
Influenza RNA is too long for ribosomes to read
The issue is strand sense, not length.
questions.note: Naked +RNA is infectious; naked −RNA is not.
questions.x: A positive-sense RNA genome has the same sense as mRNA, so host ribosomes can translate it at once to make viral proteins, including the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; naked polio RNA is therefore infectious. A negative-sense genome such as influenza's must first be copied into mRNA, and host cells lack an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, so the virion must bring its own.

questions.q: Most DNA viruses that infect animal cells replicate in the nucleus, while most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm. A key reason DNA viruses go to the nucleus is to:
o: Reach the ribosomes, which are located in the nucleus
Translation occurs in the cytoplasm.
Avoid the cytoplasm, where DNA cannot exist
DNA can be present in the cytoplasm (e.g. poxviruses).
Use host DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and replication enzymes found there
Correct: host enzymes for transcribing and copying DNA are nuclear.
Use host reverse transcriptase located in the nucleus
Host cells do not provide reverse transcriptase for viral replication.
questions.x: Cells keep their DNA-dependent RNA polymerases and DNA replication enzymes in the nucleus, so most DNA viruses go there to use them for transcription and genome copying. Most RNA viruses bring or encode their own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and can work in the cytoplasm. Poxviruses are the exception that proves the rule: they replicate in the cytoplasm because they carry their own DNA enzymes.

questions.q: After reverse transcription, which retroviral enzyme inserts the viral DNA into the host chromosome?
o: Reverse transcriptase
Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA but does not integrate it.
Protease
Protease cleaves viral polyproteins.
Integrase
Correct: integrase splices the viral DNA into host DNA to form a provirus.
DNA gyrase
Gyrase is a bacterial topoisomerase.
questions.x: Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase to make double-stranded DNA from their RNA genome, then integrase cuts the host DNA and joins the viral DNA into it as a provirus. The provirus is then transcribed by host RNA polymerase II like a cellular gene. Reverse transcriptase makes the DNA but cannot insert it.

questions.q: HIV rapidly evolves resistance to single drugs mainly because:
o: Its double-stranded DNA genome mutates when exposed to drugs
HIV virions carry RNA, and drugs select mutations rather than cause them.
Integrase deletes host genes during integration
Integration does not generate viral drug resistance.
HIV undergoes meiosis to shuffle its genes
Viruses do not undergo meiosis.
Reverse transcriptase lacks proofreading, so copying is error-prone
Correct: high error rates create many variants for selection.
questions.x: HIV reverse transcriptase has no 3′→5′ proofreading, so it makes roughly one error per genome copy, and HIV replicates in huge numbers. That constantly generates a cloud of variants, and any drug selects the resistant ones that already exist. Combination therapy works because a virus is unlikely to carry resistance to several drugs at once.

questions.q: Zidovudine (AZT) is a thymidine analog with an azido group in place of the 3′-OH. How does it inhibit HIV?
o: It blocks binding of gp120 to CD4
That describes entry inhibitors.
It inhibits viral protease
Protease inhibitors are a separate drug class.
It prevents new virions from budding
AZT acts during reverse transcription.
It terminates the growing DNA chain after reverse transcriptase incorporates it
Correct: without a 3′-OH, the next nucleotide cannot be added.
questions.x: DNA polymerases, including reverse transcriptase, add each new nucleotide to the 3′-OH of the growing chain. AZT is a thymidine analog with an azido group in place of that 3′-OH, so once reverse transcriptase incorporates it, no further nucleotide can be added and the chain terminates. HIV reverse transcriptase uses AZT much more readily than human DNA polymerases, giving selectivity.

questions.q: HIV binds and enters helper T cells but does not enter hepatocytes. What best explains this?
o: Hepatocytes lack the CD4 receptor and coreceptors HIV binds
Correct: viral host range depends on specific surface receptors.
Hepatocytes lack ribosomes
Hepatocytes have abundant ribosomes.
Hepatocytes have no nucleus
Hepatocytes are nucleated.
HIV can only enter cells that are dividing
Receptor binding, not division, determines entry.
questions.x: A virus's host range and tissue tropism depend largely on matching viral attachment proteins with specific host surface receptors. HIV's gp120 binds CD4 plus a coreceptor (CCR5 or CXCR4), found on helper T cells and macrophages but not on hepatocytes. Without those receptors HIV cannot attach and enter, even though hepatocytes have plenty of ribosomes and a nucleus.

questions.q: A retroviral virion carries its genome as:
o: One double-stranded DNA molecule
The DNA copy forms only after infection.
One negative-sense single-stranded RNA
Retroviral RNA has mRNA sense.
A circular DNA plasmid
Retroviruses package RNA, not plasmids.
Two copies of positive-sense single-stranded RNA
Correct: retroviruses are diploid, carrying two +ssRNA copies.
questions.x: Retroviruses package two identical copies of a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome, so the virion is effectively diploid. Even though the genome has mRNA sense, it is reverse transcribed into double-stranded DNA rather than translated directly on entry. The DNA form appears only after infection begins.

questions.q: HIV protease inhibitors interfere with which step of the viral life cycle?
o: Cutting viral polyproteins into functional proteins, so new virions stay immature and noninfectious
Correct: protease is needed for virion maturation.
Reverse transcription of the genome
That is blocked by reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
Integration into the host chromosome
That is blocked by integrase inhibitors.
Attachment to the CD4 receptor
That is blocked by entry inhibitors.
questions.x: HIV makes its structural proteins and enzymes as long polyproteins (Gag and Gag-Pol). After budding, viral protease cuts them into individual proteins, which reorganize to form a mature, infectious core. Protease inhibitors block this step, so particles still bud but remain immature and noninfectious.

questions.q: Plating 0.1 mL of a 10⁻⁶ dilution of a phage stock on a bacterial lawn gives 50 plaques. What is the titer of the original stock?
o: 5 × 10⁻⁴ PFU/mL
Multiplies by the dilution instead of dividing by it.
5 × 10⁷ PFU/mL
Ignores the 0.1 mL plating volume.
5 × 10⁸ PFU/mL
Correct: 50 ÷ 0.1 mL = 500 PFU/mL, × 10⁶ = 5 × 10⁸ PFU/mL.
5 × 10⁹ PFU/mL
Corrects for the volume twice.
questions.note: Titer = plaques ÷ (volume × dilution).
questions.x: Titer equals plaques divided by (volume plated × dilution). Here 50 plaques ÷ 0.1 mL = 500 PFU/mL in the 10⁻⁶ dilution, and multiplying back by 10⁶ gives 5 × 10⁸ PFU/mL in the original stock. Forgetting the 0.1 mL volume gives an answer ten times too low.

questions.q: Each clear plaque on a lawn of bacteria represents:
o: A colony of phage-resistant bacteria
Resistant colonies grow; plaques are clearings.
A zone of antibiotic killing
No antibiotic is used in a plaque assay.
An area where progeny of one infecting phage lysed the surrounding cells
Correct: one plaque traces back to one infectious particle.
A colony of lysogenic bacteria
Lysogens grow rather than clear the lawn.
questions.x: In a plaque assay, a single infectious phage infects one cell in a lawn, and its progeny infect and lyse neighboring cells in rounds, leaving a clear zone. So each plaque traces back to one infectious particle, which is why plaque counts measure plaque-forming units. Resistant or lysogenic cells grow instead of clearing.

questions.q: In a one-step growth experiment, cells artificially broken open 5 minutes after infection contain no infectious phage, even though phage DNA is being copied. Why?
o: The infecting virions disassembled on entry, and new virions are not yet assembled
Correct: this is the eclipse period.
The phage failed to infect the cells
Phage DNA replication shows infection occurred.
The phage DNA integrated permanently and stopped
Ongoing DNA replication rules out dormancy.
Host restriction enzymes destroyed all the phages
The phage DNA is replicating, so it was not destroyed.
questions.x: In the eclipse period of a one-step growth curve, the infecting virion has come apart to release its genome, and new virions have not yet been assembled. Breaking cells open at this point releases no infectious particles even though phage DNA is being copied. Later, assembly finishes and intracellular infectious phage rises before lysis.

questions.q: A culture of 10⁶ bacteria is infected so that each cell receives one phage. After lysis, 2 × 10⁸ phages are released. What is the average burst size?
o: Off by a factor of 100.
Off by a factor of 10.
Correct: 2 × 10⁸ phages ÷ 10⁶ cells = 200 phages per cell.
Off by a factor of 10 in the other direction.
questions.x: Burst size is the average number of phages released per infected cell. With every cell infected by one phage, 2 × 10⁸ phages ÷ 10⁶ cells = 200 phages per cell. Keeping exponents straight is the key: 10⁸ ÷ 10⁶ = 10², not 10¹ or 10³.

questions.q: Many enveloped viruses leave host cells by budding rather than lysis. A likely consequence is that:
o: The host cell always bursts at once
That describes lytic release.
The host cell can survive and release virions over a long period
Correct: budding need not destroy the cell immediately.
The released virions lack surface proteins
Viral glycoproteins are inserted into the membrane before budding.
The released virions gain a peptidoglycan coat
Animal cells have no peptidoglycan.
questions.x: Enveloped viruses often leave by budding: viral glycoproteins are inserted into the host membrane, and new virions push out wrapped in that membrane. Because the cell is not torn open all at once, it can stay alive and keep releasing virions for a long time, which helps chronic infections. Lytic release, by contrast, destroys the cell in one burst.

questions.q: Prions are infectious agents made of:
o: A small naked RNA circle
That describes a viroid.
Misfolded protein with no nucleic acid
Correct: prions propagate without any genome.
DNA packaged in a protein capsid
That describes a DNA virus.
Lipid vesicles containing RNA
Prions contain no RNA.
questions.x: Prions are infectious agents made only of a misfolded form of a normal host protein, PrP, with no DNA or RNA. They cause transmissible spongiform encephalopathies such as Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease. A small naked circular RNA is a viroid, a different nonliving agent.

questions.q: How does the amount of prion protein increase in an infected host?
o: Host polymerases replicate the prion genome
Prions have no genome.
Reverse transcriptase makes DNA copies of the prion
Prions have no RNA to reverse transcribe.
Prion particles divide by binary fission
Prions are not cells.
The misfolded, β-sheet–rich form induces normal PrP to adopt the misfolded shape
Correct: prions template conformational conversion.
questions.x: Prions spread by templated misfolding. The misfolded, β-sheet–rich PrP binds normal, mostly α-helical PrP made by the host and converts it into the misfolded shape, which then converts more. The amount of prion grows without any genome or replication of nucleic acid, so polymerases and fission play no role.

questions.q: An infectious brain extract stays infectious after UV irradiation and nuclease treatment but loses infectivity after harsh protein denaturants. The agent is most likely a:
o: Virus
UV and nucleases would inactivate a viral genome.
Viroid
A viroid is naked RNA and would be destroyed by nucleases.
Prion
Correct: resistance to nucleic-acid damage and sensitivity to denaturants indicate a protein agent.
Bacterium
Bacteria would be killed by UV and have DNA genomes.
questions.x: Treatments act like diagnostic tests. UV and nucleases destroy nucleic acids, so viruses, viroids and bacteria would be inactivated, while protein denaturants destroy protein structure. An agent that survives nucleic-acid destruction but fails after denaturation is made of protein, the defining property of a prion.

questions.q: Viroids differ from viruses in that viroids:
o: Are made only of protein
That describes prions.
Infect only bacteria
Known viroids infect plants.
Are a small circular RNA with no protein capsid
Correct: viroids are naked, noncoding RNA plant pathogens.
Are DNA wrapped in a lipid envelope
Viroids are RNA and have no envelope.
questions.x: Viroids are the smallest known infectious agents: short circular single-stranded RNA molecules with no capsid, no envelope and no protein-coding genes. They infect plants and rely entirely on host enzymes to replicate. A virus always has at least a genome inside a protein capsid.

questions.q: A viroid's RNA encodes no proteins. How can it still replicate and cause disease in a plant?
o: Host ribosomes translate it into a toxin
Viroids do not encode proteins.
It is reverse transcribed and integrated into the plant genome
Viroids replicate as RNA by rolling-circle copying.
It converts host proteins into a misfolded infectious form
That is prion behavior.
Host RNA polymerase copies it, and the viroid RNA interferes with host gene expression
Correct: viroids rely entirely on host enzymes and act through their RNA.
questions.x: Viroid RNA encodes nothing, so it depends on host enzymes. Host RNA polymerase is redirected to copy the circular RNA by rolling-circle replication. Disease results from the viroid RNA itself, which can interfere with host gene expression, for example through RNA silencing of plant genes.

questions.q: Influenza can undergo sudden major antigenic changes when two different strains infect the same cell. This depends on its:
o: Double-stranded DNA genome
Influenza has an RNA genome.
Reverse transcriptase activity
Influenza is not a retrovirus.
Segmented genome, which allows segments to reassort
Correct: reassortment of segments causes antigenic shift.
Lack of an envelope
Influenza is enveloped.
questions.note: Shift = reassortment; drift = gradual point mutations.
questions.x: Influenza has a segmented RNA genome of eight pieces. When two strains infect one cell, segments can be mixed in new progeny, producing reassortants with new hemagglutinin or neuraminidase genes; this abrupt antigenic shift can spark pandemics. Antigenic drift, by contrast, is the slow accumulation of point mutations from error-prone copying.

questions.q: Plant sap passed through a filter that retains all bacteria still causes disease in healthy plants. This suggests the agent is:
o: A rod-shaped bacterium
Bacteria would be retained by the filter.
A fungal spore
Fungal spores are larger than bacteria.
A protozoan
Protozoa are much larger than bacteria.
Smaller than bacteria, such as a virus
Correct: viruses pass through bacteria-retaining filters.
questions.x: Filters with pores small enough to hold back bacteria were how viruses were first discovered, with tobacco mosaic virus. If the filtered sap still causes disease, the agent must be smaller than bacteria, such as a virus. Fungi and protozoa are even larger than bacteria and would also be retained.

questions.q: A retrovirus carrying no oncogene of its own causes tumors when it integrates beside a cellular proto-oncogene. The most likely mechanism is:
o: The viral long terminal repeat promoter/enhancer drives overexpression of the nearby gene
Correct: this is insertional activation.
Reverse transcriptase directly mutates the p53 protein
Reverse transcriptase copies nucleic acid; it does not modify proteins.
The capsid binds and activates the proto-oncogene's protein
Capsid proteins do not activate host oncoproteins.
Integrase deletes the entire chromosome
Integration inserts DNA; it does not delete whole chromosomes.
questions.x: When a retrovirus integrates, its long terminal repeats carry a strong promoter and enhancer. If the provirus lands next to a proto-oncogene, these elements can drive abnormally high expression of that gene, turning it into an oncogene, a process called insertional activation. This explains how retroviruses with no oncogene of their own can still cause tumors.

questions.q: Which property distinguishes bacterial exotoxins from endotoxin?
o: Exotoxins are made only by Gram-negative bacteria
Gram-positive bacteria also make many exotoxins.
Exotoxins are secreted proteins; endotoxin is LPS from the Gram-negative outer membrane
Correct: endotoxin is a structural lipid–sugar component.
Endotoxin is a secreted protein
Endotoxin is lipopolysaccharide, not protein.
Exotoxins are heat-stable lipids
Most exotoxins are heat-labile proteins.
questions.x: Exotoxins are proteins secreted by Gram-positive or Gram-negative bacteria; they act on specific targets, are usually heat-labile, and can be turned into toxoid vaccines. Endotoxin is lipopolysaccharide, specifically lipid A, from the Gram-negative outer membrane, released mainly when cells die. Gram-positives make many exotoxins, such as tetanus and botulinum toxins.

questions.q: Mycobacterium tuberculosis stains poorly with the Gram stain but holds carbol fuchsin even after an acid–alcohol wash. This is due to:
o: Mycolic acids, waxy lipids in its cell wall
Correct: the waxy wall makes it acid-fast.
Complete lack of a cell wall
Mycobacteria have a thick, complex wall.
A lipopolysaccharide outer membrane
LPS is a Gram-negative feature.
A thick polysaccharide capsule
Acid-fastness comes from wall lipids, not a capsule.
questions.x: Mycobacteria have a thick wall rich in mycolic acids, long waxy lipids that keep out many stains, including Gram-stain reagents. Once heated carbol fuchsin gets in, the waxy wall holds it even through an acid–alcohol wash, so the cells are called acid-fast. This wall also slows growth and makes the bacteria resistant to many drugs.

questions.q: Teichoic acids are characteristic components of:
o: Gram-negative outer membranes
Gram-negative outer membranes carry LPS instead.
Archaeal plasma membranes
Archaeal membranes are made of ether-linked lipids.
Viral capsids
Capsids are made of protein subunits.
Gram-positive cell walls
Correct: teichoic acids are woven through the thick peptidoglycan.
questions.x: Teichoic acids are anionic polymers woven through the thick peptidoglycan of Gram-positive walls, with lipoteichoic acids anchored in the membrane. They help shape the wall, bind cations, and contribute to inflammation. Gram-negative envelopes carry lipopolysaccharide in their outer membrane instead.

questions.q: Why does a typical bacterium not burst in fresh water, even though water enters it by osmosis?
o: Its rigid peptidoglycan wall resists the rising internal pressure
Correct: the wall withstands turgor pressure.
It pumps water out with a contractile vacuole
Contractile vacuoles are found in some protists, not bacteria.
Bacterial cytoplasm is isotonic to fresh water
Bacterial cytoplasm is hypertonic to fresh water.
Its plasma membrane is impermeable to water
Water crosses membranes readily.
questions.x: Bacterial cytoplasm is hypertonic to fresh water, so water rushes in by osmosis and creates high internal pressure. The rigid, cross-linked peptidoglycan wall resists that pressure and keeps the cell from bursting. Contractile vacuoles do the same job in some freshwater protists, not in bacteria.

questions.q: Bacteria use restriction enzymes to cut invading phage DNA, yet their own chromosomes are not cut. Why?
o: A host methylase modifies the recognition sites in the bacterium's own DNA
Correct: methylation marks self DNA as protected.
Bacterial chromosomes lack these recognition sequences
Short recognition sites occur by chance throughout any large genome.
Bacterial chromosomes are single-stranded
Bacterial chromosomes are double-stranded.
Restriction enzymes work only outside the cell
Restriction enzymes act inside the cytoplasm.
questions.x: Restriction–modification systems pair a restriction enzyme with a methylase that recognizes the same short sequence. The methylase marks the host's own sites, and the restriction enzyme cuts only unmethylated sites, so invading phage DNA is destroyed while self DNA is spared. Short recognition sites appear by chance many times in any large genome, so host DNA cannot simply lack them.

questions.q: A bacterium survives a phage infection and later resists that same phage. Sequencing shows a short piece of the phage genome now inserted into its CRISPR array. How does this give resistance?
o: The spacer encodes antibodies against the phage
Bacteria do not produce antibodies.
The spacer converts the cell into a lysogen
Lysogeny involves integration of the whole phage genome.
The spacer methylates the phage capsid
Methylation acts on DNA, and CRISPR works by cleavage.
RNA transcribed from the spacer guides a Cas nuclease to cut matching phage DNA
Correct: CRISPR–Cas is a sequence-specific adaptive defense.
questions.x: CRISPR–Cas is an adaptive immune system in bacteria and archaea. After surviving an infection, the cell stores a short piece of the invader's DNA as a spacer in its CRISPR array. Transcribed spacer RNA guides a Cas nuclease to matching phage DNA, which it cuts, so a repeat infection by the same phage is stopped.

questions.q: During late death phase, a culture's optical density (OD₆₀₀) stays almost constant while viable plate counts fall sharply. The best explanation is that:
o: OD measures all intact cells, including dead ones, while plate counts detect only viable cells
Correct: turbidity cannot distinguish live from dead cells.
The cells are dividing faster than ever
Viable counts are falling, not rising.
The culture is contaminated with a faster-growing species
Contaminants would form colonies and raise plate counts.
Dead cells form more colonies than live cells
Dead cells cannot form colonies.
questions.x: Optical density measures how much light the culture scatters, which depends on the number of intact cells whether alive or dead. A plate count only detects cells that can still divide to form colonies. So in death phase, OD can stay high while viable counts fall, and turbidity overestimates living cells.

questions.q: Vibrio fischeri produces light only when its population density is high. This behavior is controlled by:
o: Conjugation between neighboring cells
Conjugation transfers DNA, not density signals.
Lysogenic conversion by a phage
Density-dependent light production is not phage-driven.
Transposition of light genes at high density
Gene regulation, not DNA movement, controls this response.
Quorum sensing through secreted autoinducers that build up with cell number
Correct: autoinducer concentration reports population density.
questions.x: In quorum sensing, each bacterium releases small signal molecules called autoinducers. When cells are dense, the signal builds up past a threshold, binds receptors, and switches on group behaviors such as light production in V. fischeri, biofilm formation or virulence. At low density the signal stays dilute and the genes stay off.

questions.q: Bacteria in a biofilm on a catheter often tolerate antibiotics far better than the same strain grown in liquid culture. One contributing reason is that:
o: Every biofilm cell has acquired a resistance plasmid
Biofilm tolerance occurs even without new resistance genes.
Biofilm cells lose their ribosomes
Biofilm cells still have ribosomes.
Biofilm cells become eukaryotic
Bacteria remain prokaryotic in biofilms.
The matrix slows drug penetration and many cells grow slowly
Correct: limited diffusion and low growth rate reduce drug killing.
questions.x: Bacteria in a biofilm are encased in a matrix of polysaccharides, proteins and DNA that slows antibiotic penetration. Many cells deep inside grow slowly or are dormant (persisters), and drugs that target growth, such as β-lactams, kill them poorly. This tolerance does not require new resistance genes, which is why biofilm infections on devices are so hard to clear.

questions.q: Colonic bacteria make vitamin K that the human host absorbs, and in return they receive nutrients and a stable habitat. This relationship is:
o: Parasitism
In parasitism the host is harmed.
Mutualism
Correct: both partners benefit.
Commensalism
In commensalism only one partner benefits.
Lysogeny
Lysogeny describes a phage–bacterium relationship.
questions.x: Symbiotic relationships are classified by who benefits. In mutualism both partners gain, as when gut bacteria supply vitamin K and receive nutrients and a habitat. In commensalism one gains and the other is unaffected, and in parasitism one gains at the other's expense.

questions.q: Compared with a typical eukaryotic gene, a typical bacterial protein-coding gene:
o: Contains many introns that are spliced out
Introns are rare in bacterial genes.
Requires a 5′ cap for translation
Bacteria use a Shine–Dalgarno sequence instead.
Lacks introns, so the primary transcript can serve directly as mRNA
Correct: most bacterial genes are uninterrupted.
Is transcribed inside a nucleus
Bacteria have no nucleus.
questions.x: Most bacterial genes are continuous coding sequences without introns, so the primary transcript is already usable mRNA and needs no splicing, capping or poly-A tail. Combined with no nucleus, this allows translation to begin while transcription is still going. Eukaryotic genes usually contain introns that must be spliced out.

questions.q: Many large or hydrophobic antibiotics kill Gram-positive bacteria but not Gram-negative bacteria. The main reason is that Gram-negatives have:
o: A thicker peptidoglycan layer
Gram-negatives have a thinner peptidoglycan layer.
No ribosomes
All bacteria have ribosomes.
Endospores in every cell
Most Gram-negatives do not form spores.
An outer membrane with LPS and size-limited porins that blocks entry
Correct: the outer membrane is a permeability barrier.
questions.x: The Gram-negative outer membrane is a permeability barrier: its LPS outer leaflet keeps out hydrophobic molecules, and its porins let only small hydrophilic molecules through. Large or hydrophobic drugs such as vancomycin cannot reach their targets. Gram-negatives actually have a thinner peptidoglycan layer, so wall thickness is not the reason.

questions.q: Bacteria exposed to a drug stop growing; when the drug is washed away after 6 hours, they resume growth with no loss of viable count. The drug is best described as:
o: Bactericidal
A bactericidal drug would reduce the viable count.
Lytic
Lysis would lower viable counts.
Bacteriostatic
Correct: it halts growth without killing.
Mutagenic
Nothing indicates the drug causes mutations.
questions.x: Bacteriostatic drugs stop growth without killing; when the drug is removed, cells recover with no loss of viable count. Bactericidal drugs kill, so viable counts drop and do not recover after washout. Many ribosome-targeting drugs, such as tetracyclines, are bacteriostatic, while β-lactams are bactericidal.

questions.q: A phage infects E. coli strain K but not strain B. A mutant phage that can now infect strain B most likely has an altered:
o: Amount of DNA in its head
Genome size does not determine which cells a phage binds.
Tail fiber protein that binds a receptor on strain B
Correct: host range is set mainly by attachment to surface receptors.
Lysozyme that cuts the cell wall
Lysozyme acts after attachment and is not host-specific.
Integrase that inserts into the host chromosome
Integration happens after entry and does not set host range.
questions.x: Phage host range depends mainly on attachment: tail fibers or other attachment proteins must bind a specific receptor on the bacterial surface. A mutation in the tail fiber can let the phage recognize a receptor on a new strain. Steps after entry, such as lysis or integration, do not set which cells a phage can bind.

questions.q: Salting meat helps preserve it because, in a strongly hypertonic environment, bacterial cells:
o: Gain water and burst
That happens in hypotonic, not hypertonic, surroundings.
Have their cell walls dissolved by salt
Salt does not dissolve peptidoglycan.
Lose water by osmosis, so their growth is inhibited
Correct: plasmolysis halts metabolism and growth.
Turn into endospores
Many bacteria cannot form spores, and salt does not trigger it.
questions.x: In a hypertonic environment, water flows out of the bacterium by osmosis, the membrane pulls away from the wall (plasmolysis), and metabolism and growth halt. Salting and sugaring foods preserve them this way. Bursting happens in hypotonic surroundings, and the wall prevents even that.

questions.q: During which phase of the cell cycle is the nuclear DNA replicated?
o: S phase
Correct: the synthesis (S) phase is when each chromosome is copied into two sister chromatids.
G1 phase
G1 is growth and preparation; DNA has not yet been copied.
G2 phase
G2 follows replication; the cell checks the copied DNA and prepares for mitosis.
Prophase
Chromosomes condense in prophase, but replication finished earlier in S.
questions.x: The cell cycle is G1 (growth), S (DNA synthesis), G2 (preparation) and M (mitosis). Each chromosome is copied during S into two sister chromatids that stay joined at the centromere. Prophase is tempting because chromosomes first become visible then, but condensation only packages DNA that was already replicated in S.

questions.q: Compared with the same human cell in G1, a cell in G2 has:
o: twice the DNA content and twice the number of chromosomes
Counts sister chromatids as separate chromosomes; they are not until anaphase.
twice the DNA content but the same number of chromosomes
Correct: each chromosome now has two sister chromatids joined at a centromere, so DNA doubles but the count stays 46.
the same DNA content and twice the number of chromosomes
Chromosome number does not double in S phase; DNA content does.
half the DNA content and half the number of chromosomes
Halving happens in meiosis, not between G1 and G2.
questions.note: Count chromosomes by centromeres, not by chromatids.
questions.x: S phase doubles DNA content (2C to 4C in a diploid cell) but not chromosome number, because two sister chromatids sharing one centromere still count as one chromosome. A human G2 cell therefore has 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids. Chromosome number only appears to double in anaphase, when sisters separate and each gets its own centromere.

questions.q: Mature neurons that have permanently stopped dividing are said to reside in which state?
o: G2 arrest
G2 arrest is a temporary checkpoint pause after replication.
Metaphase arrest
Metaphase arrest happens when the spindle checkpoint is triggered, not in resting neurons.
G0
Correct: G0 is a non-dividing state outside the active cycle; many neurons stay there for life.
S phase
S phase is active DNA replication, the opposite of a resting state.
questions.x: G0 is a resting state outside the cycle in which cells carry out their functions without preparing to divide. Most mature neurons and cardiac muscle cells stay in G0 for life, whereas others, like hepatocytes, can be recalled. G2 or metaphase arrest are temporary checkpoint pauses in cells that are still cycling, not a permanent exit.

questions.q: Cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) activity rises and falls through the cell cycle mainly because:
o: CDK genes are transcribed only during mitosis
CDK protein levels are roughly constant across the cycle.
CDKs are destroyed by proteasomes at the end of every phase
It is the cyclin partner, not the CDK, that is periodically degraded.
ATP becomes available only at specific checkpoints
ATP is always present; kinase activity is gated by cyclin binding and phosphorylation.
cyclin levels oscillate through regulated synthesis and ubiquitin-mediated degradation
Correct: CDK levels stay fairly constant; their activity depends on binding cyclins that come and go.
questions.x: CDKs are kinases present at fairly steady levels; they are active only when bound to a cyclin partner. Cyclins are made in specific phases and then tagged with ubiquitin (by APC/C or SCF) and destroyed by the proteasome, so CDK activity rises and falls with them. The tempting error is thinking the CDK itself is degraded each phase; it is the cyclin that oscillates.

questions.q: A mutant Rb protein cannot be phosphorylated by cyclin D–CDK4/6. What is the most likely effect on cells expressing only this mutant?
o: They enter S phase uncontrollably because E2F is permanently free
That results from losing Rb or hyperphosphorylating it, not from blocking phosphorylation.
They arrest in G2 because mitotic cyclins cannot be made
Rb acts at the G1/S transition, not the G2/M transition.
They arrest in G1 because E2F stays bound and S-phase genes are not transcribed
Correct: hypophosphorylated Rb holds E2F; without phosphorylation the G1/S transition is blocked.
They replicate DNA but skip mitosis entirely
Cells blocked at G1/S never begin replication.
questions.note: Phosphorylated Rb = released E2F = go.
questions.x: In G1, unphosphorylated Rb binds the transcription factor E2F and blocks S-phase genes. Cyclin D–CDK4/6 (then cyclin E–CDK2) phosphorylates Rb, releasing E2F so the cell can pass G1/S. An Rb that cannot be phosphorylated is a permanent brake, so cells arrest in G1. Uncontrolled S-phase entry is what happens when Rb is lost, the opposite situation.

questions.q: The G2/M checkpoint mainly ensures that, before mitosis begins:
o: every kinetochore is attached to the spindle
That is the spindle assembly checkpoint, which acts during mitosis before anaphase.
sister chromatids have already separated
Sister chromatids separate in anaphase, well after G2.
the nuclear envelope has re-formed
The nuclear envelope re-forms in telophase.
DNA replication is complete and the DNA is undamaged
Correct: the G2/M checkpoint blocks mitotic entry until DNA is fully copied and repaired.
questions.x: The G2/M checkpoint asks whether the genome is ready to be divided: replication must be finished and damage repaired, otherwise CDK1–cyclin B stays inhibited. Kinetochore attachment is checked later, by the spindle assembly checkpoint during metaphase. Keeping the two checkpoints straight (G2/M for DNA, metaphase/anaphase for attachment) is the key distinction.

questions.q: Why can a single kinetochore that is not attached to the spindle delay anaphase in the whole cell?
o: It generates a signal that inhibits the anaphase-promoting complex (APC/C)
Correct: the spindle checkpoint keeps APC/C off, so securin and cyclin B persist and separase stays inactive.
It physically holds all other chromosomes at the metaphase plate
Chromosomes are not tethered to each other; the delay is biochemical signaling.
It activates separase too early
Early separase activity would cause premature separation, not a delay.
It prevents DNA replication from finishing
Replication is complete before mitosis begins.
questions.x: An unattached kinetochore catalyzes formation of an inhibitory complex that keeps APC/C–Cdc20 inactive throughout the cell. While APC/C is off, securin is not degraded, separase stays inhibited and cohesin holds all sisters together. Because the signal is diffusible, one lagging chromosome halts everyone; separase activated early would cause premature separation, not a delay.

questions.q: Cultured cells are treated with nocodazole, which prevents microtubule polymerization. After 18 hours, most cells are found:
o: in G1 with decondensed chromatin
Microtubule loss does not block the G1 phase; cells progress until mitosis.
in early mitosis with condensed chromosomes, held by the spindle checkpoint
Correct: without a spindle, kinetochores stay unattached and the checkpoint holds cells before anaphase.
in S phase with partly replicated DNA
Nocodazole does not interfere with DNA synthesis.
as binucleate cells that have finished telophase
Cells cannot reach telophase without a functioning spindle.
questions.note: Spindle poisons arrest cells in mitosis.
questions.x: Without microtubules no spindle forms, so kinetochores never attach and the spindle assembly checkpoint keeps APC/C off. Cells progress normally through G1, S and G2, then pile up in prometaphase with condensed chromosomes. This mitotic arrest is how spindle poisons such as colchicine and vinca alkaloids work, and why they are used to make karyotypes.

questions.q: Hydroxyurea depletes the cell's deoxyribonucleotide pool. If an asynchronous culture is treated for 24 hours, flow cytometry would show most cells with:
o: about twice the DNA content of a G1 cell
Doubling DNA requires completing S phase, which needs dNTPs.
about the DNA content of a G1 cell
Correct: cells pile up at the G1/S border or very early S, before much DNA is copied.
about four times the DNA content of a G1 cell
Re-replication without mitosis is not caused by dNTP depletion.
about half the DNA content of a G1 cell
Somatic cells cannot drop below the G1 amount by blocking synthesis.
questions.x: Without dNTPs, DNA polymerase stalls, so cells cannot complete S phase. Cells in G2 and M finish dividing and then stop at the G1/S border, while cells already in S stall early, so most cells have near-G1 DNA content. A 2× (G2) content would require finishing replication, which is exactly what hydroxyurea prevents.

questions.q: Once a mammalian cell passes the restriction point late in G1, it:
o: is committed to completing the cycle even if growth factors are removed
Correct: after the restriction point, progression no longer depends on external mitogens.
immediately begins chromosome condensation
Condensation begins in prophase, after S and G2.
can no longer repair DNA damage
DNA repair remains possible throughout the cycle.
exits into G0 permanently
Passing the restriction point commits the cell to divide, not to rest.
questions.x: The restriction point is the late-G1 commitment step: once Rb is sufficiently phosphorylated and E2F drives its own cyclin E, the cycle continues without mitogens. Before it, removing growth factors sends cells to G0. Passing it does not disable later checkpoints or DNA repair; it only removes dependence on external growth signals.

questions.q: A cell line is engineered to express a form of cyclin B that cannot be degraded. What is the most likely result?
o: Cells arrest in G1 and never replicate DNA
Cyclin B acts at G2/M and in mitosis, not at G1/S.
Cells skip mitosis and re-enter S phase
Persistent CDK1 activity keeps cells in mitosis rather than skipping it.
Cells divide faster with shorter G2 phases
Failure to degrade cyclin B blocks completion of division.
Cells enter mitosis but cannot exit it
Correct: cyclin B destruction inactivates CDK1, which is required for mitotic exit.
questions.x: CDK1–cyclin B drives entry into mitosis, and exit requires APC/C to ubiquitinate cyclin B so CDK1 activity falls. With non-degradable cyclin B, cells enter mitosis and can even separate sisters, but they cannot decondense chromosomes, re-form nuclei or complete cytokinesis. The trap is G1 arrest; cyclin B works at G2/M, so earlier phases are unaffected.

questions.q: Fusing an S-phase cell with a G1 cell makes the G1 nucleus start replicating early, but fusing an S-phase cell with a G2 cell does not make the G2 nucleus replicate again. The best conclusion is that:
o: G1 nuclei contain an inhibitor that S-phase cytoplasm cannot overcome
The G1 nucleus did replicate, so no dominant inhibitor was present.
G2 cytoplasm contains a factor that triggers replication in any nucleus
The data show G2 nuclei resisting replication, not G2 cytoplasm causing it.
S-phase cytoplasm has a replication activator, and G2 DNA cannot replicate again until it passes through mitosis
Correct: the G1 nucleus is competent to respond; G2 DNA has already used its once-per-cycle licensing.
DNA replication is controlled only by signals inside the nucleus
The fusion shows a cytoplasmic factor can trigger replication.
questions.note: DNA is licensed to replicate once per cycle.
questions.x: S-phase cytoplasm contains activators that start replication at licensed origins. Origins are licensed (MCM helicases loaded) only in G1, and licensing is blocked from S until the end of mitosis, so G2 DNA cannot fire again. This once-per-cycle licensing explains both results; a dominant G1 inhibitor is ruled out because the G1 nucleus did replicate.

questions.q: The protein p21, which is made in larger amounts after DNA damage, stops the cell cycle by:
o: cutting damaged DNA out of the chromosome
Excision is done by repair enzymes, not by p21.
degrading all cyclin proteins
p21 blocks cyclin–CDK activity; it is not a protease.
phosphorylating Rb to activate E2F
Rb phosphorylation promotes S-phase entry, the opposite of arrest.
binding and inhibiting cyclin–CDK complexes
Correct: p21 is a CDK inhibitor, so Rb stays unphosphorylated and the cell pauses.
questions.x: DNA damage stabilizes p53, which transcribes p21, a CDK inhibitor. p21 binds cyclin–CDK complexes such as cyclin E–CDK2, so Rb stays unphosphorylated and E2F stays bound, holding the cell in G1 for repair. p21 is not a protease or nuclease; it simply blocks kinase activity, and phosphorylating Rb would push the cell forward rather than stop it.

questions.q: After two-thirds of a liver is surgically removed, the remaining tissue restores much of its mass within weeks. This is possible mainly because hepatocytes:
o: divide continuously throughout adult life
Hepatocytes normally divide rarely; that is why they are described as quiescent.
fuse with each other to form larger cells
Liver regrowth is driven by cell division, not by cells fusing.
can leave G0 and re-enter the cell cycle when stimulated
Correct: mature hepatocytes are usually quiescent but readily divide again after injury.
are permanently arrested like mature neurons
Permanently arrested cells could not regenerate the organ.
questions.x: Hepatocytes are quiescent (G0) in the healthy adult liver but keep the ability to re-enter G1 when growth factors such as HGF appear after injury. The remaining cells divide until mass is restored. This contrasts with neurons, which are terminally differentiated, and with continuously dividing tissues like gut epithelium.

questions.q: Chromosomes first become visible as condensed structures and the mitotic spindle begins to form during:
o: metaphase
In metaphase, chromosomes are already condensed and aligned at the plate.
prophase
Correct: condensation and spindle assembly begin in prophase.
anaphase
Anaphase is when sister chromatids move toward the poles.
telophase
In telophase, chromosomes decondense as nuclei re-form.
questions.x: Prophase begins mitosis: chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, centrosomes move apart and the spindle starts assembling; the nuclear envelope breaks down at prometaphase. Metaphase is tempting because chromosomes are most condensed and aligned there, but condensation and spindle formation start earlier, in prophase.

questions.q: The kinetochore is best described as:
o: a protein complex at the centromere where spindle microtubules attach
Correct: kinetochores link chromosomes to spindle microtubules.
the region of DNA at the tip of each chromosome
Chromosome tips are telomeres.
the organelle that nucleates spindle microtubules
That is the centrosome, which contains the centrioles.
the ring of actin that pinches the cell in two
That is the contractile ring used in cytokinesis.
questions.x: The centromere is a DNA region; the kinetochore is the protein complex assembled on it that grips spindle microtubules and senses tension. Each sister chromatid has its own kinetochore, allowing attachment to opposite poles. It is easily confused with the centrosome, the microtubule-organizing center that forms the spindle poles.

questions.q: A drug that specifically inhibits myosin II in an animal cell undergoing mitosis would most directly block:
o: chromosome condensation
Condensation relies on condensin proteins, not myosin.
cytokinesis
Correct: an actin–myosin contractile ring forms the cleavage furrow that splits the cytoplasm.
DNA replication
Replication finished in S phase and does not use myosin.
breakdown of the nuclear envelope
Envelope breakdown is driven by phosphorylation of nuclear lamins.
questions.note: Animal cells pinch apart; plant cells build a cell plate.
questions.x: Animal-cell cytokinesis uses a contractile ring of actin and myosin II beneath the membrane at the cell equator; myosin motors slide actin filaments to constrict the cleavage furrow. Chromosome condensation uses condensin, and nuclear envelope breakdown follows lamin phosphorylation, so neither requires myosin. Plant cells instead build a cell plate.

questions.q: How many chromatids are present in a human somatic cell at metaphase of mitosis?
o: That is the number of chromosomes, not chromatids.
That is the haploid chromosome number found in gametes.
Chromatids double only once, in S phase.
Correct: 46 replicated chromosomes, each made of 2 sister chromatids.
questions.x: At metaphase each of the 46 chromosomes has been replicated into two sister chromatids, giving 92 chromatids still joined at centromeres. Answering 46 confuses chromosomes with chromatids; 184 doubles twice. Counting rule: one centromere means one chromosome, regardless of how many chromatids it carries.

questions.q: A cell's single centrosome fails to duplicate before it enters mitosis. The most likely consequence is:
o: a monopolar spindle that cannot separate chromosomes into two daughter nuclei
Correct: two centrosomes are needed to build the two poles of a bipolar spindle.
failure to replicate nuclear DNA
Centrosome duplication and DNA replication are separate processes.
normal mitosis followed by failed cytokinesis only
Segregation itself depends on a bipolar spindle, so mitosis would not be normal.
immediate apoptosis in G1
The defect shows up in mitosis, not in G1.
questions.x: The centrosome duplicates once per cycle (around S phase) so that two spindle poles can form. With one centrosome, the cell builds a monopolar spindle: all chromosomes face one pole and cannot be pulled apart, so the checkpoint arrests the cell or it fails division. DNA replication is independent of centrosome duplication, so S phase is unaffected.

questions.q: Which event directly allows sister chromatids to begin moving to opposite poles?
o: Topoisomerase relaxing the DNA supercoils
Topoisomerase untangles DNA, but cohesin cleavage is the trigger for separation.
Kinetochores detaching from the spindle
Kinetochores must stay attached to pull chromatids poleward.
Separase cleaving the cohesin that holds sisters together
Correct: once APC/C destroys securin, active separase cuts cohesin and sisters separate.
Condensin degradation at the end of metaphase
Chromosomes stay condensed during anaphase.
questions.x: Sister chromatids are held together by cohesin rings. At the metaphase–anaphase transition, APC/C ubiquitinates securin, freeing separase, which cleaves cohesin's kleisin subunit; spindle forces then pull the sisters apart. Kinetochores must stay attached for poleward movement, and topoisomerase untangling helps but is not the trigger.

questions.q: During telophase of mitosis:
o: homologous chromosomes pair up
Homologs pair in prophase I of meiosis, not in mitosis.
chromosomes line up along the metaphase plate
That defines metaphase.
nuclear envelopes re-form around each set of chromosomes
Correct: telophase reverses prophase, with new nuclei forming and chromatin decondensing.
DNA is replicated in preparation for division
Replication happens in S phase.
questions.x: Telophase essentially reverses prophase: chromosomes arrive at the poles, decondense, and nuclear envelopes re-form from lamin dephosphorylation, usually overlapping with cytokinesis. Metaphase alignment comes earlier, homolog pairing is unique to meiosis I, and DNA replication occurs only in S phase.

questions.q: Clinical karyotypes are usually prepared from cells arrested in metaphase because at that stage:
o: chromosomes are maximally condensed and easiest to tell apart
Correct: condensed metaphase chromosomes show clear size, shape and banding.
the chromosome number is temporarily doubled
Chromosome number stays 46; only chromatids are doubled.
the nuclear envelope is intact for staining
The envelope has broken down by metaphase.
homologous chromosomes have fused together
Homologs do not fuse; in mitosis they do not even pair.
questions.x: Metaphase chromosomes are at maximum condensation, so each can be identified by size, centromere position and banding pattern. Cells are cultured, treated with a spindle poison to accumulate metaphases, then stained. The chromosome number is still 46 at metaphase; only the chromatid number is doubled.

questions.q: A girl's blood cells show that some have 47 chromosomes and others have 46. The most likely cause is:
o: nondisjunction during meiosis I in the mother
A meiotic error would give every cell 47 chromosomes.
fertilization of one egg by two sperm
Polyspermy produces triploidy (69 chromosomes).
crossing over between homologous chromosomes
Crossing over swaps segments but does not change chromosome number.
nondisjunction during a mitotic division after fertilization
Correct: an error in an early embryonic mitosis creates two cell lines, called mosaicism.
questions.x: Having two populations of cells (mosaicism) means the error happened after the zygote formed, during a mitotic division of the embryo. A meiotic nondisjunction gives an abnormal gamete, so the zygote and essentially all its descendants would have 47. Polyspermy yields triploidy, and crossing over exchanges segments without changing chromosome number.

questions.q: Crossing over between homologous chromosomes occurs during:
o: prophase of mitosis
Homologs do not pair in mitosis.
prophase I of meiosis
Correct: homologs synapse into tetrads and exchange segments in prophase I.
anaphase II of meiosis
Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II; crossing over is long over.
S phase before meiosis
S phase copies DNA; recombination comes later, in prophase I.
questions.x: In prophase I, homologs pair (synapsis) via the synaptonemal complex, forming tetrads in which non-sister chromatids exchange segments at chiasmata. This recombination, along with independent assortment, generates genetic variation. Homologs do not pair in mitosis, and by meiosis II there are no homolog pairs left to recombine.

questions.q: Which division reduces a human cell from diploid to haploid chromosome number?
o: Meiosis II, when sister chromatids separate
Meiosis II keeps the number at 23; it is equational, like mitosis.
Mitosis, when sister chromatids separate
Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same.
Cytokinesis after S phase
S phase is followed by G2, and cytokinesis alone does not sort homologs.
Meiosis I, when homologous chromosomes separate
Correct: separating homologs halves the chromosome number, from 46 to 23.
questions.note: Meiosis I is reductional; meiosis II is equational.
questions.x: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, so each daughter has 23 chromosomes (each still two chromatids): it is the reductional division. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids like mitosis and keeps the count at 23. The trap is thinking haploidy arrives in meiosis II because DNA content halves again then; chromosome number already halved in meiosis I.

questions.q: In human spermatogenesis, which is the first cell type that is haploid?
o: Primary spermatocyte
Primary spermatocytes are diploid cells that enter meiosis I.
Secondary spermatocyte
Correct: it forms after meiosis I separates homologs, leaving 23 chromosomes.
Spermatogonium
Spermatogonia are diploid stem cells that divide by mitosis.
Spermatozoon
Sperm are haploid, but spermatids and secondary spermatocytes come first.
questions.x: Spermatogonia (diploid stem cells) divide by mitosis; some become primary spermatocytes (2n) that undergo meiosis I to give secondary spermatocytes (n, still with sister chromatids). Meiosis II produces spermatids, which mature into spermatozoa. Haploidy begins at the secondary spermatocyte because meiosis I is the reductional division.

questions.q: In a human female, primary oocytes are present before birth and remain arrested in which stage until shortly before ovulation?
o: Metaphase II
Metaphase II arrest applies to the secondary oocyte, which is ovulated.
Anaphase I
No long-term arrest occurs in anaphase I.
Prophase I
Correct: primary oocytes pause in prophase I from fetal life until an LH surge, sometimes for decades.
G0 before DNA replication
Primary oocytes have already replicated DNA and begun meiosis.
questions.x: Oogonia enter meiosis before birth and arrest as primary oocytes in prophase I (diplotene) for years. Each cycle, the LH surge lets one dominant follicle's oocyte finish meiosis I, forming a secondary oocyte and the first polar body, which then arrests at metaphase II. Metaphase II arrest belongs to the ovulated secondary oocyte, not the fetal-stage cell.

questions.q: The cell released from the ovary at ovulation is arrested in metaphase II. When is meiosis II completed?
o: Only if a sperm fertilizes it
Correct: sperm entry triggers completion of meiosis II and release of the second polar body.
At the LH surge, before ovulation
The LH surge completes meiosis I, not meiosis II.
At puberty
Puberty starts cycles of follicle maturation, not completion of meiosis II.
During implantation
Meiosis II finishes at fertilization, days before implantation.
questions.x: The secondary oocyte is ovulated arrested in metaphase II and finishes meiosis II only when a sperm fuses with it; the Ca²⁺ wave triggers completion and release of the second polar body. The LH surge completes meiosis I, not meiosis II. An unfertilized secondary oocyte never finishes meiosis and degenerates.

questions.q: Unequal division of the cytoplasm during oogenesis produces:
o: one large egg and small polar bodies, keeping most cytoplasm in the egg
Correct: the egg keeps the nutrients and organelles the early embryo needs.
four equal-sized eggs from each primary oocyte
Equal division into four cells describes spermatogenesis.
two eggs and two polar bodies
Each primary oocyte yields at most one egg.
one diploid egg and one haploid polar body
The mature egg is haploid.
questions.x: Oogenesis divides cytoplasm unequally so that one primary oocyte yields one large ovum plus small polar bodies that degenerate. This packs the egg with the organelles, mRNAs and nutrients needed before the embryo's own genome activates. Spermatogenesis, by contrast, yields four equal, small sperm from each primary spermatocyte.

questions.q: Which cells in the seminiferous tubules nourish developing sperm, form the blood–testis barrier and secrete inhibin?
o: Leydig cells
Leydig cells sit between tubules and make testosterone in response to LH.
Spermatogonia
Spermatogonia are the stem cells that become sperm.
Sertoli cells
Correct: Sertoli cells support spermatogenesis and secrete inhibin, which suppresses FSH.
Granulosa cells
Granulosa cells are the female counterpart of Sertoli cells, in ovarian follicles.
questions.x: Sertoli cells line the seminiferous tubules, nurse developing germ cells, form the blood–testis barrier with tight junctions, secrete androgen-binding protein and inhibin, and respond to FSH. Leydig cells lie outside the tubules in the interstitium and make testosterone under LH. Granulosa cells are the ovarian analog of Sertoli cells.

questions.q: In males, the main target cells of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) are:
o: Leydig cells, which it stimulates to make testosterone
Leydig cells respond to LH, not FSH.
Sertoli cells, which it stimulates to support spermatogenesis
Correct: FSH acts on Sertoli cells; LH acts on Leydig cells.
spermatids, which it stimulates to grow flagella
Spermatids are supported by Sertoli cells rather than targeted directly by FSH.
prostate cells, which it stimulates to secrete fluid
The prostate is driven by androgens, mainly DHT.
questions.note: FSH → Sertoli (sperm); LH → Leydig (testosterone).
questions.x: In the testis, FSH acts on Sertoli cells (supporting spermatogenesis and making androgen-binding protein and inhibin), while LH acts on Leydig cells to make testosterone. The common trap is swapping these: LH targets Leydig, FSH targets Sertoli. Spermatids are not direct FSH targets; Sertoli cells relay the support.

questions.q: A boy with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) has two maternal X chromosomes that carry identical alleles at markers near the centromere, although his mother is heterozygous at those markers. The error most likely occurred in:
o: maternal meiosis I
Meiosis I nondisjunction passes both homologs, which differ at heterozygous centromere markers.
paternal meiosis I
Both X chromosomes are maternal, so the father's meiosis is not implicated.
a mitotic division in the early embryo
A mitotic error would usually cause mosaicism rather than XXY in all cells.
maternal meiosis II
Correct: sister chromatids share centromere-linked alleles, so nondisjunction of sisters in meiosis II fits.
questions.note: Centromere markers survive crossing over, so they trace MI versus MII.
questions.x: Markers near the centromere rarely recombine, so they track whether homologs or sisters were mis-segregated. Maternal meiosis I nondisjunction passes both homologs, which differ at heterozygous markers; meiosis II nondisjunction passes two sisters, which are identical there. Identical maternal alleles therefore point to maternal meiosis II.

questions.q: The many mitochondria in the midpiece of a sperm cell mainly provide:
o: ATP to power the flagellum
Correct: midpiece mitochondria supply the energy for swimming.
enzymes that digest the zona pellucida
Those enzymes are in the acrosome on the head.
mitochondrial DNA that the embryo inherits
Paternal mitochondria are normally destroyed after fertilization.
the haploid nucleus delivered to the egg
The nucleus is in the sperm head.
questions.x: The sperm midpiece is packed with mitochondria wrapped around the axoneme to supply ATP for dynein-driven flagellar beating. Acrosomal enzymes sit in the head, and paternal mitochondria are usually destroyed after fertilization, which is why mtDNA is inherited maternally.

questions.q: A man injects high doses of testosterone for several months. What would most likely happen to his sperm count?
o: It rises, because testosterone directly stimulates spermatogenesis
Systemic testosterone suppresses the pituitary, so the net effect is reduced production.
It falls, because negative feedback suppresses LH and FSH and intratesticular support for spermatogenesis drops
Correct: low gonadotropins starve Sertoli and Leydig cells, so sperm production declines.
It stays the same, because sperm production is independent of hormones
Spermatogenesis depends on FSH and high local testosterone.
It rises, because inhibin secretion stops
Inhibin falling would raise FSH, but exogenous testosterone suppresses FSH and LH overall.
questions.note: Exogenous androgens act as a male contraceptive via feedback.
questions.x: Exogenous testosterone feeds back on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, suppressing GnRH, LH and FSH. Without LH, Leydig cells make little testosterone inside the testes, where spermatogenesis needs very high local levels, and without FSH Sertoli support falls. Blood testosterone is high, yet sperm count drops, which is why androgen abuse causes infertility.

questions.q: Sperm complete their maturation and become capable of motility while stored in the:
o: seminiferous tubules
Sperm are produced there but are not yet motile.
prostate gland
The prostate adds fluid to semen but does not store sperm.
epididymis
Correct: sperm mature and gain motility as they pass through the epididymis.
urethra
The urethra is only a passage during ejaculation.
questions.x: Sperm leave the seminiferous tubules structurally complete but immotile. During transit through the epididymis (about two weeks) they gain the capacity for forward motility and are stored there until ejaculation. Full fertilizing ability still requires capacitation in the female tract.

questions.q: Undescended testes (cryptorchidism) often lead to infertility mainly because:
o: testosterone cannot be made inside the abdomen
Leydig cells usually still make testosterone; sperm production is what is most affected.
sperm cannot reach the urethra from the abdomen
The duct system still connects; the issue is the temperature for production.
the abdomen lacks a blood supply for the testes
Abdominal testes are still perfused.
spermatogenesis requires a temperature a few degrees below core body temperature
Correct: the scrotum keeps the testes cooler than the abdomen, as sperm production needs.
questions.x: The scrotum keeps the testes about 2–3 °C below core temperature, and spermatogenesis is highly temperature sensitive. In undescended testes, germ cells are damaged and sperm production falls, while Leydig cells usually keep making testosterone. Cryptorchidism also raises testicular cancer risk.

questions.q: Fructose in semen, a major fuel for ejaculated sperm, comes mainly from the:
o: prostate gland
The prostate adds a slightly alkaline, enzyme-rich fluid.
bulbourethral glands
These secrete a small amount of clear mucus before ejaculation.
seminal vesicles
Correct: seminal vesicles supply most of the semen volume, including fructose.
Leydig cells
Leydig cells secrete testosterone into the blood, not semen components.
questions.x: The seminal vesicles contribute most of semen volume, an alkaline fluid rich in fructose (fuel for sperm), prostaglandins and clotting proteins. The prostate adds a thin, slightly alkaline fluid with enzymes such as PSA, and bulbourethral glands secrete pre-ejaculate mucus. Leydig cells secrete hormones into blood, not fluid into semen.

questions.q: After a vasectomy, in which each vas deferens is cut and sealed, a man would be expected to have:
o: low testosterone levels and no semen
Leydig cells still release testosterone into the blood.
normal sperm counts but no seminal fluid
Cutting the vas blocks sperm, not gland secretions.
arrested spermatogenesis due to high FSH
Spermatogenesis continues; the sperm are reabsorbed.
normal testosterone levels and semen that lacks sperm
Correct: hormone production is untouched, and accessory glands still make most semen fluid.
questions.x: Cutting the vas deferens blocks sperm transport but leaves the testes and accessory glands intact. Leydig cells still release testosterone into the blood, sperm are still made and then reabsorbed, and the seminal vesicles and prostate still make nearly all semen volume. The man ejaculates semen that simply lacks sperm.

questions.q: An XY individual has testes but nonfunctional androgen receptors. Which set of features is expected?
o: Female external genitalia and no uterus
Correct: no androgen response feminizes the genitalia, but anti-Müllerian hormone from Sertoli cells still removes the Müllerian ducts.
Male external genitalia and a uterus
Androgens cannot act on the genitalia, and AMH still blocks uterine development.
Female external genitalia and a uterus
The testes still secrete AMH, which causes the Müllerian ducts to regress.
Male external genitalia and no uterus
Male genitalia require a functioning androgen receptor.
questions.note: AMH acts through its own receptor, so it still works.
questions.x: In androgen insensitivity, testes form (SRY) and secrete both testosterone and anti-Müllerian hormone.
