Without androgen receptors, Wolffian ducts regress and external genitalia develop as female. But AMH acts through its own receptor, so Müllerian ducts still regress and there is no uterus or upper vagina. The trap is assuming a uterus forms because the person looks female.

questions.q: In an embryo that lacks anti-Müllerian hormone, the Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts develop into the:
o: epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles
These come from the Wolffian ducts under testosterone.
oviducts, uterus and upper vagina
Correct: without AMH, Müllerian ducts persist and form female internal structures.
ovaries
Ovaries develop from the gonadal ridge, not from ducts.
prostate and urethra
These form from the urogenital sinus under DHT.
questions.x: The Müllerian (paramesonephric) ducts form the oviducts, uterus and upper vagina unless anti-Müllerian hormone from Sertoli cells makes them regress. The Wolffian ducts form the epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles under testosterone. Ovaries come from the gonadal ridge, not from either duct system.

questions.q: An XY infant lacks 5α-reductase, the enzyme that converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). Which finding is most likely?
o: Female internal ducts with male external genitalia
AMH removes Müllerian ducts, and the external genitalia lack DHT.
Ambiguous or female-appearing external genitalia with male internal ducts
Correct: testosterone alone forms Wolffian structures, but external genitalia need DHT to masculinize.
Complete absence of testes
Testes form under SRY regardless of 5α-reductase.
Normal male development, since testosterone substitutes fully for DHT
DHT is required to fully masculinize the external genitalia and prostate.
questions.x: 5α-reductase converts testosterone to the more potent DHT. Testosterone alone is enough for Wolffian ducts to form epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles, and AMH still removes Müllerian ducts. DHT is required to masculinize the external genitalia and prostate, so these infants have male internal ducts but ambiguous or female-appearing genitalia, often virilizing at puberty.

questions.q: In mammals, development of the gonads into testes is triggered mainly by:
o: the SRY gene on the Y chromosome
Correct: SRY encodes testis-determining factor, which starts testis development.
the number of X chromosomes present
One X or two, a Y with SRY leads to testes; XXY individuals are male.
maternal estrogen crossing the placenta
Maternal hormones do not determine gonadal sex.
high testosterone before the gonads form
Testosterone comes from the testes after they have formed.
questions.x: The SRY gene on the Y chromosome encodes a transcription factor (TDF) that directs the bipotential gonad to become a testis; without it the gonad becomes an ovary. Testosterone and AMH come from the testis afterward, so they cannot be the trigger. Number of X chromosomes does not decide gonadal sex: XXY individuals with SRY develop testes.

questions.q: A GnRH agonist given as a continuous infusion, rather than in pulses, lowers LH and FSH secretion. The best explanation is that:
o: the agonist blocks GnRH receptors as an antagonist
An agonist activates the receptor; the suppression comes from desensitization.
the agonist directly inhibits the gonads
The effect is at the pituitary; gonadal output falls afterward.
continuous GnRH increases inhibin secretion by the pituitary
Inhibin is made by Sertoli and granulosa cells, not the pituitary.
constant stimulation desensitizes and downregulates the pituitary GnRH receptors
Correct: gonadotropes need pulsatile GnRH; constant exposure shuts down their response.
questions.note: Pulsatile GnRH stimulates; continuous GnRH suppresses.
questions.x: Pituitary gonadotropes respond to GnRH pulses roughly every 1–2 hours. Continuous exposure, even to an agonist, desensitizes and downregulates GnRH receptors, so LH and FSH fall after a brief flare. This is why long-acting GnRH agonists treat prostate cancer and precocious puberty. The drug is an agonist, not an antagonist; suppression comes from receptor desensitization.

questions.q: Which hormonal event directly triggers ovulation?
o: A sharp drop in estrogen
Estrogen peaks just before ovulation and helps cause the LH surge.
A rise in progesterone from the corpus luteum
The corpus luteum forms after ovulation.
A surge in luteinizing hormone (LH)
Correct: the mid-cycle LH surge causes the mature follicle to rupture.
A surge in prolactin
Prolactin drives milk production, not ovulation.
questions.x: A mid-cycle surge of LH from the anterior pituitary triggers follicle rupture and ovulation about a day later, and also lets the oocyte complete meiosis I. The surge is itself caused by high, sustained estrogen switching to positive feedback, so estrogen peaks rather than drops. Progesterone rises only after ovulation, from the corpus luteum.

questions.q: During the follicular phase of the ovarian cycle, the endometrium thickens mainly in response to:
o: progesterone from the corpus luteum
Progesterone dominates later, after ovulation.
hCG from the placenta
hCG appears only after implantation.
oxytocin from the posterior pituitary
Oxytocin acts on uterine muscle at labor, not on endometrial growth.
estrogen from the developing follicles
Correct: rising estrogen drives the proliferative phase of the uterine cycle.
questions.x: In the follicular phase, growing follicles secrete estradiol, which drives proliferation of the endometrium (the proliferative phase). After ovulation, progesterone from the corpus luteum converts it into secretory endometrium ready for implantation. Progesterone is the tempting answer but it acts later; hCG appears only after implantation.

questions.q: The main role of the corpus luteum during the luteal phase is to:
o: release a second oocyte later in the cycle
Only one ovulation normally happens per cycle.
secrete FSH to recruit new follicles
FSH comes from the anterior pituitary.
secrete progesterone that keeps the endometrium ready for implantation
Correct: progesterone (with estrogen) maintains the secretory endometrium.
produce the LH surge
LH is secreted by the anterior pituitary.
questions.x: After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum under LH, secreting progesterone plus estrogen and inhibin. Progesterone makes the endometrium secretory and vascular for implantation and, through negative feedback, suppresses new follicle growth. The corpus luteum does not make pituitary hormones such as LH or FSH.

questions.q: If fertilization does not occur, menstruation begins mainly because:
o: estrogen levels rise sharply
A sharp estrogen rise is a late follicular event that leads to ovulation.
the corpus luteum regresses and progesterone levels fall
Correct: without progesterone the endometrium cannot be maintained and is shed.
LH levels surge
The LH surge triggers ovulation, not menstruation.
hCG levels rise
Rising hCG would rescue the corpus luteum and prevent menstruation.
questions.x: Without fertilization there is no hCG, so the corpus luteum regresses about 14 days after ovulation. Falling progesterone and estrogen cause the spiral arteries to constrict and the functional endometrium to be shed. Rising hCG would do the reverse, rescuing the corpus luteum and preventing menstruation.

questions.q: Home pregnancy tests detect human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) because this hormone is:
o: made by the trophoblast after implantation to keep the corpus luteum active
Correct: hCG acts like LH to keep progesterone flowing early in pregnancy.
released by the anterior pituitary at every ovulation
hCG is not a pituitary hormone and appears only in pregnancy.
secreted by the corpus luteum in every cycle
The corpus luteum responds to hCG; it does not make it.
produced by the fetal liver late in pregnancy
hCG rises within days of implantation, from placental tissue.
questions.x: After implantation, the syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG, an LH-like hormone that keeps the corpus luteum producing progesterone until the placenta takes over around weeks 8–12. Because hCG is made only by trophoblast tissue, its presence in urine or blood signals pregnancy. It is not produced in normal non-pregnant cycles by the pituitary or the corpus luteum.

questions.q: Estrogen normally inhibits LH release, yet LH surges just before ovulation. What best explains this?
o: Progesterone from the corpus luteum stimulates the LH surge
The corpus luteum forms after ovulation, so it cannot cause the surge.
Estrogen held high for about two days switches its feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary from negative to positive
Correct: sustained high estradiol from the dominant follicle triggers the LH surge.
Estrogen levels drop to zero just before ovulation
Estrogen is at its peak, not its lowest, before ovulation.
Inhibin from the follicle stimulates LH release
Inhibin selectively suppresses FSH.
questions.note: Low estrogen gives negative feedback; high, sustained estrogen gives positive feedback.
questions.x: At low or moderate levels, estrogen exerts negative feedback on GnRH and LH. When the dominant follicle keeps estradiol high (above a threshold for about 36–48 hours), feedback switches to positive, gonadotropes become very sensitive to GnRH, and the LH surge follows. Progesterone cannot cause the surge because the corpus luteum forms only after ovulation.

questions.q: Combined estrogen–progestin oral contraceptives prevent pregnancy mainly by:
o: killing sperm in the female reproductive tract
That describes spermicides.
triggering early menstruation every week
Withdrawal bleeding is scheduled by the pill regimen; it is not the mechanism.
stimulating a continuous LH surge
Without a surge, ovulation cannot occur.
suppressing GnRH, FSH and LH so that follicles do not mature and no LH surge occurs
Correct: steady exogenous steroids give negative feedback and block ovulation.
questions.x: Combined pills provide steady estrogen and progestin that exert negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, suppressing GnRH, FSH and LH. Follicles do not mature and no LH surge occurs, so there is no ovulation; progestin also thickens cervical mucus. The monthly bleed is withdrawal bleeding set by the pill-free days, not the mechanism of action.

questions.q: Compared with a premenopausal woman, a postmenopausal woman would be expected to have:
o: high FSH and low estradiol
Correct: depleted follicles make little estrogen or inhibin, so negative feedback is lost and FSH rises.
low FSH and low estradiol
Low estrogen removes feedback, so FSH increases rather than falls.
low FSH and high estradiol
The ovaries no longer make much estradiol.
high FSH and high estradiol
Estradiol falls once the follicles are gone.
questions.x: At menopause the ovarian follicles are depleted, so estradiol and inhibin fall sharply. Losing their negative feedback lets GnRH drive high FSH and LH levels. High FSH with low estradiol is the hormonal signature of ovarian failure, which rules out any option with low FSH or high estradiol.

questions.q: In humans, fertilization normally takes place in the:
o: uterine cavity
The embryo reaches the uterus as a blastocyst, days later.
ovary
The egg is released from the ovary before fertilization.
ampulla of the uterine (fallopian) tube
Correct: sperm usually meet the egg in the wide ampulla of the oviduct.
cervix
The cervix is a passage for sperm, not the site of fertilization.
questions.x: Fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla, the wide outer part of the uterine tube, within about a day of ovulation. The zygote then cleaves as it travels toward the uterus and arrives as a blastocyst around day 5, implanting around days 6–10. Fertilization in the uterus is a common misconception.

questions.q: An aromatase inhibitor given to a premenopausal woman would most directly reduce:
o: LH secretion by the anterior pituitary
LH would actually rise as estrogen feedback is lost.
androgen production by theca cells
Theca cells make androgens under LH; aromatase acts afterward.
conversion of androgens to estradiol in granulosa cells
Correct: aromatase in granulosa cells converts theca-derived androgens into estrogens.
progesterone production by the corpus luteum
Progesterone synthesis does not require aromatase.
questions.note: Two-cell model: theca make androgens (LH), granulosa aromatize them (FSH).
questions.x: In the two-cell model, theca cells make androgens under LH, and granulosa cells use FSH-induced aromatase to convert them to estradiol. An aromatase inhibitor blocks that conversion directly. Theca androgen production is upstream and unaffected, and less estrogen feedback would actually raise, not lower, LH and FSH.

questions.q: The luteal phase lasts about 14 days in most women, while the follicular phase varies. In a regular 35-day cycle, ovulation would most likely occur around:
o: day 21
Correct: 35 − 14 = 21, since the luteal phase is fairly constant.
day 14
Day 14 fits a 28-day cycle; a longer cycle lengthens the follicular phase.
day 17
This splits the extra length evenly between the phases, but the luteal phase does not stretch.
day 28
That would leave only 7 days for the luteal phase.
questions.note: Cycle length varies by the follicular phase.
questions.x: The luteal phase is fixed at about 14 days by the corpus luteum's lifespan, so cycle length differences come from the follicular phase. Ovulation occurs about 14 days before the next menses: 35 − 14 = day 21. Choosing day 14 assumes a 28-day cycle, and splitting the extra days evenly wrongly lengthens the luteal phase.

questions.q: A woman's basal body temperature rises by about 0.3 °C and stays higher for roughly two weeks. This rise is best explained by:
o: estrogen secreted before ovulation
Estrogen peaks before ovulation; the temperature rise follows ovulation.
FSH secretion early in the cycle
Early FSH is not linked to the temperature shift.
the onset of menstruation
Temperature falls back around menstruation as progesterone drops.
progesterone secreted after ovulation
Correct: progesterone from the corpus luteum has a mild thermogenic effect.
questions.x: Progesterone from the corpus luteum acts on the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center and raises basal body temperature about 0.3–0.5 °C. The rise begins after ovulation and lasts about two weeks, the life of the corpus luteum. Estrogen peaks before ovulation, so it cannot explain a shift that starts after ovulation.

questions.q: To reach the egg plasma membrane, a sperm passes through the zona pellucida by:
o: using its midpiece mitochondria to dissolve the zona
Mitochondria supply ATP for swimming, not digestive enzymes.
releasing acrosomal enzymes after binding zona glycoproteins
Correct: binding the zona triggers the acrosome reaction, which digests a path.
fusing directly with the zona pellucida
The zona is a glycoprotein coat; fusion happens with the egg membrane.
waiting for cortical granules to open the zona
Cortical granules harden the zona after fertilization.
questions.x: After capacitation, the sperm binds zona pellucida glycoproteins (ZP3 in mice), which triggers the acrosome reaction: exocytosis of the acrosome releases proteases such as acrosin that digest a path through the zona. Only then can the sperm membrane fuse with the egg plasma membrane. The zona itself is not fused with, and cortical granules harden it rather than opening it.

questions.q: An egg is injected with a strong Ca²⁺ chelator just before it is exposed to many sperm. Which outcome is most likely?
o: The acrosome reaction is blocked in the sperm
The chelator is inside the egg; the sperm acrosome reaction is unaffected.
Meiosis II finishes faster than normal
Ca²⁺ is required for egg activation, including completion of meiosis II.
The zona pellucida hardens before sperm arrive
Zona hardening needs the Ca²⁺-triggered cortical reaction.
No cortical reaction occurs, so polyspermy is more likely
Correct: the Ca²⁺ wave triggers cortical granule exocytosis, the slow block to polyspermy.
questions.note: Ca²⁺ wave → cortical granules → zona hardening.
questions.x: Sperm fusion triggers a Ca²⁺ wave in the egg, which causes cortical granule exocytosis; the released enzymes modify the zona so other sperm cannot bind (the slow block). A chelator inside the egg blocks this wave, so no cortical reaction occurs and polyspermy becomes likely. The sperm's own acrosome reaction is unaffected because the chelator is confined to the egg.

questions.q: The fast block to polyspermy, best studied in sea urchin eggs, depends on:
o: enzymes released from cortical granules
Cortical granules cause the slower, permanent block.
depolarization of the egg membrane within seconds of sperm fusion
Correct: a rapid change in membrane potential stops further sperm from fusing.
the second polar body blocking the entry point
The polar body does not physically block sperm.
digestion of extra sperm by the acrosome
The acrosome belongs to the sperm and helps it penetrate the egg coats.
questions.x: In sea urchins, sperm fusion opens Na⁺ channels and depolarizes the egg membrane within seconds; a positive membrane potential prevents further sperm from fusing. This fast block is temporary and is followed by the Ca²⁺-dependent cortical reaction, the slow, permanent block. Cortical granule enzymes are therefore the slow block, not the fast one.

questions.q: Freshly ejaculated sperm placed next to eggs in a dish fail to fertilize them unless first incubated under conditions that mimic the female tract. This incubation allows:
o: the second meiotic division of the sperm
Sperm finish meiosis in the testis.
the cortical reaction
The cortical reaction happens in the egg after fertilization.
capacitation, which changes the sperm membrane and allows the acrosome reaction
Correct: capacitation normally happens in the female tract and is needed for fertilization.
the sperm to grow its flagellum
The flagellum forms during spermiogenesis in the testis.
questions.x: Ejaculated sperm cannot fertilize until capacitation in the female tract removes cholesterol and surface glycoproteins from their membrane, raises membrane fluidity and enables hyperactivated motility and the acrosome reaction. Sperm finish meiosis and build flagella in the testis long before this, and the cortical reaction is an egg event after fusion.

questions.q: Twins share a single chorion and a single amnion. They most likely arose from:
o: splitting of one embryo after the amnion had already formed
Correct: a late split, around the second week, leaves monozygotic twins in one shared amniotic sac.
fertilization of two eggs by two different sperm
Dizygotic twins each have their own chorion and amnion.
splitting of the embryo at the two-cell stage
An early split gives separate chorions and amnions.
fertilization of one egg by two sperm
Two sperm in one egg produce a triploid zygote, not twins.
questions.x: Monozygotic twins' membranes depend on when the embryo splits. Splitting by day 3 gives separate chorions and amnions; splitting the inner cell mass (days 4–8) gives one chorion, two amnions; splitting after the amnion forms (about days 8–13) gives one chorion and one amnion. Two-cell splitting gives separate membranes, and dizygotic twins always have their own.

questions.q: During cleavage of the early embryo, cell number rises quickly while:
o: the overall size of the embryo stays about the same
Correct: cleavage divisions skip growth, so cells get smaller.
each cell grows to the size of the zygote
There is no growth phase between cleavage divisions.
the embryo implants into the uterine wall
Implantation comes later, at the blastocyst stage.
the three germ layers form
Germ layers form at gastrulation.
questions.x: Cleavage divisions are rapid mitoses with little or no G1/G2 growth, so the zygote's cytoplasm is partitioned into ever smaller blastomeres while the embryo, still inside the zona pellucida, stays about the same size. This raises the nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio. Germ layers form later at gastrulation, and implantation follows blastocyst formation.

questions.q: In the human blastocyst, the inner cell mass gives rise to the embryo, while the trophoblast gives rise to:
o: the nervous system
The nervous system comes from ectoderm of the inner cell mass.
the endometrium
The endometrium is maternal tissue.
the fetal part of the placenta
Correct: trophoblast cells form the chorion, the fetal contribution to the placenta.
the primordial germ cells
Germ cells come from the embryo proper.
questions.x: The blastocyst has an inner cell mass, which forms the embryo proper (and amnion and yolk sac), and an outer trophoblast. The trophoblast becomes the chorion, the fetal part of the placenta, and secretes hCG. The endometrium is maternal tissue (forming the decidua), so it cannot come from the embryo's trophoblast.

questions.q: If an embryo cannot escape (hatch) from its zona pellucida, which step will fail?
o: Fertilization
Fertilization has already occurred if a blastocyst is present.
Implantation into the endometrium
Correct: the blastocyst must shed the zona before it can attach to the uterine wall.
Cleavage
Cleavage happens inside the zona.
Formation of the blastocoel
The blastocoel forms while the zona is still present.
questions.x: Cleavage, compaction and blastocoel formation all occur inside the zona pellucida. Around day 5 the blastocyst hatches from the zona so the trophoblast can contact and invade the endometrium. Failure to hatch blocks implantation; fertilization and cleavage have already happened by then.

questions.q: In humans and other deuterostomes, the blastopore formed during gastrulation develops into the:
o: mouth
That is the protostome pattern.
neural tube
The neural tube comes from ectoderm folding during neurulation.
umbilical cord
The umbilical cord forms from extraembryonic tissue.
anus
Correct: deuterostome means the mouth forms second; the blastopore becomes the anus.
questions.x: The first opening formed in gastrulation is the blastopore. In deuterostomes (echinoderms and chordates, including humans) it becomes the anus and the mouth forms second; in protostomes it becomes the mouth. The terms literally mean second mouth versus first mouth, which is the key to avoiding the reversal.

questions.q: Which structure is derived from embryonic mesoderm?
o: Kidney
Correct: kidneys, along with muscle, bone, heart and blood, are mesodermal.
Epidermis
The epidermis comes from ectoderm.
Hepatocytes of the liver
Liver parenchyma buds from endoderm.
Adrenal medulla
The adrenal medulla comes from neural crest (ectoderm).
questions.x: Mesoderm forms muscle, bone, connective tissue, heart, blood and vessels, kidneys, gonads and the adrenal cortex. Endoderm forms the lining of the gut and its glands, including liver and pancreas; ectoderm forms epidermis and the nervous system. The adrenal medulla is the trap: it comes from neural crest, an ectodermal derivative.

questions.q: A carcinoma arises from the epithelial cells that line the alveoli of the lung. These cells originally came from which germ layer?
o: Mesoderm
Mesoderm forms lung connective tissue and vessels, not the lining.
Endoderm
Correct: the lung epithelium forms from an outgrowth of the endodermal foregut.
Ectoderm
Ectoderm forms the epidermis and nervous system.
Neural crest
Neural crest forms peripheral neurons, melanocytes and some facial structures.
questions.x: Endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the digestive and respiratory tracts. The lungs arise as a bud from the foregut, so alveolar and airway epithelium is endodermal, while the surrounding connective tissue, smooth muscle and blood vessels are mesodermal. A carcinoma from alveolar cells therefore traces back to endoderm.

questions.q: The adrenal cortex and adrenal medulla differ in embryonic origin. Which pairing is correct?
o: Cortex from neural crest; medulla from mesoderm
This reverses the two origins.
Both from endoderm
Endoderm forms gut-derived organs such as the liver and pancreas.
Cortex from mesoderm; medulla from neural crest
Correct: steroid-secreting cortex is mesodermal; the catecholamine-secreting medulla is neural crest.
Both from neural crest
Only the medulla, which acts like a sympathetic ganglion, is neural crest.
questions.note: The medulla is a modified sympathetic ganglion.
questions.x: The adrenal cortex, which makes steroid hormones, comes from intermediate mesoderm, like the gonads that also make steroids. The medulla comes from neural crest cells that become chromaffin cells, essentially postganglionic sympathetic neurons that secrete epinephrine into the blood. Remember: steroid-secreting tissues are mesodermal.

questions.q: Formation of the neural plate from dorsal ectoderm is induced by signals from the underlying:
o: yolk sac
The yolk sac is extraembryonic and does not induce the neural plate.
endoderm of the gut tube
The gut tube lies too far ventral to induce the neural plate.
trophoblast
The trophoblast forms the placenta.
notochord
Correct: the mesodermal notochord signals the overlying ectoderm to become neural plate.
questions.x: During neurulation the notochord, a rod of mesoderm under the dorsal ectoderm, secretes signals that induce the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate, which folds into the neural tube. This is a classic example of induction. The gut endoderm lies ventral and the yolk sac and trophoblast are extraembryonic, so they do not induce the neural plate.

questions.q: A mutation that prevents neural crest cells from migrating would most likely cause a lack of:
o: the spinal cord
The spinal cord forms from the neural tube itself.
skeletal muscle of the limbs
Limb muscle comes from somitic mesoderm.
pigment-producing melanocytes in the skin
Correct: melanocytes come from neural crest cells that migrate into the skin.
the epithelial lining of the intestine
Gut lining comes from endoderm.
questions.x: Neural crest cells delaminate from the edges of the closing neural tube and migrate widely, forming melanocytes, peripheral and autonomic neurons, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla and facial bones and cartilage. Blocked migration leaves those cells absent, as in pigment disorders and Hirschsprung disease. The spinal cord itself comes from the neural tube, not the neural crest.

questions.q: Spina bifida results from:
o: failure of the notochord to form
The notochord forms; the defect is in neural tube closure.
overgrowth of the neural crest
Neural crest is not overgrown in spina bifida.
incomplete separation of the digits
That is syndactyly.
incomplete closure of the neural tube
Correct: failure of the posterior neural tube to close causes spina bifida.
questions.note: Folate before and early in pregnancy lowers the risk.
questions.x: The neural tube forms when the neural plate folds and its edges fuse, finishing around week 4. If the posterior end fails to close, vertebral arches do not form over the cord, giving spina bifida; failure at the anterior end causes anencephaly. Adequate folic acid before and in early pregnancy lowers the risk.

questions.q: Somites, blocks of paraxial mesoderm on either side of the neural tube, give rise to:
o: vertebrae, skeletal muscle and dermis
Correct: somites form the axial skeleton, trunk and limb muscle, and dermis of the back.
the brain and spinal cord
These come from the neural tube (ectoderm).
the liver and pancreas
These are endodermal.
the epidermis and hair
These are ectodermal.
questions.x: Somites are segmented blocks of paraxial mesoderm beside the neural tube. They split into sclerotome (vertebrae and ribs), myotome (skeletal muscle of the trunk and limbs) and dermatome (dermis of the back). The brain, spinal cord, epidermis and hair are ectodermal and the liver and pancreas endodermal, so they cannot come from somites.

questions.q: When tissue from the dorsal lip of the blastopore is grafted onto the ventral side of an amphibian gastrula, a second body axis forms that is made mostly of host cells. This shows that the grafted tissue:
o: divides rapidly to build the entire second axis itself
The new axis is made mostly of host cells, not graft cells.
induces neighboring cells to change their developmental fate
Correct: an organizer signals surrounding host cells to form axial structures.
has lost its developmental potential
It clearly still has strong developmental effects.
fuses with host cells to form hybrid cells
Induction works by signaling, not cell fusion.
questions.x: The dorsal lip of the blastopore is the Spemann organizer. When grafted, it recruits host tissue that would have formed belly to instead form a neural tube and somites, a process called induction. Because the second axis is built mostly from host cells, the graft did not build it itself; it changed its neighbors' fates through signaling.

questions.q: Which statement about exchange across the human placenta is correct?
o: Maternal blood flows directly into fetal vessels
The two circulations normally do not mix.
Maternal and fetal blood stay separate, and solutes cross by diffusion and transport
Correct: placental barriers allow exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes without blood mixing.
Oxygen crosses by active transport against its gradient
O₂ moves by diffusion down its partial-pressure gradient.
Fetal red blood cells cross freely to the mother
Cells generally do not cross; leakage mostly occurs at delivery.
questions.x: In the placenta, maternal blood bathes the chorionic villi but stays separated from fetal blood by trophoblast and capillary endothelium. Gases cross by diffusion down partial-pressure gradients, glucose by facilitated diffusion, and some nutrients and IgG by active transport or transcytosis. The circulations do not mix, which is why maternal and fetal blood types can differ.

questions.q: In fetal circulation, the foramen ovale allows blood to:
o: pass from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the lungs
Correct: most oxygenated blood from the IVC crosses directly to the left heart.
pass from the pulmonary artery to the aorta
That is the ductus arteriosus.
bypass the liver on its way to the heart
That is the ductus venosus.
return from the fetus to the placenta
That is the role of the umbilical arteries.
questions.x: Fetal lungs are fluid-filled and not used for gas exchange, so most blood bypasses them. The foramen ovale lets oxygen-rich blood from the IVC flow from the right atrium to the left atrium, and the ductus arteriosus shunts pulmonary-artery blood into the aorta. The ductus venosus is the third shunt, bypassing the liver.

questions.q: Fetal hemoglobin binds 2,3-BPG weakly. How does this help the fetus obtain oxygen?
o: It lowers fetal hemoglobin's O₂ affinity so that it releases O₂ to fetal tissues faster
Weak 2,3-BPG binding raises affinity; it does not lower it.
It allows maternal red cells to enter the fetal circulation
Maternal red cells do not normally enter the fetal circulation, and 2,3-BPG binding has nothing to do with cell transfer.
It increases dissolved O₂ in fetal plasma by active transport
No active O₂ transport occurs.
It gives fetal hemoglobin a higher O₂ affinity, so O₂ moves from maternal to fetal blood
Correct: a left-shifted fetal curve loads O₂ at placental partial pressures.
questions.x: 2,3-BPG stabilizes the low-affinity T state of hemoglobin. Fetal hemoglobin (α₂γ₂) binds 2,3-BPG poorly, so its O₂ dissociation curve is left-shifted with higher affinity than maternal HbA. At the placenta this difference pulls O₂ from maternal to fetal blood. Weak 2,3-BPG binding raises affinity, so an answer claiming it lowers affinity reverses the logic.

questions.q: Which vessel carries the most highly oxygenated blood in the fetus?
o: Umbilical artery
Umbilical arteries return deoxygenated blood to the placenta.
Pulmonary vein
Fetal lungs do not oxygenate blood.
Umbilical vein
Correct: the umbilical vein brings oxygenated blood from the placenta.
Descending aorta
Aortic blood is already mixed with deoxygenated blood.
questions.note: In the fetus, the 'vein' carries oxygen-rich blood.
questions.x: In the fetus, the placenta is the gas-exchange organ. The single umbilical vein carries oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood from the placenta toward the fetal heart, while the two umbilical arteries return deoxygenated blood. Vessel names reflect direction relative to the heart, not oxygen content, which is the trap.

questions.q: The earliest blood cells of the human embryo form in the:
o: bone marrow
Marrow becomes the main site only late in fetal life.
amnion
The amnion encloses the protective amniotic fluid.
spleen
The spleen helps in mid-gestation but is not the first site.
yolk sac
Correct: blood islands in the yolk sac make the first blood cells, before the liver and marrow take over.
questions.x: Hematopoiesis begins in blood islands of the yolk sac in the third week, then shifts to the fetal liver (with some spleen contribution) in mid-gestation, and finally to bone marrow, which becomes the main site late in fetal life and after birth. Bone marrow is tempting because it is the adult site, but it is the last to take over.

questions.q: A teratogenic drug is most likely to cause major structural birth defects when taken during:
o: the first week, before implantation
Early exposure tends to be all-or-none: embryo loss or full recovery.
the last trimester
Organs are already formed; late exposure mainly affects growth or function.
weeks 3 to 8 after fertilization, during organogenesis
Correct: organ systems form then, so disruption causes major malformations.
the week before conception
No embryo exists yet to be malformed.
questions.x: During weeks 3–8 (the embryonic period), organ systems are being laid down, so teratogens cause major structural malformations. Before implantation, exposure usually has an all-or-none effect: the embryo dies or recovers completely. After week 8, organs are already formed, so later exposures mainly affect growth and function, as in the fetal brain.

questions.q: Excess retinoic acid during development can cause anterior structures to take on more posterior identities. This is best explained by retinoic acid:
o: destroying all neural crest cells
The effect described is a change in positional identity, not cell loss.
changing Hox gene expression along the anterior–posterior axis
Correct: retinoic acid regulates Hox genes, which specify positional identity.
blocking DNA replication in the embryo
Blocked replication would stop growth, not shift identities.
converting endoderm into ectoderm
The described defect involves axial position, not germ layer identity.
questions.x: Retinoic acid forms an anterior–posterior gradient and acts through nuclear receptors that directly regulate Hox genes. Hox genes encode transcription factors that give each region its positional identity. Excess retinoic acid shifts Hox expression anteriorly, so anterior structures take on posterior identities, a change in identity rather than cell death.

questions.q: A cell that can give rise to an entire organism, including extraembryonic tissues such as the placenta, is described as:
o: totipotent
Correct: the zygote and very early blastomeres are totipotent.
pluripotent
Pluripotent cells form all three germ layers but not extraembryonic trophoblast.
multipotent
Multipotent cells form only a few related cell types.
unipotent
Unipotent cells form only one cell type.
questions.x: Totipotent cells, such as the zygote and very early blastomeres, can form all embryonic and extraembryonic tissues, including trophoblast-derived placenta. Pluripotent cells, like inner cell mass and ES cells, make all three germ layers but not trophoblast. The trophoblast is the dividing line between totipotent and pluripotent.

questions.q: Embryonic stem cells taken from the inner cell mass are pluripotent. This means they can form:
o: only blood cells
That describes a multipotent hematopoietic stem cell.
derivatives of all three germ layers but not the trophoblast
Correct: ICM cells form the embryo proper, not the placental trophoblast.
every tissue including the placenta
That would be totipotent.
only one specialized cell type
That is unipotent.
questions.x: Inner cell mass cells are pluripotent: they can give rise to every derivative of ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm, plus germ cells, but not the trophoblast that forms the fetal placenta. Forming the placenta too would require totipotency, seen only in the zygote and earliest blastomeres. Restriction to one lineage, like blood, describes multipotent stem cells.

questions.q: A hematopoietic stem cell can produce red blood cells, neutrophils and lymphocytes but not neurons. It is therefore:
o: totipotent
Totipotent cells can form a whole organism.
pluripotent
Pluripotent cells could also make neurons and other germ-layer derivatives.
terminally differentiated
Terminally differentiated cells do not self-renew or produce many types.
multipotent
Correct: it is limited to one lineage family, the blood cells.
questions.x: Potency is ranked totipotent > pluripotent > multipotent > unipotent. A hematopoietic stem cell self-renews and makes all blood lineages, myeloid and lymphoid, but cannot cross into other germ-layer derivatives such as neurons. Producing many cell types within one lineage family is multipotency; pluripotent cells would also make neurons.

questions.q: A key advantage of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) made from a patient's own skin cells over embryonic stem cells for transplant is that iPSCs:
o: are genetically matched to the patient, which reduces immune rejection
Correct: autologous iPSCs carry the patient's own antigens.
cannot form tumors
Pluripotent cells, including iPSCs, can form teratomas.
are totipotent and can form a placenta
iPSCs are pluripotent, like ESCs.
do not require any transcription factors to produce
iPSCs are made by expressing reprogramming factors such as Oct4 and Sox2.
questions.x: iPSCs are made by expressing reprogramming factors such as Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc in adult cells. Because they come from the patient, derived tissues carry the patient's own MHC antigens and largely avoid immune rejection, and they avoid using embryos. Like ES cells they are pluripotent, not totipotent, and can form teratomas, so tumor risk remains.

questions.q: A nucleus from a differentiated frog intestinal cell is transplanted into an enucleated egg, which then develops into a tadpole. What does this demonstrate?
o: Intestinal cells are naturally totipotent in the adult
Reprogramming needed the egg cytoplasm; intestinal cells do not do this alone.
Egg cytoplasm supplies the genes for the tadpole
Genes come from the transplanted nucleus; cytoplasm only reprograms it.
Differentiated cells keep the genes needed to direct development of a whole organism
Correct: differentiation relies on differential gene expression, not permanent gene loss.
Differentiation happens by deleting unneeded genes
The result shows the genes were still present.
questions.note: Nuclear transfer shows genomic equivalence.
questions.x: Somatic nuclear transfer shows genomic equivalence: a differentiated cell keeps the full genome needed to build an organism. The egg cytoplasm reprograms gene expression but contributes no nuclear genes. Differentiation therefore works by turning genes on and off (differential gene expression), not by deleting unneeded genes.

questions.q: A stem cell divides to give one daughter that remains a stem cell and one that begins to differentiate. This type of division:
o: depletes the stem cell pool with every division
One daughter stays a stem cell, so the pool is preserved.
is the same as meiosis
This is a mitotic division; no chromosome reduction occurs.
maintains the stem cell pool while producing specialized cells
Correct: asymmetric division balances self-renewal and differentiation.
produces two identical differentiated cells
That would be a symmetric differentiating division.
questions.x: In asymmetric division, one daughter keeps stem identity (self-renewal) and the other becomes a progenitor that differentiates. This keeps the stem cell pool constant while supplying specialized cells, as in skin, gut and bone marrow. It is ordinary mitosis with unequal fate determinants or niche signals, not meiosis.

questions.q: The intestinal epithelium is replaced every few days. The stem cells driving this renewal are located:
o: at the base of the crypts
Correct: crypt stem cells produce cells that move up the villi and are shed.
at the tips of the villi
Villus tips are where old cells are shed.
in the smooth muscle layer
The muscularis does not supply epithelial cells.
in the bone marrow only
Blood stem cells do not routinely replace gut epithelium.
questions.x: Intestinal stem cells (Lgr5⁺) sit near the base of the crypts of Lieberkühn, supported by niche signals such as Wnt. Their progeny divide, differentiate and migrate up the villus, then are shed from the tip after a few days. The villus tip is where cells die, so it is the opposite of the stem cell location.

questions.q: Cells grown from a culture are injected into immunodeficient mice and form tumors containing neural tissue, cartilage and gut-like epithelium. This result best supports the claim that the cells are:
o: unipotent
Unipotent cells would form only one cell type.
terminally differentiated
Differentiated cells would not form multiple tissue types.
multipotent hematopoietic cells
Blood stem cells cannot make neurons, cartilage and gut epithelium.
pluripotent
Correct: making ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm derivatives shows pluripotency.
questions.note: A teratoma containing all three germ layers is the classic pluripotency test.
questions.x: A teratoma assay tests pluripotency: cells injected into immunodeficient mice form tumors, and if those tumors contain tissues from all three germ layers (neural tissue = ectoderm, cartilage = mesoderm, gut epithelium = endoderm), the cells are pluripotent. Multipotent blood stem cells are limited to blood lineages and could not make this mix.

questions.q: Ectoderm transplanted to a new location in an embryo still forms the structure it would have made in its original place. Before transplantation, the tissue was already:
o: totipotent
A totipotent cell would adopt its new surroundings' fate.
determined
Correct: determination is a commitment to a fate before visible differentiation.
undergoing apoptosis
Dying tissue would not go on to form structures.
dedifferentiated
Dedifferentiation is a loss of specialization, the opposite of commitment.
questions.x: Determination is commitment to a fate before visible differentiation; a determined cell keeps its fate even when moved to a new environment. Specified but undetermined tissue would instead adopt the fate of its new surroundings. Totipotent or uncommitted tissue would be reprogrammed by the new location, which is the opposite of what was observed.

questions.q: In fruit flies, a mutation in a homeotic (Hox) gene causes legs to grow where antennae normally form. Hox genes normally:
o: control the rate of cell division in all tissues
Hox genes set positional identity, not general growth rate.
encode structural proteins of the leg
Hox genes encode transcription factors, not structural proteins.
trigger apoptosis in extra limbs
Their main job is segment identity, not removing tissue.
specify the identity of body segments along the anterior–posterior axis
Correct: Hox transcription factors tell each segment what structures to form.
questions.x: Hox (homeotic) genes encode homeodomain transcription factors expressed in an ordered pattern along the anterior–posterior axis, telling each segment what to become. Mutations swap segment identity, as in Antennapedia, where antennae become legs. They are regulatory genes, so they do not encode leg structural proteins or set overall growth rate.

questions.q: In fly embryos, bicoid protein forms a gradient from the anterior end. When extra copies of the bicoid gene are added, head structures extend farther toward the posterior. This suggests that:
o: bicoid is required only in posterior cells
Bicoid is concentrated anteriorly and specifies anterior fates.
cells adopt fates according to the local morphogen concentration
Correct: more bicoid moves each concentration threshold posteriorly, so anterior fates expand.
head formation does not depend on bicoid
Changing bicoid dose changed head size, showing dependence.
each cell inherits a fixed fate regardless of position
Fates shifted with the gradient, so they depend on position.
questions.note: Morphogens act through concentration thresholds.
questions.x: Bicoid mRNA is localized at the anterior pole, so its protein forms a concentration gradient. Target genes switch on above specific thresholds, so cells read their position from the local concentration. Adding bicoid copies raises the gradient and pushes each threshold posteriorly, expanding head fates, which shows fate depends on position rather than lineage.

questions.q: Tissue from the zone of polarizing activity (ZPA) is grafted to the anterior edge of a chick limb bud, and a mirror-image duplication of the digits results. The best explanation is that the ZPA:
o: contains cells that become all the extra digits themselves
The extra digits come mostly from host tissue responding to the signal.
blocks apoptosis between the digits
That would cause webbing, not mirror duplication.
secretes a morphogen that specifies posterior digit identity
Correct: a second source of the signal, Sonic hedgehog, makes a mirror-image gradient.
converts limb mesoderm into ectoderm
Germ layer identity does not change.
questions.x: The ZPA at the posterior limb bud secretes Sonic hedgehog, a morphogen whose gradient specifies digit identity, with the highest concentration giving the most posterior digit. A second anterior source creates a mirror-image gradient and mirror-duplicated digits. The extra digits come mainly from host cells responding to the signal, not from the graft itself.

questions.q: Notch–Delta signaling, in which a cell with membrane-bound Delta activates Notch on an adjacent cell, is an example of:
o: juxtacrine signaling that requires direct cell contact
Correct: both ligand and receptor are membrane-bound, so the cells must touch.
endocrine signaling through the blood
Endocrine hormones travel long distances in the circulation.
autocrine signaling only
Delta on one cell signals Notch on a neighboring cell.
synaptic signaling across a cleft
Notch–Delta does not use a neurotransmitter or synapse.
questions.note: Lateral inhibition via Notch keeps neighbors from adopting the same fate.
questions.x: Juxtacrine signaling requires direct contact because both ligand and receptor are membrane-bound. When Delta binds Notch, Notch is cleaved and its intracellular domain enters the nucleus to change transcription, often producing lateral inhibition so neighboring cells adopt different fates. Endocrine and paracrine signals travel through blood or extracellular fluid instead.

questions.q: A growth factor secreted by one cell that diffuses a short distance to act on nearby cells is an example of:
o: paracrine signaling
Correct: paracrine signals act locally on neighboring cells.
endocrine signaling
Endocrine signals travel in the blood to distant targets.
autocrine signaling
Autocrine signals act on the secreting cell itself.
juxtacrine signaling
Juxtacrine signals need direct membrane contact.
questions.x: Signaling is classified by distance: autocrine acts on the secreting cell, juxtacrine needs membrane contact, paracrine diffuses locally to nearby cells, and endocrine travels in the blood. A secreted growth factor acting on neighbors over a short distance is paracrine. It is not juxtacrine, because the factor is released rather than staying on the membrane.

questions.q: A tissue that normally induces lens formation is placed next to older head ectoderm, and no lens forms. The most likely explanation is that the older ectoderm:
o: releases the inducing signal itself
If it made the signal, a lens would be more likely, not less.
has become totipotent
Older tissue loses potential rather than gaining it.
is no longer competent to respond to the inducing signal
Correct: responding tissue must be competent, for example by expressing the right receptors.
has lost all of its DNA
Differentiated cells keep their genome.
questions.x: Induction requires both an inducing signal and a competent responding tissue that has the right receptors and transcription factors. Competence is limited in time; as ectoderm ages and commits to other fates it stops responding to lens-inducing signals. Older tissue has lost potential, not gained it, and differentiated cells keep their DNA.

questions.q: Removing the optic vesicle before it contacts the head ectoderm prevents lens formation. This is an example of:
o: apoptosis
No cell death is being described.
embryonic induction
Correct: one tissue, the optic vesicle, directs another, the ectoderm, to form a lens.
senescence
Senescence is permanent arrest of aging cells.
gastrulation
Gastrulation forms the germ layers, much earlier.
questions.x: Embryonic induction occurs when one tissue signals to change the fate of another. The optic vesicle, an outgrowth of the forebrain, contacts the head surface ectoderm and induces it to form the lens placode; removing it prevents lens formation. The lens then induces the cornea, a chain of reciprocal inductions.

questions.q: When cells from two tissues expressing different cadherins are mixed, they sort into separate groups. This happens mainly because cadherins:
o: degrade the extracellular matrix
That is the role of matrix metalloproteinases.
act as receptors for steroid hormones
Cadherins are adhesion proteins, not steroid receptors.
form gap junctions between unlike cells
Gap junctions are made of connexins.
bind to the same type of cadherin on neighboring cells in a Ca²⁺-dependent manner
Correct: homophilic cadherin binding makes like cells stick to like.
questions.x: Cadherins are Ca²⁺-dependent adhesion proteins that bind mainly to the same cadherin type on neighboring cells (homophilic binding). Cells with matching cadherins stick together more strongly, so mixed populations sort into separate tissues. Gap junctions are made of connexins and degrading the matrix is the job of metalloproteinases, so neither explains sorting.

questions.q: Female calico cats have patches of orange and black fur, with the coat-color gene carried on the X chromosome. This pattern results from:
o: random inactivation of one X chromosome in each cell early in development
Correct: each patch descends from a cell that silenced a different X.
crossing over between X chromosomes in skin cells
Somatic crossing over is not the cause of calico patches.
loss of one X chromosome from half of the body
Both X chromosomes are present; one is silenced.
a new mutation in each fur cell
New mutations would arise randomly and rarely; large two-color patches reflect which X is active in each clone.
questions.x: In female mammals, one X in each cell is randomly inactivated early in development and condensed into a Barr body, and all descendants keep the same X silenced. A heterozygous female cat thus has patches expressing the orange allele and patches expressing the black allele. Both X chromosomes are still present; one is simply silenced in each patch.

questions.q: A salamander regrows an amputated limb. Regeneration depends mainly on:
o: migration of blood stem cells into the stump
Blood stem cells do not rebuild bone, muscle and skin.
a blastema of dedifferentiated and progenitor cells at the wound
Correct: cells near the stump form a blastema that rebuilds the limb.
meiosis in the stump cells
Regeneration uses mitosis, not meiosis.
enlargement of existing cells without division
Rebuilding a limb requires cell division.
questions.x: After amputation, cells near the stump lose some specialization or activate resident progenitors to form a blastema, a mass of proliferating cells under the wound epidermis. Blastema cells retain positional memory and rebuild the missing structures by mitosis and redifferentiation. Regeneration requires cell division, so enlargement alone or meiosis cannot rebuild a limb.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes apoptosis from necrosis?
o: Apoptotic cells swell and burst
Swelling and bursting describe necrosis.
Apoptosis occurs only after physical injury
Apoptosis is a programmed process that also occurs in normal development.
Apoptotic cells are removed by phagocytes without causing inflammation
Correct: contents stay packaged in apoptotic bodies, so little inflammation results.
Apoptosis does not involve enzymes
Caspases carry out apoptosis.
questions.x: Apoptosis is programmed, caspase-driven cell death: the cell shrinks, chromatin condenses, DNA fragments and the cell breaks into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies that phagocytes clear without inflammation. Necrosis results from injury; cells swell and burst, spilling contents that trigger inflammation. Swelling and bursting is the classic necrosis feature, not apoptosis.

questions.q: Cells exposed to an apoptotic stimulus are treated with a broad caspase inhibitor. The most likely result is that:
o: the cells die faster by apoptosis
Inhibiting the executioners slows or blocks apoptosis.
the cells enter mitosis immediately
Blocking caspases does not push cells into mitosis.
the cells release cytochrome c into the nucleus
Cytochrome c is released into the cytosol, upstream of caspases.
the cells fail to complete apoptosis
Correct: caspases are the proteases that carry out apoptotic cell dismantling.
questions.x: Caspases are cysteine proteases that execute apoptosis: initiator caspases (8, 9) activate executioner caspases (3, 7), which cleave cellular proteins to dismantle the cell. A broad caspase inhibitor stops this cascade, so cells fail to complete apoptosis, though they may later die by other means. Cytochrome c release is upstream and goes into the cytosol, not the nucleus.

questions.q: In the intrinsic pathway of apoptosis, which event activates the initiator caspase-9?
o: Binding of Fas ligand to the Fas receptor
That starts the extrinsic pathway through caspase-8.
Phosphorylation of Rb by CDK4
Rb phosphorylation drives the G1/S transition.
Release of cytochrome c from mitochondria to form the apoptosome
Correct: cytosolic cytochrome c joins Apaf-1 to activate caspase-9.
Fusion of lysosomes with the plasma membrane
Lysosome–plasma membrane fusion is exocytosis or membrane repair, unrelated to apoptosome assembly.
questions.x: In the intrinsic pathway, cellular stress activates Bax and Bak, which permeabilize the outer mitochondrial membrane and release cytochrome c into the cytosol. Cytochrome c binds Apaf-1, forming the apoptosome, which activates initiator caspase-9 and then caspase-3. Fas ligand binding is the extrinsic pathway, which activates caspase-8 instead.

questions.q: Overexpression of the protein Bcl-2 contributes to some lymphomas mainly by:
o: activating caspase-3 directly
Caspase activation would kill cells, not promote tumors.
speeding up DNA repair
Bcl-2 acts on mitochondrial apoptosis, not on repair.
acting as a growth factor receptor
Bcl-2 is not a receptor; it sits in the outer mitochondrial membrane and restrains Bax and Bak.
preventing mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization, so damaged cells survive
Correct: Bcl-2 is anti-apoptotic and blocks cytochrome c release.
questions.note: Some oncogenes work by blocking cell death rather than by driving division.
questions.x: Bcl-2 is an anti-apoptotic protein in the outer mitochondrial membrane that restrains Bax and Bak, preventing outer membrane permeabilization and cytochrome c release. Overexpression, often from a t(14;18) translocation, lets damaged lymphocytes survive and accumulate further mutations. It is an oncogene that blocks death rather than driving division.

questions.q: A cytotoxic T cell triggers apoptosis in an infected cell by engaging the target's death receptor, Fas. This mainly activates:
o: the extrinsic pathway through caspase-8
Correct: death receptors recruit adaptors that activate caspase-8.
the intrinsic pathway through cytochrome c release alone
The intrinsic pathway starts from mitochondrial stress, not receptor engagement.
necrosis through membrane rupture
Fas signaling causes apoptosis, not necrosis.
cell cycle entry through cyclin D
Fas signaling leads to death, not division.
questions.x: Death receptors such as Fas, when bound by their ligand, recruit the adaptor FADD and procaspase-8 into a signaling complex that activates caspase-8, which then activates executioner caspases. This is the extrinsic pathway. The intrinsic pathway begins with internal stress and mitochondrial cytochrome c release, so receptor engagement points to the extrinsic route.

questions.q: If apoptosis fails in the tissue between the developing fingers, the result is:
o: extra fingers
Extra digits come from patterning defects, not failed apoptosis.
webbed fingers (syndactyly)
Correct: programmed cell death normally removes the interdigital tissue.
absent fingers
Too much cell death, not too little, could remove digits.
shortened fingers
Failed apoptosis leaves extra tissue rather than shorter digits.
questions.x: Digits form when apoptosis removes the tissue between them in the developing hand and foot plate. If interdigital cells fail to die, the digits remain joined, giving syndactyly. Extra digits (polydactyly) reflect patterning errors, such as abnormal Sonic hedgehog signaling, rather than failed cell death.

questions.q: Cells are stained with labeled annexin V, which binds phosphatidylserine on the outer leaflet, and propidium iodide (PI), which enters only cells with damaged membranes. Which population represents early apoptosis?
o: Annexin V negative, PI negative
This describes healthy live cells.
Annexin V positive, PI negative
Correct: PS flips outward early, while the membrane is still intact and keeps PI out.
Annexin V positive, PI positive
Both signals indicate late apoptosis or necrosis with a damaged membrane.
Annexin V negative, PI positive
Membrane rupture without PS exposure suggests necrosis or damaged cells.
questions.note: Exposed PS acts as an 'eat me' signal for phagocytes.
questions.x: Healthy cells keep phosphatidylserine on the inner membrane leaflet. Early in apoptosis, PS flips outward and binds annexin V while the membrane is still intact and excludes PI. Late apoptotic or necrotic cells have damaged membranes and are positive for both. Annexin V positive with PI negative is therefore the early apoptotic population.

questions.q: An activating mutation in just one allele of a proto-oncogene can promote cancer because:
o: the resulting oncogene acts as a gain of function, so one altered copy is enough
Correct: oncogenic mutations are dominant at the cellular level.
both alleles must be lost before any effect appears
That two-hit pattern describes tumor suppressor genes.
proto-oncogenes normally stop the cell cycle
Proto-oncogenes normally promote growth; tumor suppressors stop it.
the mutation removes the gene from the genome
Activation alters or overexpresses the gene rather than deleting it.
questions.x: Proto-oncogenes normally promote growth, and activating mutations create oncogenes with gain of function, such as a constantly active protein or overexpression. One mutated allele is enough, so oncogenes act dominantly at the cellular level. Needing both copies lost (two hits) describes tumor suppressor genes, which are recessive at the cellular level.

questions.q: Children who inherit one mutant RB1 allele often develop retinoblastoma in both eyes at an early age. The best explanation is that:
o: RB1 is an oncogene that acts dominantly
RB1 is a tumor suppressor; tumors arise after both copies are lost.
the inherited allele makes Rb hyperactive
Hyperactive Rb would block division, not cause tumors.
retinal cells cannot undergo apoptosis
The key factor is the inherited first hit, not a general apoptosis defect.
every retinal cell already has one hit, so a single somatic mutation inactivates both copies
Correct: the two-hit model needs only one more mutation in an inherited carrier.
questions.note: Inherited tumor suppressor mutations: early, multiple, often bilateral tumors.
questions.x: RB1 is a tumor suppressor, so a cell must lose both copies before control is lost (Knudson two-hit hypothesis). Children who inherit one mutant allele carry the first hit in every retinal cell, so one somatic mutation in any of millions of cells is enough, giving early, often bilateral tumors. Sporadic cases need two somatic hits in the same cell, so they are later and unilateral.

questions.q: Many tumors carry Ras mutations that impair its GTPase activity. These mutations promote cell proliferation because Ras:
o: can no longer bind GTP
That would inactivate Ras and reduce signaling.
becomes a tumor suppressor
Ras is a proto-oncogene product; this mutation makes it an oncogene, not a tumor suppressor.
stays bound to GTP and keeps signaling for growth
Correct: Ras can no longer turn itself off by hydrolyzing GTP.
triggers apoptosis
Constant Ras signaling drives growth, not death.
questions.x: Ras is a small G protein that is active when bound to GTP and switches itself off by hydrolyzing GTP to GDP, helped by GAP proteins. Mutations that impair GTPase activity leave Ras locked in the GTP-bound state, continuously signaling through the MAP kinase pathway to drive proliferation. Losing GTP binding would inactivate Ras, the opposite effect.

questions.q: Loss of E-cadherin expression in carcinoma cells most directly promotes:
o: faster DNA replication
E-cadherin is an adhesion protein, not a replication factor.
increased apoptosis
Loss of E-cadherin is linked to spread, not to more apoptosis.
formation of gap junctions
Gap junctions are formed by connexins.
detachment from neighboring cells, aiding invasion and metastasis
Correct: losing cell–cell adhesion lets tumor cells break away.
questions.x: E-cadherin forms adherens junctions that hold epithelial cells together. Losing it, often during epithelial–mesenchymal transition, lets carcinoma cells detach from their neighbors, invade surrounding tissue and enter vessels to metastasize. It is an adhesion molecule, not a regulator of replication or apoptosis.

questions.q: An antibody that neutralizes vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) slows tumor growth mainly by:
o: directly killing tumor cells in S phase
Anti-VEGF targets blood vessel growth, not dividing tumor cells.
restoring p53 function
VEGF blockade does not repair p53.
blocking the formation of new blood vessels that supply the tumor
Correct: tumors larger than a few millimeters need angiogenesis for oxygen and nutrients.
reactivating telomerase in tumor cells
Telomerase activity supports, rather than limits, tumor growth.
questions.x: Tumors larger than a few millimeters need new blood vessels for oxygen and nutrients. Tumor cells secrete VEGF to stimulate angiogenesis; a neutralizing antibody (such as bevacizumab) blocks this, starving the tumor of blood supply. It does not directly kill dividing tumor cells, as a cytotoxic chemotherapy drug would.

questions.q: Which feature is the defining difference between a malignant tumor and a benign tumor?
o: A larger size
Benign tumors can be very large.
The ability to invade surrounding tissue and spread to distant sites
Correct: invasion and metastasis define malignancy.
Faster growth in all cases
Growth rate varies and does not define malignancy.
Being made of abnormal cells
Both benign and malignant tumors are made of abnormal cells.
questions.x: Benign tumors stay localized, often encapsulated, and do not invade. Malignant tumors invade surrounding tissue and can metastasize through blood or lymph to distant sites; this capacity defines cancer. Size and growth rate vary in both, and benign tumors can grow very large, so neither distinguishes them.

questions.q: A mutant cell line divides without growth factors, while normal cells arrest. Fusing a mutant cell with a normal cell gives hybrids that arrest without growth factors. The mutation most likely:
o: inactivates a tumor suppressor, and the normal allele restores control
Correct: the normal phenotype is dominant in hybrids, so the mutation is recessive loss of function.
activates an oncogene that dominates the normal genome
A dominant oncogene would make the hybrids divide without growth factors.
causes chromosome loss in the hybrid
The data are explained by the normal gene restoring control.
has no effect on the cell cycle
The mutant cells clearly show altered growth control.
questions.note: Fusion tests dominance: recessive defects are rescued by normal genes.
questions.x: Cell fusion tests whether a phenotype is dominant or recessive. If hybrids regain normal growth control, the normal genome supplies a function the mutant lacks, so the mutation is a recessive loss of function, typical of a tumor suppressor. A dominant oncogene would make the hybrids keep dividing without growth factors.

questions.q: Cultured normal fibroblasts stop dividing when they form a single layer, but transformed cells keep piling up into multilayered foci. This shows that transformed cells have lost:
o: the ability to replicate DNA
Transformed cells replicate DNA continuously.
contact inhibition
Correct: normal cells stop dividing when they touch neighbors on all sides.
dependence on glucose
Glucose use is not what the piling up shows.
their nuclei
Transformed cells still have nuclei.
questions.x: Normal cells in culture stop dividing when they contact neighbors on all sides, forming a monolayer (contact inhibition). Transformed cells lose this control and keep dividing, piling into multilayered foci, a hallmark used to detect transformation. They still replicate DNA, often faster, and still have nuclei.

questions.q: The E7 protein of high-risk human papillomavirus binds and inactivates Rb. In infected cells, this most directly:
o: arrests cells permanently in G1
Losing Rb removes a G1 brake rather than adding one.
activates the spindle checkpoint
Rb acts at G1/S, not during mitosis.
increases expression of p21
E7 removes Rb's control downstream; it does not boost p21.
frees E2F, pushing cells into S phase without normal G1 control
Correct: without Rb, E2F activates S-phase genes regardless of signals.
questions.x: Rb normally binds E2F to hold cells in G1. HPV E7 binds Rb and displaces E2F, which then activates S-phase genes regardless of growth signals, pushing infected cells into S so the virus can use the replication machinery. HPV E6 separately degrades p53. Removing Rb takes away a brake, so G1 arrest is the opposite effect.

questions.q: Most human cancer cells keep dividing well past the normal limit because they:
o: express telomerase, which maintains telomere length
Correct: telomerase lets cancer cells avoid the senescence caused by short telomeres.
lack all DNA repair enzymes
Cells need some repair to survive; this does not explain unlimited division.
have stopped replicating their DNA
Dividing cells must replicate DNA.
have permanently activated caspases
Active caspases would kill the cells.
questions.x: Conventional DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate chromosome ends, so telomeres shorten each division until senescence (the Hayflick limit). About 85–90% of cancers reactivate telomerase, which adds TTAGGG repeats to maintain telomere length and allows unlimited divisions; the rest use alternative lengthening. Losing all repair enzymes would be lethal rather than immortalizing.

questions.q: A researcher finds that a tumor cell line is resistant to DNA-damaging drugs and has lost both copies of a gene whose product halts the cycle and triggers apoptosis after DNA damage. Which statement best describes the gene?
o: It is an oncogene whose loss causes the drug resistance
Oncogenes promote growth when activated; loss of both copies describes a tumor suppressor.
It is a proto-oncogene that needs two hits to activate
Proto-oncogenes are activated by a single gain-of-function mutation.
It is a tumor suppressor gene whose loss lets damaged cells keep dividing
Correct: genes that halt the cycle or trigger apoptosis after damage are tumor suppressors.
It encodes a growth factor that the tumor depends on
A growth factor would not halt the cycle after damage.
questions.x: Genes that halt the cell cycle or trigger apoptosis after DNA damage, such as TP53, are tumor suppressors. Losing both copies removes the checkpoint, so damaged cells keep dividing and resist DNA-damaging drugs that kill through apoptosis. Oncogenes act by gain of function and a single mutation, so losing both copies of a gene points to a tumor suppressor.

questions.q: Normal human fibroblasts in culture stop dividing after a limited number of doublings, mainly because:
o: the cells run out of nutrients in the medium
Fresh medium does not restore division after the limit.
the cells become cancerous
Cancer cells avoid this limit rather than reaching it.
telomeres shorten with each division until a critical length triggers senescence
Correct: the end-replication problem shortens telomeres, setting the Hayflick limit.
the cells switch to meiosis
Somatic fibroblasts do not undergo meiosis.
questions.x: Because DNA polymerase needs a primer and works 5′ to 3′, the lagging strand's very end cannot be completed, so telomeres shorten each division (the end-replication problem). Somatic cells lack enough telomerase, so after about 50 doublings critically short telomeres trigger a DNA damage response and senescence. Fresh nutrients cannot overcome this intrinsic limit.

questions.q: Telomerase can lengthen chromosome ends because it:
o: is a reverse transcriptase carrying its own RNA template
Correct: it uses the RNA template to add repeats to the 3′ overhang.
is a DNA polymerase that needs an RNA primer at the very end
That primer requirement is what creates the end-replication problem.
joins chromosome ends together
End-to-end fusion is harmful and is prevented by telomeres.
removes damaged nucleotides from telomeres
Telomerase adds DNA rather than removing it.
questions.x: Telomerase is a ribonucleoprotein reverse transcriptase that carries its own RNA template. It base-pairs that template with the 3′ overhang of the chromosome and adds repeats (TTAGGG in humans); the complementary strand is then filled in by primase and DNA polymerase. Ordinary DNA polymerase's need for a primer is what causes end shortening, not what fixes it.

questions.q: Cellular senescence differs from quiescence (G0) in that senescent cells:
o: are dead and quickly removed by phagocytes
Senescent cells stay alive and metabolically active.
divide more rapidly than normal cells
Senescent cells do not divide.
have lost their nuclei
Senescent cells keep their nuclei.
are essentially permanently arrested even when given growth signals
Correct: senescence is a stable, mostly irreversible arrest; quiescent cells can re-enter the cycle.
questions.x: Quiescent (G0) cells are reversibly arrested and re-enter the cycle when given growth signals, like hepatocytes after injury. Senescent cells are stably and essentially irreversibly arrested, usually by p53–p21 and p16–Rb, even with mitogens. They stay alive and metabolically active, often secreting factors, so they are not dead or anucleate.

questions.q: Senescent cells accumulate in aging tissues and release inflammatory cytokines and proteases. Removing senescent cells from old mice delays some age-related decline. This suggests that senescent cells:
o: are harmless because they no longer divide
If they were harmless, removing them would have no benefit.
actively harm surrounding tissue through what they secrete
Correct: their secretions can drive chronic inflammation and tissue dysfunction.
are the main source of new cells in old tissue
Senescent cells do not divide, so they cannot supply new cells.
prevent all cancers in old animals
The data concern tissue decline, not complete cancer prevention.
questions.note: Senescence blocks tumor growth but its secretions can promote aging.
questions.x: Senescent cells stop dividing but remain metabolically active and release inflammatory cytokines, chemokines and proteases, the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Removing them improves tissue function in old mice, showing their secretions actively harm tissue. Senescence does suppress tumors early by stopping division, but non-dividing does not mean harmless.
